Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):

Sūrat al-Anbiyā' (21)

It was revealed in Makkah, as Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them both. In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit, by Abu Hayyan) it is stated that it is Makkan without any disagreement, and it stated this without exception. In al-Itqan (by al-Suyuti) he excepted from it the verse of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 44] and so on. It has one hundred and twelve verses according to the count of the Kufans, and eleven according to the count of the others, as stated by al-Tabarsi and al-Dani. The connection between it and what precedes it is clear and needs no explanation. It is a great surah containing a magnificent admonition. Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah, and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from 'Amir ibn Rabi'ah that a man from the Arabs stayed with him, and 'Amir honoured his lodging and spoke on his behalf to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The man came to him and said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for a valley, and there is no valley among the Arabs better than it. I wanted to grant you a portion of it, to be yours and to your descendants after you." 'Amir said: "I have no need of your grant. Today a surah has been revealed which has made us forget the world: ﴿The reckoning has drawn near for mankind﴾ [al-Anbiya': 1], to its end."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿The reckoning has drawn near for mankind﴾

It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, as al-Imam (al-Razi), al-Qurtubi and al-Zamakhshari stated, that the intended meaning of "mankind" is the polytheists. This is indicated by what you will hear after it, if Allah wills, of the verses, for they clearly describe the polytheists. Some of the eminent scholars said: what is in them is of the type of attributing to some what belongs to all, so this does not contradict the definite article being for the genus. The reason it is good here is that those "some" are the majority, and the majority has the ruling of the whole, both in the Shari'ah and in custom. Some people allowed that the genus is intended, and that the pronouns that follow refer to the polytheists of Makkah, even though they were not mentioned earlier in this surah, and this is no further-fetched than what preceded it. Others said: the indication of the specification by what has been mentioned is only on the assumption that the attributes are explained as those who explained them have explained them. It is possible to take each of them as a meaning shared by the disobedient monotheists, but there is no doubt that in this there is a great departure from the apparent meaning.

The lam (the preposition "li-") is a complement of "iqtaraba", as is apparent. It has the sense of ila (to) or of min (from), for iqtaraba is of the form if'talaba, derived from al-qurb (nearness), the opposite of al-bu'd (distance), and it takes both ila and min. Some restricted themselves to saying that it means ila, and it was said that this is arbitrary, since the verb "qariba" takes both. It was answered that this may be because both min and ila, which are the two complements of nearness, carry the sense of the end of the goal. But ila is established in this meaning, and min is established in the meaning of the beginning of the goal. Therefore, to express that the lam mentioned has the sense of the end of the goal, as in the one in the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Because your Lord has inspired it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 5], he chose the view that it means ila and restricted himself to it. In al-Kashf (a commentary, by al-Tibi) it is stated: on the assumption that it is a complement of "iqtaraba", the meaning is "iqtaraba min al-nas" (drew near from mankind), because the meaning of specification and the beginning of the goal are both sound and achieve the purpose. End of quote. But there is an objection to this, for what is understood from it is that the word min, with which the verb of approach is construed, should carry the sense of the beginning of the goal, and this is not so, because that meaning does not suit the contexts in which that word is used. So the truth is that it has the sense of the end of the goal, for they mentioned that min comes for this. Al-Shamni said: In al-Janی al-Dani, Ibn Malik gave as an example of the end of the goal the saying "taqarrabtu minhu" (I drew near to him), for it is equivalent to "taqarrabtu ilayhi" (I drew near to him). What supports this is that the verb of approach is used with min just as it is used with ila, and the meaning of min has been stated to include the end of the goal, as you have heard, but no one has mentioned the beginning of the goal among the meanings of ila. The basic principle is that the two complements should have the same meaning, so min is understood as ila in the sense that the intended meaning is the end. The most that can be said in justifying this is that the author of al-Kashf understood it as the beginning of the goal, because it is the best known of its meanings, to the point that some grammarians traced all its other meanings back to it, and considered its construction with min to be an analogy with its opposite which is construed with min, namely the verb of distance. Likewise the verb of selling is construed with min by analogy with the verb of buying, which is construed with min. This is what Najm al-A'immah al-Radi mentioned in the section on prepositions.

It is well known that "iqtaraba" means "qaruba" (drew near), just as "irtaqaba" means "raqaba" (watched). It is reported in al-Bahr that it is more emphatic than it, because of the added letters of its form. The intended meaning of the approach of the reckoning is the approach of its time, which is the Hour. The reason for choosing to express its approach, although the discourse is with the polytheists who deny the very resurrection of the dead and the very revival of the decayed bones, is that what the situation would normally require is to use something that expresses the actual occurrence instead of "approach", and to attribute that to the Hour itself rather than to the reckoning. This points to the fact that the occurrence of the Resurrection and the coming about of the raising of bodies and frames is a manifest matter without deception, an obvious thing about which there is no doubt, and that it has reached such clarity and manifestness that it is hardly hidden from the intelligent. And what the reins of speech are loosened to explain is some of what it entails of circumstances and terrors, such as the reckoning that causes agitation. Indeed, the occurrence of the reckoning itself needs no explanation; minds and intellects should not doubt it. What is intended to be explained here is that its time has come near and its appointed moment has drawn close. Thus the discourse expresses the realisation of the Resurrection, which is what the situation requires, in a fitting and firm way and with an excellent, sound method, whose subtlety is not hidden from one who gives ear while being a witness.

It is also permitted that the discourse is with the polytheists who asked about the time of the Hour and sought to hasten it mockingly, as in the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿They will shake their heads at you and say, "When will it be?" Say, "Perhaps it is near."﴾ [al-Isra': 51]. In that case the report about the approach is according to the apparent meaning. The choice of expressing the approach of the reckoning rather than the approach of the other occurrences that follow from the resurrection, such as the varieties of punishment and the matters of retribution, is to indicate that the mere approach of the reckoning, which is one of the beginnings and preliminaries of the punishment, is sufficient as a warning against what they hold of denial, and sufficient as a restraint against what they hold of arrogance and pride. So how much more so is the case with the punishment and the chastisement themselves.

Shaykh al-Islam Mawla Abu al-Su'ud, may Allah have mercy on him, stated that attributing that to the reckoning rather than to the Hour is because the discourse flows toward explaining their heedlessness of it and their turning away from what reminds them of it. But in this there is what there is. Then the clear aspect in the noble consideration for attributing the approach to the reckoning rather than to mankind, although the reverse is permitted, is this: when approach occurs between two things, it is attributed to the one that faces the other, moving and directed toward its direction, actually or by ruling. Indeed, if each of them is directed toward the other, it is correct to attribute it to each of them. You have heard that the intended meaning of the approach of the reckoning is the approach of its time, and this has been stated explicitly by the eminent exegetes. You know well that what is widespread and well known is the consideration of direction and of coming, from time to the one who is in time, not the reverse. Therefore time is described as passing and as future. So it was fitting that the approach be attributed to the time of the reckoning, and mankind be made the one toward whom it draws near.

Shaykh al-Islam also stated that in this attribution there is a magnification of the status of the one to whom it is attributed, and an exaggeration of its matter, which is not hidden, since it depicts that thing in the form of something coming toward them, which does not cease to seek them until it inevitably reaches them. End of quote. This is a meaning beyond what we have mentioned, whose subtlety is not hidden from the discerning critic and the knowledgeable al-Yalmai'i. The intended meaning of the approach of that to mankind, according to what the Shaykh (may his secret be sanctified) chose, is its drawing near to them after its distance from them. For at every hour it is nearer to them than it was in the hour before.

The statement of al-Zamakhshari was objected to: "The intended meaning of that is that the remaining part of the duration of the world is smaller and shorter than what has passed of it, for it is like the residue of a vessel and the dregs of a container." It was objected that this has no connection to what we are discussing, the approach derived from the form of the past tense, and there is no need for it in establishing its meaning. Yes, it may be understood from it, by custom, that it is also near in itself, and in that case this explanation is adopted. Some eminent scholars criticised this: that the claim of no connection to the approach derived from the form of the past tense is outside the bounds of fairness. For if he means that it has no connection to the occurrence derived from it, there is no basis for this, since the approach in the stated sense is a matter that occurred with the passing of most of the duration of the world. And if he means that it has no connection to the passing derived from it, there is also no basis for this, since the evidences indicate that this approach occurred at the time of the sending of the Prophet ﷺ, who was promised at the end of time, which precedes the revelation of the verse.

Then he said: "I wonder what is meant by its having no connection to what we are discussing. Indeed, it may even be claimed that the meaning he himself chose lacks relevance, for the approach in that sense is continuous from the very beginning of the world until the day the verse was revealed, and even beyond that. So what fits it is a form that indicates continuity and permanence." Then it is not hidden from people of understanding that this meaning which he objected to is more suited to what the situation requires, namely frightening the disbelieving rogues who doubt the matter of the Resurrection, because it shows its nearness as it actually is in reality. End of quote. So reflect.

It was also said that the intended meaning is the approach of that in the sight of Allah, the Exalted. This was criticised: it is not "in the sight of Allah, Mighty and Majestic", since no relation of nearness or distance applies between created things and Him, Mighty and Majestic.

It was answered that this is a failure to grasp, or a feigned failure to grasp, of the intended meaning. The intended meaning of "in the sight of Allah" is in His eternal knowledge, or in His decree and ordainment, not nearness and approach in the familiar sense. On this view the intended meaning of nearness is that its occurrence is realised in His knowledge, Exalted is He, or in His ordainment.

Some eminent scholars said: The intended meaning of the nearness being "in the sight of Allah, Exalted is He" is not that it is attributed to Him, Glorified is He, such that He is made near to it or it is made near to Him, Exalted is He far above that by a great exaltation. Rather, the intended meaning is the nearness of the reckoning for mankind in the sight of Allah, Exalted is He. The summary of this is that He, Exalted is His affair, because His forbearance has reached the limit of perfection, regards long durations as short. So the reckoning is near to mankind in the sight of His Majesty, Exalted, even if there are years and states between Him and them. On this interpretation the saying of Allah, the Exalted, is understood: ﴿They see it as far away, and We see it as near﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 6, 7]. This meaning, beyond what it conveys, necessarily establishes the affirmation that the remaining period between them and the reckoning is in reality a small thing, and what people think of as its length and their considering it great is among the satanic deceptions. The appropriate attitude for people of insight is to regard that period as short, so that they gird up their garments for a day on which the leg will be uncovered, and the return will be to Allah, Exalted is His affair.

As for the statement of Shaykh al-Islam in objecting to what was said, that there is no way to consider it here, because its nearness in relation to Him, Exalted is He, is something in which renewal and variation cannot be conceived, definitely, and its consideration is only in the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [al-Shura: 17] and its like, which carry no indication of occurrence. This is based on taking the nearness in His sight to mean nearness to Him, Exalted is He, in the sense of the presence of that in His eternal knowledge, for that is what does not admit variation, definitely. As for the nearness of things to one another in time or in place, there is no doubt that the objects of His knowledge, Glorified is He, are renewed with respect to that, so He knows it as it is, while the attribute of knowledge itself is eternal, as has been established in its place. End of quote.

Some of them chose that the intended meaning of the "in the sight of" is what you heard first, and this is a common meaning in usage. And the renewal was made a matter of the relation to the object of knowledge, as was said about the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Then We raised them up that We might know﴾ [al-Kahf: 12] and so on.

And it was said: the intended meaning of its approach is that its occurrence is realised without doubt, for every coming thing is near, and the distant is what has occurred and passed. For this reason it was said:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 1 (part 2 of 2):

Never will what he desires be nearer than tomorrow, nor will what he fears be farther than yesterday.

It must be that what is meant by the realization of its occurrence is its realization in itself, not its realization in the eternal knowledge, so that it differs from the preceding statement. Some of the distinguished scholars said: On this interpretation, the verb is not connected to the nearness conveyed by the past tense form, unless one resorts to the view that the form is stripped of its indication of occurrence in time, as in their saying: "Glory be to Him who is exalted above rivals and far removed from opposites." So reflect on this, and do not be heedless.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the subject, as Shaykh al-Islam (Abu al-Su'ud) stated, is for hastening the arousal of dread (al-muraw'a). The attribution of nearness to the polytheists from the outset distresses them, produces fear in them, and disturbs them with regard to the one who draws near.

It was objected that these polytheists would not be struck with fear or disturbance, because of what you will hear of their heedlessness, their aversion, and their failure to take seriously the signs revealed to them. So how could the hastening of distress be effected? It was answered that this does not require that warning and admonition fail to disturb them, nor that intimidation and caution fail to alarm them, since the possibility of the truth may occur to their minds even if it is less likely, so fear and apprehension arise in them.

This is supported by what some exegetes reported: when the verse "The Hour has drawn near" (al-Qamar 1) was revealed, the disbelievers said among themselves: "This man claims that the Resurrection has come near. So refrain from some of what you do until we see what will happen." When it did not come, they said: "We see nothing." Then the verse "Their reckoning has drawn near for the people" (al-Anbiya' 1) was revealed. They became apprehensive and waited for its nearness. When the days lengthened, they said: "O Muhammad, we see nothing of what you threaten us with." End of quotation.

Some have explained this as follows: nearness (al-iqtiraab) indicates turning toward and approaching something. When one says "drew near," it implies that a matter is approaching something and seeking it, without indicating what it is approaching. When "for the people" is said afterward, it shows that this matter seeks them and approaches them, while they flee from it. Thus it conveys that what draws near is something that distresses them, so fear and agitation arise in them before the reckoning is mentioned. This differs from saying "the reckoning has drawn near for the people," because in that case the reckoning's approach toward them is not understood until "for the people" is mentioned after it. Thus the realization of the benefit of hastening through fronting is beyond doubt. Moreover, there is an additional benefit: the mind wanders to determine what that dreadful matter is, in every direction, until the subject is mentioned.

It is also possible to say, regarding the wisdom of hastening the terror: the noble custom of the Prophet (ﷺ) was to warn the polytheists, caution them, and explain what troubles them. This indicates that what has been made clear as approaching them is something evil and dreadful. So when the prepositional phrase is fronted, intimidation occurs, because from the outset it is known that the speech concerns the polytheists, whom he (peace be upon him) habitually cautions. This differs from the case where the subject is fronted, since then the one who draws near is not known until the prepositional phrase is mentioned, and the indicator mentioned does not determine what draws near as it determines what is drawn near. For it is known from his noble custom (ﷺ) that when he speaks about them, he generally speaks of what distresses them, not that he (peace be upon him) generally speaks of what distresses them in most of his circumstances. There is a difference between these two customs. The fact that the realization of the subtle point of the fronting depends on adding the custom does not undermine the completeness of the intended meaning, since the meaning is complete when the fronting has a role in producing that subtle point, such that if the fronting were lost, the subtle point would be lost. You have come to know that the matter is so. There is nothing in the words of the Shaykh, may his secret be sanctified, indicating that the mentioned hastening results from fronting alone. So it is said.

You may say: The fronting is for hastening the intimidation, and that does not conflict with its not being realized, just as the non-realization of intimidation does not conflict with the revelation of the signs being for intimidation. So understand.

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the lam (of "for the people") be an emphasis on the attribution of the reckoning to them. In al-Kashshaf he said: The original is "The reckoning of the people has drawn near," because the thing approached is known. Then it is "Has drawn near for the people, the reckoning," with the prepositional phrase as a fixed adverbial placed in front, not as one that requires an omitted genitive that was deleted, because the later element explains it, meaning "the reckoning has drawn near for the people, the reckoning," as al-Tibi claimed. In the fronting, the explicit lam, and the definiteness of "the reckoning," there are intensifications not present in the original. Then "has drawn near for the people, their reckoning," so the lam becomes emphasizing the meaning of restriction (al-ikhtisas al-idafi), not merely emphasis, as in "la aba lahu" (he has no father), and as in the case where the adverbial is repeated, such as "fika Zayd raghib fika" (Zayd is desirous of you). End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari claimed that this interpretation is more unusual, on the ground that it contains intensifications and subtle points not found in the first interpretation. Shaykh al-Islam claimed that, although it is a complete affectation, it is far from what the context requires. Abu Hayyan and others also examined it. Some people defended it and rebutted objections against it. In sum, there is among the scholars a great debate and a major contention. The best course, after all this, is to make the lam connected to the nearness (al-iqtiraab).

Verse 1 has been used as evidence for the establishment of the reckoning. Al-Baydawi, in his interpretation of the words of the Exalted: "Whether you reveal what is in your souls or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it" (al-Baqarah 284), mentioned that the Mu'tazilah and the Khawarij deny it. This is supported by what Imam al-Nasafi mentioned in one of his works, where he said: The Mu'tazilah said: There is no scale, no reckoning, no bridge, no basin, and no intercession. Every place where Allah mentions the scale or the reckoning, He intends by it justice. End of quotation. However, what is mentioned in most authoritative theological works is that most of them deny the bridge, and all of them deny the scale. Their denial of the reckoning is not addressed in them. The truth is that the reckoning in the sense of recompense is something only the polytheists deny.

"While they are in heedlessness": that is, in great heedlessness and monstrous ignorance of it. It was said that it is better to generalize: that is, in complete heedlessness and comprehensive ignorance of His oneness, the faith in His books and His messengers (peace be upon them), the occurrence of the reckoning, the existence of reward and punishment, and all that the Noble Prophet (peace be and blessings upon him) brought. The mention of their heedlessness of that right after the statement of the nearness of the reckoning does not require limiting heedlessness to it, for the occurrence of their regret and remorse, and the manifestation of the effect of their ignorance and foolishness, which happen on the Day of Reckoning, was the cause of the mentioned sequence. End of quotation.

It may be said that the apparent sequence requires this. Whoever is heedless of Allah's recompense, which is what is meant by the reckoning, every error proceeds from him, and he mounts the back of every ignorance.

The prepositional phrase "for them" is attached to an omitted element that occurred as the predicate, "for them." His saying, glory be to Him: "turning away" (mu'ridun), that is, from the signs and warnings that declare this and call to belief in Him, which saves one from ruin, is a predicate after a predicate. The combination of heedlessness and aversion, in the way we have indicated, is beyond doubt. To indicate their firm establishment in heedlessness, which is the source of their continuous aversion, the speech was phrased as you have heard. The sentence is in the place of a circumstantial clause (hal) for "the people." Al-Zamakhshari said: He described them with heedlessness together with aversion, in the sense that they are heedless of their reckoning, unmindful, not reflecting on their end, and not noticing what their final outcome will return to, although their intellects require that there be recompense for the one who does good and the one who does evil. For this reason, when the staff is struck for them and they are roused from the slumber of heedlessness and become aware of this through the signs and warnings recited to them, they turn away, plug their ears, and flee. End of the quotation.

The sum of this contains a resolution of the apparent conflict between heedlessness, which is lack of alertness, and aversion, which comes from one who is alert. The resolution is that heedlessness of the reckoning is at the beginning of their affair, and aversion occurs after the staff of warning is struck; or that heedlessness of the reckoning is combined with aversion from reflecting on their end and the matter of their final outcome. In al-Kashshaf, he meant that their habitual state is heedlessness of what the rational proofs require, and then when the revealed proofs support them and they are guided to the path of reflection, they turn away. Within this is an explanation of the benefit of stating the first as a verbal sentence with the adverbial, since the particle of place indicates firm establishment, and of stating the second as a descriptive phrase that is transient, indicating a renewed kind. From this, the weakness of the view that the adverbial is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun hidden in "turning away," placed before it, becomes evident. End of quotation.

It is not hidden that the claim that the intellects require that there must be recompense is only possible on the view of the rational goodness and badness of things, and the Ash'arites deny this most strongly.

Some distinguished scholars said: The aversion may be taken in an extended sense, as in the words of the poet:

The generosity of a youth who was firmly established in lofty matters, and who spread out and grew tall in lofty matters.

Some exegetes also mentioned this in the words of the Exalted: "But when He brings you safe to land, you turn away" (al-Isra' 67). The meaning would then be: while they are extravagant in heedlessness, excessive in it.

It is also possible that heedlessness means neglect, as in the words of the Exalted: "We were never heedless of creation" (al-Mu'minun 17). Then there is no conflict between the two descriptions.

[Page 7]

﴿There does not come to them any reminder﴾: a portion sent down from the Qur'an, which reminds them in the most complete manner and makes the matter clear to them in the most thorough way, as if it were the very essence of the reminder. "Min" (from) here is a partitive? No: "min" introduces the subject (fa'iliyyah, the agent role), and the phrase that follows it is in the nominative position as the subject. The view that it is partitive (tab'idiyyah) is far-fetched. The "min" in His words, ﴿from their Lord﴾, is for the start of the end point (ibtida' al-ghayah) in a metaphorical sense, and it is connected either to "yatihim" (comes to them) or to an omitted word that is a qualifier of "dhikr" (reminder). Whichever it is, it indicates its excellence, its nobility, and the great enormity of what they did to it. Mentioning the title of Lordship (al-Rububiyyah) serves to intensify the reproach. ﴿newly revealed﴾ is in the genitive case (bi'l-jarr) as a qualifier of "dhikr."

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read it in the nominative, on the basis that it is also a qualifier of it, taking into account the position (al-mahall). Zayd ibn 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with them both) read it in the accusative, on the basis that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from it, in view of its being described by His words, ﴿from their Lord﴾. His words, glorified be He, ﴿but they listen to it﴾, form an exception of the incomplete type (istithna' mufarragh), whose position is accusative, as a circumstantial clause from the object of "yatihim" (comes to them), with "qad" either implied or not, according to the well-known difference of opinion, as it is said. Najm al-A'immah al-Radi said: when the past tense verb follows "illa" (except), its being sufficient with the pronoun without the waw is frequent, as in: "What I met him with except that he honored me," because the occurrence of "illa" is mostly before nouns, so it is by interpretation "except honoring me," and thus it becomes like the affirmative present tense verb.

It is permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from the object, because it also carries its pronoun, and the meaning does not reject it, but this is contrary to what is apparent. Even more remote than that is what is said: that it may be a qualifier of "dhikr." Although "illa" prevents this according to the majority (al-Jumhur), since incomplete exception in qualifiers is not permitted in their view, it is still permissible to presume another reminder after "illa," so that this clause becomes a qualifier of it, and that is in the position of describing the mentioned noun, meaning: no reminder comes to them except a reminder that they listen to.

His words, exalted be He, ﴿while they are playing﴾, are a circumstantial clause from the agent of ﴿they listen to it﴾.

[p. 8]

Concerning His words, glorified be He: ﴿Their hearts are heedless﴾. It is either another circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the same subject, in which case it is synonymous (mutarādifa) with the previous one, or a circumstantial clause from the waw in (yalʿabūna) "they play," in which case it is interlinked (mutadākhila). The meaning is: no new reminder (dhikr) comes to them from their Lord at any time except that they listen to it while playing and mocking it, being heedless of it; or they play with it while their hearts are heedless of it.

Ibn Abi ʿAbla and ʿĪsā read (lāhiyatun) with a nominative ending, as a predicate following another predicate about them. The reason for the difference between the two predicates is not hidden.

﴿Lāhiyatan﴾ comes from lahiya ʿan al-shayʾ (with kasra), lahiyyan and lihyānan, meaning he forgot about it, abandoned mentioning it, and turned away from it, as in al-Ṣiḥāḥ (the lexicon of al-Jawharī). In al-Kashshāf (of al-Zamakhsharī) it is stated: it is from lahiya ʿanhu, meaning he became distracted and неглected it. Since, regarding heedlessness mentioned earlier, it is required that the heedless person have no awareness at all of the thing he is heedless of, not even that it comes to his mind or strikes his hearing, it becomes problematic to describe their hearts as heedless after they have heard the verses, since by that they have been freed from heedlessness and have attained awareness, even if they were not granted faith and remained in the depths of disgrace and abandonment.

It is answered that describing them thus is based on treating their awareness, because they do not benefit from it, as if it were nonexistent. A parallel is what has been said concerning His words, exalted be He: ﴿And they certainly knew that whoever bought it would have no share in the Hereafter, and wretched is that for which they sold their souls, if only they had known﴾ [al-Baqara 2:102]. You know that there is no harm in taking the heedlessness mentioned here, in the interpretation of lahiya, to mean abandonment and turning away, as the wording of al-Ṣiḥāḥ makes clear. This has not been taken to be from the lahw that means play, as is well known, because following (yalʿabūna) with that meaning in this context does not suit the eloquence of the revelation nor agree with the sublimity of its magnificent composition, even though its meaning can be made sound through some kind of interpretation.

The "origination" (ḥudūth) that the word muḥdath requires is renewal (tajaddud), and this implies being preceded by non-existence. The reminder (dhikr) is described as such with regard to its being sent down, not with regard to itself, although that would also be correct if dhikr is taken to mean the verbal speech and one holds the view widely attributed to the Ashʿariyya (Ashʿarites) that it is originated, since it is composed of letters and sounds. What the context requires and the good arrangement demands is an explanation that whenever admonition and reminder are renewed for them, and the words of warning and caution are repeated in their ears, and the verses are sent down upon them, and the staff strikes them, and they are alerted from the slumber of heedlessness and ignorance more times than there are pebbles, and they are guided to the path of truth repeatedly, this only increases them in flight.

As for whether that reminder is originated or eternal, it has no connection to the context, as will not be hidden from people of understanding. It is also permitted that the intended meaning of dhikr is the inner speech (al-kalām al-nafsī, the speech of the soul, the attribute of God as held by the Ashʿarites and Māturīdites), and attributing coming to it is a metaphor; indeed, attributing it to speech in general is likewise. The intended meaning of origination is renewal. It may be said that describing it as such is with regard to its being sent down, so this does not contradict the view of the eternity of the inner speech held by its proponents among the People of the Sunna and the Community (Ahl al-Sunna wal-Jamāʿa). The Ḥanābila (Hanbalis), who hold that the verbal speech is eternal just like the inner speech, must necessarily hold that the description is with regard to that, so that the verse does not serve as a proof against them.

Al-Ḥasan ibn al-Faḍl said: the intended meaning of dhikr is the Prophet ﷺ, and he has been called a dhikr in His words: ﴿Indeed Allah has sent down to you a reminder, a messenger﴾ [al-Ṭalāq 65:10–11]. What points to this here is (hal) "Is this..." etc., which comes shortly, God willing. But this is open to scrutiny. In general, the verse is not one that can be used as a proof for refuting the People of the Sunna, not even the Ḥanābila, as will not be hidden.

﴿And they secretly conspired in private﴾: this is a new sentence, brought to explain another of their crimes. (Al-Najwā) is a noun from tanājī (secret conferring), and it is only done in secret, so the meaning of "secretly" is emphasis on concealing it. It is also possible that it is a verbal noun meaning tanājī (conferring), so the meaning is that they concealed their conferring by not conferring in the sight of others. This is more evident and better placed according to what is in al-Kashf (of al-Ṭībī).

Abu ʿUbayda said: al-isrār (secrecy) is among the words with two opposite meanings (aḍdād), and it may mean here disclosure (al-iẓhār). From this is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

When al-Ḥajjāj saw he had drawn his sword, he revealed (asarra) the Khārijite who had been concealing (ḍamara).

You know that the common usage is the meaning of concealment, even if we say it is among the words with opposite meanings, as al-Tibrīzī stated explicitly. There is no reason to deviate from that.

His words, exalted be He: ﴿Those who did wrong﴾ are a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in ﴿they conspired﴾, as al-Mubarrad said, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributed it to Sībawayh. This implies that they are described with gross wrongdoing in what they conspired.

Abu ʿUbayda, al-Akhfash and others said: it is the subject (fāʿil) of ﴿they conspired﴾, and the waw is a particle indicating plurality, like the waw in qāʾimūna "they stand" and the tāʾ in qāmat "she stood." This is according to the dialect of "the fleas ate me" (akalūnī al-barāghīthu), a dialect of the Azd Shanūʾa. Their poet said:

My family blame me for buying the palm groves, and all of them are the most blameworthy.

Abu Ḥayyān stated that this is a good dialect and not anomalous, as some claimed. Al-Kisāʾī said: it is the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtadaʾ), and the clause before it is its predicate, placed first for emphasis on it. The meaning is: they conspired the secret talk, so the relative pronoun was placed in place of the pronoun, to record their action as wrongdoing. It was also said that it is an omitted subject, meaning: they are those who. It was also said that it is the subject of an omitted verb, meaning: those who said, since saying is often omitted. This was chosen by al-Naḥḥās. On all these views it is in the nominative position.

It is permitted that it is in the accusative position, as a dispraise, as al-Zajjāj held; or by supposing an implied "I mean," as some held. It is also permitted that it is in the genitive position, being a qualifier (naʿt) of "people," as Abu al-Baqāʾ said, or a substitute (badal) for it, as al-Farrāʾ said. Both are as you see.

His words, exalted be He: ﴿Is this but a human being like yourselves?﴾ and so on, are in the accusative position, as an object (maf-ʿūl) of an implied speech verb after the relative pronoun and its clause. It is an answer to a question arising from what came before, as if it was said: what did they say in their secret talk? Then it is said: they said, "This..." etc. Or it is a substitute for ﴿they conspired﴾, or coordinated with it. It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: saying, "Is this..." etc., and it is the object of an implied speech verb before the relative pronoun, as al-Naḥḥās chose. It was also said that it is the object of the secret talk itself, because it has the sense of speech, and the definite verbal noun may govern its object, as Khalīl and Sībawayh held. It was also said that it is a substitute for it, meaning: they conspired this talk.

The hal (is?) here means negation, and it is not an interrogative of astonishment, as Abu Ḥayyān claimed. The hamza in His words, exalted be He: ﴿Will you then approach magic﴾ is for denunciation, and the fāʾ is for coordination with an implied element required by the context. His words, glorified be He: ﴿while you see﴾

[p. 9]

are a circumstantial clause from the subject of "you approach," confirming the denunciation and emphasizing the improbability. They meant, as has been said: "This is nothing but a human being like you," that is, of your kind, "and what he brings is magic that you know," so you approach it and attend it in acceptance and submission, "while you see" that it is magic. They said this based on what was fixed in their deviant belief: that a messenger can only be a king, and that everything that appears at the hand of a human of extraordinary acts is of the type of magic. By "magic" here they meant the Qur'an. In this there is a denial of its truth in the most emphatic way. May Allah fight them; how are they deluded!

They concealed this because it was a way of binding the covenant, arranging the beginnings of evil and corruption, and paving the way for the stratagems of deceit and plotting to demolish the matter of prophethood and extinguish the light of religion. But Allah, exalted be He, refuses except to complete His light, even if the polytheists dislike it. It was also said that they concealed it so that they could say to the Messenger ﷺ and the believers: "If what you claim is true, then tell us what we secretly conspired?" Al-Ṭībī rejected this, saying that the wording does not support it, nor does it fit the emphasis in His words, exalted be He: ﴿Those who did wrong secretly conspired﴾, nor in His words, glorified be He: ﴿Will you approach﴾ magic.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 4:

﴿He said: My Lord knows the word in the heavens and the earth.﴾ This is a report from Him, may He be exalted, of what the Prophet (ﷺ) said after He revealed to him their states and their words, as a clarification of the manifestness of their affair and the disclosure of their secret. So the subject of ﴿said﴾ is his pronoun (ﷺ), and the sentence after it is its object. This is the recitation (qira'ah) of Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, al-A'mash, Talhah, Ibn Abi Layla, Ayyub, Khalaf, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki and Ibn Jarir. The rest of the seven read ﴿Say﴾ in the imperative, addressed to his Prophet (ﷺ). The word ﴿the word﴾ is general, including both the secret and the open. Choosing it over "the secret" serves to establish His knowledge of it, may He be glorified, in the demonstrative manner, along with what it implies: that His knowledge, may He be exalted, of both matters is on a single level, with no difference between them in clarity and obscurity, definitively, as in the sciences of the Truth.

In al-Kashshaf it is stated that between "secret" (sirr) and "word" (qawl) there is a general and specific relation from one aspect. The appropriate thing in this context is to generalize "word" so that it includes both its open and its secret forms, and the more hidden. It is as if it were said: He knows this kind and what is higher than it and lower than it. In this there is an intensification in the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, may He be exalted, which is appropriate to what He related about them of excessive concealment. Choosing "secret" over "word" in some verses is for a reason that calls for it there, and every context has its own speech.

The prepositional phrase ﴿in the heavens and the earth﴾ is attached to an omitted element and functions as a circumstantial qualifier of ﴿the word﴾, meaning: existing in the heavens and the earth.

His saying, may He be glorified: ﴿And He is the All-Hearing﴾, i.e., of all things heard, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾, i.e., of all things known. It was said: i.e., the one who is intensive in knowledge of things heard and things known. Their words and their deeds enter into this by primary inclusion. A concluding parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ tadhyili) is implied, supplying the content of what precedes it and containing the threat of recompense for what proceeded from them. It is understood from the words of al-Bahr that what precedes it also contains that.

[p. 9 continued]

﴿Nay, they say: "A confusion of dreams."﴾ This is a turning away (*idrab*) from Him, exalted is He, and a transition from relating their earlier speech to relating another speech that is confused and false. That is, they did not confine themselves to saying, regarding him (ﷺ), "Is this not but a human being like you?", nor regarding what appeared at his hand of the noble Qur'an, "It is sorcery." Rather, they said that it, that is the Qur'an, is "a confusion of dreams." Then they turned away from this and said: ﴿Nay, he has invented it﴾, from his own self, without it having any basis or even the semblance of a basis. Then they turned away again and said: ﴿Nay, he is a poet﴾. What he brought is poetry, which imagines to the hearer meanings that have no reality. This confusion is the characteristic of the falsifier who has been refuted, for he keeps moving between falsehood and what is more false, and wavers between corruption and what is more corrupt. So the first "bal" (nay), as we see, is from the speech of Him, exalted and mighty is He, and it is a transitional (*intiqaliyyah*) particle. What is transitioned from is what preceded, taken in its particularity. The last two are from their reported speech, and both are cancelling (*ibtaliyyatan*), because of their wavering and bewilderment in their fabrication. The whole of what was said falls within the secret counsel (*najwa*).

[p. 10]

It is also permissible for the first "bal" to be transitional, with what is transitioned from being what preceded, taken without regard to its particularity, and the sentence not falling within the secret counsel. Both views are sound, and there is nothing in them but a difference in the meaning of "bal," and in the first being part of the narration while the last two are part of the reported speech. There is no objection to this.

It has also been allowed that the first "bal" is part of their speech and is also cancelling, connected to their saying "It is sorcery," indicated by the words ﴿Will you then approach sorcery?﴾. This was refuted on the grounds that it is valid only if the noble wording were "They said, nay, etc.," to convey the narration of their turning away. That it is inverted, and its origin is "They said, nay," is not hidden in what it contains. It has also been answered that it is a turning away from their reported statement, with the statement implied before the words of the Exalted, "Is this etc.," or from what the secret counsel contained, and the saying was repeated because of the intervening element, or because it was not expressly stated. What is in this is also not hidden. It has also been allowed that all three are from His speech, exalted and mighty is He, on the basis that this is a descent (*tanzil*) of their statements into the degrees of corruption: their second statement is more corrupt than the first, the third is more corrupt than the second, and likewise the fourth than the third. This type of turning away is called progression (*taraqqi*), but it was not described here as progression, to indicate that progression in ugliness is in reality a descent. The reason for this, as stated in *al-Kashf*, is that their saying "It is sorcery" is closer to the truth than the second, for it may be said: indeed, among eloquent speech there is truly sorcery, because confused speech that cannot be controlled has no resemblance in any way to the elegant composition that silenced every orator. Then the claim that it is, in addition to being confused, invented, is further and further removed, because the composition, in its material and form, is among the most complete proofs of truthfulness. How much more so, when added to this is that the one who uttered it (ﷺ) was known among them for trustworthiness and truthfulness. The last is the raving of the delirious, for they are the people most able to distinguish by natural disposition between the versified and the prose, and between what poetry is intended for and what this speech is intended for, which is not like the eloquent sermons of their own orators, let alone that; and between the embellishments of poetry and the embellishments of this prose. This is as far as it concerns form alone. Then, when you come to the material and the composition of poetry from imaginings and base meanings that the rustics arrive at, and this is among the certain matters of belief and the practical matters of religion on which the affairs of the Hereafter and of this life depend, and by which the nobles are distinguished, the matter becomes clearer and clearer. This is so, while the one who uttered it, peace and blessings be upon him, is one for whom poetry does not come easily, and even if he intended it, they had associated with him and tasted him for forty years. End of quotation.

As for the composition of poetry being from imaginings, this is a description of what is usual. So it is not contradicted by his saying (ﷺ): "Indeed, there is wisdom in poetry," because that is in terms of rarity. This is confirmed by the emphasis with *inna*, which indicates doubt about it. The word "poet" has also been used with the meaning of "liar." Al-Raghib said: "The word 'poet' in the Qur'an means 'liar' by nature." On this reading, they meant, may Allah fight them, "Nay, he is" and far be it from Him, "one of many fabrications." In "bal" here, on this view, there is no cancelling, but rather an affirmation of the first judgment with an addition to it, as al-Raghib explicitly stated. On whether it is used for cancelling in the speech of Allah, exalted is He, there is disagreement. Ibn Hisham affirmed it and gave as an example His saying: ﴿And they say: "The Most Merciful has taken a son." Glory be to Him! Nay, they are honoured servants﴾ [al-Anbiya' 26]. Ibn Malik, in his commentary on *al-Kafiyah*, made a mistake and denied it. The truth is that if the cancelling concerns what was said by others, then it occurs in the Qur'an. If it concerns what was said by Him, exalted is He, then it does not occur, rather it is impossible, because it would be a change of mind (*bada'*). Perhaps it may be said that Ibn Malik's intended denial is the second case. Furthermore, this view, although it has a remoteness, is not without merit, as it has been said. So reflect.

﴿Then let him bring us a sign﴾ is the answer to an omitted conditional clause, which the context makes clear. It is as if it were said: "And even if it is not as we have said, but rather he is a messenger from Allah, mighty and majestic, as he claims, then let him bring us a sign, as the first ones were sent." Al-Nisaburi assigned a different condition, saying, taking from the words of the Imam in explaining the essential meaning of the verse: "They first denied that the Messenger (ﷺ) was of the kind of human beings. Then it is as if they said: 'Granted that, but what you claim to be a miracle is not a miracle. Its utmost is that it is beyond customary habit, and not everything beyond habit is a miracle; it may be sorcery.'" This holds if we assist them in the premise that the eloquence of the Qur'an lies outside habit. But we are far from accepting this premise, for we claim that it is extremely weak and badly composed, like confused dreams. Granted, but it is of the kind of the speech of ordinary people. Granted, but it is invented by him from himself. Granted that it is speech of eloquence, but it does not exceed the eloquence of poetry. Since this miracle is in such a state, then let him bring us a sign that is not open to any of these possibilities, as the first ones were sent." End of quotation. And it is, as you see, [unclear].

The word *ma* here is a relative pronoun in the genitive position with the *kaf* (like), and the sentence after it is its relative clause, with the returning pronoun omitted. The prepositional phrase is connected to an implied verb that functions as an adjective to "sign." That is: "Then let him bring us a sign like the sign with which the first ones were sent." The lack of some of the conditions for omitting a returning pronoun governed by a preposition does no harm, since there is no agreement that this is required. Whoever requires it considers the omitted returning pronoun here to be in the accusative, by way of omission and connection (*al-hadhf wa-l-iysal*), which is a broad path. By "sign" they meant the thing compared to it, as narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: the she-camel, the staff, and similar things. The apparent expectation would have been to say: "Then let him bring us what the first ones brought," or "like what the first ones brought." However, it was diverted from this to what is in the noble wording, because it indicates what that indicates, with the added feature that it was sent with it from Allah, mighty and majestic is He. In the use of "bringing" in regard to him (ﷺ), and the diversion from the apparent form in what follows, there is an allusion that what he (ﷺ) brought is from himself, while what the first ones brought is from Allah, blessed and exalted is He. Thus there is an allusive insinuation appropriate to what preceded of fabrication. So said al-Khafaji. He also mentioned that what has been said, namely that the diversion from "as the first ones brought" is because their intent was to demand a sign like the sign of Moses and the sign of Jesus, peace be upon them both, and not others of what the rest of the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, brought, and that the scholar al-Baydawi alluded to this, is without foundation.

It has also been allowed that *ma* is verbal-source (*masdariyyah*), and the *kaf* is in the accusative as a comparative verbal noun, that is, an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. That is: "Then let him bring us a sign, a bringing being like the sending of the first ones with it." The comparison is valid in that what is meant is "like the bringing of the first ones with it," since the sending of the messengers, peace be upon them, includes the bringing mentioned, as in *al-Kashshaf*. In *al-Kashf* it is said that it indicates that His saying, exalted is He, "as the first ones were sent," is a metonymy (*kinayah*) in this context. The benefit of the diversion after the goodness of the metonymy is to establish that it is a sign accepted by all, by its like, which proves the messengership, and which no one disputes, and upon which the purpose is established. The claim that the sending which is compared is the verbal noun of the passive, and its meaning is being sent from Allah, exalted is He, with signs, does not fatten or suffice in justifying the comparison, because that is different from bringing as well, even if it does not separate from it. It has also been said that the noble wording may be taken to mean that each of bringing and sending was intended in each of the two sides of the comparison, but the mention of sending was omitted on the side of what is compared, and the mention of bringing was omitted on the side of what the comparison is made to, relying on what is mentioned in each place rather than what is omitted in the other place. Its remoteness is not hidden.

Furthermore, the apparent point is that their acknowledgment of the sending of the first ones was not from the depths of the heart, but was a matter required by their confusion and bewilderment. Some of the eminent scholars mentioned that among what favours taking the view that what precedes is a report of their confused statements, this report, is that they first denied that the Messenger could be a human being, and they settled the matter with that and built upon it what they built. Then they conceded that the first ones had been people of signs, and they demanded of him (ﷺ) that he bring something of the kind of what they had brought. And on the view of the descent of their statements into degrees of corruption, this is taken to mean that it came down from them, and the diversion to metonymy was to establish its descent from their level. End of quotation. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

[p. 12]

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 21, verse 6:

﴿No town before them believed.﴾ This is a resumptive clause (*istinaf*), brought to refute them concerning what is indicated by the close of their statement: the implicit promise that they would believe when the requested sign came. It also shows that in making this demand they are like one who seeks his own death with his own hoof.

Refraining from granting their request is itself a mercy toward them. How could it be otherwise? For if they were given what they asked for, while certainly not believing, they would have been annihilated, according to the way of God, exalted is He, with the earlier nations: those who asked for signs and were then given them, yet did not believe, were destroyed. God, glorified is He, had already decreed that this community would not be punished with the punishment of annihilation. This view is preferable to what has been said: that when they attacked the Qur'an, claiming it was not a miracle, and pressed this to the point of being rebuked by His words, ﴿Will you then come to magic?﴾ (21:3), until they reached His words, glorified is He, ﴿Let him bring us﴾ (21:5), the statement ﴿No town believed...﴾ was revealed as a consolation to him, may God bless him and grant him peace, that warning would not benefit them.

Whatever the case, His words, glorified is He, ﴿from a town﴾ are on the elision of a noun (*hadhf al-mudaf*), meaning "from the people of a town." The particle *min* (from) is extra (*mazida*), for emphasis of generality, and what follows it is in the nominative position as the subject (*fa'il*). His words, glorified is He, ﴿We destroyed it﴾ are in the genitive or nominative position as a descriptive qualifier (*sifa*) of "town." What is meant is: "We destroyed it by destroying its people, because they did not believe after the coming of the signs they had requested." It has also been said that "town" is a metaphor for its people, so there is no need to posit an elided noun.

It has been objected that "We destroyed it" contradicts this, and that the use of a term with two referents (*istikhdam*), though frequent in speech, is contrary to the apparent meaning. Some have said: you may say that its destruction is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for the destruction of its people, but what was mentioned first is preferable.

The interrogative particle *a* (hamza) in His words, glorified is He, ﴿Will they then believe?﴾ is for denying that it occurs, and the *fa* (then) is for coordination (*'atf*). This is either upon an implied element which the interrogative particle entered, so that it conveys the denial of their believing and its negation immediately after the non-belief of the earlier ones. The meaning then is: no nation of the destroyed nations believed when the signs they had requested were granted; will these believe? They would not believe even if they were given what they asked for, that is, even though they are more defiant and more insolent, as is understood from the context and from turning away from understanding it as "they will not believe" either. Or it is upon ﴿No town believed﴾, on the basis that the *fa* is considered as preceding the interrogative particle in meaning, conveying the ordering of the denial of their believing upon the non-belief of the earlier ones. The interrogative particle was placed before it only because it demands initial position (*sadara*).

The words of His, Exalted and Majestic be He: ﴿We sent before you only men﴾ are a reply to what they claimed, that the Messenger must be an angel (malak), which is the point alluded to by their saying, ﴿Is this not but a human being like yourselves?﴾, on which they built what they built. So it is connected to that claim. The reply to their saying ﴿Then let him bring us﴾ is placed before it, because they said this as a challenge (ta'jiz), so it is necessary to hasten to refuting and nullifying it. Also, this reply contains a kind of elaboration that would be disrupted by placing it earlier, which would break the harmony (tajawub) of the noble composition.

His saying, Exalted be He: ﴿to whom We reveal﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the manner of sending. The present tense form is used to narrate a past state that was continuous (hikayat al-hal al-madiyya al-mustamirra), and the object is omitted because there is no intention to specify it. The meaning is: We did not send to the nations before your sending to your community except men, not angels, to whom We reveal, through the intermediary of an angel, what We reveal of the legislations (shara'i') and rulings (ahkam) and other things, including stories (qisas) and reports (akhbar), just as We reveal to you, without any difference between them in the reality of revelation (wahy) and the reality of its signification. Just as there is no difference between you and them in being human, so what is it with them that they do not understand that you are not a novelty among the messengers, and that what has been revealed to you does not contradict what was revealed to them, so that they say what they say?

Some of the eminent scholars said: the clause is in the place of the accusative as a descriptive qualifier (sifa madiha) of ﴿men﴾, and this is what the sublime composition requires. The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read (yuha ilayhim) with the ya', in the passive form (al-mabni li'l-maf'ul), following the ways of majesty (sunan al-kibriya') and as an announcement that the agent is determined.

His saying, Exalted be He: ﴿So ask the People of the Reminder (Ahl al-Dhikr), if you do not know﴾ is a shift in the mode of address (talwin li'l-khitab), directed to the disbelievers, in order to rebuke them and bring them down from the rank of disapproval and denial (al-istib'ad wa'l-nakir), after the establishment of the truth, in the manner of addressing the Messenger of God (ﷺ), because he is the one deserving of address concerning such refined realities. As for finding out about them by asking others, that is among the tasks of the common people. His (ﷺ) being commanded to ask in some verses is not for the purpose of finding out and acquiring knowledge of what is asked about, but for another reason. The particle fa' (fa) indicates the consequence of what follows upon what precedes. The People of the Reminder are the People of the Scripture (Ahl al-Kitab), as reported from al-Hasan, Qatada and others. The conditional response (jawab al-shart) is omitted, relying confidently on what is indicated by what is mentioned. That is: if you do not know what has been mentioned, then ask, O ignorant ones, the People of the Scripture, who are acquainted with the conditions of the earlier messengers, peace be upon them, so that your doubt may be removed. They were commanded to do so because the reports of a great multitude (akhbar al-jamm al-ghafir) convey knowledge in such matters, especially since they used to support the polytheists in their enmity towards him (ﷺ) and consult them about his affair (peace be upon him). In this there is, from the indication of the complete clarity of the matter and the strength of the status of the Prophet (ﷺ), what is not hidden.

It is reported from Ibn Zayd that the People of the Reminder are the People of the Qur'an. Ibn 'Atiyya rejected this, saying: they were their opponents, so how could they be commanded to ask them? This also refutes what the Imamiyya claim, that they are his family (ﷺ). The discussion of this has already passed.

﴿Nor did We make them bodies﴾ is an explanation that the messengers, peace be upon them, were an example for the rest of the individuals of the species in the judgments of human nature. The word jasad (body), according to what is in the Qamus (al-Qamus al-Muhit), is the substance (jism) of humans, jinn and angels. Al-Raghib said: it is like jism, except that it is more specific than it. Al-Khalil said: jasad is not said of other than a human, such as the creatures of the earth and the like. Also, jasad is said of what has a colour, while jism is said of what has no visible colour, like air and water.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 8:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We did not make them bodies﴾ etc. bears witness to what al-Khalil (al-Khalil ibn Ahmad al-Farahidi) said, end. It was also said: [jasad] is a body of composite structure. Its outward meaning is that it is more general than [animal], and some have restricted it to it. Some said: it is originally a verbal noun of [jasada al-dam], meaning it clotted/adhered, and it was applied to the composite body because it has parts adhering to one another. Then, the apparent point is that whoever holds that it is restricted so as not to include non-rational animals, for example, claims at most that this is according to its original usage, and does not hold that it may not be generalized afterward. So be not heedless.

Its accusative case is either because it is a second object of [ja'ala], the meaning being making it so from the start, following the manner of their saying: "Glory to Him who made the gnat small and the elephant large." Or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun, and [ja'al] is creative. Its being singular is to refer back to the genus, which encompasses the many; or because it is originally, as you have heard, a verbal noun, and such is applied to a single masculine thing and others. It was also said: it is for the intention of distributive inclusivity in the pronoun, meaning We made each one of them [a body]. It was also said: it is with an elided genitive-governing noun, meaning [possessors of a body]. In al-Tashil it is stated that the plural and dual of the governing noun suffice instead of the dual and plural of the governed noun in proper names, and likewise what has no ambiguity among common nouns.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They did not eat food﴾ is an attribute of (jasadan), meaning: and We did not make them a body free from need of nourishment, but in need of it. ﴿Nor were they immortal﴾ meaning: remaining forever. It is permitted that [khuld] means long lasting stay, but the first is preferred, because the sentence confirms what precedes it, namely that the earlier messengers, peace be upon them, were human and not angels, as the corrupt belief of the polytheists and their worthless claim require. The apparent point is that they also believe the angels, peace be upon them, to be everlasting, as the philosophers believe about them, except that they call them pure intellects. The meaning in sum is: We made them nourished bodies, ultimately heading to death according to their terms, and did not make them angels who neither eat nor die, as you claim. It was also said: the sentence is a rebuttal of His saying: ﴿What is this messenger who eats food?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7], etc. But the first is more fitting. Yes, it, along with confirming what precedes it, contains a rebuttal of that.

In choosing (wa ma kanu) over (wa ma ja'alnahum) there is an indication that the absence of immortality and permanence is among the consequences of their innate constitution in this created state, which was pointed to by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We did not make them bodies﴾ etc., not by a newly-initiated making. Rather, if you look at all composite things made of opposing elements, you will see their lasting even a little as a strange matter, and you will rise to seek the cause for that. From here it has been said:

"Do not let your question of why the past passed follow it; turn to what remains and ask it why it remained."

Rather, it is not far-fetched that possibilities in general are like this. For they have said: when a possible thing is left to itself and its essence, it is non-existent, since non-existence does not need a cause or an influence, unlike existence. It does not follow from this that non-existence is the essence's requirement, so as to become impossible, since that returns to the priority of non-existence and its suitability relative to the essence. Something pointing to this, as has been said, is Abu Ali's saying regarding accidents: the cure for the effect in itself is that it is not, and for it, from its cause, is that it is not hopeless. And their saying that the two sides of the possible are equal relative to its essence means its equality in not being necessitated either way relative to its essence. And their saying: the cause of non-existence is the cause of existence, in the sense that non-existence does not need an influence or making, but the absence of the cause suffices for it; not that the absence of the cause is an influence on the non-existence of the effect. Perhaps in his ﷺ saying: "What God the Exalted wills, comes to be, and what He does not will, does not come to be," there is an indication of this, so reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 9:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We fulfilled the promise to them﴾. It has been said that it is coordinated (ʿatf) with what is understood from the narrative of His revelation, Exalted is He, to the messengers, on a continuous, renewing basis (al-istimrar al-tajaddudi), as if it were said: "We revealed to them what We revealed, then We fulfilled to them the promise which We made to them within the revelation, by destroying their enemies." It has also been said that it is coordinated with the earlier "We reveal" (nuhi) in the sense of "We revealed" (awhayna). The placing of the command to ask (the people of remembrance) together with what accompanies it is for the sake of binding them to account and refuting them. Al-Khafaji said: "It is coordinated with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We sent﴾, and thumma (then) indicates a remote mention (li-l-tarakhi al-dhikri), meaning: We sent messengers from among mankind, and We fulfilled to them what We had promised them; likewise Muhammad (ﷺ), so beware of denying him and opposing him. Thus the verses, just as they contain the answer, also contain a threat." End of quotation. There is consideration in this.

The accusative of "the promise" (al-waʿd) is by removal of the preposition (nazʿ al-khafid), and the original is "We fulfilled to them in the promise," and from this is the usage "they fulfilled them in fighting" (ṣadaqūhumu al-qitāl) and "he fulfilled me the age of his camel" (ṣadaqanī sinna bakrihi). It has also been said that it is in the sense of a second object, since ṣadaqa may take two objects directly without the intermediary of a preposition at all.

﴿So We saved them and whom We willed﴾, that is, of the believers in them, as a group of the exegetes hold. It has been said that it means of them and of others whom wisdom requires to be preserved, such as one who will believe, he or some of his descendants, in the Hereafter; and this is the secret in the protection of those who denied him and harmed him (ﷺ) from the punishment of total annihilation. What the group holds was preferred on account of the contrast with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and We destroyed the transgressors﴾, and this is because the definite article is taken as generalizing (al-istighraq), and "the transgressors" applies to the disbelievers absolutely, based on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the transgressors are the companions of the Fire﴾ [Ghafir: 43], on the basis that the intended meaning of "companions of the Fire" is those who abide in it and remain in it forever, and none abides in it forever in our view except the disbelievers. As for one who first generalized, he said: the intended meaning of "the transgressors" is all others than those saved. The expression "whom We willed" rather than "those who believed" or "those with them," for example, is apparently indicating that the intended meaning is the believers and others along with them, and it is not clear, on the restricted reading, what the purpose is of departing from what was mentioned to what is in the noble composition. And the use of "We willed" (nashāʾu) rather than the apparent "We willed" (shiʾnā) is to narrate the past situation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 10:

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed We have sent down to you a Book﴾ is a resumed statement (kalam mustanaf) brought to establish the truth (haqqiyyah) of the Mighty Qur'an, which, at the beginning of the blessed surah, mentioned the people's aversion to the signs that come to them from it, their mockery of it, and their confusion regarding its matter; and it explains the loftiness of its rank following the establishment of his prophethood (ﷺ), by showing that he, like the other noble messengers, peace be upon them, has been sent with the emphatic oath, to display greater concern for its content and to signal that the addressees are at the furthest degree of denial. The address is to the Quraysh.

It is also permitted that the address is to all the Arabs. The tanwin on "Kitaban" is for magnification and exaltation, meaning: a Book of great standing, with a luminous proof. His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿in it is your reminder (dhikrukum)﴾ is a qualifier of it, emphasizing what the indefinite form of exaltation (al-tankir al-tafkhimi) conveys of its being of lofty worth, by being of beautiful effects, bringing to them lofty benefits. The meaning of "dhikr" (reminder/mention), as al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from Ibn Abbas, is renown (al-sit) and nobility (al-sharaf), used metaphorically: in it is that which causes nobility for you, because it is in your language and sent down to a prophet from among you, by whose nobility you are ennobled and by whose fame you become famous, since you are its bearers, and the reference for untying its knots. That this is attributed to it is an exaggeration of its being the cause of that. And from Sufyan: it is noble character and good deeds, meaning: in it is that by which mention (i.e. good praise and good repute) is obtained, from noble character and good deeds, by calling the cause by the name of the effect; so it is metaphorical for that as well.

Several transmitted from al-Hasan that the intended meaning is what you need in matters of your religion, and some added: and your worldly affairs. It was also said that "dhikr" means "reminding" (al-tadhkir), in the passive sense, and the meaning is: in it is your admonition. This was preferred because it is most suitable to the flow (siba) and context (siyaq) of the noble composition, for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Will you not then understand?﴾ is a reproachful rebuke, containing an incitement to them to reflect upon the matter of the Book and to reflect on the varieties of admonitions and warnings within it, among which are the preceding and following calamities.

The author of al-Tahrir said: What the context of the verses requires is that the meaning in it is the mention of your ugly deeds and blameworthy conduct, and how you treated the prophets of God, upon them be blessings and peace, with denial and obstinacy. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Will you not then understand?﴾ is a rebuke against them for their not reflecting, which leads to awakening from the slumber of heedlessness, end of quote. But this is far-fetched. The "fa" is for coordination with an implied element that the statement entails, meaning: Will you not reflect, so that you do not understand that the matter is so; or: you do not understand anything of the things of which this is one,

The commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 11:

The words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And how many a town did We shatter﴾ are a kind of detailed explanation of the general statement of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿and We destroyed the transgressors﴾, and a clarification of the manner of their destruction and an alert to their great number. Thus "kam" here is khabariyyah (the "kam" used to express a large quantity), indicating multiplicity. Its position is in the accusative, as it is the object of "qasamna" (We shattered), and "min qaryatin" (from a town) is a tamyiz (specification). In the word qasm (shattering), which means breaking by separating the parts and removing their joining altogether, there is, as the use of the strong qaf suggests, an indication of the intensity of anger and the severity of wrath that is not hidden. The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿which had been wrongdoing﴾ are a description (sifah) of "qaryah" (town). It is said that the original was "ahla qaryatin" (the people of a town), which is indicated by the pronoun that comes later, if Allah the Exalted wills. So the governing noun (mudaf) was removed and the governed noun (mudaf ilayh) was put in its place, and it was therefore described by what is a attribute of the removed noun, namely wrongdoing (zulm). It is as if it were said: "And many a people of a town We have shattered, who were wrongdoers in respect of the signs of Allah the Exalted, disbelieving in them, like you."

In al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari) it says: the intended meaning of "qaryah" is its people, and for this reason it was described as wrongdoing. Thus the attribution is figurative (tajawwur fi al-taraf). Some of them said: you may say that its description with that is by figurative attribution (al-isnad al-majazi), and the words ﴿We shattered from a town﴾ are a kinayah (allusion or metonymy) for "We shattered its people," because the destruction of the town necessarily entails the destruction of its people; so there is neither majaz (figurative usage) nor hadhf (ellipsis). In any case, the intended meaning is not a specific town. Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from al-Kalbi that it is the town of Hadrawt in Yemen. Ibn Mardawayh transmitted through his chain from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, that he said: Allah the Exalted sent a prophet from Himyar called Shu'ayb, and a servant rose against him and struck him with a staff. Then Bukhtanassar marched against them, fought them, and killed them until no one remained of them. And concerning them Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And how many a town﴾, etc.

In al-Bahr (of Abu Hayyan) it says that these people were in Hadrawt, and that Allah the Exalted sent to them a prophet whom they killed. So Allah the Exalted empowered Bukhtanassar over them, as He had empowered him over the people of Bayt al-Maqdis. He sent to them an army, which they defeated; then he sent another, which they also defeated; then he went out to them himself, defeated them, and killed them. It is also transmitted from some of them that the name of this prophet was Musa ibn Misha. And from Ibn Wahb that the verse concerns two towns in Yemen, one of them Hadrawt and the other Qulabah, whose people were arrogant, so Allah the Exalted destroyed them at the hand of Bukhtanassar. It is not hidden that this is something the apparent meaning of the verse rejects, and the view that it belongs to the type of your saying: "How many dirhams of Zayd's did you take?", with the prepositional phrase "min darahim Zayd" (of Zayd's dirhams) being connected to "akhadhta" (you took) and the tamyiz being omitted, meaning: "How many dirhams did you take from Zayd's dirhams?" It is also said here that it is by the estimate of "kam sakin" (how many inhabitants), meaning: "We shattered the inhabitants of a town," or something similar. Such views should not be given attention except by refuting them. Thus it is likely that what is in the narrations is to be understood as an illustrative example (sabil al-tamthil), and many such cases are not rare.

[Page 16]

In the words of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿and We raised up after them﴾, meaning after the destruction of their people, not after that deed, as some have wrongly supposed, ﴿another people﴾, meaning that they had nothing in common with them. This is an alert to the complete uprooting of the former ones and the cutting off of their last trace altogether, and this is the secret of placing the account of the raising up of these people before the account of the beginnings of the destruction of those, in the words of Allah, glorified is He:

﴿When they perceived Our punishment﴾. The pronoun of the plural refers to the people of the town, not to another people, since they had no sin that would necessitate what this statement includes. Iḥsās (perception) means apprehension through a sense, i.e., when they apprehended Our severe punishment with their senses. Perhaps that punishment was something perceivable by one of the outward senses. It is also permissible that there is a metaphor of implicature (istiʿārah makniyyah) in "baʾs" (punishment), and that "iḥsās" is a figurative imagining (takhyīl), and that "iḥsās" is a metaphor (majāz) for apprehension in general, i.e., when they apprehended that.

﴿Behold, they were fleeing from it﴾. That is, from the town. Thus "min" is for the starting point (ibtidāʾiyyah), or it is from "the punishment," and the feminine form is because it has the meaning of retribution and adversity, so "min" is causal (taʿlīliyyah). On both possibilities, it is connected to the saying of the Exalted: ﴿racing away﴾. "Idhā" is the sudden particle (fujāʾiyyah), and the clause is the response of "lammā." "Rakaḍa," from the pattern of "qatala," means to strike the animal with its leg, and it is transitive.
