It may also be used intransitively, as in "rakaḍa al-faras" (the horse ran), meaning it ran, as Abū Zayd said, and no weight is given to one who denies it. "Al-rakḍ" here is a metonymy (kināyah) for fleeing, i.e., "behold, they were fleeing, hastening, galloping their mounts."

It is also permissible that the meaning is "likened to those who drive their mounts," on the basis that there is a serial metaphor (istiʿārah tabaʿiyyah) there. There is no obstacle to taking the speech in its literal sense, as has been said.

"Do not flee" (lā tarkudū): that is, it was said to them. The speaker may be the angels of punishment, or those believers present there, who said it mockingly toward them. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is possible, according to the previously mentioned narration, that the speaker was from the army of Bukhtansar (Nebuchadnezzar), and he intended by it to deceive them and to mock them." It was also said: it is possible that the meaning is that they are made to become (khula'a', i.e. objects of ridicule or dupes), by saying that to them, though it was not said in the sense that they had reached such a point in running and fleeing from punishment, after being pampered and living in luxury, that whoever saw them would say: "Do not run." ﴿And return to what you were given in luxury therein﴾ of the blessings and pleasures. Al-itraf is the wasting of blessing, and "fihi" is for location (zarfiyya), though it has been permitted that it be causal (sababiyya). ﴿And your dwellings﴾ in which you used to take pride, ﴿that perhaps you may be questioned﴾: you intend to be consulted, to take counsel and to plan regarding important matters and calamities; or you will be asked about what befell you and what descended upon your wealth and your dwellings, so that you answer the questioner with knowledge and witnessing; or your retinue and servants will ask you, saying, "What do you command? What do you decree? How shall we proceed, and how shall we leave things as they were before?"; or those who come seeking your bounty will ask you for your generosity, either because you used to be generous, spending your wealth to be seen by people and seeking praise, or because you used to be stingy, so it was said to them as mockery upon mockery. It was also said, according to the previous narration, that the meaning is: "that perhaps you may ask for peace, or for the jizya (poll tax), or for a matter you might agree upon with the king." It was said that by their dwellings is meant the Fire, so the meaning of "return to your dwellings" is "enter the Fire," in mockery; and by the questioning is meant the questioning about deeds, or by it is meant punishment, by way of metonymy (majaz mursal) by mentioning the cause and intending the effect, i.e., "enter the Fire so that you may be questioned or punished for your wrongdoing and your denial of the signs of God, Exalted." This is contrary to the apparent meaning, as is not hidden.

﴿They said﴾ when they despaired of escaping by fleeing and were certain that the punishment had seized them, ﴿"Woe to us!"﴾ meaning, O our destruction! ﴿"Indeed, we were wrongdoers."﴾ deserving the punishment for having been wrongdoers against the signs of God, the Exalted. This is an acknowledgment from them of wrongdoing and of its consequence, which is the punishment, and a regret over it at a time when that does not benefit them. It has been said, according to the earlier narration, that this regret and acknowledgment came from them when the swords seized them and a caller called out from the heaven: "O vengeance of the prophets!"

Page 17

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 15:**

﴿So that cry of theirs did not cease﴾: that is, they did not stop repeating that word. Calling it *da'wa* (a cry or call) is in the sense of *da'wa* (a calling out), since it is said *da'a da'wa* and *da'wa*, because the wailer is as if calling upon destruction, saying: "O woe, come! This is your time."

Al-Huwfi, al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa' permitted that *tilka* (that) be the subject (*ism*) of *zala* (to remain/continue), with *da'wahum* (their cry) as its predicate (*khabar*), or the reverse. Abu Hayyan said: Al-Zajjaj said this before them. As for our later companions, they hold that the subject and predicate of *kana* and its sisters (*kana wa akhwatuha*, the verbs of state) resemble the agent (*fa'il*) and the object (*maf'ul*). Just as it is not permitted to advance or delay the agent and the object when this causes confusion, because the grammatical case endings (*i'rab*) are not visible, it is not permitted in the chapter of *kana*. No one disputed this except Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn al-Hajj, one of the most eminent students of al-Shalubin. End quote.

Al-Fadil al-Khafaji said: What Ibn al-Hajj mentioned in his book *al-Madkhal* is that there is no confusion in it, and that it arises from failing to distinguish between *iltibas* (confusion, where what is understood is the opposite of what is meant) and *ijmal* (ambiguity, where neither of the two possibilities is specified). For this reason he permitted it. What he mentioned is open to discussion and reflection.

In the marginal notes of al-Fadil al-Bahlawan on the tafsir of al-Baydawi, it is said that this applies to the agent and object, and to the subject and predicate when the case endings are absent, and that the indication (*qarina*) is an accepted and explicitly stated principle. As for the chapter of *kana* and its sisters, it is not accepted. End quote.

The apparent view is that there is no difference between the chapter of *kana* and the other cases mentioned, even if the absence of explicit statement is granted, since what they cited as the reason for the prohibition is common to both. Moreover, that [situation] is closer to confusion than to ambiguity, especially in this verse in one opinion. So understand this.

﴿until We made them a harvested crop, extinguished﴾: that is, until We made them like harvested plants and extinguished fire in destruction. This is what the second *'Allama* (the author of the commentary on *Miftah al-Ulum*) stated in his commentary on *Sharh al-Miftah*. He then said: In this there are two metaphors (*isti'aratan*) by way of metonymy (*kinaya*) with a single expression, which is the pronoun in *ja'alnahum*, since they were compared to plants and to fire, and the pronoun was mentioned in the singular, while what was intended by it was the thing compared to them, namely the plant and the fire, by way of claim (*idda'an*), with the indication that harvesting, which is a property of plants, and extinguishing, which is a property of fire, were attributed to it. This cannot be regarded as a simile (*tashbih*) like *hum summun bukmun 'umyun* (they are deaf, dumb and blind), because the plural of *khamidin* (extinguished) in the form used for rational beings contradicts the simile, since we have no people who are "extinguished" such that the people of the town could be compared to them. Extinguishing is a property of fire, unlike deafness, for example, which is attributed to people in the phrase *hum ka-qawmin summin* (they are like a deaf people). Likewise, *hasidan* is taken to mean "reaped" (*mahsudin*), with the singular and plural being the same in the pattern *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul*, so as to agree with *khamidin*. Yes, it is permissible to liken the destruction of a people to the cutting of plants and the extinguishing of fire, in which case it is an explicit subordinate metaphor (*isti'ara tasrihiyya tab'iyya*) in both descriptions. End quote.

The same is in *Sharh al-Miftah* of al-Sayyid al-Sanad, except that it is permitted to consider *hasidan* alone as a simile, based on what is in the *Kashshaf* (of al-Zamakhshari), meaning: We made them like the harvested crop, just as you say "We made them ashes," meaning "like ashes." Many have explained the singular form of *hasid* in this interpretation, since *mathal* (example/likeness), being originally a verbal noun, is applied to the singular and to other than the singular, and it is the predicate in the sense of an eloquent simile (*tashbih baligh*). This would entail the validity of *al-rijalu asadun* (the men are lions), and this, as you see, is unacceptable.

An objection was raised to the words of the two commentators, "since there is no people of ... etc.", that there is a point of discussion in it, and that the basis of what they both stated, namely that *khamidin* does not admit of simile because its plural is the plural for rational beings, is what prevents it from being an adjective of fire. So even if it were said *khamidatan* (feminine singular), it would be a simile. The Sharif (al-Jurjani) explicitly stated this in his glosses. However, this is open to doubt, because if the application (*haml*) is valid in a simile by way of claim, why would its plural not be valid for that purpose? Had it not been so, the metaphor would not be valid either. The scholar al-Tibi and al-Fadil al-Yamani went to the view that there is a simile in both places. Thus in the verse there are four possibilities, so reflect on all of this.

*Khamidin* together with *hasidan* is in the position of the second object of *ja'ala* (to make), as in *ja'altuhu hulwan hamidan* (I made it sweet and sour). The meaning is: We made them those who gather the harvest and the extinguishing, or [we made them] resembling the reaped and the extinguished, or resembling the reaping and the extinguishing, or We made them perishing in the most complete manner. It is not intended that *ja'ala* here governs three objects, although it is among the verbs that govern two objects. Or it is a state (*hal*) from the pronoun in *ja'alnahum* (the object of the verb), or from the concealed pronoun in *hasidan*, or it is an adjective of *hasidan*. The last has several meanings. Some objected that its being an adjective of it, together with its being a simile intended for what does not reason, is rejected by its being used for rational beings.

﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾ That is, We did not fashion this raised canopy, this spread-out bed, and what lies between them of kinds of creatures, filled with forms of wonder and marvels, as tyrants fashion their ceilings, their carpets, and all their ornaments for amusement and play. Rather, We fashioned them for religious benefits and divine wisdoms, such as making them a means of taking lessons and a proof leading to knowledge, together with countless benefits and wisdoms that cannot be exhausted. The summary of this is: We did not create that empty of wisdoms and purposes, except that He expressed this by the word "play" (la'ib). And it is, as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said, "the act to which no sound purpose is directed," in order to show the perfect exaltedness of Him, the Exalted, above creating something void of wisdom, by describing it in a form about whose impossibility for Him, glory be to Him, no one doubts. It is said that this statement is a general indication that the creation of the world and the origination of the children of Adam are founded upon the foundations of consummate wisdom, which entail sublime ends, and an alert that what is recounted of the punishment descending upon the people of the towns is among the requirements of those wisdoms and their branches, according to what their deeds necessitate, along with a transition to warning the addressees. In al-Kashf it is stated that the verses are for establishing the matter of prophethood and negating those earlier slanders, as the Imam mentioned, and this is the truth, because it has been repeated in the Noble Book that the wisdom in creating the heavens and the earth and what is between them is worship and knowledge, and the recompense of one who fulfills them and one who does not. That is not completed except by the sending down of Books and the sending of Messengers, peace be upon them. Thus, one who denies the Message makes the creation of the heavens and the earth a play, exalted is He who created them and created everything, far above that and above every deficiency with a great exaltation. And one who denies the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) makes the manifestation of the miracle (mu'jizah, a supernatural sign that accompanies a prophet's claim) at his hands a matter of futility and play. In it, therefore, is an affirmation of his prophethood, peace and blessings be upon him, and the invalidity of all those slanders.

[p. 18]

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Had We wished to take a pastime, We would have taken it from Our presence﴾ is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that confirms what precedes it) affirming what came before it, namely the negation of play in the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them. The meaning of the verse, as the author of al-Kashshaf inclines to understand it, is: "Had We wished to take a pastime, the taking of a pastime from Our side would have been a divine pastime, that is, a wisdom which you would have taken as a pastime from your side. This is the very essence of seriousness and wisdom." So the sense is "had We wished it, it would have been impossible."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿if We were ever to do so﴾ is like a repetition of that meaning, for the sake of emphasizing the impossibility. The *in* (إنْ) here is conditional, and its apodosis is omitted, meaning: "(if We were ever to do so) something that is described as play by its doing, then this would be Our action." If it is taken as negative, so that it states explicitly the conclusion of the preceding clause, as the majority of exegetes hold, it would also be good and eloquent. Al-Alusi concludes here.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿from Our presence﴾ means from the direction of Our power, and he took the resulting meaning to be: "If We wished that, We would have taken it, for We are capable of everything, except that We do not will it, because wisdom turns Us away from it." The author of al-Kashshaf noted that interpreting it as power is not clear, although al-Baydawi and others also interpreted it this way. The apparent implication is that taking a pastime falls under power. It has been said that it is impossible for God, in an absolute, essential sense, and what is impossible cannot be the object of power. The answer is that the truth of a conditional does not require the truth of both its parts; this is a conditional based on the impossibility of the will. Or it may be said that wisdom does not contradict taking what is of a kind that can be played with; it only contradicts His doing an act by which He Himself becomes a player. So there is no impossibility in the taking itself, but in His being described by it. Al-Alusi concludes here.

In my own view, the truth is that futility (*'abath*), being a deficiency, is impossible with respect to God, the Exalted. Therefore, abstaining from it is obligatory for Him, glorified and exalted is He. Although we do not say that anything is obligatory upon God, the Exalted, we do say that it is obligatory with regard to Him, mighty and majestic is He. The most eminent of the later scholars, al-Kalanbawi, said: The position of the Maturidiyya (the followers of al-Maturidi), who affirm that actions have a quality that makes them good or bad before revelation arrives, is that if there is in an act a quality that requires ugliness, then that act is impossible with respect to God, the Exalted, so abstaining from it is obligatory for Him, glorified is He, although nothing is obligatory upon Him, mighty and majestic is He. This is like imposing what cannot be borne, according to them, and like lying, according to the verifying scholars of the Ash'ariyya and the Maturidiyya. If there is no such quality in an act, then that act is possible for God, the Exalted, and it is not obligatory upon Him, glorified is He. Thus they agree with the Ash'ariyya that nothing is obligatory upon God, the Exalted. Al-Kalanbawi concludes here.

Whoever denies that futility is a deficiency, as lying is, has been stubborn against his own reason. More forceful than this is that it is understood from the words of some of the verifying scholars that it is obligatory to observe wisdom in general with respect to God, glorified is He, lest one of the well-known impossibilities be entailed. The intended meaning of denying that anything is obligatory upon God, the Exalted, is the denial of obligation in particular matters, as the Mu'tazila maintain. Perhaps, in that case, obligation means that the act necessarily issues from God, the Exalted, in such a way that He cannot abstain from it, on the basis that abstaining would entail an impossibility after its cause has issued by choice, not absolutely, nor on condition that the readiness be complete, lest the principle of choice be abandoned. Just as the abandonment of this principle is not entailed by the view of Imam al-Razi, which many of the Ash'ariyya chose, that knowledge necessarily follows from reflection by reason. Nevertheless, one should avoid applying the term "obligation" to God, the Exalted, so reflect on this, for it is important.

It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿from Our presence﴾ is "from what is fitting to Our court, of the immaterial beings." That is, "We would have taken it from among them, not from the raised bodies and the placed substances, like the custom of tyrants in raising thrones and adorning them, and spreading carpets and decorating them." Al-Alusi concludes here.

It should not be hidden that most of the People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna, the Sunni community) deny the existence of immaterial beings (*mujarradat*). Moreover, even if the verse is interpreted as stated, the intended purpose is to refute those who claim that play is taken in this world, not to say that it is permissible to take it from immaterial beings. Indeed, it is even more evident that it is impossible among them. It is reported from al-Jubba'i that the meaning is: "Had We wished to take a pastime, We would have taken it from Our side in such a way that no one would be aware of it, because it is a deficiency, so concealing it is better." Or it is closer to what is more quickly understood from al-Kashshaf, and that is less far in meaning.

Al-Imam al-Wahidi said: Play (*lahw*) is the seeking of relief from the self. Then a woman is called *lahw*, and so is a child, because one finds relief in each of them. For this reason, a man's wife and child are called his "fragrant herbs" (*rayhanatan*). The meaning is: "Had We wished to take a woman who is a source of relief, or a child who is a source of relief, We would have taken him from Our presence," that is, from among what We choose and select from what We will. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had God wished to take a son, He would have chosen whom He willed from what He creates﴾ [al-Zumar: 4]. The exegetes said: that is, from among the wide-eyed maidens (*al-hur al-'in*). This is a refutation of the saying of the Jews about 'Uzayr and of the saying of the Christians about the Messiah and his mother, concerning his being a son, peace be upon him, and her being a consort. The meaning of ﴿from Our presence﴾ is "from Our side, such that no one has any control over it, because a man's child and his wife are with him, not with anyone else." Al-Wahidi concludes here.

The interpretation of *lahw* here as "child" is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi. It is also reported from al-Zajjaj that it means "child" in the dialect of Hadramawt. Its meaning as "woman" is related by Qatada from the people of Yemen, though he did not attribute it to a particular town among them. Al-Tabarsi claimed that its origin is intercourse, and it is used as a euphemism for a woman, because she is copulated with. He recited the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*Has Basbasa claimed today that I have grown old, and that a man like me cannot enjoy pastime?*

The apparent meaning, however, is to take *lahw* as you heard it first, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and what is between them, playing﴾ [al-Anbiya': 16], and because the negation of a child will come explicitly, God willing. From this it is known that taking the intended meaning as a refutation of the Christians and their like is not appropriate here.

Furthermore, the apparent sense of the context is that *in* (إنْ) is conditional, and the apodosis is omitted, relying confidently on what precedes it. That is: ﴿if We were ever to do so﴾ [then] "We would have taken it from Our presence." It is also possible that *in* is negative. Although that is good in meaning, and it was stated by a group including Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Juraij, some have objected to it that most occurrences of the negative *in* (إنْ النافية) are accompanied by the distinguishing *lam* (اللام الفارقة). However, this matter is easy.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, We hurl the truth against falsehood﴾

It is a turning away (idrab) from taking up idle play and sport, or rather from the will to take it up. It is as if it were said: "But We do not want it. Rather, Our way is to overcome the truth, of which seriousness is a part, over falsehood, of which idle play is a part." The singling out of this matter from among His other affairs, exalted is He, is for the sake of leading into what will come, God willing, of threat. It is reported from Mujahid that the truth is the Qur'an and the falsehood is Satan. It was also said that the truth is the proof, and the falsehood is their confusion and their attribution to God, exalted is He, of attributes other than His, such as offspring and the like. The general sense is the preferable one. The origin of qadhf (hurling) is throwing from a distance, as al-Raghib said, and it implies the firmness of the throw. It has been used metaphorically for "bringing forth," meaning: We bring forth the truth against falsehood.

﴿so it crushes it﴾, that is, it utterly annihilates it, as We did to the people of the overturned cities. The origin of dam'(crushing) is breaking a soft, hollow thing, and it has been used metaphorically for annihilation.

It is permissible that there is here an image (tamthil) of the truth's dominance over falsehood, until it removes it, by hurling a hard body onto the head of a soft brain so as to split it. This implies the height of the truth and the lowliness of falsehood, and that the side of the first remains while the second perishes. It is also permissible that it be a metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah), by likening the truth to a hard thing that comes from a high place and falsehood to a soft, hollow, low body. Perhaps the view that it is an image is the better one.

Isa ibn Umar recited (fa-yadmaghahu) with the accusative (nasb), and this is weak, because what follows the fa' is in the accusative only by the implied particle "an," not by the fa' itself, contrary to the Kufans' view regarding the answer after the six items (al-ashya' al-sitta). What is here is not one of them, and such a construction is not found except in poetry, like his saying:

"I will leave my dwelling to the Banu Tamim, and I will join the Hijaz, and so I rest."

However, it has been said regarding this that "astarihu" is not accusative but nominative, with the emphatic light nun, pausing on it with the alif. It has been justified that the accusative after the imperfect future resembles the wish in its expectancy. It is not hidden that the meaning in the verse is not restricted to the future, and they have said that this justification in the line is weak, so what is in the verse is weaker in its basis. The conjunction on this reading is with "al-haqq" according to Abu al-Baqa'. The meaning is: "Nay, We hurl the truth so that We crush it against falsehood," that is, We throw the truth, so its nullifying is by it.

Some of the eminent scholars mentioned that if it were classed under the pattern of "I fed her straw and cold water," it would be correct, and it was inferred that the conjunction is on the meaning, that is, We do the hurling and then the crushing. It was also read (fa-yadmuhu) with a damma on the mim and the ghayn. ﴿and behold, it is vanishing﴾, that is, utterly departing. In the sudden "idha" (idha al-fuja'iyyah) and the nominal sentence there is an indication of the completeness of hastening in departing and perishing, which is not hidden. It is as if it had been vanishing from the origin.

﴿And woe to you for what you describe﴾: a threat to the Quraysh, or to all the disbelievers of the Arabs, that they too have the like of what those have of punishment and retribution. The "ma" is causal (ta'lil), connected to the stabilizing element on which the predicate depends, or to an omitted element which is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "woe" according to the view of some, or from its concealed pronoun in the predicate. The "ma" is either verbal-masdar, or relative, or descriptive, that is: "And settled for you is woe and destruction because of your attributing to Him what does not befit the majesty of His affair, exalted is His majesty," or "by that which you describe," or "by something you attribute to Him, of offspring and the like," or "being among what you describe Him, mighty and majestic, by." That the address is to whoever you hear is something without obscurity or distance. And farthest of all from the mark is whoever said that it is an address to the people of the cities by way of iltifat (shift) from the third person in His saying ﴿So their claim did not cease to be that﴾ to it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 19:

﴿To Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth.﴾ This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) that confirms what came before it: that God, exalted is He, created all His creatures in perfect wisdom and complete order, and that He, glory be to Him, establishes the truth and eliminates falsehood. It has also been said that it corresponds to His saying, ﴿And woe to you﴾. As you can see, this is [a weak view]. That is, to Him alone, exalted is He, belong all creatures in terms of creation, ownership, management, disposal, giving life, causing death, punishing, and rewarding, without anyone having any share in that, whether independently or as a follower.

It seems that the intention here is to show greater majesty, so the word "heavens" is given in the plural, with the meaning that whoever is in each one of the heavens belongs to Him. Previously, the aim was only to show that this visible ceiling and spread-out bedding, and what lies between them, contain countless wisdoms. For this reason the singular form is used rather than the plural.

In al-Itqan (al-Suyuti's *al-Itqan fi 'Ulum al-Qur'an*): where a number is intended, "heaven" is used in the plural, and where a direction is intended, it is used in the singular.

﴿And those who are with Him﴾ are the angels, peace be upon them all, according to what is narrated from Qatadah and others. "With Him" refers to nearness of rank, not nearness of place. The nearness of rank and standing has been likened to the nearness of place and distance, so the thing being compared is expressed with a word that denotes the thing it is compared to. Thus there is an explicit metaphor (istiʿarah musarrahah).

It has also been said that they are described this way to place them, because of their honour with Him, mighty and majestic, in the position of those brought near to kings, by way of illustration. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is His saying, ﴿they do not disdain His worship﴾, that is, they do not consider themselves too great for it, nor do they regard themselves as proud, ﴿nor do they tire﴾, that is, they do not grow weary and do not become exhausted. It is said: *hasara* (the camel) and *istahsara*, meaning he became weary and exhausted; and *hasartuhu* ("I wearied him") is transitive, while *hasara* is intransitive. It is also said *ahsartuhu* with a hamza.

The apparent view is that *istihsar* (with the extra letters), where no request is involved as here, is more emphatic than *husur*, since an increase in the form indicates an increase in meaning. The unity between the two words, which is what their usage indicates, means unity in the basic meaning. The use of the more emphatic form serves to draw attention to the fact that their worship, with its burden and constancy, is truly deserving of making one weary; yet they do not grow weary. This is not a negation of intensified weariness while its basic occurrence is affirmed in general. A parallel to this is His saying, ﴿Your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat: 46], according to one of the well-known interpretations of it.

Abu al-Baqa' and others allowed that this could be coordinated with the first "those" (man). The explanation that they are the angels, peace be upon them, remains as it is. He mentioned that this coordination is because the coordinated element is more specific than the element it is coordinated with in reality, like the coordination in His saying, ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend﴾ [al-Qadr: 4], in indicating the elevated status of the coordinated element and its glorification, since it is singled out for mention even though it is included in the generality of what precedes it. It has also been said that it was singled out because it is more general in one respect: "whoever is on the earth" includes humans and similar beings, whereas "those who are with Him" includes those who surround the Throne but not others. It was also permitted that by "those who are with Him" is meant a type of angel, peace be upon them, that is exalted above settling and dwelling in the heavens or on the earth. This seems to lean toward the view that a type of angel is immaterial (mujarrad), peace be upon them. But you know that the majority of the people of Islam do not hold that any of the possible existents is immaterial. What is well known of those who hold this view is that they say the angels are immaterial absolutely, not that some of them are immaterial and others are not.

Then Abu al-Baqa' allowed that, on this interpretation, His saying, ﴿they do not disdain﴾, could be a circumstantial clause (hal) modifying the first and second "those," according to the view of one who makes the adverbial phrase (zarf) the predicate, or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the adverbial phrase that is the predicate, or from the pronoun in ("with Him"). One of the last two is required according to one who parses "whoever" (man) as a subject, since a circumstantial clause cannot come from the subject. This is not hidden.

Some eminent scholars allowed that the sentence could be a new independent sentence (mustaʾnafah), but the more apparent view is to make it the predicate of "those who are with Him." Some of the possibilities for it being a circumstantial clause involve things that are not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 21, verse 20:

The saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They glorify Him night and day﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*), coming as an answer to a question that arises from what precedes it, as if it were said: "What do they do in their worship, or how do they worship?" So it is said: (*yusabbihun*, "they glorify") etc.

It is permitted that it be in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in (*la yastahsirun*, "they do not grow weary"). And the saying of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿They never slacken﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (*yusabbihun*), on both the resumptive and the circumstantial readings. It is permitted, on the reading of the circumstantial clause, that this be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (*la yastahsirun*) as well. But on the reading of the resumptive sentence, it is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from it, because of the separation. It is also permitted that it be a resumptive sentence, and the meaning is: they exalt Allah the Exalted, magnify Him and glorify Him at all times, such that no interval at all interrupts their glorification, whether through leisure or through some other occupation.

It has been raised as an objection that the angels are all like this in an absolute sense, since among them are messengers who convey the message, and glorification cannot occur during the act of conveying. Among them also are those who curse the disbelievers, as is reported in another verse. 'Abdullah ibn al-Harith ibn Nawfal asked Ka'b about this, as Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-Azamah*, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* related. He answered that glorification was made for them like breathing, so it does not prevent them from speaking about something else. This was criticised on the ground that it is far-fetched. It has also been said that Allah the Exalted created for them tongues, so they glorify with one and convey with another, for example. It has also been said that their conveying and their cursing of the disbelievers is glorification in meaning.

Al-Khafaji said: "The apparent meaning is that if it is not taken to apply to some of them, then what is intended is hyperbole, as one says: 'So-and-so does not cease from praising you and giving thanks for your blessings.'" End of quotation. The goodness of this is not hidden. It is also possible to say that this glorification is like the presence and the inner remembrance (*al-dhikr al-qalbi*) that occurs to many of the wayfarers (*al-salikin*), and that this can coexist with conveying and other outward acts. Furthermore, the fact that the angels glorify night and day does not necessitate that there be night and day for them in the heaven, because what is intended is to convey their continuity in glorification in the customary manner.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 21:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth who raise the dead?﴾ is a report of another of the transgressions of those disbelievers, one greater than their transgression of disparaging prophethood. Am (أم) here is the disjunctive (munqati'a) "am," and it is to be estimated as bal (بل, "rather") of transition (al-idrabiyya), and the interrogative hamza (al-hamza al-inkariyya) is for denying the occurrence (al-wuqu'), not for denying what has occurred (al-waqi'). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from the earth﴾ is connected to ittakhadhu (they have taken), and min (مِن) is for the starting point (ibtida'iyya), in the sense that their taking of them begins from parts of the earth, such as stones and kinds of minerals. It is also permissible for it to be partitive (tab'idiyya).

Abu al-Baqa' and others said: It is permissible for it to be connected to an omitted element that stands as a description of gods (ālihatan), meaning gods existing from the kind of the earth. In any case, the intended meaning is belittlement, not restriction. Whoever permitted restriction was obliged to restrict the denial to the severe, and that is not sound.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they raise the dead﴾, meaning they resurrect the dead, is a description of gods (ālihatan). This is what the denial, the rebuke and the censure revolve around, not the taking itself, for that has certainly occurred. That is: "Rather, have they taken gods from the earth, they alone, despite their lowliness and inanimateness, who raise the dead?" No indeed. What they have taken as gods is far removed from that. Although they did not say this explicitly, yet in that they claimed divinity for them, it is as if they claimed for them the power to raise the dead, since that is necessarily one of the distinctive features of divinity. The restrictive sense in the fronting of the pronoun, and what was pointed to of alerting to the complete incompatibility of their state with raising the dead, which necessitates greater denial, is like the fronting of the prepositional phrase in His saying: ﴿Is there doubt about God?﴾ [Ibrahim: 10], to alert to the complete incompatibility of His affair with being subject to doubt. It is also possible to make this one of the consequences of their false claim, for divinity necessitates independence in originating and restoring. So when they claimed divinity for the idols, it is as if they claimed for them independence in raising the dead, just as they were made, by this, claimants of the very fact of raising. This is what Mawla Abu al-Su'ud said.

Some said: The fronting of the pronoun is for piety (taqwa), and what al-Zamakhshari went to, of it conveying the sense of restriction, he followed in this. In al-Kashf, what drives toward preferring it over piety is that it is a reinforcement (tarshih) of what he presented earlier, that divinity is not valid without the capacity to raise the dead, and there is no basis for permitting that it be a separating pronoun (fasl). End.

It was also permitted that the sentence ﴿they raise the dead﴾ be a new independent sentence, with an interrogative denial implied before it, to explain the reason for denying the taking. Perhaps the one who permits this does not grant that the meaning of the hamza in the disjunctive am must be denial of the occurrence; it may be denial of what has occurred. The explanation of yunshiruna as yab'athuna (they resurrect) is the well-known one and the view of the majority. Qutrub said it means yakhluqun (they create).

Page 23

Al-Hasan and Mujahid read (yanshurun) with a fatha on the ya', taking it as from nashara, and it and anshara have the same meaning. Nashara may also come intransitive, as in the saying: Allah anshara the dead (anshara Allahu al-mawta), so they were raised (fa-nushiru).

[Page 23]

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted﴾ are a refutation of the plurality of gods. The pronoun in (فِيهِما, "in them") refers to the heavens and the earth, and what is meant by them is the whole universe, both the upper and the lower. What is meant by "being in them" is a complete capacity to exercise control and governance, not dwelling and settling within them, as al-Kalanbawi (al-Fadil al-Kalanbawi) imagined. On this reading the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is linked to a verb of place. Al-Tibi (al-Tibi) said that it is an adverbial phrase attached to "gods," in the manner of the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And He is the One who is God in the heavens and God on the earth﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 84], and His words, glory be to Him: ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and in the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 3]. The attachment of the adverbial phrase to what is mentioned here is taken in terms of its implying the meaning of creating and being the one who affects.

You know that the apparent meaning is what was mentioned first, and that (illa, "except") here indicates the otherness of what follows from what precedes it. So it has the same function as (ghayr, "other than"). In meaning, it is an attribute with the function of ghayr, so that it is used to describe a noun and what follows it, which is an indefinite plural or something similar. The first case is illustrated by this verse, and more than one of the exegetes has stated explicitly that the meaning is: "Had there been in them gods other than Allah." Al-Khafaji (al-Khafaji) took this as an indication that illa here is a noun with the meaning of an attribute of what precedes it, and that its grammatical case appears in what follows it, because it has the form of a particle, as in the relative (al) in the active participle, for example.

Al-Fadil al-Shamni (al-Shamni) denied that it has the function of ghayr in being a noun, citing what is in the marginal notes of al-Allama al-Thani (al-'Allama al-Thani) at the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Neither old nor young﴾ [al-Baqarah: 68], that no one holds that illa is a noun except the one that has the function of ghayr. Then he mentioned that what is meant by its having the function of ghayr is that it has the same role as ghayr in making what follows it different from what precedes it, whether in essence or in attribute. In the commentary on al-Kafiyah by al-Radi (al-Radi), the basic function of ghayr is that it is an attribute that conveys the difference of its governed noun from the noun it qualifies, either in essence, as in "I passed by a man other than Zayd," or in attribute, as in "I entered by a way other than the one by which I left." The basic function of illa, which is the mother of the exception particles, is that what follows it differs from what precedes it, whether by negation or affirmation. When what follows illa and what follows ghayr came together in the meaning of difference, illa was treated as ghayr in the attribute, so that what follows illa became different from what precedes it, in essence or attribute, without regard to whether that difference is by negation or affirmation. And ghayr was treated as illa in exception, so that what follows it became different from what precedes it, by negation or affirmation, without that difference being in essence or attribute. However, treating ghayr as illa is more common than treating illa as ghayr, because ghayr is a noun, and inflection is more frequent in nouns than in particles. For this reason, ghayr occurs in all the positions where illa occurs. End of quotation.

You know that what is evident is that illa, when it conveys the meaning of ghayr, is a noun. As for its remaining a particle while being alone, or together with what follows it, with the two being treated as one thing that is an attribute of what precedes it, this is clearly open to question. And it is even more evident that it is so when it stands alone. Perhaps al-Khafaji would not have said what he said unless he was aware of someone who held that it is a noun. It is possible that what compelled him to hold that view was what counters the view that it remains a particle. By my life, he was right to find the mark when al-Allama said what he said. The words of al-Radi are not explicit in either of the two matters, as is not hidden from the fair-minded.

According to the majority, it cannot be an exception in terms of Arabic grammar, because (ālihah, "gods") is an indefinite plural in affirmative speech, and the view of most scholars, as stated in al-Talwih, is that it has no comprehensiveness (istighraq, the sense of including all of its class). Therefore, what follows it does not enter into it, so that it would need to be excluded by illa. They hold that the excepted item must be included in the item from which it is excepted in a connected exception, and they do not settle for the mere permissibility of inclusion, as al-Mubarrad (al-Mubarrad) and some of the usulis held. So, according to them, it is not permissible to say "A group of men came except Zayd," whether the exception is connected or disconnected. This is based on the principle that an disconnected exception must be certain that the excepted item does not enter the item from which it is excepted, and that certainty is absent here.

Whoever permitted exception in this kind of construction, such as al-Mubarrad, treated the nominative case on the noun of majesty (the divine name) as a substitution (badal). This was objected to on the grounds that there is no preceding negation. It was answered that law (lau, "if") is a conditional particle, and it is like negation. It is also reported from him that he answered that it indicates impossibility, and the impossibility of a thing is its non-existence. It was claimed that the "emptying" construction (tafrigh, where the governed element is left without an object) is permissible after it, and that an expression such as "Had there been with us except Zayd, we would have perished" would be the most eloquent speech. Sibawayh (Sibawayh) disagreed on this, for he said: "If you say 'had there been with us' the example, you would have made a mistake."

It was objected: they do not say "Had a man come to me, I would have honored him," nor "Had someone come to me, I would have honored him." If law were like a negation, that would be permissible, just as "There are no dwellings in it" and "No one came to me" are permissible. Al-Damamini (al-Damamini) pursued this by saying: al-Mubarrad could respond that we are agreed to treat (abā, "refused") as having the function of explicit negation, and we allowed emptying in it. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿But most of the people refused except disbelief﴾ [al-Isra': 89], and He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And Allah refuses except to perfect His light﴾ [al-Tawbah: 32]. Yet "a dwelling refused to come" and "no one refused to go" are not permissible. So whatever your answer is to this, that is our answer.

Al-Radi said: al-Mubarrad permitted the nominative case in the verse as a substitution, because in law there is the meaning of negation. This is like al-Zajjaj permitting substitution for "the people of Yunus" in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed?﴾ [Yunus: 98], treating the restriction as having the function of negation. The better view is not to treat those two cases as the same in permitting substitution and emptying together, since there is no established basis for that. End of quotation.

Al-Maliki (al-Maliki), in his commentary on al-Tashil, mentioned that the words of al-Mubarrad in al-Muqtadab are like the words of Sibawayh, and that emptying and substitution after law are not permissible. Likewise, exception is not valid in terms of meaning. In al-Kashf, it is stated that substitution and exception in the verse are both impossible in meaning, because in that case it would not convey what the speech was intended to convey, namely the negation of plurality. It would also lead to the gods being such that the true God does not count among them, which leads to corruption. So the negation of corruption indicates that He is among them, and He is far from corruption. Moreover, according to what Ibn Hisham (Ibn Hisham) held, the attribute is emphatic and can be omitted, like its counterpart in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿A single blast﴾ [al-Haqqah: 13]. So if it were said, "Had there been in them gods, they would have been corrupted," it would be correct and would convey the intended meaning.

Al-Shalubini (al-Shalubini) and Ibn al-Sa'igh (Ibn al-Sa'igh) said: the meaning is not correct unless illa carries the meaning of ghayr, in which case it would be a substitution and an equivalent. This was refuted by saying that the meaning then becomes: "Had there been in them a number of gods as a substitute and replacement for Him, exalted is His state, they would have been corrupted." This implies, by its concept, that if there were in them two gods, one of whom is He, the Mighty and Majestic, they would not have been corrupted, and that is false.

It was answered that the meaning of the verse in that case does not require this implied concept, because its meaning is: "Had there been in them a number of gods other than Him, or with Him, glory be to Him, as a substitute for Him alone, the Mighty and Majestic, they would have been corrupted." This is something beyond dispute, so understand it.

What the majority holds is that the intended meaning is difference. Corruption (fasad) means ruin and dissolution, or the non-coming-into-being of the universe. The verse, as more than one scholar has said, points to a rational proof of the negation of plurality of gods. It is an istithna'i syllogism (a conditional syllogism that negates the consequent), in which the contradictory of the consequent is stated in order to produce the contradictory of the antecedent. It is as if it were said: "If the god were plural in the world, it would be corrupted. But it is not corrupted. Therefore, the god is not plural." In this there is a use of law different from its well-known use.

Al-Sayyid al-Sanad (al-Sayyid al-Sanad) said: law may be used in the context of inference, so that from it is understood the connection between the existence of the conditional (al-hali) and the existence of the antecedent, together with the absence of the consequent. Thus it is known from it that the antecedent is absent. This usage, though rare, does exist in the language. One says, "Had Zayd been in the town, he would have come to us," so that it is known from it that he is not there. And among such usages is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted.﴾

Al-Allama al-Thani said: the people of logic have made law a particle of implication, indicating that the consequent follows from the condition, without intending to assert the absence of either of them. For this reason, it is valid for them to exclude the same antecedent. So they use it to indicate that knowledge of the absence of the consequent is a cause of knowledge of the absence of the antecedent, since the absence of the implying element is necessarily known from the absence of what is implied, without attention to the question of what the actual cause of the absence of the consequent is in the external world. They use it in syllogisms to acquire sciences and affirmations. There is no doubt that knowledge of the absence of the implying element does not necessitate knowledge of the absence of the implied element. Rather, the matter is the reverse. When we examine it, we find that its use according to the rule of the language is more common. However, it may be used according to their rule, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Had there been in them﴾ and so on, since it is evident that the purpose of it is to affirm the negation of the plurality of gods, not to explain the cause of the absence of corruption. End of quotation.

There is a question here that can be answered with care. You should know that some grammarians hold a view similar to this statement. Al-Shalubini and Ibn 'Usfur (Ibn 'Usfur) said: law is merely for linking two occurrences in the past, without indicating the impossibility of the first or the second, just as inna (indeed) is merely for linking in the future. The apparent view is that the specific character of the past tense is not significant here.

Some of them claimed that law here is for the absence of the second because of the absence of the first, as is commonly held about it, and the inference is complete. But what is wrong with this is not hidden from one who examines it carefully.

Then al-Allama said in the commentary on al-'Aqa'id: the argument is persuasive, and the implication is customary, as is appropriate for rhetorical discourse. The custom is that conflict and dominance occur when there are multiple rulers. Otherwise, if corruption is meant as an actual fact, that is, these two going out of this observed order, then mere plurality does not necessitate it, since it is possible for them to agree on this order. If it is meant that corruption is possible, then there is no evidence for its absence. Indeed, the texts testify to the folding up of the heavens and the removal of this order, so it is possible without doubt.

Likewise, if what is meant by their corruption is their non-coming-into-being, in the sense that if two creators were assumed, there could be mutual obstruction in their actions, so that neither would be a creator, and no created thing would then exist, the implication is not certain. This is because the possibility of obstruction only necessitates the absence of plurality of creators, and that does not necessitate the non-existence of the created thing. Furthermore, the denial of the implication is raised if what is meant is non-coming-into-being in fact, and the denial of the absence of the implied element is raised if what is meant is possibility. End of quotation.

Therefore the verse is not a proof, whether corruption (*fasad*) is understood as departing from the order (*nizam*) or as non-existence of the cosmos (*'adam al-takawwun*). In this there is a criticism of what he indicated in *Sharh al-Maqasid* (*Commentary on the Maqasid*), namely that it is a proof for the second meaning. After establishing the *burhan al-tamanu'* (the proof from mutual obstruction, *tamanu'* meaning mutual interference or exclusion), he said: "This proof is called the proof of mutual obstruction, and the reference to it is in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, both would have been ruined﴾." If what is meant is non-existence of the cosmos, its formulation is that one says: If the gods were plural, the heavens and the earth would not have come into being, because their coming into being is either by the combined power of both, or by each of them separately, or by one of them alone. All of these are invalid. As for the first, it is because the attribute of a god is perfect power. As for the last two, it is because of the mutual arbitrariness and preponderance without a preponderant cause that was mentioned earlier. If what is meant by corruption is departure from the order in which they are, its formulation is that one says: If the gods were plural, there would be conflict and mutual domination between them, and the distinction of each one's action from the other's, by the necessity of custom, would not occur. Thus this harmonious unity among the parts of the world, by which the whole becomes like a single person, would not be achieved, and the order in which the species survive and effects follow in sequence would be disrupted. End of quote.

This criticism is that the plurality of gods does not necessarily entail actual mutual obstruction, through the way in which each of them wills the existence of the world independently without the power of the other having any role in it. Rather, what is entailed is the possibility of that obstruction, and possibility does not necessitate occurrence. So it is permissible that it does not occur, but rather they agree on bringing it into being jointly, or one of them delegates to the other.

Al-Mawla al-Khayali also discussed it in other respects. Then he said: The verification (*tahqiq*) in this matter is that if the noble verse is taken to negate plurality of creators absolutely, then it is a persuasive argument (*hujja iqna'iyya*). But the apparent meaning of the verse is the negation of a plurality of creators acting upon the heavens and the earth, since what is meant by existence in them is not mere presence within them, but acting upon and being affected by them. So the truth is that the necessary connection (*mula-zama*) is definitive, since mutual interference is invalid. Their causal influence is either by way of joint action or by division of labour. Then, if one of them is not a creator, the whole or part would cease to exist, since he is either a partial cause or a complete cause. Thus the world would be corrupted, i.e., this perceptible existence would not come to be, either entirely or in part.

It is also possible to formulate the necessary connection so that it is definitive absolutely, which is to say: If the god were plural, the world would not even be possible, let alone existent. For otherwise mutual obstruction between them would be possible, and that entails an impossibility, because the possibility of mutual obstruction is a necessary consequence of the combination of two things: plurality and the possibility of any of the things. So when plurality is assumed, it follows that nothing among things is possible, so that mutual obstruction, which entails an impossibility, is not possible. End of quote.

Al-Fadil al-Kalanbawi raised five objections against the first formulation, some weak and some strong. Then he said: The truth is that the second formulation of his, for the definitive nature of the necessary connection, is correct, but not the first. Al-Allama al-Dawani has a discussion on this matter, and the aforementioned Fadil mentioned what is for and against it, through refutation and affirmation.

[Page 26]

Then he mentioned that *tamanu'* has two meanings according to them. One is that the will of one of two capable agents is for the existence of the object of power, and the other is for its non-existence. This is the meaning of *tamanu'* in the proof known as the proof of mutual obstruction. The second is that each of them wills its bringing into being independently, without the power of the other having any role in it. This is the *tamanu'* that they considered in the impossibility of one object of power between two capable agents. Their statement, "If the god were plural, nothing of the possibles would exist, because it entails one of two impossibilities: either the occurrence of one object of power between two capable agents, or preponderance without a preponderant cause," is based on this. The summary of the proof for it is that if there existed two gods, both capable of perfection, mutual obstruction would be possible between them. The consequent is invalid, for if they obstructed each other, and each willed bringing into being independently, it would necessarily follow either that no created thing comes to be at all, or that it comes to be by the power of each of them, or by the power of one of them. All of these are invalid. Its coming to be by the combined power of both with this will entails their incapacity, since the will of each would fail to be fulfilled by his will. Thus they would not be two capable gods of perfection, yet they were assumed to be so. From here it becomes clear that, on the assumption of plurality, if a created thing existed, it would necessitate the possibility of one of two impossibilities: either the possibility of joint action, or the possibility of preponderance without a preponderant cause. Both are impossible. On this basis, with the meaning of corruption taken as non-existence, it has been said that the necessary connection in the verse is definitive. So it is a persuasive proof in one respect and a definitive proof in another. The first is more suited to the common people, and the second to the elite.

Mosleh al-Din al-Lari said, after a lengthy discussion: "It has been said, and I say: I will formulate the argument derived from the noble verse in a way more suitable than what others have stated, which is that the god deserving worship must necessarily be a necessary existent (*wajib al-wujud*, one whose existence is necessary). According to the people of verification, the existence of a necessary existent is identical with its essence. For if it were other than its essence, it would be contingent, because in its being existent it would depend on something else, namely existence. So if it were plural, it would follow that it is not existence, and then things would not be existent, because the existence of things consists in their connection to existence. Thus the corruption of the heavens and the earth becomes clear in its apparent sense, not in the sense of non-existence, because that is an evident artificiality." End of quote.

You know that the meaning of non-existence is more apparent for this argument. Furthermore, this type of argument is one that the philosophers (*hukama'*) adopted, indeed most of their proofs that indicate the unity of God, which is the most sublime of divine subjects. Indeed, all of them depend on the principle that the true reality of the Exalted is pure existence, subsisting by its own essence, expressed as essential necessity and intensified existence. Whatever is characterized by necessity or existence is, in its own essence, possible, and its existence, like its necessity, is derived from another, so it is not necessary. Among the most famous of these proofs: if we assume two necessary existents, they would share in necessity of existence and differ by some matter, otherwise they would not be two. What makes them distinct is either the whole reality or a part of it. The first is impossible, because if the distinction were by the whole reality, the necessity of existence shared between them would be outside the reality of each, or outside the reality of one of them. This is impossible, because it has been established that the necessity of existence is the very reality of the necessary existent in itself. The second is also impossible, because each of them would be composed of what is shared and what distinguishes it, and every composite is in need, so it would not be necessary, because it is possible. So one of the two necessary existents, or both, would be possible. This is a contradiction.

It was objected that the meaning of their statement "necessity of existence is the very reality of the necessary existent" is that the attribute of necessity of existence appears from that very reality, not that the reality is identical with this attribute. So there is no incompatibility between two necessary existents sharing necessity of existence and being distinguished by the whole reality. It was answered that what is meant is identity. The meaning of their statement that necessity of existence is identical with the reality of the necessary existent is that its essence, by its very essence, is the instance of this judgment and the source of its abstraction, without the addition of anything else, and without considering any aspect other than the essence of the Exalted, whatever aspect it may be, real, relational, or negative. The same applies to the analogy of all His attributes, according to those among the verifiers who hold their identity with His essence. The clarification of this according to their school is: just as you may conceive the continuous, for example, as the continuous itself, like the formal part of a body insofar as it is body, and you may conceive something that is the continuous as matter, so also you may conceive the necessary existent as necessary existent, and you may conceive something that is the necessary existent, as the instance and correspondence of the judgment concerning it. In the first case, the correspondent of the subject is the reality of the subject and its essence alone. In the second, it is that together with another aspect, which is an attribute subsisting in the subject, real or abstracted. Every necessary existent that is not the very essence of necessary existence, but has a reality which is characterized by being necessary of existence, is in need, in its characterization, of the occurrence of this matter and of a maker who makes it such that this matter is abstracted from it. So in itself it is possible to exist, and by this it becomes necessary of existence. Thus it is not necessary of existence in its essence. So He is the very essence of the necessary existent in its essence. The same should be applied to the rest of His real perfect attributes, such as knowledge, power, and others.

It was also objected that why should it not be possible that the distinguishing feature is an accidental matter, not a constitutive one, so that composition would not follow. It was answered that this would entail that individuation (*ta'ayyun*) is accidental, and that contradicts what has been established by proof. Ibn Kammuna has in this matter a doubt, which is said to be extremely difficult to resolve and hard to solve, to the point that some have named it "the pride of the devils" because of how he raised it. It is this: why should it not be possible that there are two simple essences, unknown in their quiddity, differing in their whole quiddity, each of which is necessary in itself, and the concept of necessary existence is abstracted from both and predicated of them accidentally? The Imam, may Allah have mercy on him, has seen something like it in his *Mulakhkhas* (*Summary*). Perhaps, if you comprehend the truth of what we have mentioned, its solution will be easy for you. If you want clarification, listen to what has been said about it: The concept of necessary existence is either abstracted from the very essence of each of them without considering any extraneous aspect whatsoever, or with the consideration of that aspect. Both alternatives are impossible. As for the second, it has been established that whatever whose essence is not merely the aspect of abstracting necessity is possible in its essence. As for the first, the instance of predicating one concept, whose correspondent is essentially identical, regardless of any aspect whatsoever, cannot be the instance of different, mutually distinct realities that share nothing in their essence at all. Perhaps every sound-natured person judges that different things, insofar as they are different without a comprehensive aspect, cannot be the instance of a single judgment and be described by it. Yes, that is permissible if those things are similar in respect of being similar, even in a negative matter. Rather, we say: if we consider the very concept of the verbal noun (*masdari*) of existence, known in some way by immediate knowledge, it leads us, by reflection and inquiry, to the conclusion that its reality and what is abstracted from it is a matter subsisting by itself, which is the Necessary, the True Existent, the Absolute Existence, which is not mixed with generality, particularity, or plurality. For whatever has this existence cannot, supposedly, have with another thing also having this existence any complete difference or otherness at all. So there would not be two, but there would be one essence and one existence, as the author of *al-Talwihat* (Suhrawardi) hinted in his words: "Consider existence, than which there is nothing more complete. Whenever you suppose it a second time, when you look, it is the same, for there is no distinction in the consideration of something." So the necessary existence of His essence, the Exalted, which is His very self, indicates His oneness, Majestic and Exalted is He. End of quote. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 22 (part 3 of 3):

It is not hidden from you that most of the proofs for this grand matter can be derived from the noble verse, and the corruption (fasad) is then understood as non-existence of coming-into-being (ʿadam al-takwin). So turn to this derivation, even if it requires some strained interpretation (takalluf). Beware of being content with taking it as a persuasive argument (hujjah iqnaʿiyyah), as many have done, for this grand matter is far too exalted to be satisfied with persuasions built on what is well known and customary.

The master of al-Kashshaf (may his resting place be fragrant) has a statement that shows the signs of verification (tahqiq) in this station, which we shall mention, God willing, as he chose it in his interpretation of the words of the Most High: ﴿Had there been with Him other gods, each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have overcome others﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91]. Then do not imagine that the verse does not entail the negation of two or one, for the negation of gods differing from the specific individual One necessarily entails that each one of them differs from him in person, and this is more eloquent than the negation of one differing from the specific individual in person. Moreover, the Most High's words ﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth﴾ are set in antithesis to it. The existence of the implication (mulazamah) suffices for the negation of one and two as well.

The context of the noble verse has been objected to on the ground that the apparent purpose is that it was brought to nullify the worship of idols, referred to by the Most High's words ﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth, who raise the dead?﴾, since the idols are mentioned after it. Yet it only nullifies the plurality of the creating God, the capable, the governing, the one possessing complete divinity, and He is not plural in the view of the polytheists. (And if you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely say: God) [Luqman: 25; al-Zumar: 38], and they say of their gods: ﴿We only worship them so that they bring us nearer to God in closeness﴾ [al-Zumar: 3]. What they say is not nullified by the verse, and what the verse nullifies they did not say. Hence it has been said that the meaning of the verse is: If there were in the heavens and the earth gods, as the idol-worshippers say, corruption of the world would follow, because those gods they claim are inanimate objects unable to govern the world, so the world would be corrupted. It has been answered that the Most High's words ﴿Or have they taken...﴾ etc. are directed at rebuking the worship of idols, even if they do not possess complete divinity, because worship is only fitting for one who has that, and after the rebuke against that, He, glorified be He, indicated that whoever possesses what has been mentioned is only one. Moreover, the explanation of the name God (Allah) is the One who necessarily exists in Himself, the Living, the Knowing, the Willing, the Powerful, the Creator, the Governor; so whenever they apply it to something, they are bound to ascribe to it these attributes, whether they wish or not. So the verse serves to nullify what their claim entails in the most complete manner. ﴿Glory be to God, Lord of the Throne, above what they describe﴾, that is: Exalt Him with the most perfect exaltation above having any gods besides Him, as they allege. The fa' here marks the consequence of what follows upon what precedes, namely the establishment of unity. Mentioning the Majesty (al-Jalalah) in the place of a pronoun indicates the cause of the ruling, for divinity is the basis of all attributes of perfection, among which is His exaltation above partners, to cultivate awe and bring about reverence. The description "Lord of the Throne" serves to emphasize the exaltation, along with what this carries of cultivating awe. The apparent meaning is that the intended sense is the literal command to exalt Him. It has also been said that the intended sense is astonishment at those who worship those base objects of worship and count them as partners alongside the existence of the great Worshipped One, the Creator of the greatest things; and the discourse on this is also like a conclusion to what preceded it of the proof.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 23:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He cannot be questioned about what He does﴾ may be the answer to an implied question arising from the affirmation of His unity in divinity, which entails His unity in creation and disposal, and from the disbelievers' attributing to Him, glorified is He, what is not befitting. It is as if it were said: if God, exalted is He, is the god who creates and disposes, then why did He create those disbelievers and not turn them away from what they say? So He answered with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿He cannot be questioned﴾, and so on. The summary is that no one is entitled to object to Him in anything of His acts, for He is absolutely wise and does not do what would invite objection. ﴿But they will be questioned﴾ about what they do and will be called to account. This ruling concerning Him, exalted is He, is general over all His acts, and it includes the creation of the disbelievers and their existence as they are. The way of resolving the question arising from what preceded, based on what this general answer indicates, is that He, exalted is He, created the disbelievers, indeed all the accountable, according to what He knew of them in their own selves, because creation is preceded by will, will is preceded by knowledge, and knowledge follows the known. So it relates to them as they are in their unmade fixed reality, which their eternal disposition requires. Some of this is hinted at by the verses of al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him:

You created the servants according to what You knew, so in knowledge the youth and the old man proceed.

Then, after creating them according to that, He charged them, to bring out the secret of what knowledge, which follows the known, had preceded concerning obedience and refusal, which are in their eternal disposition. He sent the messengers as bearers of good news and warners, so that the motives would stir, that whoever perishes would perish after clear evidence, and whoever lives would live after clear evidence, and that people would have no argument against God, exalted is He. Thus no objection is directed at God for creating the unbeliever; rather, the objection is directed at the unbeliever for his disbelief, since it is among the consequences of his disposition in its unmade fixed reality. Some of this is hinted at by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves﴾ [al-Nahl: 118], and by His saying, upon whom be prayer and peace: "Whoever finds good, let him praise God, and whoever finds other than that, let him blame none but himself." Although this is among the matters about which there is much debate and contention, it is what many of the verifiers and eminent gnostics have approved.

Some have said: this is a resumptive statement explaining that He, because of the overwhelming greatness of His majesty and the might of His dominating sovereignty, is such that none of His creatures may dispute with Him or ask Him about what He does of His acts. This is a clear statement that He has no partner in divinity. The pronoun in "they" refers to the servants, meaning: the servants will be questioned about what they do, down to the smallest particle, because they are owned by Him, exalted is He, and made to serve Him. In this there is a warning to the disbelievers. The apparent meaning is that the negation is general over all times, meaning He, glorified is He, is not questioned about what He does at any time. al-Zajjaj restricted this to the Day of Resurrection, but the first is preferable, although the matter of warning is more evident on this view. The verse has been cited as evidence that God's acts are not causally explained by purposes and ends, so one does not say "He did this for that," for if they were so explained, the servant would have the right to ask, "Why did He do it?" The Ash'aris held this view and have rational proofs for it too, and they interpreted what apparently indicates causation either metaphorically or by making the particle there denote consequence. The position of the Maturidis, as in the Sharh al-Maqasid, and of the Mu'tazilah, is that they are causally explained by that, and the Hanbalis held this too, as al-Wafi and others said.

The scholar Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr al-Dimashqi al-Hanbali, known as Ibn al-Qayyim, said in his book Shifa' al-'Alil: God, exalted and glorified is He, is wise, and does nothing in vain or without meaning, and without a benefit and wisdom which is the purpose intended by the act; rather His acts proceed from a far-reaching wisdom, and for its sake He acted. The speech of God and of His Messenger ﷺ indicates this in countless places, and it is impossible to enumerate them all, so we will mention some types of them. He cited twenty-two types in some ten folios, then said: Were we to mention what those like us perceive of God's wisdom in His creation and command, it would exceed ten thousand instances. Then he said: Is not the nullification of the wisdoms, the fitting features, for which rulings were legislated, precisely the nullification of the Sharia altogether? And is it possible for any jurist on earth to speak of jurisprudence while believing in the invalidity of wisdom, fitness and causation, and that the Lawgiver's purpose in the rulings is the benefit of the servants? Then he said: The truth which is not permissible other than this is that He, glorified is He, acts by His will, power and volition, and acts in what He does by causes, wisdoms and praiseworthy ends; the world has been endowed with forces and natures by which creation and command subsist. This is the view of the majority of the People of Islam and most schools of the speculative theologians, and it is the view of the jurists without exception. End of quotation.

The apparent meaning is that Ibn al-Qayyim and his like among the People of the Sunnah, who hold that God's acts are causally explained, do not hold, as the Ash'aris do, that what particularizes one of two opposites in its occurrence is purely the attachment of will in the well-known sense. The verifying Mu'tazilah, such as Abu al-Hasan, al-Nizam, al-Jahiz, al-'Allaf, Abu al-Qasim al-Balkhi and others, say: the knowledge that a benefit follows from bringing the beneficial thing into being is what particularizes its occurrence, and they call this knowledge the motive, which is will in their view. It was objected to them that the Necessary Existent, exalted is He, is necessitating in the attachment of His knowledge to all known things; so if the particularizing, necessitating factor for occurrence were the knowledge of benefit, that particularizer would be necessary to His essence, and His act would then be necessary by an external, compulsory cause for the agent, which certainly contradicts choice in the stricter sense. So the Necessary Existent would not be chooser in this sense, but would revert to the view of the philosophers regarding a choice compatible with necessitation. This objection does not apply to those who hold that the particularizer is the attachment of the eternal will, because that attachment is not necessary to the essence of the Necessary Existent, exalted is He, even though it is eternal and perpetual, since its attachment to the opposite instead of the actual opposite is possible. Yes, there are objections to them that are hard to escape, which are mentioned in the books of theology. A parallel to what was mentioned has been objected to the Hanafis, for they hold causation and make knowledge of the arrangement of benefits a cause for the attachment of knowledge to occurrence. So they cannot consistently say that the Necessary Existent is chooser in the stricter sense, because the essence necessitates knowledge, knowledge necessitates the attachment of will, and the attachment of will necessitates the act. There is no escape except to say that the necessitation of knowledge of benefit and advantage for the attachment of will is denied by them; rather it is a preponderant inclination not reaching the level of necessity. What is said is that if the preponderance does not reach the level of necessity, the occurrence of the preponderant at one time and its non-occurrence at another time with that same preponderance is permissible. If the restriction of one of the two times to occurrence required the addition of something to that preponderance, the preponderance would not be a preponderance; otherwise there would be preponderance without a preponderant, or rather preponderance of the less preponderant in its non-occurrence at the other time, since occurrence was preponderant by that preponderance. This is repelled in two ways. However, it applies only to the complete cause in relation to its effect, not to the chooser agent in relation to his act. For if what is meant is the necessity of preponderance without a preponderant, as is necessary in the complete cause, then the absence of such necessity is evident; and if what is meant is preponderance without a preponderant, then the nullity of this consequence in the chooser agent is denied, otherwise what is the difference between the necessitating agent and the chooser agent? Second: a preponderant in relation to one time may not be a preponderant in relation to another time, but rather contrary to the benefit, so there is no necessity of preferring one of two equals, or the less preponderant, at another time; rather it is the necessity of preferring the preponderant at every time.
