And He, exalted is He, knows all the benefits appropriate to the times, so His will attaches to the occurrence of every possible thing at the time in which it arranges the benefits appropriate to that time upon its non-occurrence, and so there is no difficulty. This is what is relied upon, for an objector could say on the first view that preferring the less preponderant is impossible with respect to the Necessary, Wise Being, though it may be permissible with respect to other chooser agents.

It occurs in the words of the philosophers that God's acts are not causally explained by purposes and ends; their meaning, as one of them said, is the denial of causation of His act by something other than His essence, because He, majestic is His state, is perfect in agency and is not dependent on anything else for it. This does not entail the denial of end and purpose of His act absolutely. Hence they could correctly say that His knowledge of the order of good, which is the very essence of His essence, is a final cause and a purpose in bringing into being. By "necessitation" in their definition of the final cause, what they mean is that which necessitates the agency of the agent, in the absolute sense of non-separation, but they were lenient in this, relying on the understanding of those trained in the sciences. They explicitly stated that He, exalted is He, has no purpose in possible things and no intention toward their benefits, because every agent who acts for a purpose other than his essence is needy of that purpose and perfected by it, and the perfecter must be higher; so the agent's purpose must be what is above him, even if this is by conjecture, and He has no purpose in what is below Him. The occurrence and existence of possible things from Him, exalted is He, in a state of perfection and a degree of firm ordering is nothing but because His essence is such that things proceed from Him only in the most complete manner and the highest possible benefits. So the Necessary Existent, according to them, from His intellection of His essence, which is the source of every good, there follows the attainment of possible things in the most complete manner and the most upright order. The consequences are accidental ends, if by end is meant what necessitates the agency of the agent, and essential ends, if by it is meant what follows from the act by an essential, not accidental, consequence, such as the existence of the principles of evil and others in the material natures. Then, just as He, exalted is He, is an end in the sense indicated, He is also an end in the sense that all things seek Him, yearn for Him, by nature and by will, because He is pure good and the true beloved, majestic is His majesty and general His bounty.

The theosophist philosophers have ruled that the light of love permeates all existents in their differing levels, and were it not so the sphere would not turn nor the darkness be illumined. Glorified is He, a dominating God, and He is the First and the Last. The full discussion of this matter according to the approach of the theologians and philosophers is sought in its proper place.

Al-Hasan read: "lā yusal" and "yusalūna," by transferring the vowel of the hamza to the sin and dropping it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 24:

The words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿Or have they taken gods besides Him?﴾ are an *idrab* (a turning away from one line of argument to another, here meaning a shift in the discourse) and a transition from demonstrating the falsehood that what they have taken are real gods, by showing that they lack the attributes of divinity, among which is the power to raise the dead (*al-insharu*), and by establishing the decisive proof that the plurality of gods is absolutely impossible and that Allah alone is singular in divinity. This leads to the falsehood of their taking those gods, which are wholly devoid of those attributes, as partners of Allah, exalted is His majesty. It also includes rebuking them by compelling them to produce proof for their false claim, and establishing that all the heavenly Scriptures speak to the truth of monotheism (*tawhid*) and the falsehood of associating partners with Allah. It has also been permitted that this is a transition to demonstrate the falsehood of gods in general, after demonstrating the falsehood of earthly gods. The interrogative *hamza* serves to deny the aforementioned taking and to find it abhorrent and grave. The phrase *min* (from/besides) is connected to *ittakhadhu*, and the meaning is: "Rather, they have taken, transgressing beyond Him, exalted is He, despite the manifestation of His magnificent affairs that necessitate His singularity in divinity, gods, while it is manifest that they are entirely void of the properties of divinity."

﴿Say﴾ to them, by way of rebuke and silencing them (*ilqam al-hajar*, literally "stopping the mouth with a stone"), ﴿Bring your proof﴾ for what you claim, whether from the side of clear reason or sound transmission, for it is not valid to assert such a thing without evidence for it. The phrasing of the proof as belonging to them (*burhanakum*) implies that they have a proof, which is a form of mockery of them. The words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿This is the reminder of those with me and the reminder of those before me﴾ are an illumination of His proof and an indication that it is among what all the divine Scriptures have spoken of, and an added incitement for them to produce proof, in order to show the extent of their incapacity. That is: this revelation that has come concerning monotheism, which contains the decisive proof, is the reminder of my community and its admonition, and the reminder of the earlier nations. I have established it, so establish your proof as well.

The word *dhikr* is repeated, and the relative clause is not simply conjoined to the previous relative clause, which would have required it to apply to both, because the particular being a reminder of those with him and being a reminder of those before him is by way of its being, in reality, identical with the revelation that contains this.

It has also been said: the intended meaning of *dhikr* is the Book. That is: this is a Book that was sent down to my community, and this is a Book that was sent down to the communities of the prophets, peace be upon them, from the three Books and the scrolls. So consult them and see whether any one of them contains anything other than the command to monotheism and the prohibition of associating partners. This is a rebuke to them that includes the opposite of their claim.

It is also read with *tanwin* (nunation) on the first and second *dhikr*, and what follows it is placed in the accusative position as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*), because it is a verbal noun (*masdar*), and its governing (*'amal*) is the original form, as in the words of Allah, ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger, an orphan﴾ [Al-Balad: 14–15].

Yahya ibn Ya'mur and Talhah read with *tanwin* and with the *kasra* on the *mim* of *min*. On this reading, *min* is a preposition and *ma'* is in the genitive governed by it. *Ma'* is a noun indicating companionship and togetherness, and here it is used as an adverb of place like *qabl* and *ba'd*, so it is permissible to introduce *min* before it, just as it is permissible to introduce it before the other two. However, its being introduced before it is rare. Abu Hayyan states that in this case it has the meaning of *'inda* (at, with). It has also been said that *min* governs its described noun, meaning: an admonition from a Book with me and an admonition from a Book before me. Abu Hatim considered this reading weak because it involves *min* entering on *ma'*, and he did not see a justification for it. It is reported from Talhah that he read ﴿This is a reminder with me and a reminder before me﴾ with *tanwin* on *dhikr* and omission of *man*. A group read ﴿This is the reminder of those with me﴾ with the genitive construction, and ﴿and a reminder from those before me﴾ with *tanwin* and *kasra* on the *mim*.

The words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿But most of them do not know the truth﴾ are an *idrab* from Him, the Exalted, which is not part of the dictated speech, and a transition from the command to rebuke them by examining the proof, to explaining that argument against them is of no benefit, because they lack the ability to distinguish between truth and falsehood. ﴿So they﴾, for this reason, ﴿are turning away﴾, persisting in aversion from monotheism and following the Messenger, not refraining from their error and misguidance, even though the clear signs and proofs are repeated for them. Or it means: they are turning away from what has been presented to them of rational and transmitted proofs.

[p. 32]

Al-Hasan, Humayd, and Ibn Muhaysin read *al-haqqu* with *raf'* (nominative), on the basis that it is the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*), meaning: "He is the truth." The sentence is parenthetical, placed between the cause and the effect, as an emphasis on the connection between them. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the accusative form also be used for emphasis, as you would say, "This is the servant of Allah, the truth, not the falsehood." The apparent reading is that it is accusative as the direct object (*maf'ul bihi*) of *ya'lamun*, and the knowing here is in the sense of recognition (*ma'rifa*).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 25:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no deity except Me, so worship Me﴾ is a resumptive clause (istiʾnaf) confirming what preceded of the verses of tawhid (divine oneness). It may be said that in it there is generalization after specification, if what is meant by "those before me" (dhikr man qablī) is the three books. Since ﴿messenger﴾ is general in meaning, there is a wording and a meaning: he was made singular in regard to the wording in "We revealed to him," then made plural in regard to the meaning in ﴿so worship Me﴾. The construction is not "fa'budni" (so worship Me, singular). This is based on the view that "fa'budūni" (so worship Me, plural) is included in what is revealed, while it is also permitted that it is not included in the command addressed to him (ﷺ) and to his community. Most of the seven readers (al-Sabʿa) read "yūḥī" in the third-person form, in the passive voice. In either case, the imperfect form is used to narrate a past state, to bring the image of the revelation vividly before the mind.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 26:

﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son."﴾ This is a report of the offensive claim of a group of the polytheists, in order to expose its falsehood and to state that He, glory be to Him, is exalted above it, following the statement that He, exalted and high, is exalted above partners in every sense. They were the clan of Khuza'ah, who said, "The angels are the daughters of God, glory be to Him." Al-Wahidi reported that Quraysh, some of the Arabs, Juhayna, Banu Salamah, Khuza'ah, and Banu Malih said this.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah, who said: "The Jews said, 'God, mighty and majestic, intermarried with the jinn, and the angels were the offspring of that union.'" Then this verse was revealed. The well-known view is the first one. The verse censures everyone who attributes this to Him, such as the Christians who say, "Jesus is the son of God," and the Jews who say, "Uzayr is the son of God." Exalted is God far above what they say, a great exaltation.

The mention of the title "the Most Merciful," which indicates that everything other than Him is His creation and subject to His lordship, serves to reveal the full extent of the ugliness of their false statement. ﴿Glory be to Him﴾: that is, you declare Him free of this in His essence, in the manner befitting Him. Here, subhan (سُبْحانَ) is a verbal noun (masdar, the basic noun derived from the verb) of sabbaha (سَبَّحَ), meaning "after I glorify Him with His glorification." It is also said that it is used as an 'alam (a fixed term, used as a proper name) for glorification, and it is spoken by the tongues of the servants. Or the meaning is: "Glorify Him with His glorification."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾ is an idrab (a shift from one statement to another, cancelling what precedes it) and a nullification of what they said. It is as if it were said: "The angels are not as they claim; rather, they are servants, in that they are created by Him, exalted is He, and so they are His possession, and a son cannot be owned." In His saying, exalted is He: ﴿honored﴾, that is, brought near to Him, there is an indication of the source of their error. Ikrimah read *mukarramun* (مُكَرَّمُونَ) with the shadda (doubled letter).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 27:

﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾, meaning: they do not say anything until He Himself says it or commands them to say it, as is the custom of well-mannered servants. This contains an alert to the perfection of their obedience and submission to His command, azza wa jall, and to their good manners toward Him, exalted is He. The underlying sense is that their speech does not precede His speech, so the act of "preceding" is attributed to them while being related to Him, as a way of making their preceding of His speech be treated as though it were their preceding of Him, mighty and majestic is He, in order to intensify their exoneration from that and to alert to the extreme repugnance of the preceding that is aimed at those who say what He has not said. The speech has been made the locus of the preceding and its instrument by which one precedes, and the lam has been substituted for the idafah to the pronoun, according to the view of the Kufans, for specification and to avoid repetition.

It has been read as (لا يَسْبُقُونَهُ) with a damma on the ba' (لا يَسْبُقُونَهُ), taking it from the pattern of mughalaba (contest), as one says: "sabaqani fa-sabaqtuhu" and "asbuquhu", and in this case the ayn of the present tense must take a damma unless its ayn or lam is a ya'. In it there is further intensification of the repugnance of preceding, and an indication that whoever's speech precedes His speech has undertaken to contend with Him, exalted is He, in preceding, and an increased exoneration from what has been negated of them, by clarifying that this, in their view, is in the position of victory after contest. So how could it be supposed that it proceeds from them?

﴿And they act by His command﴾.

This is an explanation of their following Him, exalted is He, in actions, after the explanation of their following Him, glorified is He, in words. It is as if it were said: they speak by His command and they act by His command, not by other than His command at all, by acting of their own accord. So the restriction derived from fronting the prepositional phrase applies to what is other than His command, exalted is He, not to the command of others, glorified is He.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 28:**

﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*) that serves as a causal explanation (*ta'lil*) of what precedes it and as a preparatory introduction (*tamhid*) to what follows. It is as if it were said: they do not undertake any statement or action without His command, exalted is He, because nothing hidden is concealed from Him of what they have put forward or left behind. Thus they remain ever watchful over their conditions, since they know this. ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾, meaning, for one for whom Allah, exalted is He, has approved that intercession be made.

This is as Ibn Jarir, al-Mundhir, al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ba'th*, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas: "Whoever says, 'There is no god but Allah'." Their intercession is seeking forgiveness (*istighfar*). As is established in the *Sahih*, it occurs both in this world and in the Hereafter. The Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school) have no proof in this verse for their view that intercession does not benefit the people of major sins, for it indicates no more than that they do not intercede for one for whom intercession is not approved. Moreover, the absence of intercession by the angels does not prove the absence of intercession by others. ﴿And they, along with that﴾ ﴿are fearful of His awe﴾, meaning, because of fear of His punishment, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿apprehensive﴾, expecting [it] from a weak sign, being ever on guard and watchful, not feeling secure from the plotting of Allah, exalted is He. Thus *min* is causal (*ta'liliyyah*), and the statement contains an omitted noun (*mudaf mahdhuf*).

It may also be intended that the phrase "of His awe" refers to this same meaning, in which case there is no need for such an assumption.

It has been said: it is possible that the meaning is that they fear Allah, exalted is He, and along with that they are wary lest their fear fall short. In this case *min* is connected to *mushfiqun* (apprehensive). There is a difference between *khashyah* (awe) and *ishfaq* (apprehension): the former is fear mingled with veneration and reverence, and for this reason it is restricted to the scholars in His words: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir: 28]. The latter is fear together with concern, and it is construed with *min* just as fear is, and it may also be construed with *'ala* when the sense of tenderness and compassion is intended.

Some have claimed that *khashyah* here is a metonymy (*majaz*) for its cause, and that what is meant by *ishfaq* is intense fear, i.e., they are greatly fearful because of His majesty, exalted is He. The truth is that there is no necessity to resort to figurative usage. It is also permitted that the meaning is: they are fearful because of the fear of His punishment, exalted is He, with *min* connected to what follows it. The annexation of *khashyah* to the omitted noun is an annexation of an attribute to the thing it qualifies, i.e., they fear the punishment that inspires fear. The burden in this is evident and needless.

Moreover, this apprehension is a description of them in this world and in the next, as the nominal sentence indicates. Many reports indicating the intensity of their fear have been transmitted. Among them is what Ibn Abi Hatim related from Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said on the night I was taken on the Night Journey: 'I passed by Jibril, peace be upon him, and he was among the High Assembly, prostrate like a worn-out mat out of fear of Allah, exalted is He.'"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 29:

﴿And whoever of them says﴾, that is, of the angels, peace be upon them. It was also said: of the creatures. The first view is the one the context requires, since the discussion concerns the angels, peace be upon them, and their being far removed from what was attributed to them. The meaning is: whoever of them says, by way of supposition, ﴿Indeed I am a god besides Him﴾, that is, going beyond Him, exalted is He. ﴿That one﴾, that is, the one whom we supposed to have said what was mentioned, is a supposition that is impossible. ﴿We shall recompense him with Hell﴾, like all other criminals, and the noble attributes and pleasing deeds that preceded will not avail him. It is related from al-Dahhak and Qatada that the supposition is not to be considered, and they said: the verse refers specifically to Iblis, may the curse of God be upon him, for he called people to worship himself and established disbelief. What we have mentioned is what is relied upon. It contains an indication of the strength of His dominion, the might of His majesty, and the impossibility that the angels should be in a condition where there could be imagined of them what those disbelievers imagined, which is not hidden.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Maqri read (﴿nujzihi﴾) with a dammah on the nun, intending *nujzi'uhu* with a hamzah, from *ajza'ani* (it sufficed me, it was enough for me), and then he lightened the hamzah so that it turned into a yaʾ.

﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾ is an infinitive of resemblance (*maṣdar tashbihi*), emphasising the content of what precedes it. That is: like that dreadful recompense, We recompense those who place things in other than their proper places and transgress their limits. The restriction (*qasr*) derived from the placing of the object first is considered relative to deficiency, not to excess, that is, to recompense of a lesser degree than that.

(Page 34)

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 30 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Have those who disbelieve not seen﴾: this is a rebuke for them, for their failure to reflect on the cosmic signs that point to the immensity of His power and His control, and to the fact that all else besides Him is subdued under His dominion. (Reflecting in this way would lead them to benefit from these signs and to know that whoever is like this should not turn away from worshipping Him to worship a stone or the like, which neither harms nor benefits.) The hamza is for denunciation, and the waw is for conjunction with something implied.

Ibn Kathir, Hamid and Ibn Muhaysin read it without the waw. "Seeing" here is intellectual, meaning: "Have they not reflected and known".

﴿that the heavens and the earth were﴾: the pronoun refers to the heavens and the earth. By "the heavens" is meant their category, and that is why the pronoun is in the dual and not the plural. A similar usage is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease﴾ [Fatir: 41], and likewise the verse of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur:

"Indeed, death and calamities, both of them, watch my dwelling from beyond the sanctuaries."

The predicate is given in the singular, namely His saying ﴿ratqan﴾ ("joined"), and is not made dual, because it is a verbal noun (masdar). The predicate being singular is either because it is interpreted as a derived noun, or for the sake of emphasis, or by supposing an omitted genitive, meaning "two things joined". Ratq originally means joining and sticking together, whether by creation or by human making. From it comes the term ratqa', a woman whose sexual organ is closed and joined.

Al-Hasan, Zayd ibn Ali, Abu Haywa and Isa read ﴿ratqan﴾ with a fatha on the ta', and this is the name of the thing that is joined, like naqd and naqd (both meaning the thing that is broken). By analogy, it should have been dual here to agree with the noun. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is in the sense of an omitted qualifier, meaning "they were a joined thing" (shay'an ratqan). The word shay' is a collective noun covering the few and the many, so it is correct to predicate it of the dual as of the plural. It is made good by the fact that in the state of being joined there is no plurality in it.

Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: in this type of construction, most often the form with the vowel on the first radical is a noun in the sense of the passive participle, and the form with the quiescent second radical is a verbal noun. Both may be verbal nouns. The better reading here is that both are so, and then there is no need for what al-Zamakhshari said about the justification for the predicate. The ratq, according to what is reported from Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, means the state of non-existence, since in it there are no distinct essences. So the heavens and the earth are as one single, connected, uniform thing. The fatq, and its original meaning is separation, in His saying ﴿then We parted them﴾ ([fataqnahuma]), means bringing into existence, so that distinction occurs and some realities are separated from others by it. So it is like His saying: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 14; Yusuf: 101; Ibrahim: 10; Fatir: 1; al-Zumar: 46; al-Shura: 11], on the basis that fatr means splitting. Its apparent meaning is the denial of distinction among non-existent things. What Mawlana al-Kurani established in Jala' al-Fuhum, and defended as far as he could, is that the possible non-existent thing is distinct in reality, because it is conceived, and a thing cannot be conceived except by being distinguished from other things. Otherwise it would not be preferable to conceive of it rather than something else. Also, some non-existent things may be willed and others not, and without distinction between them that would not be understood, since intending to bring into existence something not specified is impossible. For what is not specified in itself is not distinguished in the intention from anything else. It may be said on this view that it is enough for that will that the heavens and the earth were not distinguished in the state of non-existence, when looking at the observed external world. In any case, the meaning of the verse is: "Did they not know that the heavens and the earth were non-existent, and We brought them into existence?" Their knowledge of this means their ability to know it with minimal reflection, because the two are possible things. The possible thing, considered in itself alone, is non-existent, and its being characterized by existence can only come from the Necessary Existent.

Ibn Sina said in the eighth treatise of the Ilahiyyat of al-Shifa': All things other than the Necessary Existent do not deserve existence. Rather, in themselves, and with their relation to the Necessary severed, they deserve non-existence. It is not conceivable that the existence of the heavens and the earth, with their necessary possibility, should be without a cause. As for what Demokritos held, that the existence of the world came about by chance, because its principles are small bodies that cannot be divided because of their hardness, scattered in an infinite void, of similar natures but different shapes, always in motion, so it happened that a number of them came together and gathered in a particular configuration, and from them this world was formed, this is a kind of nonsense. Abnadiklas agreed with him, as it is said, but the first held that the generation of animals and plants is not by chance, while this one held that the generation of the elemental bodies is also by chance. Yet what happens by chance, if it has a collective form suitable for survival and reproduction, survives, and what happens by chance and is not like this does not survive. This nonsense is far from this man, for they mention that he was one of the leaders of the Greeks, lived in the time of Dawud, peace be upon him, received knowledge from him, frequented Luqman the Wise, and acquired wisdom from him. Then, the existence of these two from a cause is itself originated. Rather, the sensible world and other than it is originated with temporal origination, by the consensus (ijma') of the Muslims. What is imagined from some expressions of some Sufis, that it is originated in essence but eternal in time, is interpreted away from its apparent meaning, for they are too exalted to say such a thing, since it is disbelief.

The philosophers on this question hold three opinions. A group of the early ones, who are the pillars of Miletus and Samia, held that the existing things of the world, its principles, simple things and composites, are originated. A group of the Attic school and the Stoics held that the principles, namely the intellect, the soul, the separate things and the simple things, but not the intermediate things or the composites, are eternal. For their principles are above time and duration, so temporal origination is not realized in them, unlike the composites, which are below time and duration. They denied that motions are everlasting. The doctrine of Aristotle and those who followed him among his students is that the world is eternal and that the circular motions are everlasting. This is on the basis of what is known of him, otherwise it is mentioned in the Asfar that the recognized masters of wisdom among the sect are eight: three of the Miletians, Thales, Anaxagoras and Agathodaimon, and five of the Greeks: Empedocles, Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato and Aristotle. All of them hold what the prophets, peace be upon them, and their followers said, about the origination of the world with all its substances and accidents, its spheres and its angels, its simple and composite things. Words supporting this have been reported from each of them. Likewise, things have been reported from other philosophers than these, and he extended discussion on this point. Were it not for fear of tedium, I would have quoted that, and perhaps I will quote some of it in its most suitable place, if God the Exalted wills.

It came from Ibn Abbas, in the narration of Ikrimah, al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn Jubayr, that the heavens and the earth were one thing joined together, then Allah the Exalted separated them, raised the heaven to where it is, and left the earth. Ka'b said: Allah the Exalted created the heavens and the earth joined together, then created a wind which passed between them and parted them. From al-Hasan: Allah the Exalted created the earth at the place of Bayt al-Maqdis, like the shape of a grinding stone, with smoke clinging to it. Then He raised the smoke and created the heavens from it, held the stone in its place, and spread the earth out from it. That is His saying: ﴿they were joined, then We parted them﴾. So He made seven heavens. Likewise the earth was closed as one layer, then He parted it and made it seven earths. The meaning of knowledge according to these views is also the ability to know it, but that is not through reasoning. Rather it is through inquiry from the scholars of the People of the Book who used to mix with them and accept their statements. It was also said that it is through studying the heavenly scriptures, and the Qur'an enters among them, even if they did not accept it, because it is a miracle in itself. In that there is a subtle point that is not hidden.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya reported through the chain of Abdullah ibn Dinar, from Ibn Umar, that a man came to him and asked him about the verse. He said: "Go to that shaykh and ask him, then come and tell me." He was Ibn Abbas. So the man went to him and asked him. He said: "Yes. The heavens were joined, not sending rain, and the earth was joined, not growing plants. When Allah the Exalted made the earth habitable, He parted this one with rain and parted that one with plants." The man returned to Ibn Umar and informed him. Ibn Umar said: "Now I know that Ibn Abbas has been given knowledge of the Qur'an that is true. Ibn Abbas spoke the truth; it was like this." A group, including al-Hakim, reported something with this meaning from him, and he authenticated it, and most of the exegetes adopted this view.

Ibn Atiyya said: It is a good view that combines the lesson, the proof and the enumeration of blessings, and it suits what is mentioned after it. Joining and parting are both metaphorical on it, as they are in the first view. By the heavens is meant the direction of height, or the lowest heaven, and the plural is according to the horizons, or it is in the manner of "a garment of mores". It was said that it is on its apparent meaning, and each of the heavens has a role in the rain. By "seeing" is also meant knowledge, and the knowledge of the disbelievers of this is clear.

It is permitted that the seeing be visual, but taking it as intellectual is better. Among the remote views is what is reported from some scholars of Islam, that ratq is the joining of the two belts of the first and second motions, which entails the ruin of buildings and the seasons of the year, and fatq is their separation, which requires the possibility of construction and the distinction of seasons. Indeed, it hardly holds according to the Islamic foundations established by the righteous predecessors, as is not hidden.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾ is coordinated with ﴿that the heavens﴾ and so on. There is no need to force its coordination with "We parted". The making here means creating, transitive to one object. "From" is for beginning, and "water" is the well-known thing. That is, We created from water every animal, meaning every thing characterized by real life. This is reported from al-Kalbi, and a group. It is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah created every creature from water﴾ [al-Nur: 45]. The reason water is the origin and material of the animal, and why it is singled out for this, is that it is the greatest of its materials, and the animal's extreme need for it and benefit from it is itself. It is necessary to specify the general term, because the angels, peace be upon them, and likewise the jinn, are living beings, yet they were not created from water, nor are they in need of it, according to the correct view.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 30 (part 2 of 2):

Qatadah said: The meaning is, "We created every living thing from water," so that plants are included, and "life" is taken to mean growth or something similar. Perhaps whoever claims that plants have sensation and awareness has kept "life" on its apparent meaning. Qutrub and a group said: "Water" means the drop of semen (nutfah). There must be a restriction excluding the angels, peace be upon them, and also the jinn, indeed excluding more than that, namely the animals created without semen, such as most of the terrestrial insects.

It is possible that the verb "ja'ala" (made) carries the sense of "ṣayyara" (made into), which takes two objects, and here they are "kulla" (every) and "min al-ma'" (of water). The second object is placed first for emphasis on it, and "min" is for connection (ittiṣaliyyah), as was said regarding the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "I am not from dadd, and dadd is not from me." The meaning is: We made every living thing connected to water, that is, mixed with it and not separated from it, and what is meant is that it does not live without it.

Abu al-Baqa allowed, on the first reading, that the prepositional phrase be in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to "kulla." Al-Tibi made "min" here explanatory (bayaniyyah) of the abstraction type (tajridiyyah), so that the living water is abstracted from itself as an exaggeration, as if it were the water itself.

Humayd read "ḥayyan" (living) in the accusative, taking it as an adjective of "kulla" or as a second object of "ja'ala," and the adverbial phrase is related to what follows it, "lā yaḥyā" (does not live). The word "shay'" (thing) is restricted to animals, because they are the ones described as living, though he allowed generalizing it to plants.

You know that some people say that everything in the heavens and the earth is alive with a life suited to it. These are the ones who held that the glorification of things, indicated by the saying of God Most High: ﴿And there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾ (17:44), is verbal and not merely a state. If this is said, then the thing must also be restricted if "every thing" is not made living from water. I have not found anyone among us who disagrees with this. Yes, it is reported from Thales al-Malati, who was the first to philosophize in Malatya, that the origin of all existing things is water, where he said: "Water receives every form, and from it all substances were originated, of heaven and earth." End of quotation.

Page 37

It can be interpreted according to a Sufi path, by saying that he meant by water the expansive existence (al-wujud al-inbisati), which in Sufi terminology is expressed as the Breath of the Merciful (al-nafs al-rahmani). In that case, if the reference in the verse is taken to be to that according to them, it is not far-fetched. ﴿Will they not then believe?﴾ is a denunciation of their not believing in God Most High alone, despite the appearance of the signs that necessarily require it. The "fa" (then) is for conjunction with an implied preceding clause that the denunciation calls for, meaning: "Do they know this, and then not believe?"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 31:

﴿And We placed in the earth firm mountains﴾, i.e., immovable mountains, the plural of rasiyah, from rasa al-shay' when it became fixed and firmly established. The application of the feminine plural to non-rational things in place of the masculine plural is well established and there is no doubt about its soundness. ﴿Lest it should shake with them﴾, i.e., out of dislike that it should move and quiver with them; or, "lest it should shake with them," where the lam is omitted, and it is not for fear of ambiguity. This is the view of the Kufans, but the first is preferable. In al-Insaf it is said that a better interpretation than these two is that it is like your saying, "I prepared this piece of wood lest the wall should lean," according to what Sibawayh said, that its meaning is: that I support the wall with it if it leans. The mention of shaking is given precedence out of concern for the matter, and because it is the cause of the support, and the support is the cause of preparing the wood; so the cause of a cause is treated as the cause. Thus, in what we are discussing, the underlying sense is: "And We placed in the earth firm mountains, that We might fix it when it shakes with them," so the shaking becomes the cause, just as leaning was made the cause in the example, and the sentence becomes: "And We placed in the earth firm mountains, lest it shake with them, so We fix it." Then "so We fix it" is omitted, as "We fix it" is understood, for brevity, and this is closer to reality than what was mentioned first, for its implication would be that the earth does not shake with its inhabitants because God dislikes that, and it is impossible that what He dislikes should occur, while observation is otherwise: how many earthquakes have shaken the earth until it nearly overturned. According to what we have mentioned, the meaning is that God fixes the earth with the mountains when it shakes; this does not preclude the occurrence of shaking, but it is a shaking followed by fixing, and likewise what occurs of earthquakes is only a flash, then God fixes it. End.

In al-Kashf: their saying "out of dislike that it should shake" is an explanation of the meaning, not that there is any ellipsis at all; for this reason the view of the Kufans deserves rejection. As for what is in al-Insaf, that the better reading is that it is of the type of "I prepared the wood lest the wall should lean," as was established, it returns to what we have mentioned and contradicts it not. As for his rejection on the basis of contradicting observed reality, it is not to the point, for the shaking of the earth does not occur at all, and these earthquakes are not part of it in any way. End. This is a weighty statement, as is not hidden. Some of the contemporary disbelievers have criticised what this noble verse indicates, saying that the earth, by its natural tendency toward the center, is at rest, so that shaking cannot be conceived in it even if there were no mountains in it. It was answered: first, setting aside what is in the claim of its natural pursuit of the center and its rest according to them, of disputation and argument, it is possible that God Almighty created the earth on the day He created it bare of mountains, with its parts differing in weight and lightness by a complete difference, or the said difference befell it; and despite this, He, glorified be He, did not give to its whole such weight that the weight of what God knew would move upon it of heavy bodies is not apparent in comparison to it. So it would have two distinct centers: the center of volume and the center of weight. According to them, it naturally seeks that its center of weight coincide with the center of the world; and although that requires its rest, it also requires that it move with the movement of those bodies. So God, majestic is His majesty, created the mountains in it so that it would acquire such weight that the weight of what moves is not apparent with it, and so it does not move with its movement at all. That the ratio of the height of the greatest mountains to their diameter is like the ratio of the width of a barleycorn to seven cubits is useful only regarding the sensible sphere; but as for it implying that the total of the mountains does not have considerable weight compared to the weight of the earth, that does not follow. Moreover, the creation of the mountains is not for this wisdom alone, but for countless wisdoms and benefits that cannot be enumerated; so it cannot be said that He could dispense with the mountains
[page 38]
by creating it such that no effect of the heavy moving bodies upon it is apparent in relation to its weight. Second, that by its nature it requires that it be submerged in water, such that the lines extending from its center, which coincides with the center of the world, to the convex surface of the water are equal from all sides; so the emergence of this portion that is submerged is forced. It is possible that the mountains have a part in the forcing, through the confinement of vapours in them, and the earth becoming, by reason of that, like a waterskin in water that has been blown up, so that some of it appears above the surface of the water; and were it not for that, the forcing would not be strong enough to be unopposed by what is above the earth of animals and other things, and that necessitates the shaking which may lead it to submersion. So reflect. What pertains to this topic has passed for you, so remember.

﴿And We placed in it﴾, i.e., in the earth. The repetition of the verb is due to the difference of the two things placed, together with what it contains of indicating the perfection of the favour; or it is in the mountains, according to what Ibn Jarir and al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas, and it is supported by the fact that they are the ones requiring that God place in them ﴿broad paths﴾. Fijaj is the plural of fajj. Al-Raghib said: it is a cleft flanked by two mountains. Al-Zajjaj said: every opening between two mountains is a fajj. Some said: it is a general term for the wide, whether it is a path between two mountains or not, which is why one says "a fajj wound." The apparent view is that "fijaj" is in the accusative as an object of ja'ala, and His saying, glorified be He: ﴿paths﴾ is an apposition to it; it thereby implicitly indicates that He created them and widened them for travellers, together with what it contains of emphasis, because apposition is like repetition; and on the intention of repeating the governing verb, the thing replaced is not in the status of being dropped absolutely. In al-Kashshaf it says: it is a circumstantial accusative from "subulan"; had it come later it would have been an adjective, as in His saying, exalted be He, in the surah of Nuh: ﴿that you may follow therefrom paths, broad roads﴾. It was not brought in that way but was placed first, so that it became a circumstantial, to indicate that in the state of its being made paths they were wide; and had it come as an adjective it would not have indicated that. Some made it necessary that it be the object and that "subulan" be an apposition; likewise he made necessary, in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿that you may follow﴾ etc., that "subulan" be the object and "fijaj" an apposition, saying: fajj is a noun, not an adjective, since it denotes a specific entity, which is the wide road; and a noun can be described but cannot itself be a description; this is why it occurs as a described noun in His saying: ﴿from every deep fajj﴾ [al-Hajj: 27]. Taking it as stripped of its denotation of a specific entity has no indication for it.

It was objected that we do not grant that its meaning is that; rather its meaning is the general wide, and restricting it to the road is incidental, and that does not prevent its being an adjective. Even if granted, the intention of whoever said it is an adjective is that it has the sense of an adjective in relation to "sabil," because "sabil" is the road, and it is the wide road; so when it is placed before it, its mention afterwards would be idle if it were not a circumstantial. The apparent sense of the words of al-Fadil al-Yamani in al-Matla' is that "subulan" is an explicative apposition, which is permissible with indefinite nouns, where he said: it is an explanation of "fijaj" and a clarification that those fijaj are passable; a fajj may be non-passable. It is placed first here and last in the verse of the surah of Nuh because that verse comes for favour in a general manner, whereas this one is for reflection and urging deep contemplation, and that requires detail; hence it is mentioned after His saying: "they were a closed-together mass" etc. End. You know that the more evident is to make "fijaj" accusative here as the object of ja'ala, and the reason for the difference between the two verses is not hidden, so reflect. ﴿That they may be guided﴾ to reasoning about the oneness [of God], the perfection of power and wisdom. It was also said: to their interests and needs. It was objected to the foregoing that His saying afterwards, ﴿and they turn away from its signs﴾, suffices in place of that, and that the indication of creating the paths for what has been mentioned is not apparent. End. There is what there is in this. It was permitted that the intended meaning be what is more general than guidance to reasoning and guidance to interests:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 32:

﴿And We made the sky a well-guarded ceiling﴾ from decay and change over the length of time, as was narrated from Qatadah. The meaning is that it was made preserved from that long span of time. It does not contradict this that it will be folded up on the Day of Resurrection, "like the folding of the scroll for the books." Adopting the view that it changes and decays was the position of all the Muslims and most of the eminent philosophers, as Sadr al-Din al-Shirazi (d. 1050 AH) demonstrated in his al-Asfar, and we shall mention it, God willing, in its proper place. It was also said: "[guarded] from falling." Al-Farra' said: "[guarded] from eavesdropping by means of meteors." It was objected to this view that mentioning the ceiling would then be superfluous, not fitting eloquence, let alone inimitability. As for its justification, it was said that the meaning is that its preservation is not like the preservation of the houses of the earth, since thieves may climb over their roofs, unlike this one. It was also said that it serves to indicate its being preserved from those beneath it, and it indicates its being preserved from them in the most complete way. In a hadith from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked at the sky and said: 'The sky is an elevated ceiling and a restrained wave, it flows as an arrow flows, preserved from the devils.'" If it is authentic, it is not a explicit text on the meaning of the verse, as Abu Hayyan claimed. It was also said: [guarded] from shirk and sins. What was raised against the previous view also applies to this one, as is not hidden.

﴿And they, from its signs﴾ which indicate Our oneness, Our knowledge, Our wisdom, Our power and Our will, some of which are apparent like the sun and some known through investigation into it, ﴿are turning away﴾: heedless of them, not turning the arrows of thought upon them. Mujahid and Hamid read (ʿan āyatihā), in the singular. It was explained that since each of the things in it is sufficient to indicate the existence of the Creator and His attributes of perfection, the sign was made singular for this reason. On this reading, "turning away" is taken to mean denying that it is a clear sign pointing to the Creator, as his statement in the Kashshaf indicates: that is, they are alert to what reaches them from the sky of benefits, while they are turning away from it being a clear sign of the Creator. But this is not necessary.

[Page 40]

The Almighty's saying: ﴿It is He who created the night and the day, the sun and the moon﴾, which are two of His signs. For this reason the verb was not made an explanation (bayan) of some of those signs, from which they turn away. This is an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person), which requires emphasis on the import of the speech. Since the creation of night and day is not of the same kind as the creation of animals and mountains (rawasi), the word denoting it was not made uniform. Rather, ja'l (making) is used there and khalq (creating) is used here. This was also said, though, as you see, it is not so.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿kull (each)﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), and its tanwin is a substitute for the omitted genitive noun. The author of al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari) took it as singular and indefinite, meaning each one of the sun and the moon. It has been objected that Ibn Hisham stated explicitly in al-Mughni that when the omitted noun is singular and indefinite, the pronoun referring back to kull must be singular, just as if it had been stated explicitly. Here the pronoun is plural, so it must be taken as a definite plural, meaning all of them. When it is taken this way, Ibn Hisham holds that the returning pronoun must be plural, even though, had the noun been mentioned, it would not have been obligatory. The obligation of singularity in the first case and of plurality in the second serves to draw attention to the state of the omitted word.

Abu Hayyan permits both singular and plural without restriction, so it is permissible here to take the genitive noun as singular and indefinite while the following pronoun is plural, as al-Zamakhshari did, and he is one whose high standing in Arabic you know. The Almighty's saying: ﴿in an orbit (fi falak)﴾ is its predicate. The reason for its singular form is clear, since the omitted indefinite noun denotes distributive generality (al-'umum al-badali), not comprehensive generality (al-'umum al-shumuli). Whoever takes it as a definite plural says: the intended meaning is the universal class, which is understood as plural, like the expression "He clothed them in a garment," on the basis that the collective is not in one single orbit. The Almighty's saying: ﴿swimming (yasbahun)﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal). It is also permissible for it to be the predicate, with ﴿in an orbit﴾ being a circumstantial clause or attached to it. The clause "each" etc. is a circumstantial clause for the sun and the moon, and the link is the pronoun without a waw, on the basis that this is permissible without offense. Whoever considers it offensive makes it a new sentence, and their pronoun is plural, considering multiplicity by the multiplicity of risings (matali'). Thus, for both of them, considering their conventional concept, there are external individuals in this sense, not in reality. For this reason it is said "shumus" and "aqmar" (plural forms of sun and moon), although outside there is only one sun and one moon. What made this appropriate here is the agreement of the verse-endings (fawasil). Some claimed that the two moons were given precedence because of their nobility over the rest of the stars, so the pronoun was made plural for this reason. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the stars, even though they are not mentioned, because what is mentioned points to them.

[Page 41]

It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the sun, the moon, the night and the day. Against this: the night and the day cannot fittingly be described as swimming, even if this is metaphorical for moving. Choosing the pronoun for rational beings is either because they are rational in reality, as some Muslims held, like the philosophers, or because they are rational by claim and attribution, since swimming is attributed to them, and swimming is one of the works of rational beings. The falak (orbit) in origin is anything that revolves, and from it comes the whorl of the spindle (falkat al-mighzal). What is meant here, as reported from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi, may Allah be pleased with them, is the heaven. Most of the exegetes said: it is a restrained wave beneath the heaven in which the sun and the moon run. Al-Dahhak said: it is not a body, but rather the orbit of these stars. The well-known view is that reported from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi, and in it is the statement that the heaven is spherical. In "each in an orbit" there is a hidden allusion to this, since it is not impossible by reversal, and there are many proofs for it. That it is a canopy does not contradict this. In the speech of the philosophers the term falak has been used for the heaven, and they described it as a living, knowing body that moves by will with a purely circular motion, not subject to generation, corruption, growth, withering, rupture, or reunion, whose species is limited to its individual, and which is neither hot nor cold, neither moist nor dry, neither light nor heavy. Most of these attributes branch from the premise that there is no straight inclination in its nature. This has been refuted in the theological books, and they built on the impossibility of rupture and reunion that the star moves only by the motion of the orbit. When they saw different motions, they said there are multiple orbits. The well-known view is that the universal orbits are nine: seven for the seven wandering planets, one for the fixed stars, and another to move all of them with the daily motion. The truth is that there is no decisive proof for denying anything beyond that. Do you not see that the Shaykh al-Ra'is (Ibn Sina) did not become clear to him whether the fixed stars are in one sphere or in spheres folded one within another? And their saying that the motions of the fixed stars are similar, and that whenever they are so, they are fixed in one orbit, is not certain. As for the minor premise, that is because their motions, though similar to the senses, may not be so in reality. For if we suppose that one of them completes its revolution in thirty-six thousand years and another completes it in this time but with a deficit of a tenth or less, then the portion of this degree of difference that applies to a single degree is so small that our lifetimes cannot suffice to measure it. If that is possible, the certainty of similarity falls away. What further weakens this and strengthens the possibility is that later astronomers found a star moving faster than the fixed stars and slower than the planets, which they named Herschel, and none of the earlier ones in past ages had found it. As for the major premise, it is because it is possible that different things share many necessary properties, so each may have its own orbit, and those orbits may agree in their motion in direction, pole, zone, and center. Furthermore, this possibility is not specific to the orbit of the fixed stars, but exists in all orbits. So it is possible that among the orbits of the planets there are other orbits. As for what is said in refuting this, that the nearest approach of each star equals the farthest distance of all the stars placed beneath it, this is nothing, because between the farthest distance of the moon and the nearest approach of Mercury lies the thickness of the orbit of the moon's node (jawzahar). The verifiers among the astronomers mentioned that for the epicycle orbit of each of the upper planets there are three spheres, one enveloping another, and the body of the star is fixed in the innermost sphere. Thus the thickness of four of those epicycles, from each of the lower and the higher, equals the thickness of two spheres between the nearest approach of the higher and the farthest distance of the lower. They established for the lower planets five epicycles, so the thickness between the nearest approach of Venus and the farthest distance of Mercury is the thickness of eight spheres. However, they only believed that the nearest approach of the higher equals the farthest distance of the lower because they first believed that there is nothing between these orbits that could intervene, so they could not build this on it, otherwise circularity would follow. Rather, some other proof is necessary for it. Their saying that there is no excess in the heavenly bodies, while, as you see, it is refuted by what they said about the great thickness of the outermost sphere. It is also possible that beyond the ninth of the orbits there is something that only Allah the Exalted knows. Indeed, it is possible that

[Page 42]

this ninth orbit with what is in it of spheres is fixed within the thickness of another great sphere, and within the thickness of that sphere there are a thousand thousand spheres like these spheres. This is not unlikely, for the epicycle of Mars is greater than the model of the sun. When that is conceived, what harm is there in supposing something like it that is greater still? It is also possible, as has been said, that the universal orbits are eight, since it is not impossible that all the fixed stars are fixed in the convex surface of the model of Saturn, that is, in its completing sphere which contains it, provided that it moves with the slow motion, and the eighth orbit moves with the swift motion. It has even been said that it is possible for them to be seven, by supposing that the fixed stars and the circles of the zodiac are on the convex surface of the model of Saturn, and two souls, one of which is connected to the whole seven and moves them with one of the two motions, swift or slow, while the other is connected to the seventh orbit and moves it with the other motion. So there is also no decisive proof against the orbits being fewer than nine.

Then, the apparent meaning of the verse is that each of the sun and the moon runs within the thickness of its orbit, and there is no rational objection to this. The proof of the impossibility of rupture and reunion is that if the orbit were capable of that, it would be capable of straight motion, and that is impossible for it, and it is incomplete. Even on the supposition of its completeness, that holds only for the outermost sphere (al-muhaddad). It is possible that rupture occurs in the orbit through some of its parts by circular motion. So there is no obstacle to saying that the stars in general move in their orbits like the movement of fish in water, and this does not invalidate the science of astronomy, because their motions must be uniform around the centers of their orbits, that is, they do not accelerate or decelerate, do not stop, do not retrograde, and do not bend. As for al-Suhrawardi's statement in al-Mutarahat: if the orbits were capable of rupture, and it has been demonstrated that they are living beings, then when rupture occurs in them and their parts disperse, either it is not felt, in which case the ruptured part has no relation to the other part by a perceptual unity, and the orbit has no information about its parts, and the soul that is in the body is a power that unites those parts, so the soul has no connection with its body. Or it has been said that they are living, and if they are felt, then pain is inevitable upon the dispersal of parts, for that is a perception of what is incompatible, and every perception of what is incompatible is either pain or necessitates pain. If that is so, and the stars pierce them by their motion, they would be in perpetual torment. We shall demonstrate that perpetual matters whose occurrence is impossible cannot be conceived of them. It is not hidden that this is from rhetorical arguments (khitabiyyat), indeed from what is even lower than them.

Some claimed that it is among the strong proofs, though it has no proof, from among the weak proofs. The Imam (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) claimed that just as it indicates the motion of the star, it also indicates the rest of the orbit. The truth is that it is ambiguous regarding rest and does not clearly indicate it. As for the motion of the orbit and the rest of the whole orbit, some Muslims held this, and it is reported from the Shaykh al-Akbar, may Allah sanctify his secret. It is possible that the orbit is moving and the star moves within it, either opposite to the direction of its motion or in agreement with it, either with a motion equal in speed and slowness to the motion of the orbit or different from it. It is also possible that the star is fixed in the orbit and at rest in it, as is the view of most of the philosophers, or that it moves on its own axis, as is the view of their verifiers, while the whole orbit is in motion. This is what the philosophers made necessary, though it is not granted to them and no proof of theirs establishes it.

It is also possible that the star is in a body separate from the thickness of the orbit, resembling a ring whose diameter equals the diameter of the star, and it is that by which it moves, while the orbit remains at rest. It is also possible that within the thickness of the orbit there is a void in which the star revolves, with the orbit at rest or in motion. This does not involve a claim of rupture and reunion, but rather the claim of a void, which according to us and most of the philosophers is permissible, contrary to Aristotle and his followers. The proof of permissibility is stronger than a smooth rock. As for the claim that the orbit is simple, so its simplicity prevents it from having that within its thickness, this is nothing. What they mentioned as proof of simplicity, despite its weakness, applies only to the outermost sphere and not to the rest of the orbits. Moreover, if it is permissible for the orbit to be hollow despite its simplicity, then what has been mentioned is permissible along with it, and it will hardly be established for them

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 33 (part 2 of 2):

...the escape from that. It has come in some reports that all the stars are suspended by chains of light beneath the lowest heaven, in the hands of angels who draw them wherever God Almighty wills. But this hardly holds true, though God Almighty is powerful over all things. What most of the philosophers and the astronomers (al-Hay'iyyin, those who follow the science of hay'a, cosmology) hold is that the motion specific to a star, which belongs first and essentially to its own sphere (falak), proceeds from west to east. This is the motion along the order of the zodiac (ʿalā tawālī al-burūj), and it is called the second motion and the slow motion. It is evident in the planets, and in the moon it is most evident. In the fixed stars it is hidden, which is why the earlier authorities among them did not affirm it. The motion that is not specific to the star, namely the motion of its sphere, which is secondary and accidental, proceeds from east to west. It is called the first motion and the swift motion. It occurs through the motion of the muhaddad (the outermost sphere that delimits the rest), and by it occur night and day in all the inhabited quarter (al-maʿmūra). As for at a latitude of ninety degrees or thereabouts, the motion of the second kind is, in their view, such that the star has two motions differing in direction and speed. They illustrated this with the motion of a millstone (raḥā) in one direction, swiftly, and the motion of an ant upon it in the opposite direction, slowly.

Some of the early thinkers held that there is no motion in the celestial bodies from west to east. Rather, all their motions are from east to west, because this is more fitting for these bodies, since it involves less opposition. Also, the ultimate goal of motion belongs to the outermost body, and the ultimate goal of rest belongs to the earth. Therefore, what is nearer to the outermost body must be swifter than what is farther. Also, if some of them moved from east and some from west, the star would have to move with two motions differing in direction, and that is impossible. This is because motion in a direction requires that the moving thing be present in the direction to which it moves. So if one body moved at once in two directions, it would necessarily be present at once in two places, which is impossible. There is no difference in this between the two motions being natural, or forced, or one natural and the other forced.

This is not refuted by what is observed of the ant's motion on the millstone in one direction while the millstone moves in the opposite direction, because that is only an example, and an example does not undermine a demonstration. Also, certainty about such motions (the earthly ones) is permissible, but certainty about the celestial motions is impossible. As for what was adduced to show that the motion other than the swift motion is from west to east, it does not prove this, since it may be from east while it is thought to be from west. Its explanation is that two bodies moving in one direction in a circular motion, when one of them is faster than the other, will appear, when both move in that direction, to have the slower one lagging. Thus it is supposed that it moves in the opposite direction. This is because when they are in conjunction and then both move in the direction with their respective motions, if the swift one completes a full revolution while the slow one covers the arc of the stronger (that is, the difference), the slow one appears lagging behind the swift one in the direction opposite to the direction of their motion, by that arc. They said: one must go to this, because demonstration requires it, and none of the stellar operations (al-aʿmāl al-nujūmiyya, astrological practices) refutes it.

The Imam (al-Razi) in al-Mulakhkhaṣ presented what was mentioned in the argument for the impossibility of two motions differing in direction for one body as a problem for those who hold them. He then said: "Because of the strength of this argument, some of them affirmed the daily motion for the sphere of the earth and not for the sphere of the heavens, although that is false." He mentioned it in his Tafsir and called it a conclusive proof, and he held in it the view of this group, that all motions are from east to west, but they differ in speed and slowness. But what they have mentioned is open to scrutiny. The first two objections are persuasive (iqnāʿiyya), and the third, though demonstrative, is so evidently faulty that it cannot be hidden. As for their claim that none of the stellar operations refutes it, this is false. The specific motion of the star, I mean the motion of the moon from east to west for example, through a full revolution except an arc, cannot be on the poles of the zodiac, because then it would be found parallel to the equator of the day (muʿaddal al-nahār), nor on the poles of the equator, for then it would never depart from being parallel to it, and it would not be ordered in arcs in which it falls behind each day by a great circle cutting the equator, like the circle of the zodiac, by the arcs in which the sun falls behind. Rather, it would be ordered as a small circle parallel to it. Except if the star is on the equator, to the extent that it completes a revolution by its motion, for then the ordered path would be the equator itself. But this does not exist in the stars we know. Nor can it be on poles other than its own poles, for then its course would be seen above the earth on a circle cutting the parallel circles, and the meridian circle would not divide the time from its rising to its setting into two halves, because the poles of its inclined sphere would not always be on the meridian circle, so the arcs of its visible orbits would not be divided into two halves. Also, if the matter were as they imagined, the sun would reach its apogee and perigee and its mean distances, and even the north and south, and therefore all the shadows appropriate to the sun being at these positions would have to occur on a single day, yet the actual state is otherwise.

The saying of one who says it is possible that the motion of the sun in the circle of the zodiac is toward the west is manifestly false. For if that were so, the single day with its night would fall short of the revolution of the equator by the amount of the arc the sun traversed, approximately. But the reality is otherwise, since it exceeds the revolution of the equator by that amount. Also, the sun's passage through the zodiac would be seen to be against the order (ʿalā khilāf al-tawālī), but it is not so, since it lags behind the part of the equator that is in the middle with it, each day, toward the east. So the motions of the spheres encompassing the earth are two: one in the order of succession (al-tawālī), and another in the opposite direction. As for the motions of the epicycles (tadāwīr), they are outside these two categories, because the motions of their upper parts are necessarily opposed to the motions of their lower parts, since they do not encompass the earth. If the motion of the upper part is from west to east, the motion of the lower part is the reverse, as with the mutaḥayyira (Mercury). If the motion of the upper part is from east to west, the motion of the lower part is the reverse, as with the moon.

This is the summary of what we say on this point: what the philosophers have mentioned concerning the universal and particular spheres, and the manner of their motions and positions, is a matter possible in itself, and there is no proof that it is the reality and nothing else. The people of London (Ahl Landan) and others among the observatory scientists of today have held the contrary. So too have the people of the inner heart and the spiritual ascents, such as the Greatest Shaykh (al-Shaykh al-Akbar, Ibn ʿArabi), may his secret be sanctified, who spoke at length on this in al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya. As for the pious predecessors (al-Salaf al-Salih), no detailed discussion of this is reported from them, since it is of little benefit. They stopped where the report was sound, and they said: the difference of motions and the like is by the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing. And in what is sound but whose cause is hidden, they clung to the hem of submission. What I incline to is that the heavens are according to what the prophetic reports have affirmed concerning the thickness (thakhan) and the distance between each heaven and heaven. I do not depart from the circle of this inclination. I say: it is possible that the thickness of each heaven contains a sphere for each of the planets, similar to the sphere which the philosophers have assigned to them, its essential motion being like their motion, and its accidental motion, through the motion of its heaven, being the daily motion toward the west. Thus the motions of the heavens are equal. If you refuse to accept that the heaven moves with everything in it, because some reports reject it and there is no definitive proof requiring it, I say: it is possible that there is also a mover within the thickness of the heaven, and what remains of it is still by God's power, upon its upper surface, angels who glorify night and day without ceasing.

The philosophers have a discussion on how the encompassing (al-muḥīṭ) moves the encompassed (al-muḥāṭ bihi), which the Imam (al-Razi) followed with the statement: "The correct view is that the mover of all is God Almighty by His choice. And if it is established, according to the rule of their saying, that the container moves the contained, then it moves by the power of its own essence, not by contact." As for the fixed stars, it is possible that they are in a sphere above the seven heavens, and it is possible that they are within the thickness of the seventh heaven above the sphere of Saturn. Indeed, if it is said that all the fixed stars and planets are within the thickness of the lowest heaven, moving on spheres similar to the spheres the philosophers have assigned to them, and that they have two motions as they say, it is not far-fetched. In this there is a preservation of the apparent sense of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have adorned the lowest heaven with lamps﴾ [al-Mulk: 5]. As for what they have mentioned in the science of the celestial bodies and distances, despite its confusion, we are not obliged to accept it. Therefore it does not apply that they said the distance of the fixed stars from the center of the earth is twenty-five million four hundred and twelve thousand eight hundred and ninety-nine farsakhs (a farsakh being a unit of distance),

[Page 44]

and what has come in the report, that between the heaven and the earth is five hundred years, and the thickness of the heaven is likewise, requires that between the surface of the earth and the fixed stars, on this assessment, there is a thousand years' journey, and farsakhs of that distance together with the farsakhs of half the radius of the earth, which is one thousand two hundred and seventy-three approximately, according to what has been said, far less than what was mentioned.

There is no need to say that number has no concept, and that five hundred was chosen because five is a circular number (ʿadad dāʾir), so that there is in it a hidden allusion to rotation, as is said of every sphere. And what indicates the soundness of the possibility that the sphere is within the thickness of the heaven is what Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with both of them, who said: "The sun is like a water-wheel (al-sāqiya) which runs in the heaven in its sphere. When it sets, it runs at night in its sphere beneath the earth until it rises from its east. And likewise the moon." The reports, both raised (marfūʿa) and halted (mawqūfa), concerning the stars, the heavens, and the earth are numerous.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti has mentioned some of them in a treatise he composed explaining the Sunni cosmology (al-Hay'a al-Sunniyya). When you examine them, you will see that most of them deviate from the circle of the accepted zodiac. Among them is what indicates that the star has a forced motion, like what Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from ʿIkrima: "The sun did not rise until it was stretched for it as a bow is stretched." Then, the apparent meaning is that by the swimming (al-sibāḥa) is meant the essential motion. It is also possible that what is meant is the accidental motion, indeed it has been said that this is more fitting, because that is not observed in the way this is observed; rather, common people do not know it. It has also been said that it is possible that what is meant is what encompasses both motions. Some have inferred, from the attribution of swimming to the star, that there is no vehicle carrying it that moves with its motion at all, but rather it moves by itself in the sphere, like the movement of a fish in water, since one does not say of someone sitting in a box or on a log that drifts in water that he is swimming. He chose that it runs in a channel receptive to splitting and rejoining, like water. Without affirming the impossibility of that ascent to the seventh heaven.

And God Most High knows the reality of the matter. He, glorified is He, is the Guardian of success, and upon the axis of His guidance revolves the sphere of verification. This is a portion of what we saw as fitting for this place, and another portion of what relates to this matter will come, God willing, in the words that follow.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 34:

﴿We did not grant to any human before you﴾, whoever he may be, ﴿eternity (al-khuld)﴾, that is, lasting and remaining in this world, because that would be contrary to the creative wisdom (al-hikma al-takwiniyya) and the legislative wisdom (al-hikma al-tashri'iyya). It has also been said that al-khuld means a long stay, and from this comes the saying of the people about the three stones of a cooking hearth (al-athafi) that they are "khawalid" (long-lasting). This has been used as evidence that al-Khidr (peace be upon him) is not alive, but this is open to question. ﴿So if you die, will they be the immortals?﴾ according to Our wisdom. It was revealed when they said, ﴿We await for him the misfortunes of time﴾ (al-Tur 52:30). The first fa' (fa') links the conditional sentence to what precedes it, and the hamza (of interrogation) is for denying its content. In reality, it is a denial of its consequence, namely what follows the second fa'. Yunus claimed that this sentence is the object of the denial, and that the condition is an interposed clause between them, whose answer is omitted and indicated by the sentence. But this is not the case. The denial of what is mentioned includes the denial of that on which it depends, existentially and non-existentially, namely their gloating over his death (ﷺ). It is as if it was said: "So if you die, will they be the immortals, so that they gloat over your death?" And in the meaning of this is the saying of Imam al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him:

Men wished that I would die, and if I die, that is a path in which I am not the only one.

So say to the one who seeks the opposite of what has passed: "Provide for another like it, and it is as if it had already happened."

And the saying of Dhu al-Isba' al-Adwani:

When time drags its chest over some people, it makes others kneel down.

So say to those who gloat over us: "Wake up! The gloaters will meet what we have met."

[Page 45]

Al-Allama al-Tibi mentioned, and the author of al-Kashf transmitted it with slight addition, that this is a return to what the noble surah is directed toward in terms of prophethood, in order to move from it to the establishment of another legislator. That is because when He, exalted is He, silenced those who claimed that God has a son, and those who took partners with Him, glory be to Him, and rebuked them, He mentioned what indicates their silencing, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So if﴾ and so on, because when an opponent has no further support, he wishes for the destruction of his opponent.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 35:

﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾ is a proof of what they denied concerning their immortality, and it reinforces His words, glorified is He, ﴿And We did not make﴾ etc. According to Shaykh al-Ash'ari, death is an existent quality (kayfiyyah wujudiyyah) that is opposed to life. According to al-Isfara'ini, and it is attributed to most scholars, death is the absence of life from that which is capable of life in actuality. Thus the absence of that life is like blindness that comes upon the eye, not absolute blindness. Therefore, the absence of life from the embryo when it is prepared for life does not entail that it is dead. It has also been said that death is the absence of life from that which is capable of life in an absolute sense, and this entails that the embryo is dead, and there is no harm in that, given the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God when you were dead and He gave you life, then He causes you to die, then He gives you life again﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:28]. Al-Ash'ari used as evidence that death is existent His words, exalted is He: ﴿He who created death and life﴾ [al-Mulk 67:2]. Creation (khalq) is bringing into existence and bringing out of non-existence, and death is possible, and what is possible must have an agent, while non-existence does not act. It is answered regarding the first point that the word may mean "measuring" (taqdir), which is more general than bringing into existence.
