And even if it is granted that it means bringing into existence, it is possible that by the creation of death is meant the creation of its causes, or that a noun is understood (i.e., the creation of the causes of death), and this is not rare in speech. As for the Ustadh (Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini), he said that by death is meant the Hereafter and by life the worldly life, because of what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he explained them thus. As for the second point, it is answered that the agent may intend non-existence just as he intends life, so the agent removes life just as he removes sight, for example.

Al-Laqani said: The apparent meaning supports what al-Ash'ari held, and departing from the apparent meaning without a reason is not acceptable to those who depart from it. His statement is explicit that death is an accident ('arad), while some scholars who hold that it is existent hesitated over whether it is a substance (jawhar) or an accident, because in some hadiths it is said that it is a created thing (ma'na) that God created in the palm of the Angel of Death, and in some of them it is said that God created it in the form of a ram that passes by nothing whose smell it finds except that it dies. Most of the scholars' expressions are that it is an accident that follows life, or the corruption of the body structure of the animal. The first is not comprehensive, and the second is a descriptive definition (rasm) by its effect. Close to this is what some of the learned said: it is the cessation of the faculties due to the extinction of the innate heat (al-hararah al-gharizziyyah), which is their instrument. If that is due to the extinction of the innate moisture (al-rutubah al-gharizziyyah), then it is natural death, and otherwise it is non-natural death. People know of death only as the severance of the soul's specific attachment to the body and its separation from it. By "soul" (nafs) is meant the animal soul (al-nafs al-hayawaniyyah), which in an absolute sense is more general than the human soul, just as the animal in an absolute sense is more general than the human.

According to the philosophers and those who follow them, souls are three: the vegetative (nabatiyyah), the animal (hayawaniyyah), and the celestial (falakiyyah). The term "soul" is applied to the three by homonymy (al-ishtirak al-lafzi), as the Imam related in al-Mulakhkhas from the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqin), and by synonymy (al-ishtirak al-ma'nawi), as the words of the Shaykh in al-Shifa' seem to require. The verification of this is in its proper place. Intending here what includes all of them is not something to be considered. Some of them said: By it is meant the human soul, because the discourse is directed at negating the immortality of humans. Its generality was chosen so that it would include the souls of humans, jinn and all kinds of animals, and this does not harm the context but is rather more beneficial in it. There is no doubt in the death of each individual of those kinds. Yes, it has been disputed whether it is valid to intend its generality in a way that includes the soul of every living being, such as the angel and others, or not, based on the disagreement over the death of the angels, peace be upon them, and the Houris (al-hur al-'in). Some said: All of them die, even for a moment, because of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas 28:88]. Others said: They do not die, because of what some reports indicate. By "every soul" is meant the earthly souls. The verse used as evidence is interpreted in a way that you will know, God willing. They are included in the exception in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And the Horn will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on earth will swoon, except whom God wills﴾ [al-Zumar 39:68]. The first (that all die) does not accept that every swooning is death. Some said: The angels die but the Houris do not die. Others said: Some of the angels, peace be upon them, die and some do not die, like Jibril, Israfil, Mika'il and 'Azra'il, peace be upon them. The view of the first group was preferred. It is not objected that death requires the separation of the spirit from the body, while the angels, peace be upon them, have no bodies, because the one who holds that they die says that they have bodies, but these are subtle, as is the truth indicated by the texts. Perhaps one may also deny that death requires a body. Some went to an extreme and claimed that souls themselves die after their separation from the body, even though after separation they are not possessors of a body. It seems that he is committed to interpreting death as nonexistence and dissolution. The truth is that they do not die, whether death is interpreted as mentioned or not. Ahmad ibn al-Husayn al-Kindi alluded to this disagreement in his words:

People have disputed until there is no agreement among them except on the thing that is condemned, and disagreement is about the condemned thing.

So it was said: The soul of a man escapes safe,
And it was said: It shares the body of a man in its ruin.

The Imam (al-Razi) went to the generality of the verse, except that he said: It is specific, for He, exalted is He, has a soul, as He said, exalted is He, relating the words of 'Isa, peace be upon him: ﴿You know what is in my soul, and I do not know what is in Your soul﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:116], even though death is impossible for Him, glorified is He. Likewise inanimate objects have souls, and they do not die. Then he said: A general term that has been specified remains an argument, so it continues to be acted upon in its apparent meaning in what is other than what has been excluded from it. That refutes the philosophers' view regarding human spirits, the separate intellects, and the celestial souls, that they do not die. End of quote. In this there is the following: If he intended by soul the substance attached to the body in the manner of governance and direction, as the philosophers and those who agree with them say, or the subtle, luminous, living body that moves, penetrates the limbs and spreads through them like the flow of rosewater, as the majority of the later scholars hold, and Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned a hundred proofs for it, then God is exalted above that absolutely. Likewise inanimate objects do not have the attribute of this according to the common view. Also, according to the philosophers, human spirits and separate intellects do not have a soul in either of those two senses, so how would their view be refuted by the noble verse? If he intended by it the essence (dhat), as is one of its meanings, it would be permissible to attribute it to God, exalted is He, and it has been said of it in the verse he mentioned. Likewise it is attributed to inanimate objects. But this is objected to: If he intended by death the separation of the spirit from the body, or something similar, then his statement "that refutes..." is invalid, because according to the philosophers the spirits and intellects mentioned have no bodies, so death in that sense cannot be conceived of them. If he intended by it non-existence and dissolution, it is objected that inanimate objects have that attribute, so his statement "they do not die" is invalid. In sum, it is not hidden from the one who reflects that the Imam erred in this matter.

Then, the meaning of the soul being "one who tastes death" is that it experiences it in a manner by which it suffers or takes pleasure, insofar as it is freed by it from the narrowness of the base worldly life into the realm of the dominion (malakut) and the sanctuaries of holiness. So it has been said.

It seems that every soul suffers from death, but this differs in intensity and weakness. In a hadith: "Indeed death has agonies." The mentioned escape for some people does not necessarily entail the absence of suffering. Perhaps in the choice of the word "tasting" there is an allusion to this for one who has taste, because most of what has come concerns punishment. Al-Imam said: Tasting is a specific perception, and here it is a metaphor for perception in general, and it is not possible to keep it on its literal meaning, because death is not of the kind of food that is tasted. He mentioned that by death is meant its preliminaries, the great pains, because it has been said that its entry into existence cannot be perceived, and at the time of its existence the person becomes dead, and the dead do not perceive. It is objected that the perceiver is the separated soul, and it perceives the pain of its separation from the body.

﴿And We test you﴾: the address is either to all people, by way of shifting (talwin), or to the disbelievers, by way of turning (iltifat), meaning: We deal with you as one who tests you ﴿with evil and good﴾, with the disliked and the liked, to see whether you will be patient and thankful or not.

The interpretation of "evil and good" as mentioned is related from Ibn Zayd. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that they are hardship and ease. Al-Dahhak said: poverty and illness, and wealth and health. Generalization is preferable. Evil is mentioned first because it is most fitting for those being rebuked, or because it is closer to the death mentioned before it. Al-Raghib mentioned that God's choosing of His servants is sometimes by pleasures, so that they may give thanks, and sometimes by harms, so that they may be patient. Thus both the gift and the trial are tests (bala'), so the trial requires patience and the gift requires thanks. Fulfilling the rights of patience is easier than fulfilling the rights of thanks, so the gift is the greater of the two tests. In this view 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, said: "We were tested with adversity and we were patient, and we were tested with ease and we were not patient." For this reason 'Ali, may God ennoble his face, said: "Whoever is given abundance in his worldly life and does not know that he has been deceived by it is deceived in his intellect." End of quote. Perhaps a reason for placing evil first can be known from this.

﴿Fitnah﴾, i.e., a trial (ibtila'). It is a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing "We test you," from a different root of the verb.

It is also permitted that it be an object of purpose (maf'ul lah) or a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning: We test you with evil and good for the sake of showing your excellence and your baseness, or while manifesting that. So consider this and do not be heedless. ﴿And to Us you will be returned﴾, not to any other, neither independently nor jointly, so We will repay you according to what appears from you of deeds. On the first of the two readings of the address, it is a promise and a warning; on the second, it is a pure warning. In the verse there is an allusion that what is meant by this worldly life is testing and exposure to reward and punishment.

It is recited (yurja'un) with the third-person "ya" (yurja'una), by way of turning (iltifat). That is, the verb is read in the third person plural masculine, "they are returned," shifting from the address in "We test you" to the third person.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 36:**

﴿When those who disbelieve see you, they take you only in mockery.﴾ That is, the polytheists. ﴿They take you only in mockery﴾ means: they take you only as one at whom they mock, in the sense of restricting their dealings with him ﷺ to their taking him in mockery. God treated them with His justice by making mockery their portion, not in the sense of restricting their taking him to his being a mockery, as is the immediate understanding. It is as if it were said: "What do they do to you except take you in mockery?"

It is apparent that the clause ﴿they take you﴾ etc. is the response (jawab) of ﴿when﴾ (idha). It did not need a fa' (the particle of consequence), just as its response, which is joined by ma to it, did not need one in God's words: ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them, their argument is nothing but...﴾ [al-Jathiya: 25]. This differs from the response of conditional particles other than idha when joined by ma, for in that case the fa' is required, as in: "If you visit us, then we do not wrong you." It has also been said that the response is omitted, and that it is "they say" (yaqulun), which is implied by God's words ﴿Is this the one who mentions your gods?﴾ and His words ﴿they take you﴾ etc. is an interjection. This is not so. Yes, it is necessary to supply the verb "say" in what was mentioned, and it is either coordinated with the clause ﴿they take you﴾ or is a circumstantial clause, meaning: "and they say" or "saying". The interrogative is for denial and astonishment, and both indicate that the intended meaning is: "He mentions our gods with evil." Sometimes the context alone suffices to indicate this, as in God's words: ﴿We heard a youth mention them﴾ [al-Anbiya: 60], for mentioning the enemy is only with evil. They avoided stating it explicitly out of courtesy toward their gods.

In Majma' al-Bayan it says: The Arabs say "you mentioned so-and-so," meaning "you blamed him." On this is the verse of 'Antara:

*Do not mention my dowry and what I fed her, lest your skin become like the skin of the mangy camel.*

End of quotation. The demonstrative is similar in his words:

*This is Abu al-Saqr, unique in his virtues, of the lineage of Shayban, between al-Dall and al-Salam (two trees).*

Thus there is in this some kind of clarification of "taking him in mockery."

God's words ﴿while they are disbelievers in the mention of the Most Merciful﴾ are in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the implied pronoun of the implied "say." The meaning is: they blame him, peace be upon him, for mentioning their gods, which neither harm nor benefit, with evil, while they themselves are disbelievers in the Qur'an which was sent down as a mercy. They are therefore more deserving of blame and denunciation. The first pronoun is the subject, its predicate is ﴿disbelievers﴾, and it is by this that ﴿in the mention﴾ is connected. It was placed first for the sake of the fasila (verse-ending rhyme). Its annexation is a lam-type annexation (i.e., the genitive is possessive). The second pronoun is a verbal emphasis of the first. Separating the governing word from the governed by the emphatic, and separating the emphasized from the emphasizer by the governed, is permissible.

It is also permissible that ﴿the mention of the Most Merciful﴾ means His unity, with dhikr being a verbal noun (masdar) annexed to its object, meaning: "they are disbelievers in the unity of the Most Merciful, the Bestower of blessings upon them, with that which calls for His unity and belief in Him, glorified is He." And it is permissible that it means His admonition and His guidance of creation by sending messengers and sending down scriptures, the dhikr being a verbal noun annexed to its subject. It has been said that the intended meaning of "the mention of the Most Merciful" is his ﷺ uttering this expression and applying it to God, and the intended meaning of their disbelief in it is their saying: "We do not know the Most Merciful except the Most Merciful of Yamama," so it is a verbal noun annexed to its object only, and it is not anything (valid), as is not hidden.

Al-Zamakhshari made the clause a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of ﴿they take you﴾, meaning: they take you in mockery while they are in a state which is the very root of mockery and derision, which is disbelief in the mention of the Most Merciful.

The occasion of revelation of the verse, according to what Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi: "He ﷺ passed by Abu Sufyan and Abu Jahl while they were conversing. When Abu Jahl saw him, he laughed and said to Abu Sufyan: 'This is the prophet of the Banu 'Abd Manaf.' Abu Sufyan became angry and said: 'Do you not deny that the Banu 'Abd Manaf should have a prophet?' The Prophet ﷺ heard it, so he returned to Abu Jahl, confronted him and warned him, and said: 'I do not see you ceasing until there befalls you what befell your paternal uncle al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.' And he said to Abu Sufyan: 'As for you, you did not say what you said except out of zealotry.'"

And I see that the heart is not satisfied that this is a cause of revelation. And God knows best.

[Page 48]

﴿Mankind was created of haste﴾. It means seeking a thing and eagerly pursuing it before its time. By "mankind" is meant the species. It was described thus because of its excessive hastiness and its lack of patience, as if it were created from haste itself. This is by way of treating the dispositions and character with which it was formed as though they were the elements from which it was formed, to indicate how completely haste clings to it and is never separated from it.

Abu 'Amr, Abu 'Ubayda and Qutrub said: in this verse there is a *qalb* (inversion, transposition of words). The intended sense is "haste was created from mankind," meaning that it was made part of his natures and characters because it clings to him. 'Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) read it accordingly. This is an unaccepted *qalb*. Similar usage is common in their speech when they want to express intensity. They say to one who constantly plays: "You are made of play," and from this is the poet's line:

*"And I, when the one who strikes the ram strikes it on its head, [I] throw out the tongue from the mouth."*

It was also said that by "mankind" is meant al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, because the verse was revealed concerning him when he hastened the punishment, saying: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], and so on.

Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrima, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: by it is meant Adam (peace be upon him). He wanted to stand up before the breath of the spirit had completed being breathed into him and reached his legs. It was also said that Allah created him at the end of the day, on Friday. When He had sent the spirit into his eyes and tongue but it had not yet reached his lowest part, he said: "My Lord, hasten my creation before the sun sets." This is narrated from Mujahid.

It was also said that the meaning is that he was created swiftly, not in the gradual order in which his descendants were created. Page 49 This is mentioned to show that his being created in this way is among the causes of his haste in affairs. The more apparent view is that the intended meaning is the species, although the creation of Adam (peace be upon him) and what it entails extends to his offspring. What was mentioned about the occasion of revelation does not contradict this, as is not hidden.

It was also said that *al-'ajal* means clay in the language of Himyar. Abu 'Ubayda recited for someone:

*"The nab' tree in the hard, smooth rock is its place of growth, and the palm tree's place of growth is in water and clay."*

It was objected that there is no connection between this meaning and the context here. Al-Tibi said: the purpose of this would be to belittle the status of the human species, to complete the sense of threat in His words: ﴿I will show you My signs, so do not seek to hasten them﴾. The reliance is on the first meaning. The address is to the disbelievers who sought hasty punishment. By His signs is meant His retributions, and by showing them to them is meant His afflicting them with them. That showing is in the Hereafter, as what follows indicates, and it was also said that it includes this world. The prohibition against their hastening Him to bring them is despite the fact that their souls are created with haste, so that they may restrain them from what they desire. This is not a case of commanding what is beyond one's capacity, because Allah has given them the means by which they can restrain the soul from its impulses. This prohibition returns to the command to be patient.

Mujahid, Humayd and Ibn Muqsim read ﴿*khalaqa al-insana*﴾ with *khalaqa* in the active voice and *al-insana* in the accusative.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 38:

﴿And they say, "When is this promise?"﴾ That is, when is the time of the occurrence of the Hour that has been promised. They were saying this out of impatience for its coming, by way of mockery and denial, as the answer indicates, not as a request to specify its time by way of challenge, as in the case in Surah al-Mulk. ("Matā" [when]) is in a place of raising (rafʿ), as it is a predicate (khabar) of "hādhā" [this].

It is related from some of the Kufans (al-Kūfiyyūn, the Kufan grammarians) that it is in a place of accusative (naṣb) as an adverb of time (ẓarfiyyah), and the governing element for it is an implied verb, meaning: "When will this promise come" ﴿if you are truthful﴾ that it will come. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ and the believers who recite the noble verses that report the coming of the Hour. The answer to the conditional is omitted, relying on what precedes it as an indication of it, for their saying "When is this promise?" — since it was a form of delay on their part regarding the promised thing and a request for its coming with haste — is, in effect, a request for its coming quickly. So it is as if it were said: "If you are truthful, then let it come to us swiftly."

وقولُه تعالى: ﴿لَوْ يَعْلَمُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ [Had those who disbelieved known] اسْتِئْنافٌ (*isti'naf*, a resumptive new sentence) مَسُوقٌ لِبَيانِ شِدَّةِ هَوْلِ ما يَسْتَعْجِلُونَهُ وفَظاعَةِ ما فِيهِ مِنَ العَذابِ وأنَّهم إنَّما يَسْتَعْجِلُونَهُ لِجَهْلِهِمْ بِشَأْنِهِ، وإيثارُ صِيغَةِ المُضارِعِ في الشَّرْطِ وإنْ كانَ المَعْنى عَلى المُضِيِّ لِإفادَةِ اسْتِمْرارِ عَدَمِ العِلْمِ بِحَسَبِ المَقامِ وإلّا فَكَثِيرًا ما يُفِيدُ المُضارِعُ المَنفِيُّ انْتِفاءَ الِاسْتِمْرارِ، ووُضِعَ المَوْصُولُ مَوْضِعَ الضَّمِيرِ لِلتَّنْبِيهِ بِما في حَيِّزِ الصِّلَةِ عَلى عِلَّةِ اسْتِعْجالِهِمْ.

وقالَ أبُو حَيّانَ (Abu Hayyan): الَّذِي يَظْهَرُ أنَّ مَفْعُولَهُ مَحْذُوفٌ لِدَلالَةِ ما قَبْلَهُ عَلَيْهِ أيْ لَوْ يَعْلَمُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مَجِيءَ المَوْعُودِ الَّذِي سَألُوا عَنْهُ واسْتَبْطَؤُوهُ (وحِينَ) مَنصُوبٌ بِذَلِكَ المَفْعُولِ ولَيْسَ عِنْدِي بِظاهِرٍ

﴿بَلْ تَأْتِيهِمْ بَغْتَةً﴾ is in coordination ('atf) with ﴿لا يَكُفُّونَ﴾. Ibn 'Atiyya claimed that it is a corrective clause (istidrak) with an implied negation before it, and the sense is: "Indeed, the signs do not come according to their demands, but it [the Hour / the Promise] comes upon them suddenly." It was also said that it is a corrective clause in response to His saying, ﴿لَوْ يَعْلَمُ﴾ and so on, which is negated in meaning, as if it were said: "They do not know that, but it comes upon them," and so on. The distance between this and what Ibn 'Atiyya claimed is like the distance between the heaven and the earth.

The hidden pronoun in (تَأْتِيهِمْ) refers to (al-wa'd, the Promise), by interpreting it as "the promised threat" (al-'idah), or "the appointed time" (al-maw'idah), or "the time" (al-hin), by interpreting it as "the Hour" (al-sa'ah). Or it refers to (al-nar, the Fire), which al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's al-Bahr al-Muhit) preferred. ﴿بَغْتَةً﴾ means suddenly (fajata), and is a verbal noun (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal), or an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) for ﴿لِتَأْتِيَهم﴾; it is a verbal noun not from its own verb-form. ﴿فَتَبْهَتُهُمْ﴾ means it will astonish and bewilder them, or overpower them, according to the figurative meaning (ma'na kinai).

Al-A'mash read (بَلْ يَأْتِيهِمْ) with the third-person masculine ya' (ya' al-ghaybah), and (بَغَتَةً) with a fatha on the ghayn, which is a dialectal form of it. It was said that this is permissible for every word whose middle radical is a guttural letter (harf halq). (فَيَبْهَتُهم) is also with the third-person ya', so the hidden pronoun in each of the two verbs refers to the Promise or to the time, as al-Zamakhshari said.

Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: it is possible that it refers to the Fire, by taking it to mean the punishment. ﴿فَلا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ رَدَّها﴾: the pronoun in the genitive refers to what the feminine pronoun before it referred to. It was also said that it refers to the suddenness (al-baghtah), meaning: they will not be able to turn it away from themselves entirely. ﴿وَلا هُمْ يُنْظَرُونَ﴾ means they will not be given respite so as to rest even for the blink of an eye, and in this there is a reminder of their being given respite in this world.

Page 51

﴿And indeed, messengers before you were mocked﴾, etc. This is a consolation to His Messenger (ﷺ) regarding their mockery, after he had fulfilled his purpose by mentioning the wise replies to their objections against prophethood, and what was woven into them of meanings that are the essence of the aims. In it is the indication that he, peace and blessings be upon him, had discharged what was incumbent upon him of conveying the message, and that he would be victorious in the end. For this reason, it began with mention of the noble prophets, peace be upon them, as a model to follow, and it concluded with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly written in the Psalms [Zabur]﴾ [al-Anbiya: 105], etc. The introduction of this with an oath serves to increase the confirmation of its content. The tanwin on "rusul" (messengers) is for magnification and multiplicity. "Min" (from) is connected to a omitted element which is an adjective of it, meaning: "And by Allah, indeed messengers of great station and of great number were mocked, who existed from a time before your time," with the omission of the annexed noun (mudaf, the noun governed by another) and the placing of the annexed-to noun (mudaf ilayhi) in its position.

﴿So there befell﴾, i.e., there encompassed, immediately after that, or there descended, or there alighted, or the like, for its meaning revolves around comprehensiveness and necessity, and it is hardly used except for evil. "Al-hayq" is what encompasses a person of the disliked outcome of his action. It has been said: the origin of "haqa" is "haqqa," like "zala" and "zalla," and "dhama" and "dhamma."

[Page 51 marker above is part of the source text.]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿those who mocked them﴾, i.e., of those messengers, peace be upon them, is connected to "haqa." Its placement before its subject, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿what they used to mock﴾, is for hastening to clarify that the evil reached them. The word "ma" (what) is either a relative pronoun, conveying magnification, and the pronoun referring back to it, with the preposition phrase connected to the verb after it; its placement is for the sake of the verse-endings (fawasil, the rhyming ends of verses). The meaning: "So there encompassed them that which they used to mock, by which they were destroyed." Or it is a verbal-noun (masdariyya) "ma," and then the pronoun refers to the category of the messenger, indicated by the plural, as they said.

Perhaps the preference for the singular over the plural is to draw attention to the fact that the recompense of their mockery befalls them for each one of them, peace be upon them, not the recompense of their mockery of all of them in general only. That is, the recompense of their mockery descended upon them, placing the cause in the position of the effect, to indicate the complete connection between them. Or it is the very mockery itself, if by that is meant the otherworldly punishment, based on the manifestation of deeds in the otherworldly state in forms appropriate to them in beauty and ugliness.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 42:**

﴿Say﴾: a command to him (ﷺ) to ask those mockers a question of rebuke (*taqri'*) and admonition (*tanbih*), so that they will not be deceived by the blessings of God Most High that have overwhelmed them. He says: ﴿Who will protect you﴾, that is, guard you, ﴿by night and by day from the Most Merciful﴾, that is, from His punishment, as indicated by the context of guarding. The mention of the night first is because calamities occur more often at night and strike harder.

Mentioning the title "the Most Merciful" serves as a reminder that they have no protection except through the mercy of God Most High, and it provides them with the answer, as was said regarding His words: ﴿What has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?﴾ [al-Infitar: 6]. It was also said that this is a hint that when His punishment, may He be exalted, is willed, it is severe and painful. For this reason it is said: "We seek refuge in God, Mighty and Majestic, from the anger of the Forbearing." It is also a rebuke to them, in that He punishes them even though His mercy prevails, and an indication of the extent of their wickedness.

Abu Ja'far, al-Zuhri and Shayba read *yaklukum* (يَكْلُوكم) with a light damma and without hamza. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' related *yaklawkum* (يَكْلَوْكم) with a fatha on the *lam* and a sukun on the *waw*.

God Most High's words: ﴿Rather, they are turning away from the remembrance of their Lord﴾ are a *idrab* (a shift away from the preceding statement) (*idrab*: a change of direction in speech), serving as a verdict (*tasjil*) against them: they are not among the people of hearing, and they are a people whom blessings have distracted from the Bestower, so they do not remember Him, Mighty and Majestic, until they fear His punishment, or consider the security and ease they are in as a protection and safeguard, so that they would ask about the one who guards (*al-kali'*), in the manner of the poet's saying:

"Halt, and greet the remains of the abode's encampment, with its rain-pools and stones. What will you find in them of rain-pools and stones?"

In this there is that they persist in turning away, having first been reminded and alerted. In linking the turning away to the remembrance of Him, and in the mention of the Lord, *rabb*, attached to their pronoun, which indicates that they are under His dominion, management, and nurture, Most High, there is an indication, which is clear, that they are in the furthest extreme of error and misguidance.

It was also said that it is an *idrab* from an implied premise, that is: they are not heedless of God Most High, so that asking about Him, glorified be He, would be of no use. How could that be, when they only took gods and worshipped them so that they would intercede for them with Him, Most High, and bring them near to Him in nearness (*zulfa*)? Rather, they turn away from His remembrance, Mighty and Majestic, so the reminder suits them. This, although it is apparent from the context and clearly fits the requirement of the situation, has remained hidden from the observers, and they have all been heedless of it. [End of quotation.]

It has been objected that the context is for ignorance of them and for a verdict against them, that when they are reminded they do not remember. Do you not see His words: ﴿nor do the deaf hear the call﴾ [al-Anbiya': 45]? What was mentioned implies the opposite, since it includes describing them as benefiting from warning and call, and also because His words "heedless" contradict what the noble composition indicates. So the truth is what was stated above.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 43:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Or do they have gods that protect them from Us?﴾ This is a turn away from describing them with turning away (i'rad) to rebuking them for relying on their gods and attributing protection to them. So *am* (or) is disjunctive (munqati'a), with an implied *bal* (rather) and a hamza (interrogative particle), as if it means "Rather, do they have gods...?" *Lahum* (for them) is the predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), *ālihatun* (gods) is the subject (mubtada'), and the clause *tamna'uhum* (that protect them) is its qualifier (sifa). *Min dūnina* (apart from Us) is said to be a qualifier following another qualifier, meaning: "Rather, do they have gods protecting them and preventing what comes from Us, or guarding them from Us? So they rely on them and trust in their protection."

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the sentence contains inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), and that the original order is: *am lahum ālihatun min dūnina tamna'uhum*. On this reading, *min dūnina* is also a qualifier. Al-Hawfi said that it is connected to *tamna'uhum*, meaning: "Rather, do they have gods that protect them from a punishment from Our side?" The interrogative is for the denial that they have such gods. In directing the denial and negation at the existence of gods described with what has been mentioned, rather than at the attribute itself, by saying "Do their gods protect them, etc.", there is an indication of their falling from the rank of existence, let alone the rank of protecting, which is obvious.

Some eminent scholars said: The idrab (shift) expressed by *am* refers back to the command to ask, like the earlier idrab, but it is more emphatic than it, because asking someone who is heedless about a matter is remote, and asking someone who believes the opposite is even more remote. Some understood from this that the hamza here is for taqrir (affirmation) in accordance with the claim of the disbelievers, mockingly.

It has been objected that this is not necessarily the meaning. It may be for denial, not in the sense that they did not claim this, but in the sense of "why would there be anything like it that has no reality?" In my view, the more apparent reading is to take it as referring back to the description of turning away, as you heard earlier. In the *Kashf* it is noted that within the turning away from their description as those who turn away, there is an emphatic denial, implying that they, in their turning away from His remembrance, are like one who has a guardian protecting him from Our punishment, while turning away from Him and occupying themselves with their gods. They turned away from Him, the Exalted, and occupied themselves with them. For this reason, what follows is a fitting continuation, as if it were said: "Leave the topic of turning away and look at those who turned away from their Lord, glorified is He, toward Him. This is greater and more grave," so reflect on it, for it is subtle.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They are not able to help themselves, nor will they be companioned by Us.﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (istinaf) confirming the denial that precedes it. Meaning: they are not able to help themselves, to repel what befalls them, nor will they be accompanied by help from Us or by one who repels that from them on Our part. They are in the utmost weakness and are not taken into account, so how can what is supposed about them be supposed? The pronouns refer to the gods, treating them as rational beings. This is related from Qatada. It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the pronouns refer to the disbelievers, meaning: the disbelievers are not able to help themselves through their gods, nor will help from Our side accompany them. The first reading is more suitable to the context, although this one is further from disrupting the pronoun references. The phrase *min-nā* (from Us), on both views, may be connected to the verb after it, or to an implied element that functions as a qualifier of an omitted noun.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 44:

"Nay, We gave enjoyment to these and their fathers until life lengthened over them" (﴿بَلْ مَتَّعْنا هَؤُلاءِ وآباءَهم حَتّى طالَ عَلَيْهِمُ العُمُرُ﴾) and so on: this is an idrab (a turning away from the preceding line of speech, a change of direction) with respect to what is in al-Kashf concerning the preceding discourse, which moved on to their threat, that they are among the people of istidraj (gradual enticement toward punishment), and it removed them from direct address, showing lack of concern for them. The switch from the pronoun to the demonstrative (ism al-ishara) in the verse indicates their contemptibility. In other works it is said that it is an idrab from what they imagined: that their state of being safeguarded came from the fact that they have gods who prevent calamity from reaching them. It is as if it were said: leave aside what they claim, that they are protected by the safeguarding of their gods; rather, what they are in of protection is from Us alone. We preserved them from adversity and gave them enjoyment of all kinds of ease, because they are among the people of istidraj and of immersion in what leads them to the painful punishment.

It may also be an idrab from what the preceding resumptive statement indicates, namely the falsehood of their illusion. It is as if it were said: leave aside what shows the falsehood of their illusion, that they have gods who prevent them. Know that they fell into the snare of that false illusion only because We gave them enjoyment of what they desire, until the span of their bodies' inhabitation by life grew long, so they reckoned that this would endure. They were deceived, turned away from the truth, and followed what their souls adorned for them. That is empty greed and false hope. "Do they not see" (﴿أفَلا يَرَوْنَ﴾), that is, do they not look and so not see,
صفحة 53
"that We come to the land" (﴿أنّا نَأْتِي الأرْضَ﴾), that is, the land of the disbelievers or their land, "reducing it from its edges" (﴿نَنْقُصُها مِن أطْرافِها﴾), by empowering the Muslims over it and their taking what they take from it and placing it within the realm of their dominion. The shift from "that We reduce the land from its edges" to the wording of the sublime composition is to depict the manner of its diminution and its being wrested from their hands, for it occurs through the coming of the armies of the Muslims and their conquest. The original would have been "the armies of the Muslims come," but He attributed the coming to Himself, exalted and mighty be He, to honor them and to indicate that it is by His power and His pleasure, and in this is an exaltation of jihad and of the mujahidin.

The verse, as we stated at the beginning of the surah, is Medinan, and it was revealed after the obligation of jihad, so it is not objected that the surah is Meccan and jihad was prescribed after it, such that it might be said that this is a report about the future, or it might be said that the intended meaning is "We reduce it" by removing its blessing, as reported from Ibn Abbas, or by ruining its settlements and the death of its people, as narrated from Ikrimah. It is also said that "We reduce it" refers to the death of the scholars. If this is authentically from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then there is no turning from it; otherwise, the more apparent view, considering the context, is what has preceded. This is supported by His saying: "Are they then the victors?" (﴿أفَهُمُ الغالِبُونَ﴾) over the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers.

The meaning is a denial that victory follows from what has been mentioned of the diminution of the land of the disbelievers through the empowering of the believers over it. It is as if it were said: after what has been mentioned has become manifest and they have seen it, would their victory still be imagined? In the definite article (in al-ghalibun) there is an allusion that the Muslims are those specifically designated for victory, and they are the ones known for it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 45:

﴿Say: I am only warning you﴾ after He, exalted is He, had made clear, on His part, the extent of the terror of what the hasty ones are hastening for, and the ultimate evil of their state when it comes, and had reproached them for their ignorance of this and their turning away from the remembrance of their Lord, who protects them from the nightly visitors and the calamities of the day and other of their evils, the peace and blessings of Allah be upon him was commanded to say to them: "I am only warning you of what you are hastening for, of the Hour, by the true revelation that speaks of its existence and of the awfulness of the terrors within it." That is, my task is only to warn you by informing you of it, not by bringing it about, for that conflicts with the cosmic (takwini) and legislative (tashri'i) wisdom, since faith is based on proof (burhani), not on direct sight (ayani).

As for His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And the deaf do not hear the call﴾, it is either part of the speech that was dictated (al-kalam al-mulaqqan), a concluding remark (tadhyil) to it by way of parenthetical interjection, which he, the peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, was commanded to say to them as a rebuke, reproach and recording against them of complete ignorance and obstinacy; or it is from Him, exalted is He, in the manner of His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Rather, they are turning away from the remembrance of their Lord﴾, as if it were said: "Say to them that, while they are far removed from hearing." The definite article in "the deaf" (al-summ) is either for the genus, which includes these disbelievers in a primary way, or for a specific reference (al-'ahd), so the explicit noun is placed in the position of the pronoun to record their deafness against them. The restriction of the negation of hearing by His saying: ﴿when they are warned﴾, even though the deaf do not hear absolutely, is to show the extent of the intensity of their deafness. Likewise, the choice of "call" (du'a'), which is an expression for sound and summons, over "speech" (kalam) is for this reason, since warning is customarily delivered with loud, repeated sounds accompanied by signs indicating it. So when they do not hear these, their deafness is at a degree unheard of. It has also been said that it is because the subject is warning; do you not see His saying: ﴿Say: I am only warning you by the revelation﴾? In this there is a subtle tickling that is not hidden.

Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Jubayr on the authority of Abu 'Amr, and Ibn al-Salt on the authority of Hafs read (tusmi'u) with the "ta" on the basis of address to the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, from iscmaa' (causing to hear), with "al-summa" and "al-du'a'" both in the accusative as objects. This reading supports the possibility that the sentence is from Him, exalted is He. It was also read (yasma'u) with the "ya" in the third person, with the verb attributed to his pronoun, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, with "al-summa" and "al-du'a'" both in the accusative as mentioned. Ibn Khalawayh mentioned that it was read (yusma'u) in the passive voice, with (al-summu) in the nominative as the deputy of the subject, and (al-du'a') in the accusative as the object. Ahmad ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, on the authority of al-Yazidi, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read (yusmi'u) with a "ya" in the third person and a damma, with a kasra on the "mim," with (al-summa) in the accusative as the object and (al-du'a'u) in the nominative as the subject of yusmi'u. The causative of hearing is attributed to him by way of extended usage (ittisa'), and the second object is omitted, as if it were said: "and the deaf do not cause the call to be heard to anything."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 46:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if a breath of your Lord's punishment should touch them﴾ is an explanation of the swiftness of their being affected by the very coming of the punishment, following the explanation of their not being affected by the coming of its report, in the manner of emphasis by oath. That is: "By Allah, if even the slightest part of His punishment should touch them." Exalted is He: ﴿they will surely say, "Woe to us! We were indeed wrongdoers"﴾, that is, they will certainly call down woe and destruction upon themselves and will confess upon themselves to the wrongdoing that preceded.

In ﴿a breath touched them﴾ there are three intensifications, as al-Zamakhshari said, and they are, as in al-Kashf: the mention of "touch" (massa), which is less than penetration, and attaining its reality is sufficient with the arrival of anything at all; and what the word nafh (breath) carries of the sense of slightness, for its origin is the blowing of the scent of a thing, and it is said: "the animal nafahathu" meaning it struck him with the edge of its hoof, and "nafahahu bi-'atiyyah" meaning he gave him a small portion and bestowed upon him a little; and the form of the single instance (marrah), which is for the least that the noun applies to. As for al-Sakkaki, he made the indefiniteness (tankir) its fourth intensification because of what it conveys of belittlement. The derivation of that, if it is free from the form of the single instance and the word itself, is not disturbed by it, as the author of al-Idah claimed.

Some have objected to the intensification in "touch," on the grounds that it is stronger than "striking" (isabah), because it indicates the impact upon the sense of the one touched. What has been mentioned in al-Kashf shows its refutation for one who has been touched by a breath of divine favor. Perhaps there is a fifth intensification in the verse that becomes apparent upon reflection. Then, the apparent meaning is that this touching will occur on the Day of Resurrection, as we have hinted; and it has been said that it refers to this world, based on what has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, in interpreting the "breath" as the hunger that befell Mecca.

[Page 54]

The Most High's words, ﴿And We shall set up the scales of justice﴾, explain what will happen when that which they were warned of comes.

Al-Tayyibi made the clause a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) referring back to the pronoun in ﴿they will surely say﴾, with the implied meaning "while We are setting up." It is like the construction without a returning pronoun in "I came to you while the sun was rising." It may also be said that the generality of ﴿soul﴾ that comes after has taken the place of the returning pronoun, and this is, as you see, far-fetched. The meaning is: "And We shall bring forth the just scales by which the records of deeds are weighed, as the hadith of the registers and the card, which Muslim and others reported, indicates. Or [the scales weigh] the deeds themselves, as has been said. They will appear in luminous, substantial forms if they are good deeds, and in dark forms if they are evil deeds."

The plural "scales" (al-mawazin) apparently indicates a plurality of scales in the literal sense, and this has been held. It has been said that each nation has a scale, that each responsible person has a scale, and that the believer has scales according to the number of his good deeds and the kinds of his good works. The soundest and most well-known view, however, is that there is one scale for all nations and all deeds, whose two pans are like the layers of the heavens and the earth, because the reports affirming this are sound. The plurality is nominal (i'tibari). The singular may sometimes be expressed by a form indicating the plural for the sake of exalting it, as in the Most High's words ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ ﴿so that I may do righteousness﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99], and his saying: "O God of Muhammad, have mercy on me."

The bringing forth of this scale opposite the Throne, between Paradise and Hell, and Jibril (peace be upon him) takes hold of its pillar, looking at its tongue, while Mika'il (peace be upon him) is its trustee, is as stated in Nawadir al-Usul. But is it created today, or will it be created tomorrow?

Al-Laqani said: "I have not found a text on this, just as I have not found a text on what substance it is made of." End of quote. As for what is reported, that Dawud (peace be upon him) asked his Lord, glorified is He, to show him the scale, and when he saw it he fainted, then recovered and said: "My God, who can fill its pan with good deeds?" The Most High said: "O Dawud, when I am pleased with My servant, I fill it with a date." This is a text that it is created today, but I do not know the status of the hadith, so let it be examined.

The Mu'tazilah denied the scale in its literal meaning and said: "What comes in the Qur'an about this must be understood as referring to upholding justice and fairness. For them, the setting up of scales is a figure of speech for establishing a correct reckoning and recompense according to deeds." This was reported from al-Dahhak, Qatadah, Mujahid and al-A'mash. There is no reason to depart from the apparent meaning.

[Page 55]

The singular "justice" (al-qist), although it is an attribute of the plural, is because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) which is described by it for emphasis. It may also be on the basis of an omitted modifier, meaning "possessors of justice." Abu Hayyan permitted it to be an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), as in the line: "I will not sit out of cowardice from the battle," and in that case there is no need to justify its singular form.

It was read as (al-qiṣṭ) with a ṣād. The lām in the Most High's words ﴿for the Day of Resurrection﴾ means "in," as Ibn Malik explicitly stated, and he cited as evidence its occurrence in this sense in the verse of Miskin al-Darimi:

"Those are my people; they have passed on their way,
just as 'Ad and Tubba' passed before them."

This is the view of the Kufans, and Ibn Qutaybah agreed with them. Meaning: "We shall set up the scales on the Day of Resurrection, which they were hastening." Many others said that the lām indicates cause, meaning "for the sake of the reckoning of the Day of Resurrection," or "for the sake of its people." Some made it indicate specification, as is one of two possibilities in your saying "I came on the fifth of the nights that passed of the month." The more well-known of the two possibilities, and the second, is that the lām means "in."

﴿So no soul will be wronged﴾ of souls ﴿in anything﴾ of wrongdoing, so its promised reward will not be decreased, nor its known punishment increased. Thus "anything" is in the accusative as a verbal noun, and "wronged" has its well-known meaning.

It was permitted that "anything" be a direct object, by omission and transitivity, and "wronged" remains in its basic sense: meaning "no one will be wronged in anything, by being denied reward or having punishment increased." Some interpreted "wronging" as "diminishing." It was permitted for "anything" to be either a verbal noun or a direct object without considering omission and transitivity, meaning "it will not be diminished in anything of the diminishing, or in anything of the reward." That there will be no increase in punishment is understood from the indication of the text (ishara al-nass) and the customary implication (al-luzum al-mut'araf). What was chosen was that which does not need indication or implication. The fa' (so) indicates that the absence of wrong follows from the setting up of the scales.

Perhaps this implies that everyone's deeds will be weighed. Al-Qurtubi said: "The scale is true, but it does not apply to every person, based on the sound hadith, where it is said: 'O Muhammad, admit into Paradise those of your community who will have no reckoning, from the right-hand gate...' (the hadith), and the prophets (peace be upon them) are more entitled to this." Also the Most High's words ﴿The guilty will be known by their marks, and they will be seized by the forelocks and the feet﴾ [al-Rahman: 41], His words ﴿So We will not assign for them any weight on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Kahf: 105], and His words, glorified is He: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan: 23]. The weighing remains only for whomever God, glorified is He, wills from both groups.

The judge Mundhir ibn Sa'id al-Ballluti mentioned that the deeds of the people of patience are not weighed, but rather their reward is poured out for them without measure. The apparent meanings of most verses and hadiths require the weighing of the deeds of the disbelievers. Those passages whose apparent meaning contradicts this have been interpreted, and they are few in comparison. In my view there is no definitive proof for the generality of the weighing, and I incline toward its not being general. Furthermore, just as there has been disagreement about its generality with regard to individual humans, there has been disagreement about its generality with regard to the two species, humans and jinn. The truth is that the believing jinn are like the believing humans, and their disbelievers are like the disbelieving humans, as al-Qurtubi investigated and deduced from several verses. Al-Laqani expanded on this in his large commentary on al-Jawharah. The disagreement about how the weighing is carried out will come, God willing, in its place.

﴿And if there is﴾, that is, the deed implied by the setting up of the scales. It has also been said that the pronoun refers back to "anything," on the basis that the meaning is "no one will be wronged in the recompense of any deed," ﴿the weight of a mustard seed﴾, that is, the quantity of a seed that is of mustard. The prepositional phrase is attached to an omitted element which serves as a modifier of "seed." It was also permitted for it to modify "weight," but the first is closer. The meaning is: even if it is in the utmost small and insignificant amount, for the mustard seed is a proverb for smallness.

Zayd ibn 'Ali, may God be pleased with them both, and Abu Ja'far, Shayba and Nafi' read "weight" (miṡqālu) in the nominative, on the basis that "there is" is a complete verb.

[Page 56]

﴿We bring it﴾, meaning: we bring it forth. Ubayy also read it this way. The meaning is "We bring it into presence." The preposition ba' is for transitivity, and the pronoun refers to "weight," which is feminine by virtue of its genitive complement. The clause is the answer to the conditional particle in. It was permitted for in to be a conjunctive particle, with the clause then being a new sentence, but that goes against the apparent meaning.

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-'Ala' ibn Sayaba, Ja'far ibn Muhammad and Ibn Shurayh al-Isbahani read (ātaynā) with a long vowel, as a form of the stem "to come" (mufa'alah), in the sense of requiting and repaying, because they "came" to Him with deeds and He "came" to them with reward. It has also been said that it is from "giving" (ītā'), and its original form is 'a'tayna, the second hamza being changed to alif. The meaning is "We repaid" also, as a figurative usage, and this is why it takes the preposition ba'. If it meant "We gave," as some said, it would take the direct object without a preposition, as Ibn Jinni and others said.

Humayd read (athabnā) from the reward ﴿and sufficient is Us as reckoners﴾. It was said: meaning "counting and enumerating their deeds," taking "reckoning" in its linguistic sense, which is counting. This was reported from al-Suddi. It was also permitted for it to be a metaphor for recompense.

Al-Laqani mentioned that in the customary usage of the Law, reckoning is God's calling His servants to account, except those who are excepted from among them, before they leave the place of gathering, concerning their deeds, whether good or evil, in detail, not by weighing. He also said that, as al-Wahidi and others mentioned, and as the author of Kanz al-Asrar asserted decisively, reckoning occurs before the weighing. It is not hidden that the verse contains some indication that the reckoning mentioned in it occurs after the setting up of the scales. So reflect.

The accusative of the descriptive phrase is either as a specification (tamyiz) or as a circumstantial state (hal), and the first was preferred in al-Bahr.

* * *

This (and among the subtle indications in the verses): ﴿The reckoning of people draws near, while they are heedless and turning away﴾, etc. In it is an indication of the bad state of those veiled by love of this world from preparing for the Hereafter. They became heedless of correcting their affairs, turned away from obeying their Lord, and their hearts became distracted from remembrance and oblivious to contemplating His majesty and beauty, glorified is He.

In the Most High's words ﴿And the wrongdoers conspired in secret: "Is this not but a human like you?"﴾ is an indication of the bad state of some who deny the friends of God, the Most High. Their wicked, devilish souls refuse to follow them because they see them sharing in human accidents.

﴿And how many a city have We destroyed which had been wrongdoing﴾: in it is an indication that in wrongdoing lies the ruin of civilization. Whenever a person wrongs, his heart is ruined, and this leads to the ruin of his body and its destruction by punishment.

In the Most High's words ﴿Rather, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, and thereupon it departs﴾ is an indication that constant remembrance is the cause of the clearing of darkness from the heart and its purification from the defilement of other things, to the point that nothing remains in it except Him, glorified is He.

﴿And those who are with Him﴾: it was said they are the perfected ones who are in the presence, for they neither move nor rest except in presence. Worship does not weigh on them, and trade does not distract them from Him, the Most High. Their inner selves are with the Truth and their outer selves are with creation. Their breaths are glorification and sanctification, and He, glorified is He, is the best of companions for them.

In the Most High's words ﴿But they are honored servants﴾ ﴿who do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾ is an indication that the perfected one does not choose anything, but rather his way is surrender and submission to the flow of destinies, with a contented soul. From this, it has been said that the divine pole, Shaykh 'Abd al-Qadir al-Kilani, may his secret be sanctified and his kindness cover us, did not die until he ascended from the station of entitlement to pure surrender. Shaykh 'Abd al-Wahhab al-Sha'rani explicitly stated this in his book al-Jawahir wa'l-Yawaqit.

﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾: what is in it of indication has already been mentioned.

﴿Every soul will taste death﴾. Al-Junayd, may his secret be sanctified, said: "Whoever's life is by his spirit, his death will be by its departure, and whoever's life is by his Lord, the Most High, he is transferred from the life of nature to the life of origin, which is life in truth."

﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾. It was said: that is, by subjugation and gentleness, separation and union, turning away and turning toward, ignorance and knowledge, and so on. It is not hidden that the seeker is often tested with contraction and expansion, so he should be steadfast in each, lest it lower him from his rank. Perhaps the trial of expansion is stronger than the trial of contraction, so one should guard oneself there with the utmost vigilance.

﴿And We set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection﴾. Some of the Sufis said: The scales are many. For the lovers there is a scale, for the bewildered a scale, for the workers a scale, and so on. Among these is a scale for the knowers (al-'arifin), by which their breaths are weighed, and the heavens and the earth cannot weigh a single one of them.

They mentioned that in this world there are also scales, the greatest of which is the Sharia, and the two pans of the Book and the Sunnah. By my life, the Sufis of this age have indeed neglected this scale. May God, the Most High, protect us and the Muslims from the error they are in. He, Mighty and Majestic, is the One who bestows favors of every kind.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 48:

﴿And We certainly gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion, and a light and a reminder for the God-conscious,﴾ This is a kind of elaboration (tafsil) of what was stated in summary in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send before you any but men to whom We revealed⁠—﴾ up to His words, glorified is He: ﴿and We destroyed the transgressors﴾ [al-Anbiya' 7-9]. It also indicates how they were saved and how their enemies were destroyed. Its introduction with the oath of emphasis serves to show the utmost care given to its content. By "the Criterion" is meant the Torah, and likewise by "the light" and "the reminder." The conjunction (al-'atf) is as in the line of verse:

To the sovereign, the lordly one, and the son of the champion, and the lion of the battalion in the thick of the crowd.

Al-Tibi reported that the conjunction "wa" was inserted before ﴿ḍiyā'an﴾ (light), although it is a descriptive term (sifah) in meaning but not in wording, just as it is inserted before a descriptive term that is descriptive in wording, such as His words, exalted is He: ﴿when the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease say﴾ [al-Anfal 49; al-Ahzab 12]. Sibawayh said: when you say "I passed by Zayd and his companion," it is permissible; but if you say "I passed by Zayd, then his companion" with fa', it is not permissible as it is with waw, because fa' implies sequence and the postponement of the noun from the word it is joined to, unlike waw. As for the saying of the poet:

Alas for Ziyabah, for al-Harith, the one who rose at dawn, then the one who gained spoils, then the one who returned,

it was expressed with fa' and is acceptable because it is not a descriptive term in that sense, since the alif-lam is in the meaning of "who": that is, "the one who rose at dawn, then the one who gained spoils, then the one who returned." Abu al-Hasan (al-Akhfash) permits the matter with fa' just as he permits it with waw. End of quotation.

The meaning: "And by God, We certainly gave the two of them a comprehensive Book, which is evidently a separator between truth and falsehood, a light by which one is guided in the darkness of ignorance and error, and a reminder by which people are admonished and take heed." The specification of the God-conscious for mention is because they are the ones who benefit from it, or it mentions what they need of laws and rulings, or it is an honour for them.

It has also been said: the Criterion is victory, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿on the day of the Criterion﴾ [al-Anfal 41], and it was applied to it because it distinguishes between the ally and the enemy. This is reported in a narration from Ibn 'Abbas. In that case, the light is either the Torah, or the Sharia, or the white hand. And the reminder has one of the meanings mentioned.

It is related from al-Dahhak that the Criterion is the splitting of the sea, and al-firq and al-filq are siblings in meaning. Mujahid and Qatadah adopted the first view, and it is the one most fitting to the course of the noble text, for it serves to establish the matter of the Qur'an as sharing with the other divine books, especially the Torah, in the qualities mentioned; and also because the splitting of the sea is what the disbelievers demanded the like of, by their saying: ﴿Let him bring us a sign as the earlier messengers were sent with﴾ [al-Anbiya' 5].

Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak read (ḍiyā'an) without waw, taking it as a circumstantial accusative (hal) from (al-furqan). This reading also supports the first interpretation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 49:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Those who fear their Lord﴾: it is in the genitive position (majrur al-mahall), as an adjectival qualifier of praise (sifah madihah) for "the God-fearing" (al-muttaqin), or as a substitute (badal), or as an explanatory apposition (bayan), or in the accusative or nominative by way of praise (al-madh). The meaning, under every one of these analyses, is that they fear the punishment of their Lord.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿in the unseen﴾ (bil-ghayb) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object, meaning: they fear that [punishment] while it is unseen by them and not visible to them. In this there is an implicit reference (ta'ridh) to the disbelievers, in that they are not affected by warning until they witness what they have been warned of.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is a circumstantial clause from the subject (fa'il), meaning: they fear Him while absent from the eyes of people. Ibn 'Atiyyah preferred this view. It was also said: they fear Him in their hearts. ﴿And they, of the Hour, are apprehensive﴾, that is, fearful in a manner of concern (bi-tariq al-i'tina'). The sentence may be coordinated with the relative clause (al-silah) or may be a new independent sentence (al-isti'naf). The fronting of the prepositional phrase (taqdim al-jarr) is for the sake of the rhyming endings (ri'ayat al-fawasil). The specific mention of their apprehension of the Hour after describing them with fear in general terms serves to announce that it is the greatest of created things (li-l-i'dhan bi-kawniha mu'zam al-makhluqat), and to specify their being characterized by the opposite of what characterized those who seek to hasten [the Hour]. The choice of the nominal sentence indicates that their state concerning the Hereafter is constant apprehension (al-ishfaq al-da'im).

﴿And this﴾, that is, the Noble Qur'an, is referred to with "this" to indicate that it is easy to take up and that its matter is clear. It was said that the reference is to its nearness in time. ﴿Is a reminder﴾ by which whoever remembers will be reminded. It is described with the last attribute of the Torah because it suits the context and agrees with what passed at the beginning of the noble surah, along with the inclusion of everything previously mentioned in its description in His words, glorified is He: ﴿blessed﴾, that is, abundant in good and copious in benefit. Indeed, there has returned to us, and to God Most High belongs all praise, from its blessing what has returned.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿We have sent it down﴾ are either a second attribute of ﴿reminder﴾ or another predicate of ﴿this﴾. In both cases there is in it, as regards the magnification of the matter of the Noble Qur'an, what there is. ﴿Then are you deniers of it?﴾ is a rebuke of their denial after it has become evident that it is like the Torah. It is as if it were said: after you have known that its state is like the state of the Torah, are you deniers of its being sent down from Us? For that, after observing the condition of the Torah, has no room at all. The placing of the prepositional phrase first is for the sake of the fawasil (verse-endings), or for restriction, because they acknowledge other than it among what is in the hands of the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 51:**

﴿And We had certainly given Ibrahim his right judgment﴾. That is, the rushd (right guidance) that befits him and comparable great messengers. It is complete rushd: being guided to the paths of goodness in religion and in worldly life, and guiding others by the divine laws (nawamis ilahiyya). It was said: it means the scriptures (suhuf). It was said: it means wisdom (hikma). It was said: it means being granted success in goodness from childhood. Some scholars preferred to take it in its general sense.

Isa al-Thaqafi read *rashadahu* with a fatha on the ra' and the shin. Both forms are dialectal variants, like *al-huzn* and *al-hazan* (both meaning sorrow).

﴿min qabl﴾ (before this) means before Musa and Harun. It was also said: before puberty, when he came out of the *sirb* (hiding place). It was said: before he was born, when he was in the loins of Adam (peace be upon him). It was said: before Muhammad (ﷺ). The first view is narrated from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both. Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: this is the view most suitable in both wording and meaning. As for the first view, it is because of proximity. As for the second, it is because the mention of the prophets (peace be upon them) is for consolation and encouragement to follow them. The expected order would have been to mention Nuh, then Ibrahim, then Musa (peace be upon them). However, the arrangement considered the reinforcement of consolation and encouragement, so Musa (peace be upon him) was mentioned, because his situation, what he endured from his people, the abundance of his signs and the density of his community resembled the situation of our Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him). Then he turned to mentioning Ibrahim (peace be upon him). It was also said that *min qabl* refers to this: do you not see the saying of Allah, ﴿And Nuh, when he called out before (this)﴾ [al-Anbiya: 76], meaning before these mentioned persons? It was also said: before Ibrahim and Lut. End of quote.

﴿and We were knowing of him﴾, that is, of his circumstances and the perfections in him. This is like your saying about a good person among people: "I know so-and-so," for he is among those who possess the finest qualities.

It is also permitted that this is a *kināya* (metonymy) for Allah's preserving him and not letting him be lost. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said on the day he was thrown into the fire, and when Jibril (peace be upon him) said to him, "Ask your Lord," "His knowledge of my state suffices me from asking." This, however, is contrary to the apparent meaning.

[Page 59]

﴿When he said to his father and his people﴾ is an adverbial complement (*zarf*) governing *ātaynā* (“We gave”). It is taken to mean a broad period of time in which the giving occurred, along with what followed from it of his sayings and actions. It has also been permitted that it be a *zarf* governing *Rushd* (“right guidance”) or *ʿĀlimīn* (“we knew”). It may also be a *badal* (substitute) for the position of ﴿min qablu﴾ (“before”), or be in the accusative by an implied verb, as in *aʿnī* (“I mean”) or *adhkuru* (“I mention”). He began with the mention of the father because he, peace be upon him, considered it most important to give counsel and to rescue him from error.

It is apparent that he, peace be upon him, said to him and to his people, gathered together: ﴿What are these statues to which you are devoted?﴾ He, peace be upon him, meant “What are these idols?” but expressed them as *tamāthīl* (“statues”) to belittle their status, since *timthāl* is a made image resembling a creature of God Most High, from *mathhaltu al-shayʾa bi al-shayʾ* (“I likened one thing to another”), when you liken it to it. It is said they were images of men whom they venerated, and those men had passed away. It is also said they were images of the stars, which they fashioned according to what they imagined. Pointing to them with what is used for something near also indicates belittlement. Asking about them with *mā* (“what”), by which the reality is sought to be made clear or the meaning of the name explained, is a feigned ignorance of the one who knows, as if he did not know what they were, though in fact he, peace be upon him, knows that their reality is a stone or the like.

*Al-ʿukūf* is turning to a thing and remaining attached to it out of reverence for it. It is also said that it means staying and persisting with a thing for some purpose. On both explanations it falls short of worship, and so the choice of this word implies an extreme disparagement of the act of worship. The *lām* in *lahā* (“to them”) is for specification (*bayān*), so it is connected to an implied element, as in God Most High’s words: ﴿You interpret dreams﴾ [Yusuf: 43]. Or it is for causation (*taʿlīl*), so it is connected to *ʿākifūn* (“devoted”), and it is not for transitivity, because *ʿakafa* is only transitive with *ʿalā*, as in God Most High’s words: ﴿who cling devotedly to idols of theirs﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 138]. Here the description takes the place of an intransitive verb, meaning: “those to whom you are doers of devotion.”

Abū Ḥayyān favoured the *lām* being causal, with the complement of *ʿākifūn* omitted, i.e., “devoted to their worship.” It is permitted that the *lām* means *ʿalā* (“upon”), as was said regarding God Most High’s words: ﴿and if you do evil, it is for yourselves﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 7]. In that case it is connected to *ʿākifūn* on the basis that it is for transitivity.

It has also been permitted that *al-ʿukūf* be interpreted as *al-ʿibāda* (“worship”), and then the *lām* is, as was said, a support particle (*diʿāma*), not a transitive one, since the verb is transitive by itself. This view is preferred because of what follows. It was said that it is not far-fetched for the *lām* to indicate specification, with the prepositional phrase connected to an implied element that serves as the predicate, and *ʿākifūn* is a second predicate. You know that a negation following it is obstinacy.

Some people did not accept the interpretation of *al-ʿukūf* as worship, because of what Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Abī al-Dunyā in *Dhamm al-Malāhī* (“The Condemnation of Diversions”), Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and al-Bayhaqī in *Shuʿab al-Īmān* transmitted from ʿAlī, may God honour his face, that he passed by people playing chess and said: “What are these statues to which you are devoted? For one of you to touch a live coal until it is extinguished is better for him than to touch them.” There is an obvious problem with this. Yes, it is not far-fetched that the better reading is to keep *al-ʿukūf* on its apparent meaning. Nevertheless, the primary purpose is to inquire about the reason for the worship and to rebuke them for it in the gentlest manner. When they did not find anything to rely upon regarding their practice, they resorted to clinging to mere blind imitation (*taqlīd*), where

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verses 53–54:

﴿They said: "We found our fathers worshipping them."﴾ And he, peace be upon him, refuted that by way of emphatic oath, where ﴿he said: "Indeed you and your fathers have been in clear error"﴾, those whom you found thus, ﴿in error﴾, of a wondrous kind whose extent cannot be measured, ﴿clear﴾, manifest and evident, such that it is not hidden from anyone of sound intellect that it is error, because you and they relied not on any proof but on followed desire and obeyed Satan. ("You") is an emphasis for the connected pronoun in ("you were"), and it is necessary according to the Basrans (the grammarians of Basra), because of the permissibility of coordinating (a noun) with such a pronoun. The meaning of "you were in error" is the absolute continuity and firm establishment of their being in it, not their past state of continuity that occurred before the time of address, which encompasses them and their fathers. In choosing ("in error") over ("erring") there is evident emphasis on their error. The verse is evidence that falsehood does not become truth by the multitude of those who adhere to it. ﴿They said﴾: when they heard his statement, peace be upon him, (they said it) as an expression of disbelief that what they were upon was error, and of amazement at his misguiding them, peace be upon him, in the most complete manner.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verses 53–54:

﴿They said: "We found our fathers worshipping them."﴾ And he, peace be upon him, refuted that by way of emphatic oath, where ﴿he said: "Indeed you and your fathers have been in clear error"﴾, those whom you found thus, ﴿in error﴾, of a wondrous kind whose extent cannot be measured, ﴿clear﴾, manifest and evident, such that it is not hidden from anyone of sound intellect that it is error, because you and they relied not on any proof but on followed desire and obeyed Satan. ("You") is an emphasis for the connected pronoun in ("you were"), and it is necessary according to the Basrans (the grammarians of Basra), because of the permissibility of coordinating (a noun) with such a pronoun. The meaning of "you were in error" is the absolute continuity and firm establishment of their being in it, not their past state of continuity that occurred before the time of address, which encompasses them and their fathers. In choosing ("in error") over ("erring") there is evident emphasis on their error. The verse is evidence that falsehood does not become truth by the multitude of those who adhere to it. ﴿They said﴾: when they heard his statement, peace be upon him, (they said it) as an expression of disbelief that what they were upon was error, and of amazement at his misguiding them, peace be upon him, in the most complete manner.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 55:**

﴿Have you brought us the truth?﴾ That is, in earnest. ﴿Or are you among the players?﴾ That is, among the jesters. The interrogative here is not meant literally. It is an interrogative of disbelief and astonishment. Their words ﴿or are you…﴾ and so on are a parallel to it, a fair statement that subtly hints, in the most delicate way, that the established case is the second alternative, because of the various kinds of emphasis it contains. Al-Zamakhshari (author of al-Kashshaf), as noted in al-Kashf, indicated that the original form would be: "Is what you have brought to us earnestness and truth, or is it play and jest?" However, he departed from this to the wording the noble text has, for the reason already indicated.

The author of al-Miftah (al-Sakkaki) said: that is, "Have you newly renewed and introduced among us the pursuit of truth, or are these still the habits of youth continuing?" This is closer to the apparent meaning, and it contains an indication of the benefit of deviating from the expected parallel, whether apparently, or in clarifying what is meant by "coming." The apparent sense of the words of the two shaykhs (al-Zamakhshari and al-Sakkaki) is that "am" (ام) is connected (muttasila, i.e., the disjunctive question linked to a preceding question). Al-Allama al-Tibi (al-Tibi, the commentator on al-Kashshaf) preferred that it is disconnected (munqati'a, i.e., "am" introducing a new question), and said: When they heard from him, peace be upon him, what indicates the belittling of their gods and the misguidance of them and their fathers in the most eloquent manner, and they witnessed from him harshness and earnestness, they asked him, peace be upon him, for proof. It is as though they said: "Grant that we have followed our fathers in what we are in; do you have any evidence for what you claim? Have you brought us the truth?" Then they turned away from that and came with "am," which includes the meaning of "bal" (بل, "rather") of disengagement and the implied interrogative hamza. So they disengaged with "bal" from what they had affirmed for him, and affirmed with the hamza, by way of emphasis and certainty, the opposite of it. For they decided that he is a player and not truthful at all, because their placing him among the players, that is, "You are immersed in play, included in the group of those whose utmost aim in establishing claims is play and frivolity," indicates by allusive metonymy (al-kinaya al-ima'iyya) that proof and evidence are not his concern. This metonymy makes you aware that "am" cannot definitely be connected, and likewise "bal" in what follows. The truth is that the permissibility of disconnection is beyond doubt, but as for its being obligatory, there is what there is in that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 56:

﴿He said: "Rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the One who originated them"﴾ That is, who brought them into being together with what is in them of created things, among which are you, your fathers, and what you worship, without any model to imitate or any pattern to follow. This is a shift from their misguidance in worshipping idols, and from denying that these deserve such worship, to clarifying the truth and specifying the one who deserves to be worshipped.
