The pronoun in ﴿fataranna﴾ ("who originated them") either refers to the heavens and the earth, which is what Abu Hayyan inclined to, and his description of Him, exalted is He, as the one who brought them into being right after describing Him as their Lord serves to establish the truth and to alert that whatever is not like this is far removed from the lordship which is the source of the right to be worshipped. Or it refers to the images (al-tamathil), and this was preferred on the grounds that it is included in establishing the truth and guiding the addressees to it. This pronoun is not among the pronouns that are specific to rational feminine beings, as Ibn Atiyya assumed, so as to require a strained justification for its returning to what is not rational. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I am of those who bear witness to that﴾, it is a concluding statement (tadhil) containing a rejection of their attribution to him, peace be upon him, of play and jest. The demonstrative refers to what was mentioned. The first preposition-phrase is connected to an omitted element, meaning: "And I am a witness to that among the witnesses," or it is in the sense of explanation, meaning: "I mean, concerning that." Or it is connected to the adjective after it, although it is within the relative clause of "al" (the definite article), due to the widely known opinions on the broad usage of adverbial expressions. The meaning is: "And I am, concerning that which I have mentioned, among those who know it in truth, establishing it by proof, and I am not among the players." For the witness to a thing is one who verifies it and establishes it, and his testimony to that is his presenting the proof for it and affirming it by it.

Shaykh al-Islam said: His saying ﴿Rather, your Lord﴾, etc., is a turning away from what they based their statement on, namely the belief that those images are their lords. As if it were said: "The matter is not so; rather, your Lord, etc." Al-Qadi said: It is a turning away from his, peace be upon him, being a player by establishing proof for what he claimed. Al-Tibi took it as a turning away from that as well, and said: This answer comes in the wise style, and it would have been apparent that he, peace be upon him, should answer them with his saying "Rather, I am among those who are truthful and I am not among the players." Instead he said ﴿Rather, your Lord﴾ and the verse, so as to alert, by it, that my refuting what you are devoted to and my misguiding you is something that needs no proof, because it is clear; but look at this great matter, which is that you abandon the worship of your Creator, the owner of your affairs, your provider, the owner of the worlds, and the One who originated what you are devoted to, and you occupy yourselves with worshipping it instead of Him. What falsehood could be more manifest than that, and what misguidance could be clearer than it?

His saying ﴿And I am of those who bear witness to that﴾ is a concluding statement to the answer, with what corresponds to their saying ﴿Or are you of the players?﴾ in terms of style, which is metonymy (kinaya), and in terms of structure, which is making the predicate depend on the pronoun. It is as if he said: "I am not among the players in claims, but among those who know them by decisive proofs and manifest arguments, like the witness by whom we cut off claims." And it is not hidden that this can be applied to the possibility that "am" is a connected interrogative particle, so understand, reflect, and so it becomes clear to you which of the interpretations of this turning away is preferable.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 57:

﴿And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols﴾ That is, I will strive earnestly to break them. The root of kayd (plotting) is to devise a scheme to cause harm while displaying the opposite of it, and this requires striving, so it is used figuratively to mean that. It also signals the difficulty of seizing the opportunity and its dependence on using stratagems, so that they would take precautions in guarding them, and thus the attainment of the target would be more complete in rebuking them. This was a resolve on his part, peace be upon him, to guide them away from their misguidance by another means. And it is not contradicted by what is narrated from Qatadah, who said: "We consider that he, peace be upon him, said that out of their sight." It is also said that one man among them heard it, and it is said that some of their weaker ones, among those who walked at the back of the people on the day they went out to the festival, heard it. The idols were seventy; and it is said seventy-two.

Qara'a Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Ahmad ibn Hanbal (﴿بِاللَّهِ﴾) with the letter ba' (bi-), which is the second of the letters, and it is the original of the particles of oath, since it enters upon both nouns and pronouns, and it is used with the verb of swearing either explicitly or omitted. The ta' (in tallah) is a substitute for the waw, as in tujah (in front of). The waw stands in place of the ba' because of the affinity between them, in that both are labial (shafawiyyah), and in that the waw conveys a meaning close to the meaning of ilsaq (adherence), as many grammarians have stated. Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr criticized this, saying that no evidence supports it. Al-Suhayli assigned it a different reading, and what analysis requires is that none of these particles is originally derived from another. Some differentiated between the ba' and the ta' by saying that the ta' (tuthannah) carries an added meaning, namely wonder (ta'ajjub), and the wonder here is at his, peace be upon him, undertaking a matter fraught with risk. The statements of the grammarians are that the ta' may or may not carry wonder, while the lam is the one that necessarily carries wonder in oaths. Others differentiated between them in usage, saying that the ta' is used only with the glorious name of Allah, or with Rabb (Lord) when attached to the Ka'bah, rarely.

﴿After you have turned away, retreating﴾ from worshipping them to your festival. Isa ibn Umar read (تَوَلَّوْا) from tawallī, with one of the two tas deleted, which is the second according to the Basrians and the first according to Hisham. This reading is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they turned away from him, retreating﴾ [al-Saffat: 90].

The fa' in His words ﴿So he made them﴾ is explicative (faṣīḥa), meaning: they turned away, so Abraham, peace be upon him, came to the idols and made them ﴿judhādh﴾, i.e., fragments (quṭaʿan). It is fuʿāl in the sense of mafʿūl (broken), from al-jadd, which is cutting (al-qaṭʿ). The poet said:

Banū al-Muhallab—may God cut off their root (jadda Allāhu dābirahum),
they became ashes, with neither root nor branch (fa-lā aṣlun wa-lā ṭarfun).

So it is like al-ḥuṭām (debris) from al-ḥaṭm, which is breaking (al-kasr). Al-Kisāʾī, Ibn Muḥayṣin, Ibn Muqsim, Abū Ḥaywa and Ḥumayd read (jiḏāḏan) with a kasra on the jīm. In one narration al-Aʿmash read it likewise. Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Nahīk and Abū al-Sammāl read (jaḏāḏan) with a fatḥa. The ḍamma is the reading of the majority (al-Jumhūr). As related from Ibn Jinnī, from Abū Ḥātim, these are dialectal forms (lughāt), the best of which is the ḍamma. Quṭrub stated that in its three forms it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that is neither dualised nor pluralised. Al-Yazīdī said: judhādh with a ḍamma is the plural of judhādha, like zujāj and zujāja. It was also said that with a kasra it is the plural of jadhīdh, like karīm and kirām. It was also said that with a fatḥa it is a verbal noun like al-ḥaṣād, in the sense of the mahṣūd (the harvested thing).

Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb read (judhudhan) with two ḍammas, the plural of jadhīdh, like sarīr and sururr. It was also read (judhadhan) with a ḍamma then a fatḥa, the plural of juddha, like qubba and qubab, or the lightened form of fuʿul with two ḍammas.

It is related that Āzar took him out with them to a festival of theirs. They began with the house of the idols, entered it, prostrated to them, and placed food among them, which they took out with them, saying: "Until we return, may the gods bless our food." They went off. When Abraham, peace be upon him, was on the road, his resolve to go with them was turned back, so he sat down and said: "Indeed I am sick." He entered upon the idols while they were arranged in rows, and there was a great idol facing the door, which was of gold, with two jewels in its eyes that shone at night. He broke them all with an axe that was in his hand, and left none except the largest, and hung the axe around its neck. It was also said that it was in its hand. This is His words, exalted is He: ﴿except a great one among them﴾, i.e., the idols, as is apparent from what will follow, God willing. The pronoun for rational beings here and in what preceded is according to the belief of the disbelievers. The "greatness" is either in rank according to their belief as well, or in bodily size. Abū Ḥayyān said: it is possible that the pronoun refers to the worshippers. It was said: this is supported by the fact that had it referred to the idols, it would have said "except their chief."

﴿so that they may return to him﴾ is a resumption (istiʾnāf) explaining the reason for the breaking and the sparing of the great one. The pronoun in (ilayhi), according to the majority, refers to Abraham, peace be upon him, i.e., so that they may return to Abraham, peace be upon him, and not to anyone else, so that he may argue with them and rebuke them with the answer that will follow, God willing. It was also said: the pronoun refers to God, exalted is He, i.e., so that they may return to God, exalted is He, and to His oneness, when they ask him, peace be upon him, and he answers them, showing the impotence of their gods. From this it is known that His words, glorified is He, ﴿except a great one among them﴾ are not extraneous to the context according to this view, as was supposed. Yes, its distance is not hidden.

It is related from al-Kalbī that the pronoun refers to the great one, i.e., so that they may return to the great one, as one returns to the learned in resolving difficulties, so they say to him: "What is wrong with these, broken, and what is wrong with you, intact? And the axe is in your neck, or in your hand?" At that point it becomes clear to them that he is powerless, neither benefiting nor harming, and it becomes evident that they are in great ignorance in worshipping him. It seems this was based on Abraham's assessment of them, peace be upon him, from what he had tested and experienced of their obstinacy against their reason and their belief in their gods and their veneration of them. It is also possible that he, peace be upon him, knew that they would not return to him, but that this was by way of mockery and ridicule, and taking into account the state of the great one in their eyes, for the analogy of one who is prostrated to and deemed fit for worship is that one should return to him in resolving difficulties. On both possibilities there is no difficulty in the entry of la-ʿalla into the speech, and this view is the quickest of the views to come to mind. But the majority of the exegetes hold the first view. The prepositional phrase is attached to (yarjiʿūna), and the fronting (taqdīm) is for restriction (ḥaṣr) according to the three views, as it is said. It was also said: it is definite for that in the first view, and not definite for it in the last two; rather, it is permissible that it is for fulfilling the requirement of the verse-ending (fāṣila). So reflect.

The act of Abraham, peace be upon him, in breaking the idols may be taken as a supporting indication for those of our scholars who said that there is no liability on one who breaks what is made of pottery, for example, of figurines (ṣuwar) for children and the like to play with. This is the well-known opinion among the majority.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 59:

﴿They said﴾ — that is, when they returned from their festival and saw what they saw — ﴿"Who has done this to our gods?"﴾ — this great deed. They said it in the manner of denunciation, reproach and vilification. The expression "gods" (ālihah) is used here rather than "idols" (aṣnām), or "these" (hāʾulāʾ) is used, for the sake of emphasis in the vilification.

صفحة 63

And His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿"Indeed, he is among the wrongdoers"﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'nāf) confirming what precedes it. Abu'l-Baqa' permitted that "man" (man) be a relative pronoun (mawṣūla), the subject of a nominal sentence, and this clause be in the place of nominative predicate (khabar) of it, meaning: "The one who did this smashing and breaking to our gods — indeed he is counted among the ranks of the wrongdoers," either because of his audacity in humiliating them, while they are deserving of veneration, or because of exposing himself to destruction, or because of his excess in the smashing and breaking. And "ẓulm" (wrongdoing) in all three aspects means placing a thing in other than its proper place.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 60:

﴿They said﴾, that is, some of them, namely those who heard his saying, peace be upon him: ﴿By Allah, I will surely plot against your idols﴾ in the presence of some people, ﴿We heard a young man mentioning them﴾, that is, disparaging them, ﴿so perhaps he is the one who did this to them.﴾ The verb "sami'a" (to hear), as some of the eminent scholars said, should by its nature take one object, like the rest of the verbs of the senses, as al-Suhayli (al-Suhayli, d. 581 AH, a grammarian and exegete) established. It often takes its object directly, and it may also take it with "ila" (to), "li" (for) or "ba'" (with). As for whether it takes two objects, scholars disagreed. al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash al-Awsat, d. 215 AH, a grammarian) held this view. al-Farisi (Abu 'Ali al-Farisi, d. 377 AH, a grammarian), in al-Idah, and Ibn Malik (d. 672 AH, a grammarian) and others held that if the verb is followed by something that can be heard, it takes one object, as in "sami'tu al-hadith" (I heard the speech), and this is agreed upon. If it is followed by something that cannot be heard, it takes two objects, the second of which indicates a sound.

Some scholars stipulated that it must be a clause, as in "sami'tu Zaydan yaqulu kadha" (I heard Zayd say such-and-such), not "qa'ilan kadha" (saying such-and-such), because the latter indicates an essence that cannot be heard. As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Do they hear you when you call?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 72], it is by supposing an elided noun, meaning "Do they hear your call?" It has been said that the noun to which the adverbial phrase is attached stands in for it, but this is open to scrutiny. Some scholars said that the verb governs one object, with an elided noun "masmu'" (heard) before the noun denoting the essence, and the clause, if it is a circumstantial clause (hal) after a definite noun or a qualifying clause (sifa) after an indefinite noun, cannot be a second object, because it is not so except in verbs that govern a subject and predicate, and this verb is not one of them.

This was objected to on the grounds that it belongs to the verbs that are cognate with the verbs of knowledge ("'ilmiyya"), because hearing is a means of knowledge, as in al-Tashil (Ibn Malik's al-Tashil) and its commentaries. Thus it was permitted here that "fata" (young man) be the first object and the clause "yadhkuruhum" (who mentions them) be the second object. It was also permitted that "fata" be the object and the clause be a qualifying clause for it, since it is indefinite. It was said that the clause is an apposition (badal) to it. Some scholars preferred this by saying that it avoids any figurative use or implied elision, since the clause is what is heard, and the apposition is what is intended in relation to the sense. Apposition of a clause to a singular noun is permissible. In al-Hama' (al-Hama' by al-Suyuti, a grammar work), it is stated that the apposition of a clause to a singular noun is "badal al-ishtimal" (partial apposition, where the second term includes or relates to the first). In al-Tasrih (Sharh al-Tasrih by Khalid al-Azhari, d. 905 AH), it is stated that a clause may be an apposition to a singular noun in the sense of "badal kull min kull" (whole-for-whole apposition). So pay attention. Some scholars said that the clause being a qualifier is more eloquent in ascribing the mention to him, peace be upon him, because it places the action on the one who is heard, and makes him as if he were the one heard, as an exaggeration of the absence of any intermediary. This indicates that they heard him without any intermediary.

Some scholars assigned the eloquence to other reasons than those mentioned, which have been discussed. Perhaps the reason mentioned is what is possible under the possibility of apposition, so the emphasis is not lost on it. It may be said that this construction, however it is parsed, is more eloquent than your saying "sami'na dhikra fatan" (we heard the mention of a young man) and the like, where no two objects are needed by consensus. This is because "sami'na" (we heard), when it is connected to "fata", indicates in general that what was heard is something like his mention, since it makes no sense for the essence itself to be heard. Then, when "yadhkuruhum" (who mentions them) is mentioned, that is known a second time. Also, the judgment is strengthened by the repetition of the predication, as explained in the science of rhetoric ('ilm al-ma'ani). For this reason the style of the verse was preferred over others, so reflect.

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿He is called Abraham﴾, it is a qualifying clause for "fata". It was also permitted that it be a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani). The first is more apparent. "Ibrahim" is in the nominative case as the deputy subject of "yuqal" (is called), according to the preference of al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH, exegete and grammarian) and Ibn 'Atiyya (d. 541 AH, exegete). What is meant is the word itself, that is, this word is applied to him. Scholars differed over whether the object of a verb of saying may be a single word that does not express its meaning as a full clause, like "qultu qasidatan" (I said a poem) and "khutbatan" (a sermon), or be a verbal noun of a saying or its qualifier, like "qultu qawlan" (I said a saying) or "haqqan" (truly). al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH, grammarian), al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kharuf (d. 609 AH, grammarian) and Ibn Malik held that it is permissible when the single word is intended as its own wording. Al-Dunushari (d. 6th century AH, grammarian) mentioned that if the single word that follows the saying is intended as its own wording, it must be quoted and its inflection preserved. Others held that it is not permissible. Abu Hayyan (d. 745 AH, grammarian and exegete) said: "This is the correct view, since it is not preserved in their speech that they said 'Zayd is Zayd' or that they said 'darab' (he struck). The saying in their speech occurs only to quote sentences and what has a similar meaning." Those who prohibited it made "Ibrahim" nominative as the predicate of an elided subject, meaning "he is" or "this is Ibrahim", and the clause is quoted by the saying, as in the saying of the poet:

When I tasted her mouth, I said: "It is the taste of wine."

It was also permitted that it be the subject of an elided predicate, meaning "Ibrahim" is the one, or that it be a vocative from which the vocative particle is elided, meaning "He is called, when he is summoned: 'O Ibrahim!'" In my view, the verse is clearly in accordance with what al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya chose, and clarity is sufficient to decide in such matters. Al-A'lam (al-A'lam al-Shantamari, d. 476 AH, grammarian) held that "Ibrahim" is nominative by default ("al-ihmal"), because no governing word preceded it that affects its form. The saying does not affect anything except a single word that contains the meaning of a clause, so it remained unaffected, and an unaffected word, when joined to another, takes the nominative, as in the common expression "wahid wa ithnan" (one and two) when they count and do not introduce a governing word either in form or in implication, and they coordinate some numerals with others. It is not hidden that the speech of this al-A'lam is not uttered except by the most ignorant, and for a man to be more successful and more knowledgeable would be better for him than to utter the like of it or speak it.

﴿They said﴾: those who said this. ﴿Who did this﴾, etc., if the matter is so. ﴿Then bring him﴾, i.e., produce him, ﴿before the eyes of the people﴾, present and in plain view before them, in the most complete manner, as the preposition ʿalā (on, upon) used metaphorically (isti'ara, metaphor) conveys, for the sake of making the seeing firm. ﴿So that they may bear witness﴾, i.e., that they may attend our punishment of him. It has also been said that they will bear witness to his deed or to his saying that, in which case the pronoun does not refer to the people in general but to some of them, unspecified or known. The first view is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and the second from al-Ḥasan and Qatāda. The expression of hope (al-tarajjī) is more fitting to it.

﴿They said﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new sentence that answers an implied question), arising from the narration of their statement. It is as if it were said: "What did they do with him after that? Did they bring him or not?" So it is answered: ﴿They said: "Did you do this to our gods, O Ibrahim?"﴾ The narration is limited to their address to him, peace be upon him, to draw attention to the fact that bringing him and their haste to do so is a certain matter that needs no explanation. The interrogative particle, as the scholar al-Taftazani said, is the hamzah (الهَمْزَةُ) used for affirmation regarding the agent, since the disbelievers' intention was not to make him, peace be upon him, admit that the breaking of the idols had occurred, but to make him admit that he was responsible for it. How could it be otherwise, when they pointed to the act in their words: ﴿Did you do this?﴾ And also

This is the commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 63:

﴿He said, "Rather, this one, their chief, did it."﴾ If the question were a rebuke by means of the act, the answer would have been "I did it" or "I did not do it." Al-Khatib objected to this, saying that the interrogative (istifham) may remain on its original sense, since nothing in the context indicates that they knew he, peace be upon him, was the one who broke the idols, so that it would be impossible to read it as a true question. This was answered by saying that what precedes the verse indicates it, namely that he, peace be upon him, had sworn, saying, ﴿By God, I will surely scheme against your idols﴾, etc. Then, when they saw the idols broken, they said, ﴿Who did this?﴾ etc. Thus it is apparent that they knew this from his oath and his disparagement of the idols. It may be said that the oath, as many have said, was in secret, or that only one man heard it. His, exalted is He, saying, ﴿They said, "We heard"﴾ etc., from His saying, ﴿They said, "Who did this?"﴾ etc., indicates that some of them did not know that he, peace be upon him, was the one who broke the idols. So it is not far-fetched that ﴿Did you do this?﴾ was the statement of that group. It may also be said that after they discussed the matter of the idols, and some of them informed the others of what convinced them that he, peace be upon him, was the one who had broken them, they all became certain that he was the breaker.

Page 65

So "Did you do this?" was addressed to the one in question, as a rebuke by means of the doer. In his answer, he, peace be upon him, took an allusive course (ma'arid) that led him to his aim, which was to establish the proof against them in the most subtle and best manner, prompting them to reflect on the condition of their gods. This course also guarded against lying. The chief expressed a statement in the manner of one directly performing the act, by attributing it to himself, just as he presented it in that manner as an act, by placing the axe on his neck or in his hand. He intended to attribute it to himself by way of causation (tasabbub), since he saw their veneration of him was greater than their veneration of all the other idols that were with him, arranged in rows for worship besides God, exalted is He. So he became exceedingly angry about this, and attributed the act to himself by way of rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), in view of his being the one who motivated it. The original would be "I did it, because of the increase in my anger at the increase in the veneration of this." He did not break them, though that was what his anger required, so that the proof would become evident. Calling that a lie, as stated in the authentic hadith, is by way of metaphor, since allusive speech resembles it in form. Thus the argument based on what was mentioned, against the lack of infallibility ('ismah) of the prophets, peace be upon them, is invalid.

It was also said in explaining this that it is a report of what follows from their doctrine as permissible. That is, since they held that he is the greatest of the gods, his supreme divinity requires that no other be worshipped alongside him, and requires the destruction of whoever shares with him in this. So it is as if it were said: "This great one did it according to the requirement of your doctrine," and the proposition is possible.

It is related that he, peace be upon him, said: "This, their chief, did it, being angered that these should be worshipped alongside him, though he is greater than them." It was said: then this would be an illustration, by which he, peace be upon him, intended to alert them to the anger of God, exalted is He, against them for associating others with Him by worshipping idols. It was also said that he, peace be upon him, intended by that only to affirm the act for himself in the most eloquent manner, including in it mockery and misguidance, as when someone unlettered says to you, regarding something you wrote in an elegant hand, while you are famous for beautiful handwriting: "Did you write this?" and you reply to him: "Rather, you wrote it." You did not intend to negate it from yourself and affirm it for the unlettered one. You only intended to affirm and establish it for yourself, along with mockery of your interlocutor.

The author of al-Fara'id criticized this, saying that it is valid only if the act revolves between him, peace be upon him, and their chief, and does not admit a third party.

It was answered that this is not valid, because the question in "Did you do this?" is a rebuke, not a true interrogative, as you have heard from the 'Allamah, and as Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir and Imam al-Sakkaki stated explicitly. Thus the possibility of a third party is ruled out. Even if it were granted that the interrogative is on its apparent sense, the indication in the answer, by ascribing the act to what is not fit for it, with the particle bal (idrab, "rather"), is sufficient, because its meaning is that the question has no basis, and that no one but me is fit for this act. Yes, it may be objected that their being directed toward this, namely reflection on the state of their gods and establishing the proof against them, is as indicated by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Ask them, if they can speak.﴾ That is, if they are among those who can speak, which is not apparent in this case. It was also said that ﴿He did it, their chief﴾ is, in meaning, the answer to His saying ﴿if they can speak﴾, and His saying "Ask" is a parenthetical clause linked by the fa' (then), as in the line of poetry: "Know, for a man's knowledge benefits him." So the chief's being the doer would be conditioned upon their speaking and dependent on it, and that is impossible, so what it depends on is likewise impossible. Ibn Qutaybah pointed to something like this, but it is contrary to the apparent sense.

It was also said that the speech is complete at His saying ﴿He did it﴾, and the concealed pronoun in it refers to "a youth" (fata) or to Ibrahim. But it is not hidden that neither "a youth" nor Ibrahim was mentioned in a statement that was uttered in the presence of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, such that the pronoun could refer to him. Also, the particle of retraction (idrab) is not in its proper place in that case, and the fitting answer would be "Yes" (na'am). There is no reason to depart from the apparent sense here, as it has been said. It is also attributed to al-Kisa'i that he made the pause at ﴿He did it﴾ as well, except that he said the doer is omitted, meaning "He did it, the one who did it."

Page 66

Abu al-Baqa' criticized this, saying that it is far-fetched, because omitting the doer is not permissible, according to the majority. Otherwise al-Kisa'i holds that its omission is permissible.

It was also said that one may say he meant by omission the concealment (idmar), and most of the readers today pause at that, but this is not valid. It was said that the pause is at "their chief," and by it he meant him, peace be upon him, himself, because a human being is greater than any idol. In my view this interpretation is a kind of nonsense (hadhayan). Similar to it is that it could be meant as God, mighty and majestic, for He, exalted is He, is the greatest of the gods, and what they intended by them is not considered. It is attributed to al-Farra' that the fa' in "He did it" is conjunctive, and "'alah" means "la'allahu" (perhaps he), shortened.

He cited in support of this the reading of Ibn al-Sumayqa' "fa'allahu" with a doubled lam. But it is not hidden that the speech of God, the Mighty, exalted is He, should be above such an interpretation. The verse, on this reading, is extremely obscure, and what has been mentioned of its meaning is far from its wording. Some claimed that the verse is on its apparent sense, and asserted that it is permissible for the prophets, peace be upon them, to utter a lie for a benefit. But this entails the removal of trust in the laws, since there is the possibility of lies in them for a benefit. Therefore the truth is that there is no lie at all, and that in allusive speech there is ample room to avoid lying. He, peace be upon him, said ﴿if they can speak﴾ rather than "if they can hear" or "if they can understand," even though the question also depends on hearing and understanding, because the outcome of the question is the answer, and their not speaking is more evident, and rebuking them with it is more effective. This was achieved, as was expressed by

**Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 64:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So they returned to themselves﴾ meaning they reflected, pondered, and remembered that whatever cannot ward off harm from itself, nor inflict harm on the one who broke it in any way, is impossible to be able to ward off harm from others or bring benefit to them. So how could it deserve to be worshipped?

﴿Then they said﴾ meaning some of them said to others among themselves: ﴿Indeed, you are the wrongdoers﴾ meaning: by worshipping that which does not speak. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Or, by your questioning Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and your turning away from questioning them, that is, your gods. This was mentioned by Ibn Jarir. Or, by the very act of your questioning Ibrahim (peace be upon him), since it contained a rebuke that entails punishment, as has been said. Or, by your negligence regarding your gods and your failure to protect them. Or, by worshipping the lesser ones alongside this great one. Wahb said both of these. Or, by your accusing Ibrahim (peace be upon him) while the axe was on the neck of the great one. This was said by Muqatil and Ibn Ishaq. The restriction (ḥaṣr) here is relative (iḍafi), with reference to Ibrahim (peace be upon him).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 65:

﴿Then they were turned upside down onto their heads.﴾ The root meaning of al-naks (reversal, overturning) is turning a thing so that its upper part becomes its lower part. The mention of "the head" is not superfluous; it is either for emphasis or is considered a specification (tajrid). The word naks may also be used linguistically for the general turning of a thing from one state into another, and "the head" is mentioned for depiction and for censure.

Al-Zamakhshari, as reported in al-Kashshaf, mentions three interpretations of what is meant here.

The first is that it is a return from the upright and sound thinking, in regard to wronging themselves, to corrupt thinking, in permitting their worship while acknowledging that their condition falls short of that of an animal, let alone being in a position of divinity. So the meaning of ﴿Certainly you know that these do not speak﴾ is: it is not hidden from us and from you, O one who reproves them, that they do not speak; yet we take them as gods while knowing their attribute. The evidence for this is Ibrahim's (peace be upon him) reply that follows. The second is that it is a return from disputing with him (peace be upon him) in falsehood, in their saying ﴿Who has done this to our gods?﴾ and their saying ﴿Was it you who did this?﴾, to arguing for him with the truth in their saying "Certainly you know." For it is a denial of power from them and an acknowledgment of their impotence, and that they are not fit for divinity. It is called a "naks" even though it is true, because it did not give them a firm conviction; it is a naks relative to what they were upon of falsehood, since they acknowledged their impotence and yet persisted. In Lubab al-Tafsir there is something close to this in its basis, except that it estimates the return from disputing with him in their saying ﴿Indeed you are the wrongdoers﴾ to be arguing with him (peace be upon him) in falsehood in their saying "Certainly you know."

The third is that naks is an intensification of their lowering of their heads in shame, and their saying "Certainly you know" etc. is a throwing out of bewilderment; for this reason they uttered that which is an argument against them. It is permissible that it be taken as a metaphor for the intensity of bewilderment and the collapse of their argument, for this does not contradict the literal sense. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: this is a fine interpretation, and so is the first.

That the intended meaning is naks in opinion was narrated by Abu Hatim from Ibn Zayd, and it applies to the first two interpretations. Mujahid said: the meaning of ﴿they were turned upside down onto their heads﴾ is that the base ones turned back upon the leaders. Thus "the heads" refers to the leaders. My own view is that the third interpretation is the more apparent. In any case, the prepositional phrase ("onto their heads") is connected to nukisu (they were turned upside down).

It is also permitted that it be connected to an omitted verb functioning as a circumstantial clause (hal), and the sworn clause is a quoted speech of an implied saying, meaning: saying "Certainly..." etc. The address in ("you know") is to Ibrahim (peace be upon him), not to everyone who is fit to be addressed. The negated clause occupies the position of the two objects of "knew" if it takes two objects, or the position of a single object if it takes one. The intended meaning is the continuation of the negation, not the negation of continuation as the form of the present tense may suggest. Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi Abla, Ibn Muqsim, Ibn al-Jarud and al-Bakrawi, both of them from Hisham, read "nukkisu" with a doubled kaf. Ridwan ibn Abd al-Ma'bud read "nakasu" with a single kaf in the active voice, meaning they turned themselves upside down; it is also said that they turned back upon their leaders, in accordance with what Mujahid's interpretation requires.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 66:

﴿He said﴾ — upon him be peace — rebuking them: ﴿Do you then worship﴾, i.e., do you know this and yet worship, ﴿besides Allah﴾, i.e., going beyond worshipping Him, the Exalted, ﴿that which can neither benefit you at all﴾ in the way of benefit; and it has been said: "with anything." ﴿Nor harm you﴾, for knowledge of its state, which is incompatible with divinity, is among the things that definitively necessitate abstaining from worshipping it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 67:

﴿Uff to you and to what you worship besides Allah!﴾ This is an expression of exasperation on his part, peace be upon him, at their persistence in falsehood after the excuse had been cut off and the truth had become clear. The origin of uff ( uffin) is the sound made by one who is disgusted at the filthiness of something, as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said; then it became a verb-noun (ism fi'l) meaning "I am exasperated." It has many dialectal forms. The lam (la) is for specifying the one at whom the complaint is directed, and the mention of the noble Name (Allah) in the place where a pronoun might have been used is for the greater emphasis on the ugliness of what they did. ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ That is, will you not reflect, so that you would understand the ugliness of your action?

﴿They said﴾, that is, some of them said to others when they were unable to argue and their stratagems had run out. This is the habit of the falsehood-follower who is refuted: when he is confounded by the proof and still has some power, he resorts to hostility. ﴿Burn him﴾, for fire is the severest of punishments, and for this reason it has been said that none punishes with fire except its Creator. ﴿And support your gods﴾ by avenging them, ﴿if you are going to act﴾, that is, if you are going to be supporters of your gods with real support. So choose this for him. Otherwise you have neglected to support them, and it is as if you had done nothing for them at all. The turn away from "support your gods" to "burn him" in the noble text suggests this. Nimrod ibn Kan'an ibn Sanharib ibn Nimrod ibn Kush ibn Ham ibn Noah, peace be upon him, gave this counsel according to the well-known account, and all of them approved it.

Ibn Jarir reported from Mujahid, who said: I recited this verse to Abdullah ibn Umar, and he said: "Do you know, O Mujahid, who it was who advised the burning of Abraham, peace be upon him, with fire?" I said: "No." He said: "A man from the Arabs of Persia, meaning the Kurds." He specified that he was a Kurd: Ibn Atiyya. It is mentioned that God caused the earth to swallow him, and he is still sinking into it until the Day of Resurrection. His name, as Ibn Jarir reported, [is given]

[page 68]

by Ibn Abi Hatim from Shu'ayb al-Jabbai as Hayun, and it was said Hadir. In al-Bahr it is stated that they mentioned a name for him about which there is disagreement, and no certain reality can be established concerning it. It is also reported that when they resolved to burn him, they imprisoned him, then built for him a structure like an enclosure at Kuthā, a village among the villages of the Nabataeans within the borders of Babylon in Iraq. This is the saying of God Most High: ﴿They said: Build for him a structure and cast him into the blazing fire﴾ (37:97). They gathered for him hard firewood of various kinds over a period of forty days, then they kindled a great fire, so intense that no bird could pass over it in the upper air because of its fierce heat. They did not know how to cast him into it, so Iblis came to them and taught them the making of the catapult (manjaniq), and they made it. It was also said that the Kurd who had advised burning made it. Then he was swallowed by the earth. Then they went to Abraham, peace be upon him, and placed him in the catapult, bound and shackled. The angels of the heavens and the earth cried out: "Our God, there is no one on Your earth who worships You except Abraham, peace be upon him, and he is to be burned for Your sake. So permit us to support him." He, exalted and majestic, said: "If he seeks help from any of you, let him help him. If he calls on none but Me, then I know him best, and I am his Protector. Leave him to Me, for he is My friend, I have no friend other than him, and I am his God, he has no god other than Me." Then the keeper of the winds and the keeper of the waters came to him, asking his permission to extinguish the fire. He, peace be upon him, said: "I have no need of you. God is sufficient for me, and He is the best Disposer of affairs."

It is reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he said: When they bound him to cast him into the fire, Abraham, peace be upon him, said: "There is no god but You, glory be to You, to You belongs all praise, to You belongs the dominion, You have no partner." Then they threw him, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, came to him and said: "O Abraham, do you have any need?" He said: "As for you, no." Gabriel, peace be upon him, said: "Then ask your Lord." He said: "My knowledge of my condition is enough for me in place of asking."

It is also related that the gecko (wazagh) was blowing on the fire, and this is found in a narration of al-Bukhari.

In al-Bahr, the exegetes mentioned things said to have come from the gecko, the mule, the swallow, the frog, and the bat, and God Most High knows best concerning that. When he, peace be upon him, reached the enclosure, God Most High made it, by the blessing of his saying, a garden, and that

God's saying, exalted is He: ﴿O fire, be cool and safe for Abraham.﴾ That is, "Be cool and safe": "be of coolness and safety," meaning "cool yourself with a coolness that does no harm." For this reason 'Ali, may God honour his face, said, as related by Ahmad and others: "Had He not said *and safety* (wa salaman), its coolness would have killed him." The verse contains several intensifications: the fire, which is subjected to God's power, is made obedient and submissive; the phrase "be of coolness" is used in place of "cool yourself"; and the genitive ("the coolness of") is omitted, with the thing it modifies put in its place. It has also been said that *salaman* is in the accusative governed by a verb implied in the sentence, meaning "and We made safety for him," so that the clause is coordinated with *We said* (qulna). This is contrary to the apparent sense, which the reports support.

It is related that the angels took hold of Abraham's arms and set him down on the ground, and there was a spring of sweet water, red roses and narcissus, and the fire burned nothing except his bonds, as related from Ka'b. It is also related that he remained in it for forty or fifty days, and he said: "I never had a more pleasant life than when I was in it." Ibn Ishaq said: "God sent the angel of shade in the form of Abraham to keep him company." They also said: "God, Mighty and Majestic, sent Gabriel with a shirt of Paradise silk and a carpet (tanfasa). He dressed him in the shirt, seated him on the carpet, and sat with him conversing. Gabriel said: 'O Abraham, your Lord says: Do you not know that the fire does not harm My beloved?'"

Then Nimrod looked out from a high place of his and saw him sitting in a garden, with the angel seated beside him and the fire surrounding him. He called out: "O Abraham, how great is your God, whose power has reached the point of coming between you and what I see! O Abraham, can you come out of it?" Abraham said: "Yes." He said: "Do you fear that if you sleep in it, it will harm you?" He said: "No." He said: "Then get up and come out of it." So he rose and walked in it until he came out. Nimrod met him, honoured him, and said: "O Abraham, who was the man I saw with you in your likeness, sitting beside you?" He said: "That was the angel of shade, whom my Lord sent to keep me company in it." Nimrod said: "O Abraham, I will offer to your God a sacrifice (qurban), because of what I have seen of His power and might in what He did for you, when you refused anything but His worship and His unity. I will sacrifice to Him four thousand cows." Abraham said to him: "God, exalted is He, will not accept from you what you did while following your religion, until you abandon it and return to my religion." He said: "I cannot give up my kingdom, but I will sacrifice them to Him." So he sacrificed them, and he left off from Abraham.

At that time Abraham was sixteen years old. In some reports, when they saw that he had not burned, they said: "He has enchanted the fire," so they threw into it an old man of their own, who burned. In another report, when they saw him safe and that nothing of him had burned except his bonds, Haran, the father of Lot (ﷺ) [as the text states], said: "The fire does not burn him because he has enchanted it. But put him on something and light a fire beneath him, for the smoke will kill him." So they placed him on chaff and lit a fire beneath him, and a spark flew to Haran's beard and burned him.

'Abd ibn Humayd related from Sulayman ibn Surad, who had met the Prophet (ﷺ), that Abu Lut said, and he was his paternal uncle: "The fire did not burn him for the sake of his kinship to me." So God sent a tongue of fire that burned him. The reports about this story are numerous. But al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan) said: "People have said much about what happened to Abraham, but what is sound is what God mentioned: that he was cast into the fire, and God made it cool and safe for him."

Then the apparent meaning is that God Himself is the one who said to it "Be cool," and that there was a real speech. It has been said that the speaker was Gabriel, by God's command. It has also been said that this speech is a metaphor for making it cool. The apparent meaning also is that God, Mighty and Majestic, stripped it of its distinctive properties of heat and burning and left in it its light and brightness. It has been said that it turned into pleasant air, and that in this form it is one of the greatest extraordinary events. It has also been said that it remained as it was, but God, whose power is exalted, repelled its harm, as one sees with the salamander, as His saying ﴿for Abraham﴾ suggests. This is because what is mentioned is contrary to the customary, so it is specific to the one to whom it was given, and with respect to others it remains on the original basis, without regard to the concept of the designation (mafhum al-laqab), since most scholars do not consider it valid. Some of the earlier reports support this.

Whatever the case, it is a great sign. Something similar may occur for some of the righteous of the Muhammadan community as a karamah (a miracle granted to a saint) for them, because they follow the beloved Prophet (ﷺ). What is observed of this occurring to some of those who claim affiliation to the presence of the perfect saint, Shaykh Ahmad al-Rifa'i, may his secret be sanctified, from the wicked who came close, because of the extent of their wickedness, to being unbelievers, is said to be a kind of sorcery, the disbelief of whose practitioner and whose execution are disputed. They have names of unknown meaning which they recite when entering the fire and when striking themselves with weapons. It is not far-fetched that these are disbelief, even if they are accompanied by things that are not disbelief. Some have mentioned that at that moment they say: "Talsaf talsaf, hayf hayf, I seek refuge in the perfect words of God from the evil of what He created. I adjure you, O fire, or O weapon, by the truth of the living, the adorned, the light of the Sabhi, and Muhammad (ﷺ), that you not harm me, or that you not harm the youth of the path." This did not happen in the time of Shaykh al-Rifa'i, may his mighty secret be sanctified, for he was the most attached of people to the sunnah (the Prophet's practice) and the most careful to avoid the places of innovation (bid'ah). His companions followed his way and clung to the hem of his guidance, may his secret be sanctified. Then some of those who claimed affiliation with him experienced what they experienced.

In al-'Ibar (of al-Dhahabi) he said: "Corruption has multiplied among the companions of the Shaykh, may his secret be sanctified, and satanic states have appeared among them since the Tatars took Iraq: entering fires, riding wild beasts, and playing with snakes. This is something the Shaykh did not know, nor did his righteous companions. We seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan." End of quotation.

The truth is that reciting anything over them is not a condition for not being affected by entering fire and the like. Many of them call out, when the fire is lit for them and the tambourines are beaten, "O Shaykh Ahmad! O Rifa'i!" or "O Shaykh so-and-so!" naming a shaykh from whom they took the path, and they enter the fire and are not affected, without reciting anything at all. Most of them, when they recite the names over the fire without the tambourines being beaten for them, and without any change of state in them, are not able to touch a live coal. Sometimes it happens that one of them recites the names, the tambourines are beaten for him, and he calls on whichever shaykh he calls on, then he enters and is affected.

In sum, we have not seen for them any firm rule. However, the general pattern is that when the tambourines are beaten for them and they call for help from their shaykhs and become wild, they do what they do and are not affected. I have seen some of them take a skin of wine, call on whoever they call on, enter a large oven in which the fire blazes, sit in the fire, drink the wine, and remain until the fire goes out. Then they come out, and nothing of their clothing or body has burned. The closest thing said about such cases is that it is *istidraj* (a gradual lure leading to ruin) and a trial. As for saying that God, Mighty and Majestic, honoured the presence of Shaykh Ahmad al-Rifa'i, may his secret be sanctified, by making his followers, whoever they are, unaffected by fire and the like, and by weapons and other things, when they cry out his name or the name of one of his followers in certain circumstances, that is far-fetched. Indeed, I think you would say it is not permissible. It may happen to some believers in some circumstances as a help to them. Some people take fire in their hand and are not affected, because of substances they smear on their hands, which have the property that fire does not harm the body when it is smeared with them. The one who does this then gives the impression that it is a karamah.

Furthermore, those who say that God has placed in each thing a specific property, as His wisdom requires, have cited this verse as evidence. The difference between water and fire, for example, is not merely that God's custom is to create burning and the like in the presence of fire, and quenching and the like in the presence of water. Rather, He placed in this the specific property of quenching, for example, and in that the specific property of burning, for example. But this does not burn, and that does not quench, except by His permission, mighty and majestic is He. For if He had not placed in the fire heat and burning, He would not have said to it what He said. There is no one who holds a distinction. So reflect.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 70:**

﴿They intended a scheme against him﴾: a great plot, to harm him and to overpower him. ﴿So We made them the greatest losers﴾: that is, the greatest loser of every loser, since their effort to extinguish the light of the truth, by word and by deed, returned as a decisive proof that he, peace be upon him, was upon the truth while they were upon falsehood. It also raised his rank, peace be upon him, and made them deserving of the severest punishment. It has also been said: He made them the greatest losers in that He, glorified is He, gave power over them to something among His most insignificant and weakest creatures, namely the gnat, which fed on their flesh and drank their blood. He also gave power over Nimrod to a gnat, which kept tormenting him until he died, may God curse him. But the one relied upon is the first interpretation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 71:

﴿And We saved him and Lot﴾. He, according to what has preceded, was the son of his paternal uncle. It is also said that he was the son of his brother, and this is narrated in al-Mustadrak from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. The verb ﴿najjaynahu﴾ (We saved him) carries the sense of ﴿akhrajnahu﴾ (We brought him out) through what grammarians call tadmin (implying one verb in the sense of another). For this reason it takes ﴿ila﴾ (to) in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿to the land which We have blessed for the worlds﴾. It is also said that the phrase is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning "reaching the land," so there is no tadmin. By "this land" is meant the land of al-Sham (Greater Syria). It is also said to be the land of Mecca, and it is said to be Egypt, but the first view is the correct one. He described it with general blessing because most of the prophets, peace be upon them, were sent there, and their laws, which are the sources of perfections and of religious and worldly goods, spread throughout the world. He did not say "which We have blessed it" in order to emphasise by making it encompassing in blessing. It is also said that by the blessings is meant worldly favours such as fertility and other things, but the first view is clearer and more fitting to the condition of the prophets, peace be upon them.

It is narrated that he, peace be upon him, left Iraq with Lot and Sarah, the daughter of his paternal uncle Haran the Elder. Both of them had believed in him, peace be upon him. He sought to flee with his religion, so he descended at Harran and remained there for as long as Allah the Exalted willed. Some have claimed that Sarah was the daughter of the king of Harran and that he, peace be upon him, married her there, and that her father stipulated that he would not turn her away from her religion, but the first view is the correct one. Then he came to Egypt, then he left it for al-Sham, and he settled at al-Sab' (Beersheba) in the land of Palestine. Lot settled at al-Mu'tafikah, at a distance of one day and night's journey from al-Sab', or nearer. In the verse there is praise of al-Sham, of what it contains. In a hadith: "There will be a migration after a migration, and the best of the people of the earth will be those who most cling to the place of migration of Abraham." It was recorded by Abu Dawud.

Page 71

And from Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Blessed (tuba) are the people of al-Sham." I said: "And what is that, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Because the angels, peace be upon them, spread their wings over it." It was recorded by al-Tirmidhi from Bahz ibn Hakim, from his father, from his grandfather.

As for Iraq, al-Ghazali, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned in the chapter on tribulation (al-mihnah) in al-Ihya' the consensus of a group of scholars on its blame, on the disliking of residing in it, and on the recommendation of fleeing from it. Perhaps the reason for this is too evident to need explanation, so we will not delve into it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 72:

﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob as a nāfilah (an extra gift)﴾, that is, a gift, as has been narrated from Mujahid. And ʿAṭāʾ said: it derives from nafalahu, meaning aʿṭāhu (he gave him). It is, according to what Abu Hayyan chose, a verbal noun like al-ʿāqibah and al-ʿāfiyah, in the accusative governed by "We gave," on the pattern of qaʿadtu juluusan (I sat, a sitting). A group chose that it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from Isaac and Jacob, or that it means "a child was born" or "an addition to what he (peace be upon him) asked for," and that is Isaac; so it would be a ḥāl from Jacob. There is no ambiguity in this, due to the clear indicator. ﴿And each﴾ of those mentioned, namely Abraham, Lot, Isaac, and Jacob, peace be upon them, not some of them without others, ﴿We made righteous﴾, by granting them success in righteousness in religion and in worldly life, so they became perfect.

And We made them leaders (a'imma) who are followed in matters of religion, ﴿guiding﴾ the community to the truth ﴿by Our command﴾ to do so, and by Our sending them, until they became perfecters (of others). ﴿And We inspired them to do good deeds﴾ so that perfection would be complete by joining action to knowledge. According to what al-Zamakhshari and those who followed him held, its origin is that the verb is formed as ﴿yuf'alu al-khayrat﴾ (the good deeds are done), in the passive voice, with ﴿al-khayrat﴾ in the nominative as a deputy for the subject (na'ib al-fa'il). Then it became ﴿fi'lan al-khayrat﴾ (an act of good deeds), with the verbal noun (masdar) carrying tanwin and ﴿al-khayrat﴾ still in the nominative as deputy subject of the passive verbal noun. Then it became ﴿fi'la al-khayrat﴾, with the tanwin removed and the verbal noun put in construct with its object, which stands in place of its subject. The argument, as it has been said, is that ﴿fi'la al-khayrat﴾ in the verbal-noun sense is not "inspired"; what is inspired is that they should do (an yaf'ala). The verbal noun of the passive form and the resulting thing (al-hasil bi-l-masdar) are like two synonyms. Also, revelation is general to the prophets mentioned, peace be upon them, and their communities, and therefore the verb was put in the passive form.

Abu Hayyan criticized this, saying that forming the verbal noun as a passive (with a deputy subject) is disputed. al-Akhfash permitted it, but the correct view is that it is prohibited. What was mentioned about the generality of revelation does not necessitate this here, since the verbal noun may be active and, in meaning, annexed to an omitted apparent noun that includes those who were inspired and others, i.e., "the deeds of the responsible people (al-mukallafin) are good deeds." It may also be annexed to those who were inspired, i.e., "that they should do good deeds." And if they were inspired with that, then their followers proceed in the same way, and it does not necessarily follow that it is specific to them. End of quotation.

It has been defended for al-Zamakhshari that what he mentioned is an explanation of a matter established in grammar, and the reason for it is two matters. The second is what was mentioned about the generality of revelation, which has been objected to; the first is free from objection. al-Khafaji mentioned most of this, then said: The apparent meaning is that the verbal noun here is for command, like "darb al-riqab" (striking the necks). In that case, the apparent meaning is that the address is to the prophets, peace be upon them, so the inspired thing is God Most High's saying: "Do good deeds." That is because revelation contains the meaning of speech, as they say, so it is connected to it, not to the act. However, it has been said that this is refuted by what was pointed out earlier, that what was mentioned is not among the rulings specific to the prophets, peace be upon them. But the matter here is easy. It is also permitted that the meaning is: We legislated for them the doing of that by inspiration to them. So reflect.

The discussion of His saying, Most High: ﴿and the establishment of prayer and the giving of zakat﴾ is in this same pattern. As many have said, it is conjoining the particular to the general (ʿatf al-khass ʿala al-ʿamm), to indicate its excellence and distinction. The original form of (iqam) is iqwam; its waw was changed to an alif after its vowel was moved to the preceding consonant, and one of its two alifs was deleted because two unvocalized letters met. Most often, a ta' (ة) is substituted for it, so one says iqamah. The ta' may also be omitted, either absolutely, as Sibawayh held, and the usage of Arabic supports this; or on condition of annexation, so that the annexed noun takes its place, as al-Farra' held. Abu Hayyan said this is a weaker view. What made the deletion good here is the (rhetorical) harmonization (mushakala) with the surrounding words. The verse clearly indicates that there was prayer and zakat in earlier communities, a matter on which the texts agree. However, these two were not like the prayer and zakat prescribed for this Muhammadan community, may God's best prayers and most complete salutations be upon its Prophet.

﴿And they were worshipping Us﴾ alone, to the exclusion of others, ﴿not letting anything other than Our worship occur to their minds.﴾ It is as if God Most High, by this, indicated that they fulfilled the covenant of servanthood, after He indicated that He, glory be to Him, fulfilled to them the covenant of lordship.

Page 72

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 74:

﴿And Lot﴾. It has been said that it is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb (idmar) that is explained by His words, ﴿We gave him﴾. That is, "And We gave Lot, We gave him," and the clause is conjoined to ﴿We granted him﴾. Glorified is He, in His words ﴿And We delivered him and Lot﴾, He gathered Abraham and Lot together. Then He specified the blessing bestowed on each of them individually, and what came between them is a general statement. Al-Tabarsi (al-Tabarsi) took the meaning of His words ﴿And each﴾ etc. to be: each of Abraham and his two sons, Isaac and Jacob, ﴿We made...﴾, so Lot, peace be upon him, is not included there. This has a basis. As for the view that the meaning is "each of Isaac and Jacob," it has no basis, and it requires strained effort to justify the plural that follows it. It has also been said that the verb "mention" (adhkur) is implied, and that the clause ﴿We gave him﴾ is a new sentence. ﴿Judgment (hukman)﴾ means wisdom, and by it is meant what is obligatory to do; or prophethood, since the prophet is a judge over his community; or the deciding of disputes between adversaries in judgment. It has been said that it means preserving the scrolls of Abraham, peace be upon him, but this is far-fetched. ﴿And knowledge﴾ of what is fitting for the knowledge of the prophets, peace be upon them all. ﴿And We delivered him from the town that used to do the vile deeds﴾. It has been said: that is, sodomy (liwat). The plural is used in view of the multiplicity of its types. It has also been said that what is meant is vile deeds in general, though the most abominable of them is sodomy. Ishaq ibn Bishr, al-Khatib and Ibn Asakir reported from al-Hasan who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Ten traits the people of Lot did, and for them they were destroyed: the mounting of men upon one another; throwing with the slingshot (julahiq) and the flicking of pebbles (khadhf); playing with pigeons; beating the frame drums (duff); drinking intoxicants; shaving the beard; lengthening the moustache; whistling (safr) and clapping; wearing silk; and my community will add to them one trait: the mounting of women upon one another.'"

That deed is attributed to the town by omitting the modifier and placing the modified noun in its position, so the epithet is causal (sababi), as in the saying: "A man came to me whose servant committed adultery." If the attribution were taken as figurative (majaz), without any omission, or the town were taken as a figurative reference to its people, that would also be permissible. The name of the town is Sodom (Sadum). It has been said that its villages were seven, and it referred to them by one of them because it is the best known. Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr said that it referred to them in the singular because its people were united in the vile act. It is also reported that all of them were overturned except Zaghar, because it was the home of those who believed in Lot, peace be upon him. The well-known view is that all of them were overturned.

﴿Indeed they were a people of evil, deviators﴾, that is, going out of obedience, not submitting to Lot, peace be upon him. The clause is a reason for ﴿used to do the vile deeds﴾. It has also been said that it is the reason for ﴿We delivered him﴾, and that, as you see, is weak.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 75:

﴿And We admitted him into Our mercy⦆ That is, into the people of Our mercy; that is, We made him one of them and counted him among them. Thus the sense of "into" (al-zarfiyyah, the sense of enclosure) is figurative. Or, "into Our mercy" means "into Our Garden," in which case the sense of "into" is literal, and "mercy" is a metaphor, as in the hadith of the two Sahihs: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said to Paradise: "You are My mercy; I show mercy through you to whomever I will of My servants." It is also permissible that "mercy" be a metaphor for prophethood, and that the sense of "into" be figurative too, so reflect upon this. ﴿Indeed, he is among the righteous⦆ who had the good reward preceded for them from Us. The sentence is an explanation (ta'lil) of what came before it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 76:

﴿And Noah﴾: that is, mention Noah, meaning his story, peace be upon him. Ibn 'Atiyyah claimed that Noah (Nuh) is conjoined (ma'tuf, 'atf) to Lot (Lut), who is the object of "We gave" (ātaynā), in the sense of "and We gave Noah." Abu Hayyan did not consider this unlikely, but it is not right (laysa bi-shay'). It is said that when He, glorified is He, mentioned the story of Abraham, peace be upon him, who is the father of the Arabs, He followed it with the story of the father of mankind, who is the second father, just as Adam, peace be upon him, is the first father. This is based on the well-known view that all the people who remained after the Flood are his descendants, peace be upon him. He is the son of Lamak ibn Matushalakh ibn Akhnukh, and he is Idris, it is said, and he is the longest-lived of the prophets, peace be upon them, according to what is in al-Tahdhib. Al-Hakim mentioned in al-Mustadrak that his name was 'Abd al-Ghaffar, and that he was called Nuh because of his excessive weeping over himself. Al-Jawaliqi said: the word Nuh is non-Arabic, arabicized (mu'arrab). Al-Kirmani added that its meaning in Syriac is "the one who rests" (al-sakin).

﴿when﴾ he called out, that is, he invoked God Most High with his words: ﴿I am overcome, so help [me]﴾ [al-Qamar 10], and his saying: ﴿My Lord, do not leave upon the earth any of the disbelievers as a dweller﴾ [Nuh 26]. Idh is an adverbial of time (zarf) governed by the omitted genitive-annexed noun (al-mudaf al-muqaddar), as we indicated. Whoever does not posit this omission makes it a comprehensive apposition (badal ishtimal) from Noah.

﴿from before﴾: that is, from before these who have been mentioned. We have already mentioned another view concerning qabl. ﴿So We answered him﴾ in his supplication ﴿and We rescued him and his family from the great distress﴾, which is the Flood, or the harm inflicted by his people. The root of karb is intense grief. It is said that it may derive from karb al-ard, meaning the turning over of the earth by digging, since grief stirs the soul in the way that stirs (the earth). Or it may derive from karabat al-shams, when the sun draws near to setting, since from intense grief the sun of the spirit almost sets. Or it may derive from al-karb, a thick knot in the rope of a bucket, since grief is like a knot upon the heart. Describing it as "great" (ʿazīm) is an emphasis on what the word itself already indicates.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 77:

﴿And We helped him against the people who denied Our signs﴾. That is, We protected him and defended him from them by destroying them and delivering him. It has also been said: that is, We helped him against them, so "min" (from) here means "ʿalā" (against). Some of the scholars said: the verb naṣara (to help) is transitive with both ʿalā and min. In al-Asās (Asās al-Balāgha by al-Zamakhshari), it says: "God Most High helped him against his enemy" and "helped him from his enemy." The distinction between them is made as follows: the verb transitive with ʿalā indicates mere assistance, while the verb transitive with min indicates that this assistance leads to retribution against the enemy and victory over him. ﴿Indeed they were a people of evil﴾, plunged deeply into wickedness. This clause gives the reason for what precedes it and paves the way for what follows, namely God's words: ﴿So We drowned them all﴾. Denying the truth and immersing oneself in evil is something that, in earlier nations, definitely results in destruction. As for the accusative of "ajmaʿīn" (all), it has been said that it is in the circumstantial (ḥāl) position relative to the object pronoun, but as you see, this is weak. Abu Hayyan said: it is in the position of emphasis (taʾkīd) for it. Indeed, the emphasis with ajmaʿīn not following kull (all) is frequent in the Qur'an, and this serves as evidence against Ibn Malik's claim that emphasis with it in this way is rare, while its more common usage is as a follower of kull, end of quote.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 78:

﴿And Dawud and Sulayman﴾. This is either a conjunction with (Nuh), governed by its verb, namely "mention" (udhkur) in the sense of "remember," as Ibn 'Atiyyah claimed. Or it is an object of an implied verb that is conjoined to that same verb, with an omitted noun in the sense "the story of Dawud and Sulayman." Dawud, son of Iyasha, son of 'Ubar, son of Ba'ir, son of Salmun, son of Yakhshun, son of 'Ami, son of Yarib, son of Hadrun, son of Faris, son of Yahudha, son of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, was, as narrated from Ka'b, red-faced, straight-haired, white-bodied, long-bearded with curly hair in it, and beautiful-voiced. Prophethood and kingship were combined for him. Al-Nawawi related from the historians that he lived one hundred years, and the period of his kingship within them was forty. He had twelve sons, and Sulayman, peace be upon him, was one of his sons. He, peace be upon him, was consulted in many of his affairs despite his young age, because of the abundance of his intellect and knowledge.

Ka'b mentioned that he was white, large, handsome, fair, humble and submissive. He became king, as the historians say, at the age of thirteen, and died at the age of fifty-three.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿when they both judged﴾ is an adverbial clause of time governed by that implied verb. Its being a substitution (badaliyyah) in the same manner as what has passed was also permitted. The meaning is "when they both judged." The verb is in the present form in order to narrate a past situation, to bring its image to mind. By "al-harth" (tilth) is meant here the crops.

Page 74

A group related from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that it means the vineyard. It was also said that the word is used for both, but in the sense of crops it is more common. Al-Khafaji said: perhaps it is used in the sense of vineyard metaphorically, by analogy with crops. The meaning is: when they both judged concerning the tilth. ﴿When the sheep of the people strayed into it﴾: this is an adverbial clause of time governing the judgment. Nafsh (straying) is the grazing of livestock at night without a shepherd, just as hamal is their grazing by day without one. Its original sense is spreading out and scattering, that is, when they scattered and dispersed. ﴿The sheep of the people grazed in it﴾ by night without a shepherd, so they grazed it and ruined it. ﴿And We were witnesses to their judgment﴾, that is, present in knowledge. The plural pronoun was said to refer to Dawud and Sulayman, and this is supported by the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, "to their judgment" (li-hukmihima) with the dual pronoun. From this, those who hold that the minimum of the plural is two derived their evidence. It is also permissible that the plural is for magnification, as in ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ (Al-Mu'minun: 99).

It was also said that the pronoun refers to the judges and the litigants. It was objected that attributing a judgment to the agent, in the sense of its occurrence by him, and to the object, in the sense of its happening to him, while both are in meaning governed by it, makes it unclear how they can be brought together in one phrase. It was answered that "judgment" here means "the matter," and there is no consideration here of his knowledge; consideration is given to it only when it is a pure verbal noun. More evident than this, as in al-Kashshaf, is that the specification comprises both the occurrence and the happening, and this is the meaning of the annexation (idafah). No regard remains for the action after it, neither verbally nor in meaning. So the meaning is: "and We were witnesses to the judgment that occurred among them." The clause is a parenthetical insertion confirming the judgment. It may also be said that it is praise for them, as if it were said: "and We were watching over their judgment, not allowing any flaw in it to stand." This is in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, you are under Our eyes﴾ (At-Tur: 48), in conveying care and protection.

And His saying, ﴿So We gave Solomon the understanding of it﴾, is a conjunction with ﴿judged﴾, for it has the sense of the past tense, as it passed.

Ikrimah recited (fa-afhamnaha) with the hamzah of causation (hamzat al-ta'diyah), and the pronoun refers to the judgment or the ruling (al-hukumah aw al-futya) understood from the context. It is narrated that there was a devout woman among the Children of Israel who had devoted herself (tabattalat) to worship, and she had two beautiful maidservants. One of them said to the other: "The trial has lasted long upon us. As for this woman, she does not desire men, and we will not cease to be in evil so long as we serve her. So let us disgrace her, so that she is stoned, and we will then go to the men." They took egg-white (ma' al-bayd), came to her while she was prostrating, uncovered her garment, and smeared it upon her rear, and they cried out that she had committed adultery (bagha). Whoever committed fornication among them, its punishment was stoning. She was brought before Dawud, and the egg-white was on her clothing, so he intended to stone her. Solomon said: "Bring fire, for if it is the semen of a man it will scatter, and if it is the egg-white it will coagulate." Fire was brought and he placed it upon it, and it coagulated, so he averted the stoning from her. Dawud, upon him be peace, was moved (`atafa) toward him and loved him greatly.

It happened that two men entered upon Dawud, upon him be peace, and one of them said: "This man's sheep entered my field at night and ruined it." He judged in his favor with the sheep. They went out and passed by Solomon, who was sitting at the door from which the litigants leave, and he said: "How did my father judge between you two?" They informed him, and he said: "Other than this is more gentle to both parties (arfaq bil-janibayn)." Dawud, upon him be peace, heard him, called him, and said to him: "By the right of prophethood and fatherhood, will you not tell me what is the gentler?" He said: "I think that you should give the sheep to the owner of the land, so that he may benefit from their milk, offspring and wool, and the field to the owner of the sheep, so that he may tend it until it returns to what it was; then they should exchange (yataraddaa)." He said: "The judgment is what you have judged," and he enforced the ruling accordingly. At that time his age was eleven years.

Many have held that their judgment, upon them both be peace, was by ijtihad (independent reasoning), and that is permissible for the prophets, upon them be peace, as is explained in the books of legal theory (al-usul). I too say this, for the statement of Solomon, upon him be peace, "other than this is more gentle", and then his saying "I think that you should give…" etc., is explicit that it was not by way of revelation; otherwise he would have decided the matter definitively and Dawud, upon them both be peace, would not have asked him to reveal what he had, but rather it would have been obligatory upon him to disclose it immediately and forbidden for him to conceal it. Moreover, it is apparent that he, upon him be peace, was not a prophet at that age, and it necessarily follows that the earlier judgment was likewise, since it is impossible for a judgment based on a text to be annulled by ijtihad. In al-Kashf it is stated that the claim that both rulings were by ijtihad is invalid, because the judgment of Solomon abrogated the judgment of Dawud, upon them both be peace, and ijtihad is never annulled by ijtihad. This indicates that both of them judged by revelation, and what was revealed to Solomon, upon him be peace, abrogated the ruling of Dawud, upon him be peace; or the judgment of Solomon alone was by revelation. And His saying, ﴿We gave him the understanding﴾, does not indicate that this was ijtihad.

It has been objected: if by "ijtihad is not annulled by ijtihad" he means that it is not annulled by the ijtihad of another so that one would be obliged to follow him in it, then this is not our concern; and if he means that it is not annulled by one's own ijtihad a second time, which is an expression for the change of one's ijtihad due to the appearance of another proof, then this is not invalid, as evidenced by the fact that the mujtahid may have two opinions reported from him on a single issue, like the old (qadim) and new (jadid) positions of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, and by the return of senior Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, to the opinions of some of them, though they were mujtahids. It has been said: it is possible that Dawud, upon him be peace, was revealed to retract his ijtihad and judge by what Solomon, upon him be peace, had judged by ijtihad. It has also been said: the non-annulment of ijtihad by ijtihad is among the special features of our Sharia. Moreover, it is reported in some traditions that Dawud, upon him be peace, had not finalized the judgment in that matter until he heard from Solomon, upon him be peace, what he heard.

Among those who chose that both judgments were by ijtihad is Shaykh al-Islam Mawlana Abu al-Su'ud, may his secret be sanctified. Then he said: "Rather, I say, and Allah the Exalted knows best: the opinion of Solomon, upon him be peace, was istihsan (juristic preference), as his saying 'more gentle to both parties' indicates, and the opinion of Dawud, upon him be peace, was qiyas (analogy), just as when a slave commits a homicidal offense, his master, according to Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, hands him over to the victim or ransoms him and sells him for that purpose, or ransoms him according to Imam al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him." End of quotation.

It has been reported that there was no discrepancy between the value of the field and the value of the sheep. As for Solomon, upon him be peace, he showed preference by making the benefit of the sheep equivalent to what was lost of the benefit of the field, without the owner's ownership of the sheep ceasing, and he obliged the owner of the sheep to work on the field until the harm he caused is removed. This is like what some of al-Shafi'i's companions said regarding one who usurps a slave who then runs away: he must pay the value, and the usurped owner benefits from it in exchange for the benefits the usurper deprived him of; then when the runaway is found, they exchange. End.
