As for the ruling on this issue in our Sharia: according to Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, there is no liability if there is no driver or leader with the animal, based on what al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from his saying (ﷺ): "The wound caused by an animal is unpaid (jubar)." There is no restriction in it to night or day. According to al-Shafi'i, liability is required at night but not during the day, based on what is in the Sunan, that the she-camel of al-Bara' entered a man's orchard and damaged it, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ruled that owners of property must guard it by day, and owners of livestock must guard it by night.

It has been answered that there is confusion (idtirab) in the hadith, and there is discussion about the men in its chain, and it is also possible that al-Bara' had released the camel (arsalaha), just as it is possible in this story that it was the same; thus there is no evidence in it.

﴿And to each﴾ of Dawud and Solomon ﴿We gave judgment and knowledge﴾, abundantly. Among that knowledge is knowledge of the way of ijtihad, not Solomon alone. So the clause is to dispel this misconception, and in it is evidence that an error by a mujtahid does not disqualify him from being a mujtahid. It has been said that the verse is evidence that every mujtahid in a matter where there is no decisive proof is correct, and the ruling of Allah the Exalted regarding him and his follower is what his ijtihad leads to in it, and there is no ruling of His, glory be to Him, prior to ijtihad. This is the view of the majority of the theologians among us, such as al-Ash'ari and al-Qadi, and among the Mu'tazila such as Abu al-Hudhayl, al-Jubba'i and their followers. It is also transmitted from the four Imams, may Allah be pleased with them, the view that every mujtahid is correct and that truth is one while some are in error; and al-Ash'ari is counted in al-Ahkam among those who hold this view. It has been refuted that Allah the Exalted singled out Solomon with understanding the truth in the case by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿We gave him the understanding﴾

(page 76) and that indicates that Dawud, upon him be peace, did not understand it in this case, for otherwise the specification would not be meaningful. Al-Amidi responded to this, saying: "One may say: the most that can be said of His saying, ﴿We gave him the understanding﴾, is the specification of him, upon him be peace, with the understanding, and it has no indication that this was not the case for Dawud, upon him be peace, except by way of implication (mafhum), which is not a valid proof. Even if we accept that it is a valid proof, it has been reported that both of them judged by the text with one ruling, and then Allah the Exalted abrogated the ruling in similar cases in the future, and Solomon knew of the abrogating text but Dawud, upon them both be peace, did not; so this was the understanding that was attributed to him. What indicates this is His saying, ﴿To each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾; and if one of them had been mistaken, then he would not have been given judgment and knowledge in that case. And even if we accept that their rulings differed, it is possible that both judged by ijtihad with permission to do so, and both were correct in the ruling, except that revelation descended in accordance with what Solomon, upon him be peace, had judged, so what he judged became the definite truth by the descent of revelation concerning it, and the understanding was attributed to Solomon, upon him be peace, for that reason. And even if we accept that Dawud, upon him be peace, was mistaken in that case, yet there was a text in it of which Solomon was informed and Dawud was not; and we concede error in a case such as this. The dispute is only where they judged by ijtihad and there is no text in the case." End of quotation.

Most reports support that the one who attained the judgment of Allah the Exalted in this case was Solomon, upon him be peace. What has been mentioned is not free from consideration, so reflect and ponder.

﴿And We subjected the mountains to Dawud, glorifying [Us]﴾: this begins an explanation of what is specific to each of them, upon them both be peace, of the honours of Allah the Exalted, after mention of the general honour to both of them, upon them both be peace. ﴿Glorifying﴾ (yusabbihna): they sanctify Allah the Exalted with the tongue of speech, as the pebbles glorified in the palm of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and people heard it. According to most, it was saying "Glory be to Allah the Exalted." Dawud alone heard it, according to what Yahya ibn Sallam said. It was also said that everyone heard it. It was also said that it was a voice that appeared to him from their direction though it was not from them, and this is contrary to the apparent meaning, and it does not contain the display of honour that the first view contains. Rather, if this is the echo, then it is nothing at all. Below that is what has been said: that it was by the tongue of state (lisan al-hal). It was also said: (yusabbihna) means "yasirna" (they travel), from sibahah (swimming). It has been objected that this contradicts the apparent meaning, and moreover this meaning was not mentioned by the lexicographers, nor does any other verse or report mention the mountains traveling with him, upon him be peace.

It was also said: the attribution of glorification to them is metaphorical, because they used to travel with him and they led whoever saw them to glorify, so it was attributed to them; and this, as you see, is weak.

Al-Jubba'i and Ali ibn Isa interpreted the meaning of glorification as travel as metaphorical, because travel is a cause of it, so there is no need to say it is from swimming; yet despite this, what it contains is not hidden. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) relating to ﴿the mountains﴾, or a resumptive clause explaining the manner of subjection. ﴿With﴾ (ma'a) is connected to the subjecting. Abu al-Baqa' said: "yasbahna" (they swim), and this is like His saying, ﴿O mountains, echo the glorification with him﴾ [Saba': 10]. The placing of the object first is for specification. From this one knows what is implied by taking glorification as glorification by the tongue of state and as what occurs through echo. ﴿And the birds﴾ is conjoined to ﴿the mountains﴾, or is an object with ma'a. In the reports there is explicit statement that they too glorified with him, upon him be peace, like the mountains. It was recited ﴿and the birds﴾ in the nominative (wa-al-tayru), as a beginning, with the predicate omitted, i.e., "and the birds are subjected." It was also said: it is conjoined to the pronoun in ﴿glorifying﴾, and this is permissible according to the Kufans. His saying, ﴿and We were doers﴾, is a concluding clause for what precedes it, i.e., it is part of Our way to do the like of it, so it is no novelty from Us, even if it is a wonder in your eyes.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 80:

﴿And We taught him the craft of making coats of mail﴾, i.e., the making of the coat of mail (dir'). Originally the term (libas, "garment") refers to anything worn. Ibn al-Sikkit cited:

"Wear for every circumstance its garment, whether its blessings or its hardships."

It was also said that (libas) is a name for all weapons, whether a coat of mail or otherwise. Al-Tabarsi preferred this view and cited al-Hudhali describing a spear:

Page 77

"With me is a (libas) for the fierce one, as if it were a horn on the forehead of a horned one, a gathering of sheep."

Qatadah said: "Coats of mail were previously plates. The first to weave and link them was Dawud (peace be upon him), so they combined lightness and protection." It is narrated that two angels descended from the sky and passed by him (peace be upon him), and one of them said to the other: "How excellent a man Dawud is, except that he eats from the public treasury." So he asked Allah, exalted is He, to provide him from his own earnings, and He softened the iron for him, and he made the coat of mail from it. It was also read (lubusa) with a damma on the lam. (Lakum) is related to a deleted element that occurs as a qualifier of (libas). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be related to (allamna) or to (san'ah).

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿so that it may protect you﴾ is related to (allamna), or it is a substitution of inclusion for (lakum) with the preposition repeated; it explains the manner of the particularity and the benefit derived from the lam of (lakum). The hidden pronoun refers to (libas), and the feminine form is according to the interpretation of "coat of mail," which is feminine by hearing, or it refers to "craft."

A group read (liyuhsinakum) with the yaa' (third person), on the basis that the pronoun refers to (libas) or to Dawud (peace be upon him), it was said, or to the teaching. It was also permitted that it refers to Allah, exalted is He, by way of iltifat (shift of person). This was supported by the reading of Abu Bakr from 'Asim, (linuhsinakum) with the nun. All these readings have a sukun on the ha' and are light (unstressed). Al-Faqimi, from Abu 'Amr, and Ibn Abi Hammad, from Abu Bakr, read with the yaa', a fatha on the ha', and a shaddah on the sad; Ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read with the taa' (second person) and the shaddah. ﴿from your might﴾: it was said, i.e., from the war of your enemy, and what is meant is what occurs in it; and it was said the statement is on the assumption of an elided noun, i.e., from the instrument of your might, such as the sword. ﴿Will you then be thankful?﴾ is a command that comes in the form of a question, because it contains a rebuke, by implying a shortcoming in gratitude, and by emphasis, indicating that gratitude is deserved to be performed without a command; so it asks whether that command, which must necessarily be carried out, has been carried out or not.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 81:**

﴿And to Solomon the wind﴾, meaning: We subjected the wind to him. The lam (preposition *li-*, "to/for") is used here but not with the first (the subjection of the wind follows a different construction from the earlier subjection mentioned in the verse), to indicate the difference between the two subjections. The subjection of what was subjected to him, peace be upon him, was by way of complete submission to him and obedience to his command and prohibition. This differs from the subjection of the mountains and the birds to David, peace be upon him, which was by way of following and emulating him, peace be upon him, in the worship of God, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿Violently blowing﴾ (*ʿāṣifatan*) is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative) from *al-rīḥ* (the wind), and its governing element (*al-ʿāmil*) is the implied verb, meaning: "And We subjected the wind to him while it was violently blowing." Describing it this way here does not contradict its description elsewhere as *rakhāʾ* (gentle), meaning good and mild, because *rakhāʾ* describes it in itself, while *ʿaṣf* (violence) describes it in terms of its covering a great distance in a short time, like a violent storm in itself. Thus, although it is gentle, it acts like a violent storm.

It is also permissible that it is described by each of the two descriptions relative to the time that Solomon, peace be upon him, wished it to be in. It was said that it was described as gentle in its going and as violent in its returning, following the custom of people in hastening back to their homeland. So it was violent at one time and gentle at another.

Ibn Hurmuz and Abu Bakr, in one narration, read *al-rīḥu* (the wind) in the nominative, in the singular.

Al-Hasan and Abu Raja' read *al-riyāḥa* (the winds) in the accusative, in the plural, and Abu Haywa read it in the nominative, in the plural. The reading in the accusative is clear. As for the nominative, it is that the nominative noun is the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), and the predicate is the fronted adverbial phrase (*al-ẓarf al-muqaddam*), while *ʿāṣifatan* (violently blowing) is a *ḥāl* from the pronoun of the subject within the predicate, and its governing element is what is contained in it of the sense of "being situated" (*al-istiqrār*).

﴿Running by his command﴾, meaning: by his will and in accordance with his desire, and this is a common usage. It is also possible that he commands it literally and God Most High creates for it an understanding of his command, as was said regarding the coming of the tree to the Prophet ﷺ when he called it. The clause is either a second *ḥāl* or a *badal* (substitution) from the first, as has been said, and you have already been reminded not far back of the discussion of substituting a clause for a single word, so remember that. Or it is a *ḥāl* from the pronoun of the first.

﴿To the land which We had blessed﴾, and it is [Page 78] Syria, as Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from al-Suddi. He, peace be upon him, had his dwelling there. So the meaning is that it runs by his command to Syria in the evening, after it had set out from there in the morning. Because it was widely known that he, peace be upon him, lived in that land, he did not mention its running by his command from there, and confined himself to mentioning its running to it, which is more evident as a favour. It was also said that his dwelling was Istakhr, and he, peace be upon him, would ride the wind from there, and it would run by his command to Syria.

It was said: It is possible that the land is more general than Syria. He described it as blessed because when he, peace be upon him, alighted in a land, he commanded the killing of its unbelievers, the establishment of faith in it, and the spreading of justice, and there is no blessing greater than that. It is unlikely that what is understood is that that land was blessed before arriving at it, whereas what has been mentioned implies that it is blessed after him. Even more remote is the view of Mundhir ibn Saʿid, who said: The speech is complete at His saying, Most High, ﴿to the land﴾, and *allatī bāraknā fīhā* (which We had blessed) is a description of *al-rīḥ* (the wind), and in the verse there is fronting and delaying, and the original is: "And to Solomon the wind which We had blessed, violently blowing, running by his command." Indeed, it is not hidden that the speech of God Most High, the Mighty, should not be interpreted in such a way, and the speech of the least of the eloquent would be above that. Then, the apparent meaning is that by *al-rīḥ* (the wind) is meant this well-known element, which is common to all its famous types. It was said: What is meant by it is *al-ṣabāʾ* (the east wind).

Some reports contain what apparently indicates this. Concerning Muqatil, he said: The devils wove for Solomon, peace be upon him, a carpet of gold and silk, a *farsakh* by a *farsakh* (about six kilometres square), and they placed for him a pulpit of gold on which he would sit, and around him were thrones of gold on which the prophets, peace be upon them, would sit, and thrones of silver on which the scholars would sit, and around them all the people, and around the people the jinn, the devils and the birds, shading him from the sun, and the east wind would lift the carpet a month's journey from morning to afternoon and from afternoon to morning.

What has been mentioned, that it is carried upon the carpet, is the well-known view, and perhaps that was at some times; otherwise Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd that he said: Solomon, peace be upon him, had a vessel of wood, and in it were a thousand compartments, and in each compartment were a thousand rooms, and he would ride in it with him the jinn and humans, and beneath each compartment were a thousand devils who would lift that vessel. When it rose, the gentle wind came and carried it along, and they travelled with it, so that the people did not know until the armies and troops had overshadowed them from it. It was said, concerning the reason for the plural, that the carpet was on the vessel mentioned, but this is not so.

It is related from al-Hasan that God Most High's honouring of Solomon, peace be upon him, through the subjection of the wind was in return for what he did with the horses, when, because of them, he missed the afternoon prayer. That was because he abandoned it for the sake of God Most High, so God, Glory be to Him, compensated him with something better than it, in terms of speed together with ease. It is strange that the people of London have wearied themselves for a long time in constructing a ship that runs elevated in the air wherever they wish, by means of vapours they confine within it, deceived by what appeared some years ago of a ship that runs on water by means of machinery moved by vapours within it. That has not succeeded for them, and I do not think it will succeed according to their desire in the most perfect manner. Some of those well informed have told me that they have built a ship that runs in the air, but not wherever they wish; rather, to wherever it casts its load.

﴿And We were Knowing of everything﴾, so We did not give him what We gave him except for the wisdom that We know.

[p. 79]

**﴿And of the devils﴾**, that is, and We subjected to him from among the devils **﴿those who dive for him﴾**. *Man* (مَن) is in the accusative position, governed by *sakharna* ("We subjected"). It is also permissible for it to be in the nominative position as the subject of a nominal sentence, with its predicate being what precedes it. On both readings, according to what Abu Hayyan preferred, it is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*). According to what a group of scholars chose, it is an indefinite qualified noun (*nakirah mawsufah*, an indefinite noun described by a following clause). The reason for preferring the relative reading is that there is no specific reference here, and the relative pronoun can sometimes denote a mental reference (*al-'ahd al-dhihni*, a reference to something known in the mind), which is contrary to the apparent meaning. The plural pronoun was used in view of the meaning, and a preceding plural made it preferable. **﴿For him﴾**: diving (*al-ghaws*) is entering under water and bringing something out of it. Since the diver may dive for himself or for others, it was said *"lahu"* (for him) to indicate that the diving was not for their own sake but for his sake, upon him be peace.

He, upon him be peace, would order them, and they would dive in the seas and extract precious things for him. **﴿And they would perform﴾** for him a great deal of work, **(other than that)**, that is, other than what has been mentioned, such as building cities and palaces and inventing wondrous crafts, in accordance with the words of the Exalted: ﴿They make for him whatever he wishes of prayer niches and statues﴾ [Saba': 13]. It has been said that the bathhouse, depilatory cream, mills, glassware and soap are among their works, and al-Imam al-Razi mentioned this in his tafsir. However, there is disagreement over whether soap is among their works. In *al-Tadhkirah* it is stated: "Soap is an ancient craft; it is said that it was found in the books of Hermes and Andukhiya, and this is the most apparent view." It has also been said: "It is from the craft of Buqrat (Hippocrates) and Jalinus (Galen)," and the quotation ends. It has also been said that it is from the craft of al-Farabi, and that he first made it in Damascus of the Levant, but this is not correct. What is widely claimed, that the first to make it was al-Buni, is among the lies and superstitions of the common people. Then, these [workers] are either the first group or others, due to the generality of the word *min* (from), as if it were said: "and whoever else they perform [work]." The devils are subtle, fiery, rational bodies, and the ability to perform arduous labour in a subtle body is not far-fetched, for that is comparable to the air lifting heavy bodies. Al-Jubba'i said: "He, glorified is He, made their bodies especially dense, strengthened them and increased their size so that this would be a miracle for Sulayman, upon him be peace. When he died, He returned them to their original creation, lest their remaining [in that state] lead to the deception of the false prophet (*al-mutanabbi*)." This is a statement that falls below the level of acceptability, as is not hidden.

The apparent meaning is that those subjected were disbelievers, because the word "devils" is most often applied to them, and this has been explicitly stated in some reports. This is supported by the words of the Exalted: **﴿And We were their guardians﴾**, that is, from turning away from His command or corrupting [things]. Al-Zajjaj said: "He would protect them from corrupting what they had done during the day." It has also been said: "Guardians of them from stirring up anyone." The more fitting interpretation with the closing phrase (*tadhyil*) is the one mentioned before. It is also mentioned, regarding their protection, that He assigned to them a group of angels, upon them be peace, and a group of believing jinn. Moreover, in the stories of Dawud and Sulayman, upon them both be peace, there is what indicates the greatness of the power of Allah, the Exalted.

Al-Imam said: The subjection of the densest bodies to Dawud, upon him be peace, namely the stone, when Allah the Exalted made it speak in glorification, and the iron, which He, glorified is He, made soft for him; and the subjection of the most subtle bodies to Sulayman, upon him be peace, namely the wind and the devils, who are made of fire and used to dive in water without being harmed. This is a clear proof of the overwhelming power of Him, glorified is He, and of the manifestation of opposite from opposite, and of the possibility of reviving decayed bones and making dry earth into a living creature. So when the truthful one reports its occurrence, it is obligatory to accept it and believe in it.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 21, verse 83:**

﴿And Ayyub﴾. The discussion of him is as was mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Dawud and Sulayman﴾. ﴿When he called out to his Lord: "Indeed, [I]﴾, that is, ﴿that [harm] has touched me﴾. ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read ﴿Innī﴾ with a kasra on the hamza (إنِّي), which, according to the Basrans, is due to an implied verb of saying, meaning "saying: indeed I." The view of the Kufans is that nādā (نادى, "called out") is treated like qāla (قال, "said"). ﴿al-Durr﴾ with a fatha (الضَّرُّ) is common to every kind of harm, while with a damma (الضُّرُّ) it is specific to what afflicts the self, such as illness, emaciation, and the like. ﴿And You are the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾, that is, You are greater in mercy than anyone who is described with mercy in a general sense. Otherwise there is no truly merciful one except Him, may His majesty be exalted and high. It is not hidden what is in describing Him, exalted is He, with the utmost mercy after he had reminded Himself of that which necessitates it, being content with that from presenting the request, by soliciting the clouds of mercy in the most gentle manner.

It is related, regarding gentleness in making a request, that a woman complained to one of the sons of Saʿd ibn ʿUbadah about the scarcity of mice in her house. He said: "Fill her house with bread, ghee, and meat."

[He, peace be upon him, according to Ibn Jarir, is the son of Amus ibn Ruzah ibn ʿIs ibn Ishaq.] Ibn ʿAsakir relates [p. 80] that his mother was a daughter of Lut, peace be upon him, and that his father was among those who believed in Ibrahim, peace be upon him. Accordingly, he was before Musa, peace be upon him. Ibn Jarir said: he was after Shuʿayb, peace be upon him. Ibn Abi Khaythamah said: he was after Sulayman, peace be upon him.

Ibn Saʿd related from al-Kalbi, who said: "The first prophet to be sent was Idris, then Nuh, then Ibrahim, then Isma'il and Ishaq, then Yaʿqub, then Yusuf, then Lut, then Hud, then Salih, then Shuʿayb, then Musa and Harun, then Ilyas, then al-Yasaʿ, then Yunus, then Ayyub, peace be upon them all." Ibn Ishaq said: "The correct view is that he was from the Children of Israel, and nothing has been authentically established regarding his lineage, except that the name of his father was Amus."

He, peace be upon him, as related by al-Hakim through the chain of Samurah from Kaʿb, was tall, with curly hair, wide-eyed, of good character, short-necked, broad-chested, and thick in the shins and forearms. Allah, exalted is He, had chosen him and expanded the world for him, and He multiplied his family and wealth. He had seven sons and seven daughters, and he owned various kinds of livestock and five hundred plowlands, each accompanied by five hundred servants, and each servant had a wife and a child. Then Allah, exalted is He, tested him by the death of his children when a house collapsed upon them, by the loss of his wealth, and by illness in his body for eighteen years, or thirteen years, or seven years and seven months and seven days and seven hours, or three years. At that time his age was seventy years, and it was said eighty years, and it was said more. The duration of his life, as narrated by al-Tabarani, was ninety-three years, and it was said more.

It is narrated that his wife, and she was Madir bint Maysha ibn Yusuf, peace be upon him, or Rahmah bint Ifra'im ibn Yusuf, [and this is only possible according to some of the earlier narrations, in his time, peace be upon him,] said to him one day: "If only you would supplicate to Allah, exalted is He." He said: "How long was the period of ease?" She mentioned a long period. In some narrations it is eighty years. He, peace be upon him, said: "I am ashamed before Allah, exalted is He, to supplicate to Him, for the period of my trial has not reached the period of my ease."

It is narrated that Iblis, may the curse be upon him, came to her in a great form and said to her: "I am the god of the earth. I did to your husband what I did because he abandoned me and worshipped the god of the heavens. If he were to prostrate to me once, I would return to him and to you everything I took from you both."

In another narration: "If you prostrate to me once, I would return the wealth and the child, and cure your husband." She returned to Ayyub, peace be upon him, who was lying on a dunghill (al-Kunasah) in Bayt al-Maqdis, where no one approached him. She told him the story. He, peace be upon him, said: "Perhaps you have been tempted by the words of the accursed one. If Allah, mighty and majestic, cures me, I will certainly strike you one hundred lashes, and it is forbidden for me to taste any of your food or drink after this." So he drove her away, and he remained lying on the dunghill, with no one from the people coming near him. At that point he fell down in prostration and said: ﴿My Lord, indeed harm has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾.

Ibn ʿAsakir related from al-Hasan that he, peace be upon him, said this when two men passed by him, and one of them said to his companion: "If Allah, exalted is He, had any need in this, He would not have brought him to all of this." He, peace be upon him, heard this, and it grieved him, so he said: "My Lord..." and so on.

Anas related with a raised (marfuʿ) chain that "he, peace be upon him, once rose to pray but could not stand up, so he said: 'My Lord...' and so on." It has been said otherwise, but this last report is perhaps the most reliable of the views.

His affliction in his body was extremely severe. Ibn Jarir related from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: "There would emerge on his body something like women's breasts, which would then burst open." Ahmad in al-Zuhd related from al-Hasan that he said: "Nothing remained of Ayyub, peace be upon him, except his two eyes, his heart, and his tongue. Worms would crawl over his body." Abu Nuʿaym and Ibn ʿAsakir related from him that a worm would fall from the body of Ayyub, peace be upon him, and he would put it back in its place and say: "Eat from the provision of Allah, exalted is He." Iblis did not inflict on him in his illness anything except groaning, as al-Bayhaqi related in Shuʿab al-Iman.

The cause of his trial, as related by Ibn ʿAsakir through the chain of Juwaybir from al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas, was that a poor man sought his help to repel an injustice from him, but he did not help him.

[p. 81] Ibn ʿAsakir related from Abu Idris al-Khawlani regarding this that Syria suffered a drought. Pharaoh wrote to him, peace be upon him: "Come to us, for you will find abundance with us." So he set out with what he had, and Pharaoh gave him land. It happened that Shuʿayb entered upon Pharaoh while Ayyub, peace be upon him, was with him. Shuʿayb said: "Are you not afraid that Allah, exalted is He, will become angry with an anger such that the people of the heavens and the earth, the mountains and the seas, will become angry because of His anger?" Ayyub remained silent. When they left from his presence, Allah, exalted is He, revealed to Ayyub: "Did you remain silent about Pharaoh because you went to his land? Prepare for trial." He said: "Then my religion [is ...]." He, glorified is He, said: "I will leave it to you." He said: "I do not mind." And Allah, exalted is He, knows best the authenticity of these reports.

Then, when he, peace be upon him, prostrated and said that, it was said to him: "Raise your head, for your supplication has been answered. Strike with your foot." So he struck with his foot, and a spring of water gushed forth from beneath him, and he bathed in it, and no animal remained on the outward part of his body except that it fell off, and no wound remained except that it healed. Then he struck once more, and another spring gushed forth, and he drank from it, and no illness remained in his inward parts except that it came out, and he returned healthy. His youth and beauty returned to him, and that...

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 84:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So We answered him and removed the affliction that was upon him﴾. Then he was clothed in a robe and sat in a conspicuous place, and his wife did not know of this. Compassion for him overcame her, and she said to herself: "Suppose he has driven me away. Shall I abandon him to die of hunger and be eaten by beasts? I will certainly go back to him." When she returned, she did not see that dunghill or that condition. So she began to wander around the place where the dunghill had been, weeping, and she was too awed by the man in the robe to approach him and ask him. Then Ayyub (peace be upon him) called to her and said: "What do you want, O servant of Allah?" She wept and said: "I want that afflicted man who used to lie on the dunghill." He said to her: "What was he to you?" She wept and said: "My husband." He said: "Would you recognize him if you saw him?" She said: "Could he be hidden from me?" He smiled, and she said: "I am he." She recognized him by his smile and embraced him. ﴿And We gave him his family and the like of them with them﴾. The apparent reading is that this is a conjunction (*atf*) with "We removed" (*kashafna*). In that case it must be included within the scope of the detail of the answering of the supplication. This is somewhat unclear, because it is not evident that the bringing mentioned was something he had asked for. If it is conjoined with "We answered" (*istajabna*), this does not necessarily follow. The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about this verse. Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir narrated through the route of Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: "I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And We gave him﴾, etc. He said: Allah returned his wife to him and increased her youth, until she bore him twenty-six sons." According to this, the meaning is that We gave him in this world a number of family equal to his original family, plus another equal number. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and Qatadah said concerning the verse: Allah revived for him the children who had died during his affliction, and he was given the like of them in this world. The apparent reading is that the "like" refers also to his own offspring (*sulb*), peace be upon him. It was also said that they were additional (*nawafil*). A report states that he (peace be upon him) had two granaries, one for wheat and one for barley. Allah sent two clouds: one poured gold into the wheat granary until it overflowed, and the other poured silver into the barley granary until it overflowed. Ahmad, al-Bukhari and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "While Ayyub (peace be upon him) was bathing naked, a swarm of golden locusts fell upon him, and Ayyub (peace be upon him) began to gather them into his garment. His Lord, glorified is He, called out to him: 'O Ayyub, did I not make you independent of what you see?' He said: 'Yes, by Your might, but I have no independence from Your blessing.'" Ayyub (peace be upon him) lived after his deliverance from the affliction, according to what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), seventy years. This indicates, together with the view that his age when the affliction struck him was seventy, that the duration of his life was well over ninety-three years. When he (peace be upon him) died, he left a bequest to his son Harmal, as reported from Wahb. The verse clearly indicates that "family" does not refer only to the wife. ﴿A mercy from Us and a reminder for the worshippers﴾, that is: We gave Ayyub (peace be upon him) what has been mentioned, as a mercy from Us, and as a reminder to others among the worshippers, so that they may be patient as he was patient and be rewarded as he was rewarded. Thus "mercy" (*rahmatan*) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*, the object expressing the reason for an action), and "for the worshippers" (*lil-'abidin*) is connected to "reminder" (*dhikra*). It is also permissible that "mercy and reminder" be an instance of dispute (*tanazu'*, where two governing words compete for the same element) over it, meaning: "And We gave him the worshippers, among whom was Ayyub (peace be upon him), and Our remembrance of them with goodness and Our not forgetting them."

Abu al-Baqa' permitted the accusative of "mercy" (*rahmatan*) as a verbal noun (*masdar*, the noun of the action), and it is as you see [i.e., it is weak].

[Page 82]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 85:

﴿وإسْماعِيلَ وإدْرِيسَ وذا الكِفْلِ﴾ That is, mention them. The arrangement of Dhu al-Kifl within the row of the prophets, peace be upon them, apparently indicates that he is one of them, and this is the view taken by most scholars. There is disagreement about his name. It is said that he was Bishr, the son of Ayyub (peace be upon him), whom God Most High raised as a prophet after his father, and He named him Dhu al-Kifl and commanded him, glorified be He, to call people to His Oneness. He lived in al-Sham (Greater Syria) for his whole life, and he died at the age of seventy-five, and he bequeathed (his affairs) to his son Abdan. al-Hakim recorded this from Wahb. It is also said that he was Ilyas, the son of Yasin, the son of Finhas, the son of al-Izar, the son of Harun, brother of Musa, the son of Imran (peace be upon them all). The practice of some scholars suggests that they chose this view. It is also said that he was Yusha' ibn Nun. It is said that his name was Dhu al-Kifl. It is said that he was Zakariyya. al-Kirmani related all of this in al-'Aja'ib. It is also said that he was al-Yasa' ibn Akhtub ibn al-'Ajuz. The Jews claimed that he was Hizqiyal, and that prophethood came to him while he was among the captives of Bukhtnassar, by the river Khuwar.

Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Mujahid said: he was not a prophet, but a righteous servant whom al-Yasa' (peace be upon him) appointed as his successor, as recorded by Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim from Mujahid, on the condition that he fast by day, stand in prayer by night, and not become angry. He did so. Mujahid did not mention what his name was.

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: He was a judge among the Children of Israel. When death approached him, he said: "Who will take my place on condition that he does not become angry?" A man said: "I will," and he is named Dhu al-Kifl. The report (continues)... Also recorded from Ibn Hujayra al-Akbar: He was a king among the kings of the Children of Israel. When death approached him, the chiefs of the Children of Israel came to him and said: "Appoint over us a king to whom we may turn for refuge." He said: "Who will undertake for me three things, so that I may entrust him with my kingdom?" No one spoke except a young man among the people, who said: "I will." He said: "Sit down." Then he repeated it a second time, and no one spoke except the young man, who said: "I will." He said: "Undertake for me three things and I will entrust you with my kingdom: you will stand in prayer at night and not sleep, you will fast and not break your fast, and you will judge and not become angry." He said: "Yes." He said: "I have entrusted you with my kingdom." The report (continues)... In it, as in the previous report, is the story of Iblis, may the curse be upon him, seeking to make him angry, and God Most High protecting him from it.

Al-Kifl means guarantee, portion, and weakness. Applying this word to him, if it was not his name, is either because he undertook a matter and fulfilled it, or because he had a portion (share) from God Most High. It is also said that it is because he had double the deeds of the prophets, peace be upon them, in his time, and double their reward.

As for the one who says that he is Zakariyya (peace be upon him), he says that the application of this (title) to him is because of his guardianship of Maryam, and this falls under the first aspect. In al-Bahr it is said: "Regarding his being named Dhu al-Kifl, there are conflicting statements that are not sound. And God Most High knows best."

﴿كُلٌّ﴾ That is, each one of these ﴿مِنَ الصّابِرِينَ﴾ [of the patient], that is, patient under the hardships of the obligations and the severity of calamities. This is known from the mention of these (prophets) after Ayyub (peace be upon them). The clause is a resumptive (istinaf) clause, which came as an answer to a question that arose from the command to mention them.

﴿And We admitted them into Our mercy﴾ The discussion of this is in the same manner as the similar expression mentioned a little earlier.

﴿Indeed, they were among the righteous﴾ That is, those perfect in righteousness, because of their being protected from sins. The clause is in the position of *ta'lil* (giving a reason), and there is no case of a thing being explained by itself without any need to make *min* (مِنْ) an inceptive *min* (*min ibtida'iyyah*, denoting the starting point), as is evident upon the slightest consideration.

[p. 83]

**"And Dhu'l-Nun"**: that is, remember the companion of the fish, Yunus (Jonah), peace be upon him, son of Matta, and Matta is the name of his father, according to what is in the Sahih of al-Bukhari and others, which Ibn Hajar (Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani) authenticated.

He said: I have not come across anything in the reports that establishes his lineage. It has been said that he lived in the time of the kings of the Tawa'if (the petty kings) of the Persians. Ibn al-Athir and others said that it is the name of his mother, and no prophet other than him and 'Isa (Jesus), peace be upon them both, has been attributed to his mother.

The Jews said what has been mentioned above, except that they named him Yunah ibn Amitay. Some of them say Yunan ibn Amafi. Al-nun is the fish, as we have indicated, and it is pluralized as ninan, as in al-Bahr (the Bahr al-Muhit of Abu Hayyan), and also as anwan, as in al-Qamus (the dictionary of al-Firuzabadi).

**"When he went off in anger"**: that is, angry with his people, because of the severity of their obstinacy and the persistence of their insistence despite his long calling to them. His going away was a migration (hijrah) from them, but he had not been commanded to do it. It has been said: he was angry with the king Hizqil. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: Yunus and his people lived in Palestine. A king attacked them and took captive nine and a half tribes from among them. Allah the Exalted revealed to the prophet Sha'ya': "Go to King Hizqil and tell him to dispatch five of the prophets to fight this king." He said: "I will dispatch Yunus ibn Matta, for he is strong and trustworthy." The king summoned him to go out. Yunus said: "Has Allah the Exalted commanded you to send me out?" He said: "No." He said: "Has He named me to you?" He said: "No." Yunus said: "Then there are other prophets besides me here." They insisted with him, so he went out angry. He came to the Sea of Rome and found a people who had prepared a ship, so he boarded with them. When they reached the deep water, the ship tilted with them and was about to sink. The sailors said: "There is a disobedient man with us, or a runaway slave. Our custom, when we are afflicted with this, is that we cast lots, and whoever the lot falls upon, we throw him into the sea; and for one of us to drown is better than for the ship to sink." They cast lots three times, and each time the lot fell upon Yunus, peace be upon him. He said: "I am the disobedient man and the runaway slave," and he threw himself into the sea. A fish came and swallowed him. Allah the Exalted revealed to it that it should not harm him in the least, "for I have made your belly a prison for him, and I have not made him food." Then Allah the Exalted delivered him from its belly and cast him onto the bare ground, his skin having become delicate. He caused a gourd plant (yaqtin) to grow over him, under whose shade he sheltered and from whose fruit he ate until he grew strong. When the plant dried up, Yunus, peace be upon him, grieved over it. He (Allah) said to him: "Do you grieve over a plant, and you did not grieve over a hundred thousand or more, since you did not go to them and did not seek their comfort?" Allah the Exalted then revealed to him and commanded him to go to them. He set out toward them until he entered their land, and they were not far from him. He came to them and said to their king: "Allah the Exalted has sent me to you, so send with me the Children of Israel." They said: "We do not know what you are saying. If we knew that you were truthful, we would have done it. We have already come upon you in your homes and taken you captive. If the matter were as you say, Allah the Exalted would have protected us from you." He went around among them for three days calling them to that, but they refused him. Allah the Exalted revealed to him: "Tell them that if they do not believe, the punishment will come upon them." He conveyed it to them, but they refused, so he left them. When they missed him, they regretted their deed and set out seeking him, but they could not find him. Then they recalled their affair and the affair of Yunus, peace be upon him, to the scholars who were among them. They said: "Look and seek him in the city. If he is in it, then it is not as he mentioned about the descent of the punishment; and if he has gone out, then it is as he said." They sought him, and it was said to them: "He went out in the evening." When they despaired, they closed the gate of their city and did not let their animals or anything else enter it. They separated each mother from its young, and likewise the children from the mothers. Then they stood waiting for the morning. When the morning broke, the punishment descended from the sky. They tore their garments, pregnant women gave birth to what was in their wombs, and the children and animals cried out. Allah the Exalted then lifted the punishment from them. They sent to Yunus until they met him, and they believed in him, and they sent the Children of Israel with him.

It has also been said: "angry with his Lord, mighty and majestic." Various descriptions have been related of this anger, and al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan) objected to this, saying that this view must be discarded, since such a thing is not fitting for the station of prophethood. It should be interpreted for those scholars who said it, such as al-Hasan (al-Basri), al-Sha'bi, Ibn Jubayr and others among the Successors (tabi'un, the generation after the Companions), and Ibn Mas'ud among the Companions (sahabah, the Prophet's companions), may Allah be pleased with them, so that the meaning of their saying "angry with his Lord" is "for the sake of his Lord, the Exalted, and out of zeal for His religion." Thus the lam is the lam of cause (lam al-'illa), not the lam that transmits the action to the object.

That the intended meaning is "angry with his Lord, mighty and majestic" is consistent with the claim of the Jews, for they assert that Allah the Exalted commanded him to go to Nineveh and warn its people, but he fled from that to Tarshish, went down to Jaffa, and boarded a ship. The waves grew mighty and the ship was about to sink, so its people cast lots, and the lot fell upon him. He threw himself into the sea, the fish swallowed him, then cast him out, and he went to Nineveh, and what happened happened. It is not hidden that such flight is something from which prophets, peace be upon them, are far removed, and the Jews are a people of slander.

The accusative of **"angry"** (mughadaban) is the circumstantial accusative (hal), and it comes from the mufa'alah (form of reciprocity) which does not imply sharing, as in "I punished the thief" ('aqabtu al-liss) and "I travelled" (safartu). It seems this form is used here for emphasis. It has also been said that the mufa'alah is in its literal sense, for he, peace be upon him, was angry with his people because of their disbelief, and they were angry with him for his departure, fearing the punishment would befall them. Abu Sarf read (mughdaban) as a passive participle.

**"So he thought that We would not decide against him."** That is: indeed the matter is that We would not decide over him with punishment and the like, or We would not constrict him in his affair with imprisonment and the like. The first interpretation is supported by the reading of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and al-Zuhri (nuqaddara), with the nun vowelled with a damma, the qaf with a fatha, and the dal with a kasra and shaddah; and by the reading of 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and al-Yamani (yuqaddara), with the ya' vowelled with a damma, the qaf with a fatha, and the dal shaddah. For the verb in both is from taqdir meaning qada' and hukm (decree and judgement), as is well known. It may also mean constriction (tadyiq), for it has come with this meaning too, as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) mentioned. Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with him, understood it as from qudrah (power), and this was found problematic, since no one thinks, let alone a prophet, that Allah the Exalted lacks power over him. He turned to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and he answered him with what we mentioned first. It was also permitted that it is from qudrah, with the meaning of its metaphorical sense, "exercising" it: that is, "he thought that We would not exercise Our power over him," or the speech is by way of tamthil (an illustrative figure), that is, he acted as one who thinks that We would not have power over him in opposing his people without waiting for Our command. It has been said: it is permissible that such a thought occurred to his mind, peace be upon him, through the whispering of Satan, and then he repelled it and refuted it with proof, as the believer who is truly verifying does with the impulses of Satan and what he whispers to him at all times. Among this is the verse: **"And you think of Allah thoughts"** [al-Ahzab 33:10], and the address is to the believers.

Sahib al-Fara'id (author of al-Fara'id) objected to this, saying that such a thing is far-fetched even for a believer, let alone the infallible prophet, for it would be disbelief. The verse "you think" etc. is not of this kind, and it is inclusive of the sincere and others. Also, what passes through the mind without settling is not called thought (zann), and impulses are not blameworthy. Also, if this had been the motive for going out, it would not have been of the kind of whispering. It is answered that thought in the sense of a passing idea in the mind without preponderance is a commonly used metaphor, and the reproach was for his going off in anger; and there is no way to make it the motive for going out; yet this is a view with no merit.

Ibn Abi Layla, Abu Sarf, al-Kalbi, Humayd ibn Qays and Ya'qub read (yuqadara), with the ya' vowelled with a damma, the dal with a fatha, and lightened. 'Isa and al-Hasan read it with ya' with a fatha and the dal with a kasra.

**"Then he called out in the darknesses."** The fa' is an eloquent fa' (fa' fasihah), meaning: so what happened of the casting of lots and the swallowing by the fish happened, and then he called out **"in the darknesses,"** that is, in the intense, thick darkness in the belly of the fish. Its darkness, because of its intensity, was made as though it were darknesses. Al-Sirafi recited:

*And a night, of whose darknesses people say, the sound-eyed and the blind are alike.*

Or the plural is on its literal sense, and what is meant is the darkness of the belly of the fish, the darkness of the sea and the darkness of the night. It has been said: a larger fish swallowed his fish, so he was in the darkness of the bellies of the two fish, and the darkness of the sea and the night.

**"There is no god but You."** That is: that there is no god but You, where "an" is the lightened form of the heavy "anna," the preposition is understood, and the pronoun of the affair is omitted. Or: "there is no god but You," where it is explanatory (mufassirah).

**"Glory be to You."** That is: I glorify You with a glorification fitting for You, that anything should overpower You, or that my trial with this should come without any cause from my side. **"Indeed I have been among the wrongdoers."** Against themselves, by exposing themselves to destruction, since I hastened to migrate without a command, contrary to the customary practice of the prophets, peace be upon them. This is a confession from him, peace be upon him, of his sin and a display of his repentance, so that He would relieve his distress.

﴿So We answered him﴾, that is, his supplication which he made within his confession and his manifestation of repentance, in the most gentle and finest manner.

Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī, al-Ḥakīm in *Nawādir al-Uṣūl*, al-Ḥākim (who graded it sound), Ibn Jarīr, al-Bayhaqī in *al-Shuʿab*, and a group of others narrated from Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The supplication of Dhū'l-Nūn (Jonah) when he was in the belly of the fish: *There is no god but You, glory be to You, indeed I was among the wrongdoers*. No Muslim has ever invoked Allah with it for anything except that He answers him." Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from al-Ḥasan that this is the Greatest Name of Allah, and al-Ḥākim narrated the same from Saʿd as a marfūʿ report. I have myself witnessed the effect of supplicating with it, and praise be to Allah, when someone whose sainthood I believe in, among the strangers residing in the presence of the white falcon, instructed me to do so, at a time when I had been afflicted with trials that only Allah the Exalted knows. Its explanation is lengthy, and you are weary.

It is also narrated from Anas, as a marfūʿ report, that when [Jonah], peace be upon him, invoked with this, his supplication rose and surrounded the Throne. The angels, peace be upon them, said: "This is a weak voice, familiar, coming from a distant land." Allah the Exalted said: "Do you not recognize it?" They said: "O Lord, who is it?" He said: "That is My servant Jonah." They said: "Your servant Jonah, for whom a righteous deed has always been raised, and whose supplication is answered. O Lord, will You not have mercy on him for what he used to do in ease, and rescue him from the trial?" He said: "Indeed." So He commanded the fish and it cast him out. This is His statement, the Exalted: ﴿and We saved him from the distress﴾, that is, the distress he suffered when the fish swallowed him, by casting him onto the shore after several hours.

Al-Shaʿbī said: "It swallowed him in the forenoon and spat him out in the evening." It is narrated from Qatādah that he remained in its belly for three days, which is what the Jews claim. It is narrated from Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he remained for seven days.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Abū Mālik that he remained for forty days. It has been said that the distress refers to the distress of sin, but the former interpretation is more apparent. He, exalted is His majesty, did not say ﴿fa-najjaynāhu﴾ [so We saved him] as He said in the story of Job, peace be upon him: ﴿fa-kashafnā﴾ [so We removed]. Some of the eminent scholars said: because he invoked for deliverance from harm, the removal mentioned is consequent upon His answering him, whereas Jonah, peace be upon him, did not invoke, so the basis of the sequence in his answering was not found.

This was refuted: the *fa* in the story of Job, peace be upon him, is explanatory, and the conjunction here is also explanatory, and variation of style is a recognized method in eloquence. Furthermore, we do not concede that Jonah, peace be upon him, did not invoke; and even if there had been no supplication from him, the answering would not have been realized. End of quotation.

Al-Khafājī criticized this, saying it has no clear meaning, and that its being an explanation does not dispel the question, since its essence is: why was *fa* used here, and not *thumma* [then], nor was it used here? The apparent view is to say that the first [the supplication of Job] was a supplication for the removal of harm in a gentle manner, so when the answer was stated in summary, and the request was by way of allusion, it was fitting to use the detailed *fa*. As for here, when [Jonah], peace be upon him, emigrated without a command, that was a sin in relation to him, peace be upon him, as he indicated by his saying: ﴿Indeed I was among the wrongdoers﴾. So what was revealed to him was the supplication for not being held accountable for what proceeded from him. Thus the answering is an expression for the acceptance of his repentance and the non-accountability for him. What follows is not an explanation of it, but rather an increase in kindness beyond what he sought; for this reason it is joined with *wa* [and]. End of quotation.

It is not hidden that what he mentioned does not hold in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And Noah, when he called before, so We answered him and saved him and his family from the great distress﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 76].

[Page 86]

Regarding His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And Zakariyya, when he called out to his Lord: "My Lord, do not leave me alone (without an heir), though You are the best of inheritors."﴾

﴿So We answered him and granted him Yahya﴾ [al-Anbiya 21:90]. Here the request of Nuh, peace be upon him, was not made in the manner of an allusion (ima'), even though He, exalted is He, said in his story ﴿So We rescued him﴾ with the particle fa' (then). Zakariyya, peace be upon him, had not done anything that counts as a sin in relation to him, so that he would need to be gentle in asking for the removal of punishment. Yet He, glorified is He, said in his story ﴿and We granted him﴾ with the conjunction wa' (and). It is therefore necessary at this point to state a reason for the choice of expression in each of these two places other than the one already mentioned. What al-Shihab mentioned about the last verse will come, God willing. It may be said that the detailed particle fa' (al-fa' al-tafsiliyya, the "then" that elaborates) was used in the stories of Nuh and Ayyub, peace be upon them both, to give importance to the matter of the answering, because of the situation of generality and detail, given the greatness of what they were in and its extreme severity. Do you not see how the proverb is struck with the affliction of Ayyub, peace be upon him, since it affected his self, his family and his wealth, and continued for as long as God willed? And how God, exalted is He, described what God, glorified is He, rescued Nuh from, when He, mighty and majestic, said ﴿So We rescued him and his family from the great distress﴾. It is not so with what Dhu al-Nun and Zakariyya, peace be upon them both, were in, in relation to that. Therefore, in their two verses the wa' was used. Although wa' also comes for explanation, the use of fa' for this purpose is more common.

What al-Khafaji mentioned concerning this verse does not seem far-fetched to me: that the answering is an expression for the acceptance of his repentance, peace be upon him, and the rescue is an addition of kindness beyond what he asked for. The same will be said about what is coming, which you will hear, God willing.

﴿And thus﴾, that is, like that complete rescue, ﴿We rescue the believers﴾ from distresses in which they called upon God, exalted is He, with sincerity. There is no rescue lesser than it.

The reading of al-Jahdari is (nunajji) with a shadda, the present tense of najja (to rescue). Ibn Amir and Abu Bakr read (nujji) with a single nun, damma on it, a shadda on the jim, and the ya' sukun. Abu Ubayda preferred this reading over the reading with two nuns, because it agrees better with the Uthmanic orthography (rasm), since the written form has a single nun. Abu Ali said in al-Hujja: It is narrated from Abu Amr that he read (nujji) with idgham (assimilation), and the nun is not assimilated into the jim. It is only concealed (ikhfa'), because it is a sakin (quiescent) that comes out of the nasal passages. So it is omitted in writing while it is present in pronunciation. Whoever says it is assimilated has erred, because this nun is concealed with the letters of the mouth, and these are called the "tree letters" (al-ahruf al-shajariyya), namely the jim, the shin and the dad. Making it clear is a lahn (a solecism). So when it was concealed, the listener thought it was assimilated, end of quote.

Abu al-Fath Ibn Jinni said: Its origin is (nunajji), as in the reading of al-Jahdari. The second nun was then deleted to avoid two identical letters in succession, and the first was kept for a meaning. The heaviness arises only from the second. This is like the deletion of the second ta' in ﴿tuzahiruna﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:4]. It does not matter that it is original (asliyya), and likewise it does not matter that its vowel is not identical with the vowel of the first nun, because the motive for deletion is the gathering of two identical letters together with the impossibility of assimilation. Therefore, the statement of Abu al-Baqa', that this explanation is weak for two reasons, is refuted. One is that the second nun is original and is the fa' of the word, so deleting it is very far-fetched. The second is that its vowel differs from the vowel of the first nun, so the gathering of the two is not burdensome. This is unlike (tuzahiruna), which is not within the realm of acceptance. The deletion was prevented in ﴿tatajafa﴾ [al-Sajda 32:16] only for fear of confusion with the past tense. This is unlike what we are discussing, because if it were a past tense its final letter would not be quiescent. The claim that it became quiescent for lightness is contrary to what is apparent. It has been said that it is a past verb in the passive voice (mabni li-ma lam yusamma fa'iluhu), and the ya' became quiescent for lightness, as in the reading of one who read ﴿And leave what remains of the interest﴾ [al-Baqara 2:278], and in the line of verse:

He is the caliph, so be content with what he is content with for you, one whose resolution is firm, in whose judgment there is no bias.

The substitute for the agent is the pronoun of the verbal noun (masdar). ﴿And the believers﴾ is the direct object. Al-Akhfash, the Kufans and Abu Ubayd permitted the verbal noun to stand in the place of the agent even when the direct object is present. They based on this the reading of Abu Ja'far ﴿that He may recompense a people﴾ [al-Jathiya 45:14], and the line of verse:

Even if a poor woman bore a dog's pup, that dog would be cursed, and dogs would be cursed because of it.

[Page 87]

The well-known position of the Basrans is that whenever the direct object is present, nothing else stands in the place of the agent. It has also been said that (al-mu'minin) is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning: and thus it was rescued, that is, the rescue, We rescue the believers. It has been said that it is in the accusative by the pronoun of the verbal noun. All of these, as you see, are far-fetched.

﴿And Zakariyya﴾, that is, recall his story, peace be upon him. ﴿When he called out to his Lord: "My Lord, do not leave me alone"﴾, that is, solitary, without a son who would inherit from me, as the closing phrase indicates with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿though You are the best of inheritors﴾. If the meaning were "without a son who would accompany me and help me," it would have said "though You are the best of helpers." The meaning of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿though You are the best of inheritors﴾ is: You are the best living being who remains after the dead. This contains praise of Him, exalted is He, for His permanence, and an indication of the perishing of all others among the living. In this is seeking the rain-clouds of His gentleness, mighty and majestic is He. It has also been said that by this he intended to return the matter to Him, glorified is He, as if he said: If You do not grant me a son to inherit me, then You are the best of inheritors, and You are sufficient for me.

It has been objected that this does not suit the context of supplication, since among the etiquettes of the one who supplicates is that he should pray with earnestness, diligence and resolve.

In the two Sahihs, from the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, he said: "When one of you supplicates, let him not say: O God, forgive me if You will; have mercy on me if You will; provide for me if You will. Let him make his request with resolve, for God, exalted is He, does whatever He wills, and none can compel Him."

In a narration in Sahih Muslim: "But let him make his request with resolve and let him make his desire firm, for nothing is great to God, exalted is He, when He gives."

It may be said: This is not of the type "provide for me if You will," since its purpose is only to show contentment and reliance on God, mighty and majestic, should He not answer his supplication. And the purpose of "provide for me if You will" is not that. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 90:

﴿So We answered him﴾ his supplication ﴿and gave him Yahya﴾, and the explanation of how this came about has already passed ﴿and We made his wife fit for him﴾, i.e., We made her fit for living with him by improving her character. She had a bad temper and a sharp tongue, as is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi and ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allah. Or it means: We made her fit for him, (peace be upon him), by restoring her youth to her and making her able to bear children, for she had been barren, as is related from Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah. On the first interpretation, this clause is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿We answered﴾, because he (peace be upon him) had not prayed for the improvement of his wife's character.

Al-Khafaji said: It is also permissible to conjoin it upon ﴿and gave﴾, and then its conjunction with the particle "wa" (and) becomes clear, because of the additional benefit beyond what was requested, it is not conjoined with the detailed "fa" (then). On the second interpretation, the conjunction is upon ﴿and gave﴾. He (may God be exalted) placed the gift of Yahya before the making of the wife fit for childbearing, though the former depends on the latter, because Yahya was the greater thing sought. The particle "wa" does not imply sequence, so there is no need for what has been said: that the meaning of "gift" is its intention. Al-Khafaji said: He (glory be to Him) did not say "so We gave" because the intent is to bestow favour, not to explain, and there is no need for explanation; moreover, explanatory conjunction is not necessarily with "fa", but may be with "wa". End of quotation. There is no concealing what is in it, so reflect.

His exalted saying: ﴿Indeed, they used to hasten to good works﴾ is a justification (taʿlil) for the various forms of His favour detailed concerning the aforementioned prophets (peace be upon them), so the plural pronouns refer to the earlier prophets.

It has been said: they refer to Zakariyya, his wife and Yahya, and the clause is a justification for what is understood from the discourse, namely the attainment of nearness, closeness and high ranks for them. Or it is a resumptive clause (istinaf) which came as an answer to an implied question: "What was their condition?" The reliance is on what preceded. The meaning is that they used to strive and eagerly pursue all kinds of good deeds. Often "asraʿa" is followed by "fi", because of the sense of striving and eagerness in it, so "fi" is not here in the sense of "ila" (to) nor for causation, nor is the expression of the type of the line of poetry: "yajrahu fi ʿarāqībihā nuṣalli" (they wound her hamstrings, we pray).

﴿And they called upon Us with hope and fear﴾, i.e., desiring Our bounties and fearing Our vengeance, or desiring the acceptance of their deeds and fearing its rejection. So "raghaban" and "rahaban" are two verbal nouns (maṣdar) in the position of a circumstantial state (hal), by interpreting them as active participles. It is also permissible that this is by implying a noun, i.e., possessors of desire and fear. It is also permissible to leave them in their apparent form for emphasis. It has been permitted that they are plurals, like "khadam", the plural of "khadim" (servant), but they said: this plural is attested in rare words. It has also been permitted that they are accusative for causation, i.e., for the sake of desire and fear. Abu al-Baqa' permitted their accusative as verbal nouns, like "qa'adtu juluusan" (I sat sitting), and it is as you see.

It is related in Majma' al-Bayan that the supplication in hope is with the palms facing down and in fear with them facing up, and some of our scholars have held this. The apparent meaning is that the clause is conjoined upon the clause ("yusari'una") so it is included with it within the scope of ("kanu"). Not repeating it is a sign that the aforementioned supplication is a consequence of that hastening. One group read ("yad'una") with the deletion of the nun of nominative case, and Talhah read ("yad'unna") with a doubled nun, assimilating the nun of nominative case into the nun of the accusative pronoun. And they read ("raghban") and ("rahban") with a fatha on the ra' and sukun after it, and ("rughban") and ("ruhban") with a damma and sukun. ﴿And they were humble before Us﴾, i.e., humbly submissive, supplicating, or constantly fearful. The sum of the justification is that they attained from God, exalted is He, what they attained because of their being characterised by these praiseworthy qualities.

And His saying, ﴿and she who guarded her chastity﴾. It is in the accusative, like its similar preceding examples. It was also said that it is in the nominative, as the inchoative (al-ibtida', the subject of a nominal sentence), with the predicate omitted, meaning: "[It is] among what is recited to you," or the predicate is His saying, ﴿So We breathed into her of Our Spirit﴾, with the fa' (so) being superfluous according to those who permit that. The relative pronoun refers to Maryam, peace be upon her. The word ihsan (guarding, chastity) is used in its linguistic sense, which is prevention in general. Al-farj (the private part) originally means the gap between two things, like a cleft, and what lies between the two legs. It is used as a euphemism for the private parts, and its use became so frequent that it became almost explicit in this meaning. According to a group, this is what is meant here, i.e., she prevented her private part from marriage in both its forms, as she said, ﴿No man has touched me, and I have not been unchaste﴾ [Maryam: 20]. Celibacy (al-tabattul) was prescribed for women and men at that time. It was also said that al-farj here means the opening of her shirt collar, which she prevented Gabriel (peace be upon him) from reaching when he came close to her to breathe, since she did not recognize him.

She was described in this way to magnify her status and to declare her free from what they alleged concerning her. By "the Spirit" is meant its well-known meaning, and its attribution to His pronoun (ﷻ) is for honor. Breathing the spirit is an expression for giving life, and there is no literal breathing there. Then, this giving of life was for Jesus, peace be upon him, and since he was in her womb, it is correct to say, "We breathed into her," because what is in a thing is considered to be in it. Thus it does not necessarily mean "We gave her life," and that is not the intended meaning. This is like the flute player who says, "I blew into the house of so-and-so," while he was blowing the flute in his house. Abu Hayyan said: the statement is according to an omitted noun, meaning, "So We breathed into her son."

It is also possible that by the Spirit is meant Gabriel, peace be upon him, as was said regarding His saying, ﴿So We sent to her Our Spirit﴾ [Maryam: 17]. Min (of) is for origin (ibtida'iyyah), and there was actual breathing, while its attribution to Him (ﷻ) is metaphorical, meaning, "So We breathed into her from the direction of Our Spirit." Gabriel (peace be upon him) breathed from the opening of her garment, and the breath reached her inside, so it is correct that the breathing was into her, without dust that needs blowing away. Then, the verb nafakha (to breathe) is intransitive, but it may be transitive, so one says, "The spirit breathed us" (nafakhana al-ruh).

Some irregular readings (shadhdh) have come concerning this, and some eminent scholars have stated it. Denying it is due to lack of knowledge. ﴿And We made her and her son﴾, meaning, We made their story or their condition, ﴿a sign for the worlds﴾. Whoever reflects on their condition will realize the perfection of His power, mighty and majestic. So by "sign" is meant what came about through the two of them, along with the abundance of signs in each one of them. It was also said that by "sign" is meant the genus, encompassing the independent signs of each of them. It was also said: the meaning is, "We made her a sign and her son a sign," and the first was omitted because the second indicates it. It was argued from the mention of Maryam, peace be upon her, alongside the prophets in this surah, that she was a prophetess, since she was mentioned together with them.

However, mentioning her with them does not necessitate that she was one of them, and perhaps she was mentioned only on account of Jesus, peace be upon him. The mention of the two of them here fits with the story of Zakariyya, his wife, and their son Yahya, because of the kinship among them, peace be upon them.

This is an address to all of mankind. The demonstrative refers to the religion of tawhid and Islam, and it is used in the manner of ﴿This is the parting between me and you﴾ [al-Kahf: 78] and "This is your brother." It represents the thing pointed to as being present in the mind and then indicated, and it implies that the referent is distinguished to the utmost degree of distinction. For this reason it is not specified by a descriptive attribute.

According to what the author of al-Mațla' (Sahib al-Mațla') said, the original meaning of ummah (community) is a people who gather upon one religion. Then the term was extended until it was applied to the religion itself. The more common view is that it refers to people who gather upon a matter or in a particular time, and applying it to the religion itself is metaphorical. The apparent sense of al-Raghib's words is that it is also a literal usage, and this is the meaning intended here. By the declarative sentence is intended the command to preserve that religion and to observe its rights. The meaning is that the religion of Islam is your religion, which you must safeguard within its limits and observe its rights, so do that.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿one community﴾, are in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of (ummah), and the governing element in it is the demonstrative. It is permissible for the governing element of the circumstantial qualifier to differ from that of its referent, although the more common practice is identity, as in Abu Hayyan's commentary on Sharh al-Tas-hil. It was also said that it is a substitute (badal) for (this). The meaning of its unity is the agreement of the prophets, upon them be peace, upon it. That is, this your community is one community, not differing among the prophets, upon them be peace, but all of them unanimously agreed upon it, so it was not altered in any age, as the branches (furu') were altered. It was also said that the meaning of its unity is that no other religion shares with it, namely polytheism, in being accepted and in the validity of following it.

It is also permitted that the demonstrative refers to the way of the prophets mentioned, upon them be peace, and that what is meant by it is also tawhid. It was said that it refers to the way of Ibrahim, upon him be peace, and that the discourse is connected to his story, but this is very remote. Even more remote by many stages is what was said: that it refers to the religion of Isa, upon him be peace, and that the discourse is connected to what precedes it, as if it were said: "We made her and her son a sign for the worlds," saying to them: "Indeed, this, that is, the religion with which Isa was sent, is your community," and so on. Rather, it should not be considered at all.

It was also said that (this) refers to the group of the prophets mentioned, upon them be peace, and (community) means group. That is, these are your group, whom you must follow, gathered upon the truth, not differing. There is in this a good aspect, as is not hidden. The first view is the best, and it is the view of the majority of the exegetes, and it is related from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada. Some permitted that the address is to the believers in general, while al-Tibi made it specific to the obstinate deniers, stating regarding the arrangement of the noble composition: this surah was revealed to explain prophethood and what relates to it, and those addressed are the obstinate ones from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). When he finished explaining prophethood and repeating it as confirmation, and mentioning the prophets, upon them be peace, as consolation, he returned to addressing them with His words, exalted is His majesty, ﴿Indeed, this your community...﴾ and so on. That is: this religion which I have repeated to you is one religion which I have chosen for you so that you may hold fast to it, and to the worship of God, exalted is He, and to the affirmation of tawhid. It is the one to which I call you, so that you may hold on to it with your molars, because all the other books were revealed concerning it, and all the prophets were sent to call to it and agree upon it.

[Page 90]

Then, when He knew of their persistence, it was said: ﴿and they cut up﴾, etc. The sum of the meaning is: the religion is one, the Lord is one, and the prophets, peace be upon them, agree on it. These distant ones made the matter of the one religion among themselves into pieces, as a group divides a single thing among themselves. End quote. The more apparent view is generality. The structure of the discourse is taken on this basis from the words of al-Tayyibi with slight consideration. Al-Hasan read ﴿أمتكم﴾ (*ummatakum*) in the accusative, as a *badal* (substitution in apposition) of ﴿هذه﴾, or an *ʿatf bayān* (explicative apposition) of it. [Page 90 continues] And ﴿أمة واحدة﴾ (*ummatun wāḥidatun*) in the nominative, as the *khabar* (predicate) of *inna* (the predicate of *inna*). He also read, and Ibn Ishaq, al-Ashhab al-ʿUqayli, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, al-Jaʿfi, and Harun from Abu ʿAmr, and al-Zaʿfarani, both in the nominative, as the predicate of *inna*. It is said: the first is the predicate, and the second is a *badal* of it, a substitution of an indefinite for a definite. Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is one community. ﴿وأنا ربكم﴾ (*wa-anā rabbukum*), meaning: I am your God, one God. ﴿فاعبدون﴾ (*fa-ʿbudūn*), exclusively. Explaining *al-Rabb* (the Lord) as *al-Ilah* (the God) is because the command to worship is ordered upon it. The indication of unity is from the unity of the religion. In the word *al-Rabb* there is a hint of this, in that if one supposed that its plurality were possible in itself, it would not be possible for each thing nurtured to have more than one lord, because He is the bestower of existence and its perfections together. In the turn to the word *al-Rabb* there is a preference for the side of mercy, and that He, exalted is He, calls them to His worship in the language of encouragement and expansiveness, as stated in *al-Kashf*.

﴿وتقطعوا أمرهم بينهم﴾ (*wa-taqaṭṭaʿū amrahum baynahum*), meaning: they made the matter of their religion among themselves into pieces, on the basis that *taqaṭṭaʿa* is implicitly used with the meaning of *jaʿala* (made), which is why it takes ﴿أمرهم﴾ directly as its object. Abu al-Baqaʾ said: *taqaṭṭaʿū amrahum* means *fī amrihim* (in their matter), i.e. they scattered. It is said: it takes the object directly because it means *qaṭṭaʿū* (they cut up), i.e. they divided. It is said: ﴿أمرهم﴾ is a *tamyīz* (specification accusative) transferred from the subject, meaning: their matter was cut up. End quote. What was mentioned first is more apparent. The *amr* of the *tamyīz* is not hidden from anyone who has discernment. Then the original of the speech was: "you cut up your matter among them" in the second person. So it turned to the third person in order to censure them for what they did of dispersion in the religion and making it into scattered divisions, and to convey that to others, as if it were said: do you not see the magnitude of what these people committed against the religion of God, exalted is He, upon which all the prophets, peace be upon them, agreed? In that is a reproach of disagreement regarding the fundamentals.

﴿كل﴾ (*kull*), meaning: each one of the divided sects, or each individual of each one of those sects. ﴿إلينا راجعون﴾ (*ilaynā rājiʿūn*), returning to Us by resurrection, not to other than Us, so We will then requite them according to their deeds. There is no hiding what the sentence contains of indication of establishment and certainty.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 94:
