His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever does righteous deeds﴾ is a specification of the reward, meaning: whoever does some of the righteous deeds, or some portion of the righteous deeds, ﴿while he is a believer﴾ in what belief in it is obligatory, ﴿then there will be no denial of his effort﴾, meaning there will be no deprivation of the reward for that his deed. He expressed it by kufran (denial), which is the concealing of a blessing and the rejecting of it, in order to show the complete purity of Him, Exalted is He, from it, by depicting it in the form of something whose occurrence from Him, glorified is He, is impossible, namely the vices. The bringing forth of the reward in the context of matters obligatory upon Him, Exalted is He, and His negation by a negation of the genus (lā kufrāna), which implies generality, is for the sake of emphasis in declaring Him free of such things. The apparent structure is in the pattern of (lā māni'a limā a'ṭayta, "there is no preventer of what you have given"), and the discussion of this is well known among the scholars of Arabic (ʿulamāʾ al-ʿarabiyyah). He expressed the deed by the word effort (saʿy) to show its importance. In the reading of Ibn Masʿud it is (fa-lā kufra), and the meaning is one. ﴿And indeed, We are recording it﴾, meaning, for his effort. It has been said that the pronoun refers to "whoever," but this is not correct. ﴿for it﴾, meaning, recording it, i.e., preserving it in the record of his deed, so that it is never lost in any way whatsoever. The verse has been cited as evidence that the acceptance of a righteous deed, in every case, is conditional upon faith. This is the view of some of them. Others said: faith is a condition for the acceptance of those deeds that require intention (niyyah), and its verification is in its proper place.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 95:**

﴿And it is forbidden upon a town﴾: that is, upon the people of a town. So the speech is either with an elision (taqdir) of a noun (mudaf), or "the town" is a metonymy (majaz) for its people. "Forbidden" (haram) is used figuratively for "that whose existence is impossible," on the basis that each of the two is not hoped to occur. Al-Raghib said: "Haram is what is prevented, either by a divine subjugation, or by a compulsory prevention, or by a prevention from the side of reason, or from the side of the Sharia, or from the side of one whose command is followed." It has been mentioned that in this verse it has been understood as prohibition by subjugation, as in His saying, ﴿And We had forbidden him the wet-nurses﴾ [al-Qasas: 12]. Abu Hanifa, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr, Talha, al-A'mash, and Abu 'Amr in one narration read (wa-hirmun) with a kasra on the ha' and a sukun on the ra', and this is the end of the quotation.

Page 91

Qatada, Matar al-Warraq, and Mahbub, from Abu 'Amr, read with a fatha on the ha' and a sukun on the ra'. 'Ikrima read (wa-hurimun) with a damma on the ha' and a kasra on the ra' with tanwin. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima also, Ibn al-Musayyib, and Qatada also read with a kasra on the ra' and a fatha on the ha' and the mim, in the past tense (al-madi). Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima, with a difference of narration from them, and Abu al-'Aliya and Zayd ibn 'Ali, read with a damma on the ra' and a fatha on the ha' and the mim, also in the past tense. In another narration from Ibn 'Abbas, he read with a fatha on the ha', the ra', and the mim, also in the past tense.

al-Yamani read (wa-hurrima) with a damma on the ha', a kasra on the ra' with shadda, and a fatha on the mim, as a past verb in the passive voice (mabni li-ma lam yusamma fa'iluh).

﴿We destroyed it﴾: that is, We decreed its destruction, or We judged it in pre-eternity, because of their extreme transgression and obstinacy in what continues.

Al-Silmi and Qatada read (ahlaktuha) with the ta' of the speaker (ta' al-mutakallim). His saying, ﴿that they do not return﴾, is in the interpretation of a nominative noun (ism marfu') in the position of a subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject), whose predicate (khabar) is (haram). Ibn al-Hajib said in his Amali: "It is then obligatory to place it first (i.e., the predicate), because of what is established in grammar that the predicate of (anna) must be placed first." It is also permitted that (haram) be the subject (mubtada') and (annahum) a doer (fa'il) for it that stands in place of its predicate, even if it does not depend on a negation or interrogation, according to the view of al-Akhfash, for he does not stipulate that dependence in this, unlike the majority, as is well known.

Ibn Malik held that raising a descriptive word that stands as a subject, which is sufficient without a predicate, without dependence, is permissible without disagreement; the disagreement is only about whether it is good style (istihsan) or not. Sibawayh says: "It is not good." Al-Akhfash says: "It is good," and so do the Kufans, as in the explanation of al-Tashil. The sentence serves to confirm what precedes it, His saying, ﴿all of them are returned to Us﴾, and the meaning of "indeed" (anna) as affirmation is considered in the negation that is implied in (haram), not in the negated element. That is: it is absolutely impossible that they not return to Us for recompense, not that their actual non-return is impossible. The specification of the impossibility of their non-return by mention, despite the impossibility covering the non-return of all, as His saying ﴿all of them are returned to Us﴾ indicates, is because they are the ones who deny the resurrection and the return, not others. This meaning is related from Abu Muslim ibn Bahr, and Abu Hayyan transmitted it from him, but he said: "The purpose of the sentence according to this is to refute the saying of one who denies the resurrection, and to confirm what came before, that there is no ingratitude for anyone's effort, and that it will be rewarded on the Day of Resurrection." What is in this is not hidden.

Abu 'Utba said: The meaning is: "And impossible upon a town which We have decreed to destroy, or judged for destruction, is their return to Us," that is, their repentance, with (la) being an emphatic particle like its use in His saying, ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ [al-A'raf: 12], according to one view. It was also said that (haram) means "obligatory," as in the saying of al-Khansa:

"Indeed, a forbidden thing: I do not see time weeping
over a grief, except that I weep over Sakhr."

And from this is His saying, ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you: that you not associate anything with Him﴾ [al-An'am: 151], etc., for abandoning association is obligatory. On this basis, Mujahid and al-Hasan said: ﴿they do not return﴾ means they do not repent from association.

Qatada and Muqatil said: ﴿they do not return﴾ means they do not return to the world. The apparent meaning on this is that what is meant by "We destroyed it" is that We brought its destruction into actual existence, and what is meant by destruction is physical destruction. It is also possible, on the view that what is meant by non-return is non-repentance, that what is meant is spiritual destruction by disbelief and sins.

It is read (innahum) with a kasra on the hamza, on the basis that the clause is a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf ta'lili), explaining what precedes it. So (haram) is the predicate of an elided subject (mubtada' mahdhuf), meaning: "It is forbidden for it that," that is, what was mentioned in the previous verse of righteous deeds accompanied by faith and appreciated effort. Then He gave the reason with His saying, ﴿that they do not return﴾, their disbelief to which they are attached, so how would that not be prevented? It is also permissible to interpret the speech according to the recitation of the majority with a fatha on this meaning, by omitting the particle of reasoning, meaning: "because they do not return." Al-Zajjaj estimated the subject in this as "that their deed be accepted," and said: "The meaning is: and it is forbidden upon a town which We have judged for its destruction that their deed be accepted, because they do not repent."

Page 92

What indicates this is His saying before it: ﴿so there is no ingratitude for his effort﴾, since what is meant by it is that his deed is accepted.

And "ḥattā" (until) in His words, ﴿until, when Gog and Magog are let loose﴾, is *ibtidā'iyya* (introductory, marking the start of a new clause), and the speech after it is an *ghāya* (an end-point or limit, a clause expressing the limit of what precedes). It is as if it were said: they continue in the state of destruction they are in, until, when the Resurrection comes, they return to Us and say, "Woe to us," and so on. Or it is a *ghāya* for the prohibition (*ḥurma*), meaning: the prevention of their return to repentance continues, until, when the Resurrection comes, they return to it, and that is at a time when returning will not benefit them. Or it is a *ghāya* for the non-return from disbelief, meaning: they do not return from it until, when the Resurrection comes, they return from it, and that is at a time when this will not benefit them. This is according to the multiplicity of opinions about the meaning of the preceding verse, and the distribution (*tawzī'*, i.e. the division of these possibilities) is not hidden.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "ḥattā" is connected to His words, ﴿they have cut up﴾ (*taqaṭṭaʿū*), and so on. Abū Ḥayyān said: "In this there is a remoteness due to the great separation, but in terms of meaning it is good. Its summary is that they will not cease to be divided, not gathered upon the religion of truth, until the approach of the coming of the Hour. Then, when the Hour comes, that divergence ends, and everyone knows that their Lord is the Truth, and that the saving religion was the religion of monotheism."

The attribution of the opening (*fatḥ*) to Gog and Magog is a metaphor (*majāz*), while it is literal (*ḥaqīqa*) with respect to the barrier (*sadd*). Or the speech is elliptical, with the omission of the *muḍāf* (the governed noun), which is "the barrier," and the *muḍāf ilayh* (the governing noun) being placed in its position.

A group recited ﴿futtiḥat﴾ with the doubling (*tashdīd*) of the letter, and the discussion of "Yājūj wa-Mājūj" has preceded.

﴿And they﴾, that is, Gog and Magog. It is said: the people. And it is narrated from Mujāhid: ﴿from every slope﴾, that is, elevated from the earth, such as a mountain or a hillock.

Ibn ʿAbbās recited (*jadath*) with the letter *jīm* and the *thāʾ* with three dots (*thāʾ muthallatha*), and it means the grave. This reading supports the return of the pronoun to the people.

It was also read with the *jīm* and the *fāʾ*, and the *fāʾ* is a substitution (*badal*) for the *thāʾ* according to the tribe of Tamīm. Their substitution is not restricted to the end of the word, for they say *maghthūr* in place of *maghfūr*.

﴿they hasten﴾, that is, they hurry. The original meaning of *nasalān* (with two fatḥas) is approaching the stride together with haste. It is said that it is specifically, by convention, applied to wolves, and in that case it is a metaphor here.

Ibn Isḥāq and Abū al-Simāl recited the *sīn* with a *ḍamma*.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 97:**

﴿And the true promise draws near.﴾ That is, it draws near. It has also been said that *iqtaraba* is more emphatic in nearness than *qaraba*. ﴿The true promise﴾ is what follows the second blast (*nafkha*, the blast of the Trumpet): resurrection (*al-ba'th*), reckoning, and recompense, not the first blast. The clause is coordinated (*'atf*) with ﴿when Gog and Magog are released﴾. Moreover, this opening occurs at the time of the descent of Jesus, peace be upon him, from the sky, and after his killing of the Dajjal (the Antichrist) at the Eastern Gate of Ludd. Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah have related, in a lengthy hadith:

""Indeed, Allah, exalted is He, will reveal to Jesus, peace be upon him, after he has killed the Dajjal: 'I have brought forth servants of Mine whom no one has the power to fight. So take My servants to the mountain (*al-Tur*).' Then Allah, exalted is He, will send forth Gog and Magog, and they are, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿from every mound they swarm﴾. Jesus, peace be upon him, and his companions will then turn to Allah, mighty and majestic is He, and He will send against them a worm (*naghaf*) in their necks, and they will become dead as one soul dies. Then Jesus, peace be upon him, and his companions will descend, and He will send against them birds like the necks of camels (*bakht*), which will carry them and cast them wherever Allah, exalted is He, wills. Allah, mighty and majestic is He, will send down a rain that no house of clay or wool will be able to withstand for forty days, and it will wash the earth until it leaves it like a mirror. It will be said to the earth: 'Bring forth your fruit,' and on that day a company will eat from a pomegranate and shelter under its husk. Blessing will be placed upon milk, so that a she-camel's milk will suffice a large group of people, a cow's milk will suffice a clan, and a sheep's milk will suffice a household. While they are in that state, Allah, exalted is He, will send a pleasant wind beneath their armpits, which will seize the soul of every Muslim, and the wicked of people will remain, copulating openly like donkeys, and upon them the Hour will be established.""

And there has come a hadith related by Ahmad and a group (of scholars):

""Indeed, the Hour, after Gog and Magog have perished, will be like a pregnant woman at full term, whose family does not know until it surprises them with her delivery, by night or by day.""

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Juraij, who said: "It has been mentioned to us that

[Page 93]

the Prophet ﷺ said: ""If a mare were to foal at the time of their emergence, its foal would not be ridden until the Hour is established.""" This is an exaggeration in expressing nearness, like the report preceding it.

﴿Then, behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved will be fixed in horror.﴾ *Fa-idha* is the response (*jawab*) of the conditional (*shart*). *Idha* here is the particle of sudden occurrence (*lil-mufaja'a*), and it takes the place of the responding *fa'* in linking the clauses, not as a substitute for it. Thus, when the nominal clause that serves as the response is accompanied by it, the *fa'* is not needed, as in ﴿then they despair﴾ (al-Rum: 36). When both are brought together, as here, the link is strengthened. The pronoun (*al-damir*) refers to the matter and situation (*lil-qissa wa al-sha'n*), and it is the subject (*mubtada'*), with ﴿fixed﴾ (*shakhisatun*) as a fronted predicate (*khabar muqaddam*), and ﴿the eyes﴾ (*absaru*) as a delayed subject (*mubtada' mu'akhkhar*). The clause is the predicate of the pronoun. It is not permissible for *shakhisatun* to be the predicate with *absaru* in the nominative governed by it, because the predicate of the pronoun of the matter can only be a complete clause with both its parts explicitly stated. Some Kufans permitted it to be a singular noun, in which case what was mentioned is permissible according to them.

It is reported from al-Farra' that *hiya* is a pronoun referring to *absar*, so it is an ambiguous pronoun (*damir mubham*) explained by what follows in the sphere of its predicate. Returning a pronoun to a later-mentioned noun, both verbally and in rank, in such a case is permissible according to Ibn Malik and others, as with the pronoun of the matter, and of this is his statement: "He is the earnest one, until the eye surpasses its sister." Rather, it is related from al-Farra' that whenever the speech indicates the referent and something explaining it is mentioned after it, even if it is not in the sphere of its predicate, its preceding does no harm. He recited the verse:

"By her father, my companion will not say, 'Malik ibn Abi Ka'b has fled from me.'"

It is also related from him that *hiya* is a separating pronoun (*damir fasl* or *'imad*), which could take its place as *huwa*, and he recited the verse:

"With a garment, a dinar, a sheep and a dirham, is he then the raised one, with what is here a head?"

This does not work except according to one of the two opinions of al-Kisa'i, namely his permission of placing the separating pronoun together with the predicate before the subject, and according to the opinion of one who permitted its occurrence before a predicate that is an indefinite noun. Al-Tha'labi mentioned that the speech is complete at His statement ﴿then, behold, it﴾, meaning: then, behold, it, that is, the Hour, is present, or manifest, or occurring. Then a new sentence begins: ﴿fixed are the eyes of those who disbelieved﴾. This is a strained view, with a jarring construction. It has also been said that the response of the conditional is ﴿draws near﴾, and the *waw* is a sword of the orator (*saif khatib*, i.e., an ornamental, superfluous *waw*). This is reported in Majma' al-Bayan from al-Farra'. It is reported from al-Zajjaj that the Basrans do not permit the addition of the *waw*, and that the response according to them is His statement ﴿O woe to us!﴾, with the saying implied before it, so it is by the implied "they said: O woe to us!" Whoever makes the response what preceded also implies the saying here and makes it a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the relative pronoun: "saying" or "they say, 'O woe to us!'" It is also permitted that the clause "they say: O woe to us!" be a resumptive new sentence (*isti'naf*).

The fixing of the eyes is the raising of their eyelids upward without blinking, and this happens to the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection from the intensity of terror. By the cry of woe they intended lamentation, as if they were saying: "O our Protector, come, for this is the time of your presence!"

﴿Indeed we were﴾ in the worldly life ﴿in heedlessness﴾ complete ﴿concerning﴾ this which has overtaken us, namely the resurrection and the return to Him, mighty and majestic is He, for recompense. It has also been said: "concerning this day, and we did not know that it was true." ﴿Rather, we were wrongdoers﴾. This is a turning away (*idrab*) from describing themselves as heedless, meaning: we were not heedless of it, since He alerted us to it through the signs and the warnings, but rather we were wrongdoers by abandoning the signs and the warnings, denying them, or wronging ourselves by exposing ourselves to the everlasting punishment through denial.

The Exalted's saying: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾. This is an address to the disbelievers of Makkah and an explicit statement of their final fate. Although this was already understood in general terms from what preceded it, it is stated here for emphasis in warning and to remove excuses. The word *ma* (what) refers to their idols. Using *ma* for them is in its proper usage, since according to the prevalent view idols are among things that do not reason. Therefore, it cannot be objected that Jesus, Ezra and the angels, peace be upon them, were worshipped besides Allah, while the ruling does not include them.

[Page 94]

It is widely reported that ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zibaʿrā al-Qurashī raised this objection against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ before his conversion. The Messenger, peace be upon him, said to him: "O boy, how ignorant you are of the language of your people! I said (*wa-ma taʿbudūna*, 'and what you worship'), and *ma* is for what does not reason, and I did not say (*wa-man taʿbudūna*, 'and whom you worship')."

Ibn Ḥajar, in his *Takhrīj Aḥādīth al-Kashshāf*, criticised this, saying: "It is famous on the tongues of many scholars of non-Arab origin and in their books, but it has no basis. It has not been found in any book of ḥadīth, whether with a chain of transmission or without one. Its fabrication is evident. It is strange that some ḥadīth scholars have transmitted it." End of quotation.

This conflicts with what we have said, since Abū Dāwūd in his *Nāsikh* (*al-Nāsikh wa-l-Mansūkh*), Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Ṭabarānī report from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "When ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship﴾ and the rest was revealed, it weighed heavily on the people of Makkah, and they said: 'Do you revile our gods?' Ibn al-Zibaʿrā said: 'I will argue against Muḥammad for you. Call him to me.' He was called, peace be upon him, and he said: 'O Muḥammad, is this for our gods only, or for everyone who is worshipped besides Allah, the Exalted?' He said: 'Rather, it is for everyone who is worshipped besides Allah, the Exalted.' Ibn al-Zibaʿrā said: 'You have been defeated, by the Lord of this edifice!'" — meaning the Kaʿbah. "Do you not claim, O Muḥammad, that Jesus is a righteous servant, that Ezra is a righteous servant, and that the angels are righteous?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then these Christians worship Jesus, these Jews worship Ezra, and these Banū Mulayḥ worship the angels." Then the people of Makkah clamoured and rejoiced, and there was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has preceded from Us﴾ and so on, and ﴿And when the son of Mary is cited as an example, at once your people turn away from it﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 57], and so on.

Other narrations support this, since the apparent meaning of that is that *mā* here includes both rational beings and others. It is answered that the inclusion of rational beings which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ claimed was through the indication of the text (*dalālat al-naṣṣ*, the implication understood from the text's wording and sense rather than its direct expression), by the common factor of being worshipped besides Allah, the Exalted. When he ﷺ pointed to the generality of the verse through this implicative indication, Ibn al-Zibaʿrā raised what he raised and imagined that he had achieved his aim. Then Allah, the Exalted, Himself answered with His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has preceded from Us﴾, to the end of the verse. Its essence is the restriction of the generality understood from the implicative indication of the text to other than the righteous ones for whom the best reward has preceded. Thus, the devils who were worshipped besides Allah, the Exalted, remain included in the ruling by the implicative indication of the text. After this restriction, the text indicates, both by its direct expression and by its implication, the ruling concerning the idols and the devils, and the objection is dispelled.

Some have said: *mā* includes rational beings and others. This is the view of the majority of the imams of the Arabic language, as the second ʿAllāma said in *al-Talwīḥ*. The evidence for this is the text, usage and meaning. As for the text, it is the Exalted's saying: ﴿And by He who created the male and the female﴾ [al-Layl: 3], His saying: ﴿And by the sky and He who built it﴾ [al-Shams: 5], and His saying: ﴿Nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ [al-Kāfirūn: 3]. As for usage, it is in two respects. First, *mā* is sometimes used in the sense of *alladhī* (who/which), by the consensus of the people of the language, and what is validly used for the one who reasons is used in the sense of *alladhī*, as in the expression "the one (*alladhī*) who came is Zayd," but *mā* is not so used. Second, it is valid to say: "Of the slaves in my house, *mā* are free," (meaning, those who are free). As for meaning, there are also two respects. First, the polytheists of Quraysh, as is reported through many chains from Ibn ʿAbbās, when they heard this verse, objected with Jesus, Ezra and the angels, peace be upon them. They were among the most eloquent of the Arabs, so if they had not understood the generality, they would not have objected. Second, if *mā* were specific to what does not know, there would be no need for the Exalted's saying: "besides Allah." Since it is general and includes Him, the Mighty and Majestic, there is need to qualify it with the saying of the Glorified: "besides Allah." In that case the verse includes the worship of those noble ones, peace be upon them, and the answer which Allah, the Exalted, gave Himself becomes an answer by restriction. In this is an argument for al-Shāfiʿī's position that a general term may be restricted by an independent but subsequent statement, contrary to the Ḥanafīs.

It is answered that what has been cited of texts and usages only shows the permissibility of applying *mā* to one who knows. It does not follow from this that it is apparent in that sense or in what includes it. Rather, it is apparent in reference to what does not know, especially here, because the address is to idol-worshippers. Since it is apparent for what does not reason, it must be interpreted accordingly. As for the first point mentioned in meaning, it is not explicit that the objectors objected because they understood generality from *mā* by its literal form. It is possible that this was because they understood it from the implicative indication of the text, as already explained. As for the second point mentioned, that there is no need for the Exalted's saying "besides Allah," this is valid only if it had no benefit. Its benefit, together with emphasis, is to censure what they were upon. Even if we grant that *mā* is literally for the one who reasons, we do not grant that the explanation of the restriction was not accompanying the verse. Rational indication is suitable for restriction, contrary to a small deviant group among the theologians. Reason has established the impossibility of punishing anyone for a crime committed by another, unless the one punished was pleased with the other's crime. None of the rational people had in mind that Christ, Ezra and the angels, peace be upon them, were pleased with the worship of those who worshipped them. Such a rational argument is not absent from the verse. As for the Exalted's saying: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has preceded from Us﴾ and so on, it came only as emphasis, by adding the legal evidence to the rational evidence, while being independent of the original (rational) evidence. It cannot be that it alone is the sole explanation. The Messenger ﷺ not addressing the rational argument was not because it did not exist, but because, when he saw them, they did not pay attention to it and turned away from it. So they objected with what they objected to, despite its clarity. He awaited what would strengthen it from the transmitted evidence. Or it is because revelation preceded him, peace be upon him, so the verse was revealed before he alerted them to that. It has been said: they were stubborn, using a kind of metaphor, so there was revealed what repels it. It has also been said: this is a report without legal obligation, and the disagreement over the permissibility of delaying explanation applies only to what involves obligation. But this needs consideration.

The ʿAllāma Ibn al-Kamāl said: "There is no disagreement between us and al-Shāfiʿī on restricting a general term to some of what it covers by an independent but subsequent statement. The disagreement is whether this is a specification (*takhṣīṣ*), such that the general term becomes probabilistic (*ẓannī*) concerning what remains, or abrogation (*naskh*), such that it remains as it was. There is no basis for arguing from the Exalted's saying: ﴿and what you worship besides Allah﴾, because what is established by it, if complete, is the restriction of the general term by a subsequent statement, and the disagreement concerns what lies beyond that, while the evidence is insufficient to explain it. Nor is there a basis for the answer that *taʿbudūna* does not include Jesus, Ezra and the angels, peace be upon them, not because *mā* is for non-rational beings, which is contrary to the view of the majority, but because they were not actually worshipped, as the Messenger ﷺ made clear when Ibn al-Zibaʿrā said: 'Did not the Jews worship Ezra, the Christians worship the Messiah, and the Banū Mulayḥ worship the angels?' He ﷺ replied: 'Rather, they worshipped the devils who commanded them to do so.' The Exalted's saying: ﴿Indeed, those for whom…﴾ is for removing the thought that it includes them, based on the apparent sense."

His ﷺ answer with this is among what Ibn Mardawayh and al-Wāḥidī transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, in which: "Then Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has preceded﴾," and so on. In accordance with this, the answer of the angels, peace be upon them, came in the Exalted's saying: ﴿And the Day He will gather them all, and say to the angels, "Did these worship you?" They will say, "Exalted are You! You are our Guardian, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn"﴾ [Saba': 40–41].

The reconciliation between this narration and the previous one is that after he ﷺ told Ibn al-Zibaʿrā that the verse is general for everyone worshipped besides Allah, the Exalted, by the indication of the text, and Ibn al-Zibaʿrā said: "Did not the Jews…" and so on, he ﷺ mentioned that those mentioned, peace be upon them, were not included, because they did not share with the idols in being worshipped besides Allah, the Exalted, since they neither commanded it nor approved of what the disbelievers were doing. Perhaps there is in this a hidden allusion to the rational evidence for their not being held accountable. Then the verse was revealed as emphasis for their not being included. However, it should not be overlooked that if this narration is sound, it implies that the idols are not worshipped either, since they did not command the worship. So *mā* does not apply to them, but only to the devils, on the basis that they are the ones who command and approve of this. Thus they are the objects of worship. For this reason, Abraham, peace be upon him, said: ﴿O my father, do not worship Satan﴾ [Maryam: 44], although he was openly worshipping idols.

[Page 96]

The reason for applying the feminine form to them, on the basis that they are not rational beings, is that they were treated like inanimate objects because of their disbelief. His (ﷺ) saying ﴿الَّتِي أمَرَتْهم﴾ ("which commanded them"), rather than ﴿الَّذِينَ أمَرُوهم﴾ ("those who commanded them"), points to this. Furthermore, there is considerable remoteness in the verse not including the idols here, so it may be that this report is not authentic. Our master Abu al-Su'ud has a statement based on the report that the Prophet (ﷺ) answered Ibn al-Za'bari (Ibn al-Za'bari) with the words: "How ignorant you are of the language of your people," and so on. You already know what al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar (al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar) said about it, and he and those like him are the ones relied upon in such matters. Therefore one should not be deceived by its mention in al-Amidi's (al-Amidi) *Ahkam*, the commentary on *al-Mawaqif*, *Fusul al-Badai'* of al-Fanari, and other works that are too numerous to count. "So it is water, but not like *sada'*; a pasture, but not like *sa'dan*."

It was objected to the view that the generality (*'umum*) is by indication of the text (*dalalat al-nass*) and the specification (*takhsis*) is by what was revealed after the discussion of specification by an independent, separated (*mutarakhi*) text, that the answer to this can be known from what has preceded. It has also been said, in addition to that, that this is not one of the cases of the disputed general term (*al-'amm al-mukhtalaf fihi*), because the general term there is a single expression indicating two or more named entities absolutely together, which is evident in what it indicates by its literal sense ('ibarah), whereas the generality here is understood only from the indication of the text. It is not hidden that the matter preventing delay is evident in the lack of difference, so reflect on this, for the context is worthy of it.

*Al-hasab* is that which is thrown and by which fire is kindled, from *hasabahu* ("he pelted him") with *al-hasba'* (small stones). It is specific in its lexical meaning but general in its usage. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it means firewood in Zanji (Zanj language). 'Ali, Ubayy, 'A'ishah, Ibn al-Zubayr and Zayd ibn 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with them) read *(hatab)* with *ta'* (ط). Ibn Abi al-Sumayqa, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, Mahbub and Abu Hatim, on the authority of Ibn Bashir, read *(hasb)* with the *sad* (ص) sukun. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them). It is a verbal noun (*masdar*) described by it for emphasis. In another narration from him, he read *(hadab)* with a *dad* (ض) fatha. Also from him is the sukun of the *dad*, and Kuthayyir 'Azzah read it so. The meaning of all of them is one, namely the meaning of *al-hasab* with *sad*.

﴿أنْتُمْ لَها وارِدُونَ﴾ ("You are to enter it") is a grammatical resumptive clause (*istinaf*) emphasizing what precedes it, or it is an apposition (*badal*) to ﴿حَصَبُ جَهَنَّمَ﴾ ("the fuel of Hell"). A clause may be an apposition to a single noun, and it does not harm that it is in the position of a consequence (*natijah*). Abu al-Baqa' allowed the clause to be a circumstantial state (*hal*) of *(jahannam)*, but as you see, this is far-fetched.

The *lam* here substitutes for *'ala* ("upon"), to indicate specificity and that their entering is for its sake. This is based on the view that the original construction of *al-wurud* (arriving/entering) takes *'ala* for that meaning, as al-Fayruzabadi indicated in the *Qamus* by defining it as "overlooking the water," and this is frequent in usage. Otherwise, it has been said that it is transitive by itself, as in the Exalted's saying ﴿ورَدُوها﴾ ("they will enter it"), so the *lam* is for reinforcement because the object is placed first and the governing verb is secondary. It has also been said that the *lam* means *ila* ("to"), as in the Exalted's saying ﴿بِأنَّ رَبَّكَ أوْحى لَها﴾ ("because your Lord has inspired it," Az-Zalzalah 99:5), but this is not correct.

The apparent meaning is that the *wurud* here is the *wurud* of entering, the address is to the disbelievers, and what they worship is included by way of predominance (*taghlib*).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 99:

﴿If these were gods﴾ as you claim, O worshippers, who worship them, ﴿they would not have entered it﴾. And since their entering it has been shown in the most complete manner, in that they are the fuel (haṣab) of Jahannam, it is necessarily impossible that they be gods. This is evident in that what is intended by "those they worship" is the idols and not the devils, for the purpose of the verse is to establish the opposite of what they claim. They claim the divinity of the idols, not their non-divinity, so that their entering the Fire could be used as evidence against it. Yes, the devils who are worshipped are included in the ruling of the text by way of implication (dalalah), so do not overlook this.

﴿And each﴾ of the worshippers and those worshipped ﴿therein will abide forever﴾, remaining for eternity.

[p. 97]

﴿For them therein is wailing﴾: it is the sound of the breath of one in distress, coming out from the depths of the chest. The original meaning of *zafir* (wailing), as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said, is the repeated drawing of breath until the ribs swell from it. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in *lahum* (for them) refers to all of them, namely the worshippers and the worshipped. In this there is *taghlib* (giving precedence to the rational over the non-rational, a rhetorical device whereby rational beings are given priority in grammatical reference), since the pronoun of rational beings is used to refer to the whole, as opposed to the idols. The same applies to *khalidun* (abiding) as well. Likewise, those among them who are capable of wailing and who possess life are given precedence over others among the idols, since wailing is attributed to all of them. It is also permissible that God Most High bestows life upon the idols that were worshipped, so that their state is like the state of those with them, and they have what those have; then there is no *taghlib*. It has also been said that the pronoun refers only to those addressed in ﴿Indeed you﴾, by way of *iltifat* (a shift in the grammatical person of address), so there is no need at all to say there is *taghlib*. This has been refuted on the grounds that it would produce discord in the noble arrangement of the discourse (*nazm*). Do you not see the words of God Most High: ﴿You are its certain entrants﴾, how it combines them together by *taghlib* of those addressed? So if ﴿For them therein is wailing﴾ were restricted to them, it would necessitate disjunction. The same discussion applies to His words, Most High: ﴿and they therein will not hear﴾, meaning that some of them do not hear the wailing of others because of the intensity of the terror and the severity of the punishment, according to what has been said. It has also been said: they do not hear, even if they were called to, because of the intensity of their wailing. It has also been said: they do not hear the words that would please them, since they are addressed only with what they dislike. It has also been said that they are afflicted with deafness in reality, relying on the apparent meaning of His words, Most High: ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, mute and deaf﴾ [al-Isra’: 97]. But this, as you see, is far-fetched.

It has been mentioned, regarding the wisdom of placing the polytheists in the Fire together with what they worshipped, that it is an increase in their grief by seeing them tormented like themselves, though they had hoped for their intercession. It has also been said that it is an increase in their grief by seeing them with them, while they are the cause of their punishment. Thus it has been said:

Enduring harm and seeing the one who inflicted it
is a nourishment by which bodies are worn away.

The apparent meaning of some reports is that the final state of those who abide [in the Fire] is that none of them sees another. Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) and a group related from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: When those who will abide in the Fire remain in it, they are placed in coffins of iron with iron nails, then those coffins are placed inside other coffins of iron, then they are cast into the bottom of the Blazing Fire, so that none of them sees that anyone else is being punished in the Fire. Then he recited the verse: ﴿For them therein is wailing, and they therein will not hear﴾. From this there is known another opinion regarding ﴿they will not hear﴾. And God Most High knows best.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 101:

﴿Indeed, those for whom the best (al-husna) has already preceded from Us﴾. That is, the most excellent quality, which is happiness (al-sa'ada). It was also said: it is success in obedience (al-tawfiq li-l-ta'a). What is meant by "has preceded" is its decree in eternity (al-azal). It was also said: al-husna is the good word (al-kalima al-husna), which includes the good tidings of their reward and the appreciation of their deeds. What is meant by "has preceded" is its prior mention in the words of God Most High: ﴿So whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer, his effort will not be denied, and indeed We are recording it for him﴾ [al-Anbiya' 94]. This is contrary to the apparent meaning. The apparent meaning is that the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) refers to everyone who is characterized by the description in the relative clause, and the specificity of the occasion of revelation (khusus al-sabab) does not restrict the general wording. As for what is mentioned in some reports, that it was interpreted as referring to Jesus, Ezra and the angels, peace be upon them, this is an instance of restricting the general to some of its individual members, since they were the cause of the revelation. It is appropriate to classify as restriction what Ibn Abi Shaybah and others transmitted from Muhammad ibn Hatib, from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he interpreted the relative pronoun as referring to Uthman and his companions, may Allah be pleased with them.

Ibn Abi Hatim and a group related from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir that Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, recited the verse and said: "I am among them, and Umar is among them, and Uthman is among them, and al-Zubayr is among them, and Talha is among them, and Sa'd and Abd al-Rahman are among them." Thus I saw it in al-Durr al-Manthur. And I saw in other sources a count of the ten who were given the good tidings (al-'ashara al-mubashshara), may Allah be pleased with them. The two prepositional phrases (al-jarrān) are related to "has preceded."

Abu al-Baqa permitted that the second one be related to an omitted element, and that it occurs as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "al-husna." God's words ﴿Those﴾ are a reference to the relative pronoun in view of its being characterized by what is within the scope of the relative clause. The sense of distance in it serves to signal the loftiness of their rank and the remoteness of their station in nobility and merit, that is, "those who are described with what has been mentioned of the description." ﴿From it﴾, that is, from Hell, ﴿will be kept far away﴾, because they are in Paradise, and how far apart are it and the Fire.

Page 98

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 21, verse 102:

﴿They will not hear its faintest sound﴾: that is, its sound that is perceived from its movement. The clause is a *badal* (substitute, or apposition) for "*mub'adun*" (kept far away). It is also permitted that it be a *hal* (circumstantial clause) from its pronoun, or a predicate following another predicate (*khabar ba'da khabar*). It is preferred that it be a *mu'akkidah* (emphatic restatement) of what the first clause conveys of their being kept far from it. It has been said that the keeping away occurs after nearness, so it is understood from this that they had been brought near to it first. Since this was the likely cause of harm from it, it was removed by His words, glorified is He, ﴿they will not hear﴾. Thus it is a new clause (*mustanaffah*) to remove that. On this view, not hearing the faint sound occurs before entering Paradise. Whoever holds this says: this happens at the time of crossing the *Sirat* (the Bridge). That is because, as has come in some reports, they pass over it while it is extinguished, with no movement, to the extent that they think, while they are in Paradise, that they did not pass over it.

It has been said that they do not hear it because of the speed of their passing. This is the apparent meaning of what Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said concerning the verse: "Those are the friends of Allah, the Exalted. They pass over the Sirat in a passing faster than lightning, so it does not touch them, and they do not hear its faint sound, while the disbelievers remain kneeling." However, a different report came from him, also transmitted by Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir, that he said concerning ﴿they will not hear﴾ and so on: "The people of Paradise will not hear the faint sound of the Fire when they have descended to their abodes in Paradise." It has also been said that the keeping away from it occurs before entering Paradise as well, and the meaning of that is Allah's protection of them from falling into it, as one says: "Allah, the Exalted, kept so-and-so far from doing evil." The more evident view is that both matters occur after entering Paradise, and that is an explanation of their deliverance from the destructions and the perils.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿and they will abide in what their souls desire﴾ explain their attainment of their desires after that deliverance. The meaning is that they will remain forever in the utmost comfort. The fronting of the adverbial phrase serves restriction (*qasr*), emphasis, and the observance of the verse-endings (*fawasil*).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 103:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾ is an explanation of their being completely saved from terror, after their being saved from the Fire. For if the greatest terror does not grieve them, then by necessity nothing else grieves them. So it has been said. But this should be considered together with what has come in the reports that the Fire will roar on the Plain of Gathering (al-mawqif) a single roar, such that no prophet or angel will remain but he will fall to his knees. If we say that this does not contradict the absence of grief, then there is no difficulty. If we say that it does contradict it, then it is problematic, unless it is said that because of the brevity of its duration and the speed of the security that follows it, it takes the place of non-existence. So reflect. Fazaʿ (terror), as ar-Raghib said, is a contraction and aversion that befalls a person from a frightening thing, and it is of the same kind as jaza' (anguish). It is also used for departing swiftly out of what terrifies.

The time of this terror has been disputed. From al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Juraij it is reported that it is at the moment the people of the Fire are driven away to the Fire.

It is reported from al-Hasan that he explained "the greatest terror" as this very driving away, so that "terror" would mean the departure mentioned earlier. From ad-Dahhak it is reported that it is at the moment the lid of Hell closes over it and it is shut upon those within it; this is also found in a report of Ibn Abi ad-Dunya from Ibn ʿAbbas. It has been said: at the moment the people of the Fire are called, ﴿Be silent therein, and do not speak to Me﴾. It has been said: at the moment death is slaughtered between Paradise and the Fire. It has been said: on the day the heaven is folded up. It has been said: at the final blast (an-nafkhah al-akhirah). Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted this from Ibn ʿAbbas. The apparent meaning is that by it is meant the blast for rising from the graves to the Lord of the worlds.

Concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the angels will receive them﴾, i.e., they will welcome them with mercy when they rise from their graves. It has been said: with greeting upon them at that time, saying, ﴿This is your day which you were promised﴾ in the world, its coming, and you are given good tidings of the rewards in it for you because of faith
صفحة 99
and obedience. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid that he said concerning the verse: "the angels who were their companions in the world will receive them on the Day of Resurrection, and they will say, 'We are your allies in the life of this world and in the Hereafter; we will not part from you until you enter Paradise.'" It has been said: they receive them at the gate of Paradise with gifts or with greetings. The more evident view is that this occurs at rising from the graves, and it serves as an indication that the absence of grief is at the final blast. The apparent sense of most of the clauses requires that the angels are not included in the preceding relative clause; indeed, His saying, Exalted is He, "And the angels will receive them," etc., is explicit on this. So perhaps the attribution in that case, according to those who include the angels, peace be upon them, in the generality of the relative clause by way of the occasion of revelation, is by way of precedence (taghlib); or it may be said that their exception from the preceding generality of this verse is by way of the indication of the text (dalalat al-nass), just as their inclusion in what came before was in that manner. Abu Ja'far read ﴿لا يُحْزِنُهم﴾ as the present tense of aḥzana, and it is the dialect of Tamim, while ḥazina is the dialect of Quraysh.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 104 (part 1 of 2):

﴿The Day We fold up the heaven﴾ is in the accusative, governed by "remember" (udhkur). It has also been said that it is an adverbial phrase of time (zarf) for "they will not be grieved" (la yuhzinuhum), and it has been said it is for "the terror" (al-faza'). The definite verbal noun (al-masdar al-mu'arraf), although weak in governing, especially since it has been separated from its object by a foreign element, is nevertheless permissible, because the adverbial phrase is a place of latitude (tawassu'); so said al-Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf.

Al-Khafaji said: the qualified verbal noun does not govern according to the correct view, even if the adverbial phrase may be given latitude. It has also been said that it is an adverbial phrase for "will meet them" (tatalaqqahum). It has been said that it is a substitute (badal) for the omitted returning pronoun in ﴿you are promised﴾, a substitute of the whole for the whole, and it has been imagined to be a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal). It has been said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) of that returning pronoun, which is supposed (muqaddarah), because the Day of folding comes after the promise.

Shayba ibn Nisah and a group read (yatwi) with the ya' and the active form, its subject being Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Abu Ja'far and another read with the upper ta' and the passive form, with "the heaven" (al-sama') in the nominative as deputy subject (naiba). Al-tayy is the opposite of spreading out (al-nashr). It has also been said that it means annihilation and removal, from your saying: "fold up this talk from me" (utwi 'anni hadha al-hadith). Ibn al-Qayyim denied the annihilation of the heaven and its complete extinction, and claimed that the texts only indicate its alteration and change from one state to another. What makes the view of annihilation remote is the evident comparison in His Exalted saying: ﴿like the folding of the scroll﴾, and the scroll (al-sijill) is the sheet (sahifa), as Ibn Jarir and others transmitted from Mujahid, and in Majma' al-Bayan it is attributed to Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Kalbi as well. Some restricted it to the sheet of a covenant. It has also been said: it is originally a stone on which writing is inscribed, and then every thing written upon, whether paper or otherwise, was named by it. The prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) is in the position of an adjective to an omitted verbal noun, meaning a folding like the folding of the sheet.

Abu Hurayra and his companion Abu Zur'a ibn Amr ibn Jarir read (al-sujull) with two dammas and a shadda on the lam; al-A'mash, Talha and Abu al-Sammal read (al-sajl) with a fatha on the sin; al-Hasan and Isa with a kasra on it. The jim in these two readings is sukun and the lam is light. Abu Amr said: the people of Makka read like al-Hasan.

The lam in His saying ﴿for the books﴾ is connected to an omitted element which is a circumstantial clause (hal) of ﴿al-sijill﴾ or an adjective to it, according to the view of one who permits omitting the relative pronoun together with part of its clause, meaning: like the folding of the scroll being for the books, or the one being for the books. For "the books" refers to the sheets and what is written in them, so the scroll is part of their parts, and folding is literally connected to it. Al-A'mash read (lil-kutbi) with sukun on the ta'. The majority read (lil-kitab) in the singular. It is either a verbal noun, and the lam is for causation, meaning: as the scroll (al-tumar) is folded for writing, i.e., so that writing may be done in it. This is a metaphor for its being prepared and placed smooth and folded, so that when writing is needed there is no need to smooth it; therefore it is not objected that the known practice is unrolling the scroll for writing, not folding it for it. Or it is a noun like "imam," and the lam is as mentioned first.

Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that al-Sijill is the name of an angel. Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Asakir transmitted that from al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with him. Ibn Jarir and others transmitted something similar from al-Suddi, except that he said: he is entrusted with the sheets; when a person dies his book comes to him, so he folds it and raises it until the Day of Resurrection. The lam according to this view has been said to be connected to "folding," and it has been said it is a sword of an orator (sayf khatib), and that it is in the sense of "upon" (ala) is as you see. This view has been objected to on the ground that the comparison is not good with it, since the thing compared to is neither stronger nor more well-known. It was answered that it is stronger in consideration, due to what is in the minds of common people of the strength of the folder and the weakness of the folded thing and its smallness relative to the heaven; i.e., in view of the combination of both matters in their minds. So reflect.

Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and a group, including al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, transmitted and authenticated from Ibn Abbas that al-Sijill was a scribe of the Prophet ﷺ. A group transmitted something similar from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both. This has been judged weak, and indeed it has been said it is a very baseless view, because no companion, may Allah be pleased with them, is known by the name al-Sijill, and the comparison does not become good upon it either. Al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Asakir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the man (al-rajul)... Ibn Mardawayh added: in the language of Abyssinia; and this was related from al-Zajjaj. Some said: it is possible to carry the earlier narration from Ibn Abbas upon this, and most upon what has been said regarding interpreting al-sijill as the sheet.

There was disagreement over whether it is Arabic or arabized. The Basrans held that it is Arabic, while Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said the more correct view is that it is Persian, arabized. Then, the verse is an explicit text on the effacing of the heaven, which contradicts what has spread from the philosophers. Yes, Sadr al-Din al-Shirazi mentioned in his book al-Asfar that the view of the leading ancient philosophers is the saying of effacement (al-dutur), and the saying to the contrary is only from their later ones, due to the deficiency of their insight and the lack of purity of their hearts. Among the leaders is Anaximenes of Miletus (Ankisimaises al-Malti), who said: the persistence of this world is only by the measure of the little light of that world it contains, and by "that world" he meant the world of pure immaterial beings; otherwise it would not endure for an instant. Its persistence continues until its mixed part is purified from its mixed portion; when the two parts are purified, then the parts of this world are effaced, destroyed and remain dark, and the defiled souls remain in this darkness having no light, no joy, no rest, no tranquility, and no consolation.

Among them is Pythagoras, of whom it is transmitted that he was asked: why did you say the world is annihilated? He said: because it reaches the cause for which it existed; when it reaches it, its motion stops. Among them is Plato. Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Amiri related that he mentioned in his well-known book Timaeus that the world is created, that the Creator, Exalted, has turned it from disorder to order, that its substances are all composed of matter and form, and that every composite is subject to dissolution. Yes, he said in Asulutiqus, meaning the management of the body: the world is eternal, uncreated, and everlasting. Abraqlis relied on this, so there is contradiction between his two statements; his disciple Aristotle reconciled them with what is open to question, and perhaps the most suitable thing to say according to their school is that by the eternal world he meant the world of pure separate beings.

Among them is Aristotle, who said in the book Athulujia that intelligible things necessitate sensible things, while the Exalted Creator does not necessitate sensible and intelligible things; rather He, Glorified, sustains all things. However, intelligible things are true essences, since they originate from the First Cause without intermediary, while sensible things are circular essences, since they are the traces and likenesses of the true essences; their subsistence and permanence are by generation and reproduction, so that they may endure, imitating the intelligible things which are fixed and everlasting. He said in the book of Lordship: the intellect produced the form of the soul without moving, in imitation of the True One, for the intellect was produced by the True One while He was at rest; the soul was produced by the intellect, which is also at rest; however, the True One produced the quiddity of the intellect, and the intellect produced the form of the soul. Since it was an effect of an effect, it was not able to act its act without motion, but acted with motion, and produced an idol (sanam). It was called an idol because it is a perishing act, not fixed nor lasting, because it came about through motion, and motion does not bring about a fixed and lasting thing, but only a perishing one; otherwise its act would be nobler than it, and that is very ugly. One of the dahriyya asked him: if the Originator has always been, and there was nothing other than Him, and then He originated the world, why did He originate it? He said: "why" is not permissible regarding Him, because "why" requires a cause, and the cause is borne in what it causes from a causer above it, and He is not composite that bears causes in His essence, so "why" is negated from Him. He only did what He did because He is generous. It was said: then He must be an agent who has always been, since He is generous and has always been. He said: the meaning of "has always been" is that it has no beginning, and the act of an agent requires a beginning, and the combination of what has no beginning and what has a beginning in word and essence is purely contradictory. It was said: then does He annihilate this world? He said: Yes. It was said: then if He annihilates it, generosity is annihilated. He said: He annihilates it in order to shape it into the form that does not admit corruption, because this form admits corruption. Among them is Porphyry, author of the Isagoge, who said: all created things come into being only by the coming into being of form, by way of change, and they perish by the emptying of form, and other things of that kind from the philosophers and their sayings.

To mention all of that leads to tedium, and whoever wants it should return to al-Asfar and other books of al-Sadr. The truth is that much has occurred in the sayings of the earlier philosophers which is clearly contrary to the meaning of the noble verse and scarcely admits interpretation, and it is what their principles require; and whatever seems to agree with it agrees only in general, and the commitment to harmonize what Muslims say about the whole world with what the philosophers say about it is like harmonizing the lizard (dabb) with the nun, or rather like combining motion and rest.

O you who marry the Pleiades to Suhayl, by your life, Allah, how can the two meet?
She is Syrian when she departs, and Suhayl, when he departs, is Yemeni.

So hold fast to what the Clear Book has stated, or what is authentically related from the Trustworthy Truthful one ﷺ, and there is nothing upon you if you oppose the philosophers, for most of what they brought is ignorance and folly. By my life, many people have gone astray by their words, and the whispering tempter has laid eggs and hatched in their breasts. Their talk is noise without grinding, and clatter like the clatter of a waterskin. Were it not for the necessity which I do not disclose, and the cause whose remedy is hard to find, I would not have wasted the prime of my youth on studying and teaching it, nor would I have mentioned any of it within the lines of my book. This, while I ask Allah, Exalted, for success in holding fast to the firm rope of truth. Then, the apparent sense of the sound reports is that the Throne is not folded as the heaven is folded. If it is the encompassing sphere (al-muhaddad), as the philosophers and those who follow their traces claim, then the non-effacement of it in particular has been stated explicitly by Alexander of Aphrodisias, one of the great companions of Aristotle, although he differed from him on some questions; whoever interprets his words otherwise has been forced and has brought what is not granted to him. The apparent sense of the noble verse also indicates that it is not folded, since it restricts folding to the heaven. The common usage is that the term is not applied to the Throne. Then, folding is not restricted to one heaven rather than another, but all of them are folded, according to His saying: ﴿and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand﴾ [al-Zumar: 67].

﴿As We originated the first creation, We will repeat it﴾. The apparent view is that the kaf is a preposition and ma is verbal (masdariyya), the verbal noun being governed by it, and the prepositional phrase is an adjective to an omitted verbal noun. "First" (awwala) is the object of "originated" (bada'na), meaning: We will repeat the first creation by a repetition like Our origination of it, i.e., in ease and absence of difficulty. It has been said: i.e., in its being an existence after non-existence, or a gathering of scattered parts. It is not hidden that in regard to the repetition being an existence after non-existence absolutely, there is an issue. Yes, al-Laqani said: the view of most is that Allah, Glorified, annihilates the essences entirely and then restores them; this is the saying of the People of the Sunna and of the Mu'tazila who hold that annihilation upon bodies is valid, indeed that it occurs.

Al-Badr al-Zarkashi and al-Amidi said: it is the correct view. The saying that repetition is from pure dispersal is the saying of the minority, and it was related from

Collection in the form of hedging, but in al-Mawaqif and its commentary: Does God, exalted is He, annihilate the bodily parts and then restore them, or does He disperse them and restore the composition in them? The truth is that nothing has been established regarding this, neither negating nor affirming it, due to the absence of evidence for either side.

In al-Iqtisad by Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali: If it is said, "Are substances and accidents annihilated and then both restored together, or are accidents annihilated without substances and the accidents restored?" We say: All of that is possible, and the truth is that there is no decisive evidence in the Shari'ah specifying any one of these possibilities.

Some have said: The truth is that both occur: the restoration of what was annihilated in its very self, and the restoration of what was dispersed with its accidents. You know that the reports have been authenticated regarding the preservation of the "ajb al-dhanab" (the coccyx, the small bone at the base of the spine) of a human being, so the restoration of the human is not like his initial creation. Likewise it has been narrated that God, Mighty and Majestic, forbade the earth to consume the bodies of the prophets, and this is a hadith that is hasan according to Ibn al-'Arabi, while others said it is sahih. Something similar has come regarding those who call the adhan for the sake of reward, and their hadith is in al-Tabarani; and regarding the bearers of the Qur'an, and their hadith is with Ibn Mindah; and regarding one who never committed a sin, and their hadith is from al-Marwazi, so do not be heedless. Likewise, as for the initial creation being a gathering of scattered parts: if it holds for a compound of elements such as the human being, it does not hold for the elements themselves, for example, because they were not first created from scattered parts, by the consensus of the Muslims. So perhaps what we have mentioned regarding the aspect of the resemblance is further from dispute and debate.

It has been objected to making (awwal) the object of "bada'na" (We initiated), that connecting the beginning to the first part of the thing begun is weak; one does not say "I began the first of such-and-such" but rather "I began such-and-such," because the beginning of a thing is the thing begun, and what is begun necessarily coincides with the first, so mentioning it would be redundant.

This has been examined: the intended meaning of "We initiated" is that which was first and prior in existence, and "the first" does not mean the first of the parts, so as to suppose what was mentioned. It has also been said: "awwal khalq" (the first creation) is the object of "nu'idu" (We restore), which is explained by "nu'iduhu" (We restore it), and the kaf is restrained by ma, meaning: We restore the first creation, We restore it; the speech is complete with that, and "kama bada'na" (as We initiated) is a separate sentence, in the sense: that has been realized just as its realization was; and the meaning is not a restoration like the initiation. The place of the kaf, in such a case, is nominative, as the predicate of an elided subject, brought in for emphasis, and the context requires it, as the rebuke indicates. So it should not be said that there is no need to commit to something contrary to the apparent meaning. The indefinite "khalq" is for the purpose of detailing, and it stands in place of the plural in conveying the inclusion of all, so it is as if it were said: We restore the earlier created beings.

It has also been permitted that the kaf be put in the accusative by a hidden verb explained by "nu'iduhu," with ma being a relative pronoun and "awwal" being an adverb of "bada'na," because the relative pronoun requires a returning pronoun; when that is estimated here it becomes the object. And "awwal" has the capacity to be accusative as an adverb of time, so it is put in the accusative by it. It may also be in the position of a circumstantial clause from that returning pronoun. The resulting meaning: We restore the like of that which We initiated at the first creation, or being the first creation. The "khalq" in the first case is a verbal noun, and in the second it means the created thing. It has also been permitted that ma is descriptive and the rest of the speech remains as it is.

Abu Hayyan objected to the accusative of the kaf on the grounds that it is a view that it is a noun, and this is not the position of the majority; it was only held by al-Akhfash. The position of the Basrans is other than this: that its being a noun is restricted to poetry. He cited something similar against the view that its place is nominative in the earlier aspect. And if it is said that the restrained kaf has a complement, as some have chosen, contrary to al-Radi and those with him, then its complement should be the predicate of an elided subject there. It was preferred that the intended meaning is: We restore the like of that which We initiated at the first creation, based on what Ibn Jarir transmitted from A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered upon me while with me was an old woman from the Banu 'Amir. He said: "Who is this old woman, O A'ishah?" I said: "One of my maternal aunts." She said: "Ask God to admit me to Paradise." He, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed Paradise is not entered by the aged." The old woman was seized by distress, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed God, exalted is He, will create them a creation other than their creation." Then he said: "You will be gathered barefoot, naked, uncircumcised." She said: "Far be it from God, exalted is He, from that!" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Yes indeed, God, exalted is He, said: 'As We initiated the first creation, We shall restore it.'" A similar meaning results from what Ibn al-Hajib permitted, that "kama bada'na" is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "nu'iduhu," meaning: We restore the first creation resembling that which We initiated. Do not be heedless of what the comparison requires of the difference between the two sides. In any case, the intended meaning is the announcement of the resurrection, and none of the aspects is specific to the heavens, since the meaning does not indicate that, nor does the wording support it. Ibn Jarir also transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that the meaning of the verse is: We shall destroy every thing as it was the first time. This requires reflection, so reflect.

"Wa'dan" (a promise) is a verbal noun in the accusative, governed by its elided verb, as an emphasis for it; the sentence emphasizes what precedes it. Or it is accusative by "nu'idu," because it is a promise of restoration. This is the view of al-Zajjaj. Al-Tabarsi preferred the first, arguing that the readers pause at "nu'iduhu 'alayna" (We shall restore it upon Us) in the position of a qualifier for "wa'dan," meaning: a promise binding upon Us, and the intended meaning is that its fulfilment is obligatory, without any need to strain with the device of istikhdam. "Innا kunna fa'ilina" (Indeed We were ever doers): that is, We will certainly do that in actuality. Future acts that God knows will occur are like past ones in their certainty; for this reason the future is expressed by the past in many places in the Noble Book. Or it means: capable of doing that. This was chosen by al-Zamakhshari, and it has been objected to this that it is contrary to the apparent meaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 105:

﴿And We have certainly written in the Zabur﴾ The apparent meaning is that it is the Zabur of Dawud (David), peace be upon him, and this is related from al-Sha'bi.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it means "the Books," and the Reminder in His saying, ﴿after the Reminder﴾, is the Tawrah (Torah). This explanation is also related from al-Dahhak. He said regarding the Zabur: "The Books after the Tawrah." He also reported from Ibn Jubayr that the Reminder is the Tawrah and the Zabur is the Qur'an.

He reported from Ibn Zayd that the Zabur is "the Books which were sent down upon the Prophets, peace be upon them," and the Reminder is the "Mother of the Book" (Umm al-Kitab) in which things are written before that, and it is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), as in some reports. Al-Zajjaj chose this explanation. Applying the term "Reminder" to it is a metaphor. It occurs in the hadith of al-Bukhari from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah existed and nothing was before Him, and His Throne was upon the water. Then Allah created the heavens and the earth, and wrote in the Reminder everything." It has also been said that the Reminder is knowledge, and this is what is meant by the Mother of the Book.

The root meaning of Zabur is every book written in thick (heavy) script, from "zabartu al-kitab, azburu" with the letter ba' either fatha or damma, as in al-Muhkam (a classical Arabic lexicon), when one writes it in a thick hand. In common usage it is restricted to the book revealed to Dawud, peace be upon him. Some have said it is a name for a book confined to wisdom of the intellect, without the legal rulings of the Shari'ah, and for this reason the one revealed to Dawud, peace be upon him, is so called, since it contains none of the legal rulings.

The apparent meaning is that it is an Arabic name in the sense of "the written" (al-mazbur), and for this reason it is permitted to attach ﴿min ba'd﴾ to it, just as it is permitted to attach it to "katabna" (We have written). Hamza said it is a Syriac name. Whichever is the case, if by it is meant "the Books," then the lam in it is for the genus, meaning: We have written in the genus of the Zabur.

﴿that the earth - My righteous servants will inherit it﴾ Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and others reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the intended earth is the earth of Paradise. The Imam said: This is supported by His saying, ﴿And He has caused us to inherit the earth, to settle in Paradise wherever we will﴾ [al-Zumar 39:74], and it is the earth which is specific to the righteous, since it was created for them, and others who enter it do so only by way of following them. Also, the verse was mentioned right after the mention of the Return (of creation), and after the Return there is no earth in which the righteous settle and with which they are favoured, other than the earth of Paradise. This view is related from Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrima, al-Suddi and Abu al-'Aliyah.

In another report from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, the intended meaning is the earth of this world, which the believers will inherit and over which they will gain control. This is the view of al-Kalbi, and it is supported by His saying, ﴿He will surely grant them succession upon the earth﴾ [al-Nur 24:55].

Muslim, Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi reported from Thawban, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah gathered the earth for me, so I saw its easts and its wests, and the dominion of my Ummah will reach what was gathered for me of it." This is a promise from Him, exalted is He, of the manifestation of the religion, the honouring of its people, and their gaining control over most of the inhabited world, which the travellers frequently traverse. Otherwise, there are parts of the earth which the believers have not trodden, such as the land known as the New World and the Western India. And even if we say that all of that will be under the control of the believers in the days of the Mahdi, may Allah be pleased with him, and the descent of 'Isa, peace be upon him, then there is no need for what has been mentioned.

It has been said that the intended meaning is the Holy Land (al-Ard al-Muqaddasah), and it has been said that it is al-Sham (Greater Syria). Perhaps the survival of the disbelievers alone over the whole earth at the end of time, as the reports affirm, does not harm this inheritance, because between their independent possession of the earth at that time and the establishment of the Hour there is a short period which is not significant, and this has been counted among the near signs of the Day of Resurrection. The better view is to interpret the earth as the earth of Paradise, as the majority have held, and this is more suitable to the context.

Among the strange accounts is the story of Sultan Selim's optimism (tafa'ul) by this verse when he intended to make war upon al-Ghawri, and Ibn Kamal's good tidings to him, taking from what the verse hints at, the kingdom of Egypt in such-and-such a year, and the matter occurring as he had announced. It is a well-known story, but such matters are coincidental, and one should not rely upon the like of it.

[p. 104]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 106:

﴿Indeed, in this﴾ i.e., in what has been mentioned in this noble surah of reports, profound admonitions, promise and threat, and conclusive proofs indicating the Oneness (tawhid) and the soundness of prophethood. It has also been said: the reference is to the whole Qur'an. ﴿is surely a message﴾ i.e., a sufficiency, or a means of reaching the desired aim, or the very attainment of it, by way of emphasis (mubalaghah). ﴿for a people who worship﴾ i.e., for a people whose concern is worship rather than habit. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan that they are those who pray the five prayers in congregation.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited that and said: it refers to the five prayers in the Sacred Mosque in congregation." The pronoun in (هي, "they/it") refers to the worship implied by (عابدين, "worshipping"). Abu Hurayrah, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Mujahid said: it refers to the five prayers, without restricting it to anything. From Ka'b al-Ahbar, its interpretation is the fasting of the month of Ramadan and the five prayers. The apparent meaning is generality, and what has been mentioned is from the category of confining the statement to some of the individual instances for a particular reason.

[p. 105]

﴿And We have not sent you﴾ with what has been mentioned, and with its like of laws and rulings and other things that are the basis of the happiness of both abodes, ﴿except as a mercy to the worlds﴾. This is an exception from the most general of the causes (*'ilal*, causes or motives), meaning: We did not send you with what has been mentioned for any cause except that you might show mercy to the worlds by your being sent. Or it is an exception from the most general of the states (*ahwal*, circumstances), meaning: We did not send you in any state except as a mercy, or as one possessing mercy, or as one who shows mercy to them by conveying what you were sent with.

The apparent meaning is that "the worlds" (*al-'alamin*) includes the disbelievers. The justification for this is that he, upon him be blessings and peace, was sent with what is a cause of the happiness of both abodes and the benefit of both lives. However, the disbeliever has deprived himself of benefiting from this, and turned away from what is there because of the corruption of his receptivity. Therefore this does not harm the fact that he, may God bless him and grant him peace, was sent as a mercy with respect to him as well, just as the presence of a sweet spring, for example, is beneficial even though the lazy man does not benefit from it because of his laziness. This is clear, contrary to those who have disputed it.

As for whether "the worlds" also includes the angels, upon them be peace, there is a disagreement based on the disagreement over the universality of his mission (*'umum ba'thatihi*) to them, may God bless him and grant him peace. If we say it is universal, as al-Barizi of the Shafi'is, Taqi al-Din al-Subki, and al-Jalal al-Mahalli in his *Khasa'is* preferred, and among the Hanbalis Ibn Taymiyya, Ibn Hamid and Ibn Muflih in *Kitab al-Furu'*, and among the Malikis 'Abd al-Haqq, then we say that "the worlds" here includes them. The fact that he, upon him be blessings and peace, was sent as a mercy with respect to them is because he also came with what involves imposing on them commands and prohibitions, even if we do not know what they are. And there is no doubt that in the compliance of the one under obligation with what he is obligated to there is benefit and happiness for him.

If we say there is no universality, as al-Halimi, al-Bayhaqi, al-Jalal al-Mahalli in his commentary on *Jam' al-Jawami'*, and Zayn al-Din al-'Iraqi in his *Nukat* on Ibn al-Salah among the Shafi'is, and Mahmud ibn Hamza in his *al-'Aja'ib wa al-Gharayib* among the Hanafis, have definitively affirmed, indeed al-Burhan al-Nasafi and al-Fakhr al-Razi in their two commentaries reported a consensus (*ijma'*) on it. And even if this is not accepted, we say that they are not included here and that others besides them are intended. It has also been said: they are included here in the generality, even if we do not hold that he was sent to them, because through the sending of him, upon him be blessings and peace, they came to be acquainted with many sciences and great secrets from what was deposited in his Book, in which is the foundation of what was and what will be, by expression and by allusion. And what happiness is greater than adorning oneself with the adornment of knowledge?

As for the fact that they, upon them be peace, do not ignore anything which no one among the Muslims has held, it has also been said: this is because of their superiority, which was manifested upon the tongue of the Noble One as it was manifested.
