Some have said: the mercy with respect to the disbelievers is their safety, through his mission, upon him be blessings and peace, from being swallowed up by the earth, transformed, pelted with stones, or annihilated. This was reported by al-Tabarani, al-Bayhaqi and a group from Ibn 'Abbas. It has been mentioned that with respect to the angels, upon them be peace, the mercy is safety from something like what Harut and Marut were tested with. This is supported by what the author of *al-Shifa'* mentioned: "The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said to Jibril, upon him be peace: 'Has any of this mercy reached you?' He said: 'Yes. I used to fear the consequence, so I was made secure by God, exalted is He, praising me in the Qur'an by His saying: ﴿Possessor of strength, esteemed with the Lord of the Throne﴾ [al-Takwir 81:20].'" If this hadith is authentic, then it necessarily follows that "the worlds" includes the angels, upon them be peace. However, al-Jalal al-Suyuti mentioned in *Tazyin al-Ara'ik* that no chain of narration (*isnad*) for it has been found.

It has also been said that the intended meaning of "the worlds" is all creation, for "the world" (*al-'alam*) is everything other than God, exalted is He, and His attributes. It was pluralized with the plural of rational beings out of precedence (*taghlib*) given to the more noble over others.

That he, may God bless him and grant him peace, is a mercy to all is with regard to his being, upon him be blessings and peace, the intermediary of the Divine overflow (*al-fayd al-ilahi*) upon possible beings according to their receptacles. For this reason his light, may God bless him and grant him peace, was the first of created things. In a report: "The first thing God, exalted is He, created was the light of your Prophet, O Jabir." 

And there has come: "God is the Giver and I am the Distributor." The Sufis, may their secrets be sanctified, have in this matter words beyond that. In *Miftah al-Sa'ada* Ibn al-Qayyim said that were it not for the prophethoods, there would be in the world no beneficial knowledge whatsoever, no righteous deed, no soundness in livelihood, and no stability for any kingdom; people would be like beasts, wild predators and rabid dogs, some of which attack others. Every good in the world is from the effects of prophethood, and every evil that has occurred or will occur in the world is because of the obscurity and effacement of the traces of prophethood. The world is a body whose soul is prophethood, and there is no existence for the body without its soul. For this reason, when the sun of prophethood is eclipsed from the world and nothing of its traces remains on earth, its heaven is split, its stars scattered, its sun folded up, its moon eclipsed, its mountains blown away, its earth shaken, and those upon it destroyed; there is no subsistence for the world except by the traces of prophethood. End of quote.

If this is accepted, it becomes known through an intermediary that he, may God bless him and grant him peace, is the most perfect of the prophets, and that what he brought is more majestic than what they brought, upon them be peace. Although there is no difference in the fundamentals regarding the aspect of his being sent as a mercy to the worlds, this is not free from investigation.

Some have claimed that "the worlds" here is specific to the believers, but this is not correct. One of the excellent scholars has a lengthy discussion on this noble verse in which he refuted, argued, prevented and conceded, yet I see no source for it except scarcity of acquaintance with the truth worthy of being followed. Whenever you take care of yourself after becoming acquainted with it, its refutation will be easy for you, and its seriousness and levity will not alarm you.

What I choose is that he, may God bless him and grant him peace, was sent as a mercy to each and every single one of the worlds: their angels, their humans and their jinn. There is no difference between believer and disbeliever, human or jinn, in this. The mercy varies in degree; some of the worlds have the highest and most exalted share of it. What appears not to be mercy is either mercy upon careful examination, or is not intended primarily, like the other evils occurring in the world, according to what has been established in its place that evil is not included in God's decree (*qada'*) in its essence.

Among what is clearly evident regarding the generality of "the worlds" including the disbelievers is what Muslim reported from Abu Hurayra, who said: "It was said, O Messenger of God, invoke curse upon the polytheists. He said: 'I was not sent as a curser; I was only sent as a mercy.'" Perhaps this supports the accusative of "mercy" (*rahmatan*) in the verse as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), like his saying, may God bless him and grant him peace, which al-Bayhaqi reported in *al-Dala'il* from Abu Hurayra: "I am only a bestowed mercy." The possibility of causal interpretation (*ta'lil*) is not harmed by the view of the Ash'aris that God's acts are not subject to causation, for the Maturidis, and likewise the Hanbalis, held otherwise and refuted it with what needs no addition. Moreover, there is no barrier to saying about it what has been said about all other texts whose apparent meaning is causation. The existence of a barrier here is pure delusion, so reflect. Then it is not hidden that the attachment of "for the worlds" (*lil-'alamin*) to "mercy" is the apparent one.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is possible that it is attached to 'We have sent you'." In *al-Bahr*: "It is not permissible, according to the well-known view, for a prepositional phrase to be attached after *illa* (except) to a verb that precedes it, unless the governing verb is left free for it, as in: *ma marartu illa bi-Zayd* (I passed by none except Zayd)."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 108:

﴿Say: Only it is revealed to me that your God is one God.﴾ A group of scholars held that there are two restrictions (ḥaṣrān) in the verse, on the basis that inna (إنَّ) when it is opened (anna, أنَّ) conveys this meaning just as when it is pointed (inna, إنَّ, with a kasra) does. The first restricts the attribute to the one described, and the second restricts the one described to the attribute. In the second, God Most High is restricted to oneness (waḥdāniyyah), and in the first, the revelation is restricted to oneness. The meaning is: "What is revealed to me is nothing but the exclusivity of God Most High with oneness." It was objected: how can revelation be restricted to oneness when many other matters were revealed to him ﷺ, such as obligations (takālīf) and narratives (qiṣaṣ)? It was answered in two ways. The first: the meaning of restricting it to this is that it is the essential principle, and whatever else exists returns to it, or is not considered in comparison with it; thus it is a restriction by claim (qaṣr idde'ā'ī). The second: it is a restriction of reversal (qaṣr qalb) relative to the polytheism issuing from the disbelievers; and the same discussion applies to the second restriction.

Abu Ḥayyan denied that anna (أنَّما) with the fatḥa conveys restriction, because it is interpreted as a verbal noun (maṣdar) and a single noun, and it is not like the kasra form (inna mā), which is interpreted with mā and illa (إلّا). He said: "We know of no disagreement that it does not convey this, and the disagreement concerns only whether the kasra form inna mā conveys it."

You know that al-Zamakhshari and most of the commentators held that it does convey this, and the truth is with the group. What supports it here is that it is in the sense of the kasra form, because it occurs after "revelation" (al-waḥy), which has the sense of speech (al-qawl), and because it is in reality the object of "say" (qul). There is no doubt that it conveys emphasis (ta'kīd). When the context requires restriction, as in what we are discussing, it is combined with emphasis, but not by lexical convention as in the kasra form. Thus there occurs what does not bear it, such as His saying Most High: ﴿And David thought that We had only tested him﴾ [Ṣ: 24]. For this reason al-Zamakhshari explained it by saying "We had tested him without doubt," despite his explicit affirmation of restriction here. Yes, regarding the direction of the restriction here, in terms of it being the restriction of God Most High to oneness, as you have heard, there is what you heard at the end of Surat al-Kahf, so remember.

It was permitted that mā in ﴿innamā yūḥā﴾ be a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), but this is contrary to the apparent meaning. Its permissibility in what follows is very remote and necessitates an evident artificiality. ﴿So will you be submitting?﴾ That is, submitting (muntaqūn) to what is revealed to me of the tawḥīd. This is an interrogative that implies a command to submit. Some explained Islam (al-islām) by its necessary consequence, which is sincerely devoting worship to Him Most High, but what we have indicated is better.

Page 107

The fa' (ف) indicates that what precedes it necessitates what follows it. They said: in it there is an indication that the attribute of oneness may be established by revelation (samʿ), unlike the affirmation of the Necessary Being (al-wājib), whose path is reason ('aql), lest circularity (dawr) follow.

In Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid he said: the sending of the prophets, peace be upon them, and their truthfulness do not depend upon oneness, so it is permissible to rely on the revealed proofs (al-adilla al-samʿiyyah), such as the consensus of the prophets, peace be upon them, on calling to tawḥīd and negating partners, and such as the definitive texts of the Book of God Most High on that. As for what is said, that plurality entails possibility, [this is so] because you know the proofs of tawḥīd; and if you did not know that God Most High is Necessary Being, transcending all possible things, the establishment of prophethood and messengership would not be achieved. This is not a valid objection, because the most that the necessity [of His existence] entails is unity, not that knowing Him entails knowing it, let alone depending upon it. The cause of the error is failing to distinguish between the existence of a thing and knowledge of its existence. End.

The branching of the interrogative here is clear in establishing oneness by what has been mentioned. As for the statement of the author of al-Kashf: that the verse is not suitable as evidence for that, because it is revealed to him ﷺ only as demonstrated, not according to the rule of rhetoric (khaṭābah), so perhaps its descent was accompanied by rational proof, this is nothing, because it is evident that the branching is upon this very revelation, while the descent's being accompanied by rational proof and the branching in consideration of it is not apparent.

﴿Then if they turn away﴾ from Islam and do not heed what it requires, ﴿say﴾ to them, ﴿"I have announced to you"﴾, meaning: I have informed you of what I was commanded, or of my hostility toward you. *Al-idhan* (announcing, giving notice) is a causative form derived from *idhn* (permission). Its original sense is knowledge accompanied by permission regarding something, and it is then loosened and extended to mean knowledge in general. Verbs are formed from it, and it very often carries the sense of warning and admonition. It takes two objects, of which the second is omitted, as has been indicated.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿equally﴾ (*ʿalā sawāʾin*) are in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*) relating to the first object: that is, you are all equal in being informed of this, and I did not single out any one of you over another.

It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial qualifier relating both to the subject and to the object together: that is, I and you are equal in the enmity, or in the knowledge of what I have informed you of, namely the oneness of God, exalted is He, because the proofs for it are established. It has been said that what the Prophet (ﷺ) informed them of may be this, or that it may be the outbreak of war between them and the equality of their knowledge of it came from his informing them, since they knew that he, peace and blessings be upon him, was the truthful and trustworthy one, even if they denied some of what he reported out of obstinacy. So reflect.

It is also permitted that the preposition and its object be in the position of an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: an announcement made ﴿equally﴾. And that it be in the position of the predicate of an omitted *inna* (that is, "I have informed you that I am ﴿equal﴾"), meaning: upright and of sound judgment, with clear proof. This, however, is highly contrary to what comes first to mind.

In al-Kashshaf it is stated that His words, exalted is He, ﴿I have announced to you﴾ and so on, are an extended metaphor (*istiʿārah tamthīliyyah*, a figurative image built from a whole scene), likened to one who has a truce with his enemies, then senses their treachery, so he throws the covenant back at them, openly declares the breaking of it, makes it widely known, and announces it to all of them. This is of great eloquence.

﴿And I do not know﴾, meaning: I do not know ﴿whether what you are promised is near or far﴾, namely the victory of the Muslims over you and the rise of the religion, or the Gathering, even though it is certainly coming. The clause is in the position of an accusative complement of *adrī* (I know not). The structure did not come as "whether what you are promised is near or far," for the sake of the verse-endings (*fawāṣil*, the rhyming line-endings of the Qur'anic verses).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verses 110–111:

﴿Indeed, He knows what is spoken aloud﴾, i.e., what you openly utter of disparagement of Islam and denial of the verses, among which is what has stated the coming of the promised one. ﴿And He knows what you conceal﴾ of enmities and grudges toward the Muslims, so He will requite you for it, even for a speck (naqir) and a trifle (qitmir). ﴿And I do not know: perhaps it is a trial for you﴾, i.e., I do not know whether the delay of your recompense is a gradual leading on (istidraj) for you and an increase in your seduction, or a test for you, so that He may see how you act. The clause "perhaps it is" and so on is in the position of the object (maf'ul) by analogy with what preceded.

The Kufans treat la'alla like hal in being suspending particles (ta'liq). Abu Hayyan said: "I know of no one who held that la'alla is among the particles of suspension, although that is apparent in it." It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, in one report, that he read "adriya" with a fatha on the ya' in both places, likening it to the ya' of possession in pronunciation, although it is the ya' of the verb, and it is not vocalized with a fatha except by a governing element. Ibn Mujahid denied the fatha of this ya'.

﴿And enjoyment until a time﴾, i.e., and a provision for you and a delay until a determined term, which His will, founded on profound wisdoms, requires, so that this becomes a proof against you. It was said that the time refers to the Day of Badr. It was said it refers to the Day of Resurrection.

[Page 108]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verses 110–111:

﴿Indeed, He knows what is spoken aloud﴾, i.e., what you openly utter of disparagement of Islam and denial of the verses, among which is what has stated the coming of the promised one. ﴿And He knows what you conceal﴾ of enmities and grudges toward the Muslims, so He will requite you for it, even for a speck (naqir) and a trifle (qitmir). ﴿And I do not know: perhaps it is a trial for you﴾, i.e., I do not know whether the delay of your recompense is a gradual leading on (istidraj) for you and an increase in your seduction, or a test for you, so that He may see how you act. The clause "perhaps it is" and so on is in the position of the object (maf'ul) by analogy with what preceded.

The Kufans treat la'alla like hal in being suspending particles (ta'liq). Abu Hayyan said: "I know of no one who held that la'alla is among the particles of suspension, although that is apparent in it." It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, in one report, that he read "adriya" with a fatha on the ya' in both places, likening it to the ya' of possession in pronunciation, although it is the ya' of the verb, and it is not vocalized with a fatha except by a governing element. Ibn Mujahid denied the fatha of this ya'.

﴿And enjoyment until a time﴾, i.e., and a provision for you and a delay until a determined term, which His will, founded on profound wisdoms, requires, so that this becomes a proof against you. It was said that the time refers to the Day of Badr. It was said it refers to the Day of Resurrection.

[Page 108]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 21, verse 112:

﴿He said: "My Lord, judge with truth."﴾ This is a narration of his (ﷺ) supplication. Most readers recited (قُلْ, "say") in the imperative form. The judgment (al-hukm) means decision, and the truth (al-haqq) means justice. The meaning is: "My Lord, decide between us and the people of Makkah with the justice that requires hastening the punishment and making it severe against them." It is therefore a supplication for hastening and severity. Otherwise, all of Allah the Exalted's decisions are just and true. This was answered when they were punished at Badr with a severe punishment.

Abu Ja'far recited (رَبُّ, "Lord") with a damma, taking it as a singled-out vocative (munada mufrad), as the author of al-Lawami' said. This was criticized on the grounds that omitting the vocative particle from a common noun (ism al-jins) is anomalous (shadh), and its proper place is poetry. Abu Hayyan said: it is not a singled-out vocative, but rather a vocative construction of a noun annexed to the first-person pronoun (ya), in which the annexed noun was omitted and the word was built on damma, like (قَبْلُ and بَعْدُ, "before" and "after"). This is a dialect that Sibawayh related concerning a noun annexed to the first-person pronoun when it is addressed, and there is no anomaly in it.

Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, al-Jahdari and Ibn Muhaysin recited (رَبِّي, "my Lord") with a silent ya, and (أَحْكَمُ, "most judging") in the comparative form, meaning: "most effective," or "most just in judgment," or "greatest in wisdom." Thus "my Lord is most judging" is a subject and predicate.

A group recited (أَحْكَمَ) as a past-tense verb. (﴿And our Lord, the Most Merciful﴾) is a subject and predicate, meaning: abundant in mercy towards His servants. His saying, glorified is He, (﴿the one sought for help﴾), meaning the one from whom help is requested, is another predicate of the subject. It is also permitted that it is an adjective of (al-Rahman, "the Most Merciful"), on the basis that it is treated as a proper name.

The attribution of the Lord in what preceded to his (ﷺ) pronoun is specific, because supplication is among the duties specific to him, peace be upon him. Likewise, its attribution here to the plural pronoun that includes the believers is because seeking help is among the general duties of them all.

(﴿Against what you describe﴾) refers to the situation: they used to say that the association (with idols) would remain for them, that the banner of Islam would flutter and then subside, and that if what they were threatened with were true it would have descended upon them. Other such things that contain no good were also said. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, answered the supplication of His Messenger (ﷺ), frustrated their hopes, changed their conditions, gave victory to His allies over them, and there befell them on the Day of Badr what befell them. This sentence is a concluding parenthetical remark (i'tiradh tadhyili), which affirms the content of what came before it.

It is related that the Prophet, peace be upon him, recited to Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with him, (يَصِفُونَ, "they describe") with the third-person ya (the ghayba form). This was also narrated from Ibn Amir and Asim. Moreover, placing the Seal of the Prophets, peace be upon them, and what is connected to him as the conclusion of Surah al-Anbiya' is excellent, as al-Tibi said: "the musk of sealing wafts from it."
* * *
Among the allusive (ishari) interpretations of the verses: (﴿And We had already given Ibrahim his right guidance before﴾). It was said that this guidance is preferring the Truth, glorified is His affair, over all else, glorified is He. Al-Junayd was asked: "When did he receive that?" He said: "When there was no 'when'." (﴿He said: "Do you then worship, besides Allah, what can neither benefit you at all nor harm you?"﴾) In it is an allusion that seeking help from one who is himself needy, from a needy one, is foolishness in opinion and error in intellect, end quote.

Hamdun al-Qassar said: seeking help from creatures from creatures is like the seeking of help by a prisoner from another prisoner. (﴿We said: "O fire, be coolness and safety upon Ibrahim."﴾) Ibn Ata said: That was due to the soundness of Ibrahim's heart, peace be upon him, his freedom from attention to causes, and the soundness of his trust in Allah the Exalted. For this reason he, peace be upon him, when Jibril, peace be upon him, said to him, "Do you have a need?" replied, "As for you, no." (﴿So We made Sulayman understand it﴾). In it is an allusion that favor is in the hand of Allah the Exalted, who gives it to whom He wills, and that it has no connection with youth or age. How many a young person is far better than an elder!

(﴿And to each We gave judgment﴾) it was said: knowledge of the matters of lordship (al-rububiyyah). (﴿And knowledge﴾) knowledge of the matters of servitude (al-ubudiyyah). (﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] along with Dawud﴾). It was said: he, peace be upon him, would seclude himself in caves for the remembrance and glorification of Him, and the mountains would join him in that, glorifying along with him. Some have mentioned that the mountains, being empty of the works of creation, are adorned with the lights of the power of the Real. Lovers love seclusion in them, and for this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) used to seclude himself in the Cave of Hira'. Many of the righteous chose to devote themselves to worship in them.

(﴿And Ayyub, when he called to his Lord: "Indeed, harm has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾) It is mentioned that he, peace be upon him, said that when a worm targeted his heart and a worm targeted his tongue, and he feared that the place of his thought and the place of his remembrance would be occupied. Ja'far said: that was from him, peace be upon him, a request for a response from the Real, glorified is He, so that he might find tranquility in it, and it was not a complaint. How could the lover complain to his beloved, when everything the Beloved does is beloved? He, peace be upon him, preserved the etiquette of address. (﴿And Dhu al-Nun, when he went off in anger, thinking that We would not decree against him﴾). It was said: that was a drop from the wine-jar of endearment (al-dalal). They mentioned that the station of humble endearment is below the station of pure servitude, because the will does not pass away in it. For this reason he, peace be upon him, cried out: (﴿There is no deity but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been of the wrongdoers﴾), meaning: because there arose within my secret that I might will other than what You willed. (﴿And Zakariyya, when he called to his Lord: "My Lord, do not leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors."﴾) It was said that he, peace be upon him, desired a son fit to be a receptacle for the disclosure of the divine secrets to him, for the knower, when he is alone and finds no one to whom he may disclose the secret, becomes constricted in his ability to bear it. (﴿And they used to call upon Us in hope and in fear﴾). It was said: that is, desire for Us and fear of other than Us; or desire for meeting Us and fear of being veiled from Us. (﴿And they were humbly submissive to Us﴾).

Abu Yazid said: humility is the quieting of the heart from claims. It was also said: it is annihilation beneath the skirts of greatness and the mantle of majesty. (﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾). Most of the Sufis, may their secrets be sanctified, hold that the intended meaning of "the worlds" is all creation, and he (ﷺ) is a mercy to each of them, although the shares differ. All share in the fact that he, peace be upon him, is the cause of their existence. Indeed they said: the entire world was created from his light (ﷺ). Shaykh Abd al-Ghani al-Nabulsi, may his secret be sanctified, clearly stated this in his saying, which has been cited more than once:

*Taha the Prophet, all creation was formed from his light,*
*and had the quail been left [alone]...*

By his saying "and had the quail been left" he alluded to the fact that everything is from his light, peace be upon him, and to the aspect of the division into believer and disbeliever after its formation, so reflect. This, and we ask Allah the Exalted to make our portion of His mercy a generous portion, and to ease for us the affairs of this world and the Hereafter by His abundant kindness.
